f: 3. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the maximum age at which breastfeeding establishes a Mahram relationship?
b: Thirty months.

f: 4. According to Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muhammad, what is the maximum age at which breastfeeding establishes a Mahram relationship?
b: Twenty-four months (two years).

f: 5. What is the evidence used by those who hold that the breastfeeding period is thirty months?
b: The verse: "His bearing and his weaning is thirty months" (Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:15), together with the minimum gestation period of six months.

f: 6. Can breastfeeding establish a Mahram relationship after the breastfeeding period has ended?
b: No. Breastfeeding after the valid period creates no new prohibition.

f: 7. What is the general rule regarding prohibitions established through breastfeeding?
b: Whatever is prohibited by blood relationship is also prohibited by breastfeeding.

f: 8. What is the Hanafi exception to the rule that breastfeeding prohibits what blood relationship prohibits?
b: It is permissible to marry the mother of one's suckling sister.

f: 9. Why is it permissible to marry the mother of one's suckling sister?
b: Because unlike a blood sister's mother, she is neither one's biological mother nor one's father's wife.

f: 10. May a person marry the suckling sister of his own child?
b: Yes. This marriage is permissible.

f: 11. Why is it permissible to marry the suckling sister of one's child?
b: Because the prohibition in the blood relationship depends upon lineage, which is absent in this breastfeeding relationship.

f: 12. Do the prohibitions concerning the wife of one's father or the wife of one's son apply equally through breastfeeding?
b: Yes. These prohibitions apply through breastfeeding just as they do through blood relationships.

f: 13. What is meant by Laban al-Fahl (the husband's milk)?
b: The husband of the breastfeeding woman is legally regarded as the suckled child's father through breastfeeding.

f: 14. What legal effect does Laban al-Fahl have?
b: The suckled child becomes a Mahram to the husband and to his relatives just as if he were the child's father.

f: 15. If human milk is mixed with water, when does breastfeeding prohibition become established?
b: Only when the human milk is the dominant component.

f: 16. If human milk is mixed with food, does breastfeeding prohibition become established according to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. The prohibition is generally not established because the food is regarded as the primary nourishment.

f: 17. If human milk is mixed with medicine, when is breastfeeding prohibition established?
b: When the human milk is the dominant component of the mixture.

f: 18. If human milk is mixed with animal milk, when does breastfeeding prohibition become established?
b: Only if the human milk is the dominant component.

f: 19. According to Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how is a mixture of milk from two women treated?
b: The prohibition follows the milk that is predominant in the mixture.

f: 20. According to Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Zufar, how is a mixture of milk from two women treated?
b: Breastfeeding prohibition is established through both women regardless of which milk predominates.

f: 21. Does breastfeeding by a virgin woman establish a Mahram relationship?
b: Yes. If a virgin woman produces milk and breastfeeds a child during the valid breastfeeding period, the prohibition is established.

f: 22. Does breastfeeding with milk collected from a woman after her death establish a Mahram relationship?
b: Yes. The prohibition is established because the milk itself remains the legal cause of the prohibition.

f: 23. Why does milk collected after a woman's death still establish a Mahram relationship?
b: Because the milk itself causes the legal prohibition, even though the woman's legal status changes after death.

f: 24. Does administering breast milk through an enema (ihtiqan) establish a Mahram relationship?
b: No. It does not establish the prohibition.

f: 25. Why does breast milk administered by enema not establish a Mahram relationship?
b: Because the legal growth associated with breastfeeding is linked to ingestion through the upper digestive tract.

f: 26. If a man produces a fluid resembling milk and feeds it to a child, does a Mahram relationship result?
b: No. It is not considered biological milk.

f: 27. Does drinking animal milk establish a Mahram relationship between humans?
b: No. Animal milk does not create breastfeeding prohibitions between humans.

f: 28. Why does animal milk not establish a Mahram relationship?
b: Because there is no biological relationship (juz'iyyah) or lineage between humans and animals.

f: 29. What happens if a man is married to an adult wife and an infant wife, and the adult wife breastfeeds the infant wife?
b: Both marriages become prohibited because the adult wife becomes the infant wife's suckling mother, and a man cannot remain married to both a mother and her daughter.

f: 30. Why do both marriages become prohibited if one wife breastfeeds the other?
b: Because breastfeeding creates a mother-daughter relationship, and combining a mother and daughter in marriage is prohibited.

f: 31. If the marriage with the adult wife was not consummated, is she entitled to her dowry after breastfeeding the infant wife?
b: No. She receives no dowry because the dissolution resulted from her own action.

f: 32. If the marriage with the infant wife was not consummated, what dowry is she entitled to after the marriages are dissolved?
b: She is entitled to half of her dowry because the separation was not caused by her own culpable act.

f: 33. When may the husband recover from the adult wife the half-dowry paid to the infant wife?
b: Only if the adult wife knowingly and intentionally breastfed the infant in order to invalidate the marriage.

f: 34. Is the adult wife liable if she breastfed the infant out of necessity or without knowing about the marriage?
b: No. She is not liable in those circumstances.

f: 35. According to the Hanafi school, how must breastfeeding be proven in court?
b: By the testimony of two men, or one man and two women.

f: 36. According to the Hanafi school, is the testimony of women alone sufficient to establish breastfeeding?
b: No. Women's testimony alone is not sufficient.

f: 37. Why do the Hanafis require the normal legal standard of testimony to establish breastfeeding?
b: Because breastfeeding in this context results in the dissolution of a marriage, which requires the standard of proof used for legal rights and contracts.

f: 38. According to the Maliki school, how may breastfeeding be proven?
b: By the testimony of a single trustworthy woman.

f: 1. What are the three categories of divorce according to the Hanafi school?
b: Ahsan (best), Hasan (good), and Bid'i (innovated/sinful).

f: 2. What is the definition of Talaq Ahsan (the best form of divorce)?
b: It is a single pronouncement of divorce during a period of purity (tuhr) in which no intercourse occurred, followed by abstention from marital relations until the completion of the 'Iddah.

f: 3. Why is Talaq Ahsan considered the best form of divorce?
b: Because it leaves room for reconciliation and minimizes regret while causing the least disruption to the marriage bond.

f: 4. What is Talaq Hasan (the good form of divorce)?
b: It is pronouncing one divorce during each of three consecutive periods of purity (tuhr).

f: 5. Why is Talaq Hasan called "Sunnah divorce"?
b: Because it follows the recommended method of gradually separating the spouses through three separate pronouncements.

f: 6. What types of divorce are classified as Bid'i (innovated/sinful)?
b: Pronouncing three divorces at once, divorcing during menstruation, or divorcing during a period of purity in which intercourse occurred.

f: 7. Does a Bid'i divorce take effect according to the Hanafi school?
b: Yes. Although sinful, the divorce is legally effective.

f: 8. Is a person who issues a Bid'i divorce considered sinful according to the Hanafi school?
b: Yes. He is considered sinful for violating the Sunnah method of divorce.

f: 9. Why does the Hanafi school consider Bid'i divorce sinful but still valid?
b: Because the rules of Sunnah regulate the proper manner of using divorce, but the legal mechanism of divorce remains effective when improperly used.

f: 10. Why did some scholars argue that Bid'i divorce should still be valid despite being disliked?
b: Because divorce is a legally recognized means of ending marriage, and violating the preferred method does not necessarily invalidate the act itself.

f: 11. What is the underlying principle regarding divorce according to the Hanafi school?
b: Divorce is originally restricted (hazr) because it destroys a beneficial marital relationship and is only permitted due to necessity (hajah).

f: 12. Why is pronouncing three divorces at once considered Bid'i?
b: Because one divorce is sufficient to achieve the purpose of separation, making three simultaneous divorces unnecessary.

f: 13. What are the two categories of Sunnah divorce?
b: Sunnah in number and Sunnah in time.

f: 14. What does Sunnah divorce "in number" refer to?
b: It refers to the recommended number of divorce pronouncements, which is a single pronouncement.

f: 15. Does Sunnah divorce in number apply to both consummated and unconsummated wives?
b: Yes.

f: 16. What does Sunnah divorce "in time" refer to?
b: It refers to issuing divorce during a period of purity (tuhr) in which intercourse has not occurred.

f: 17. Why is divorce during a pure period without intercourse considered Sunnah?
b: Because it avoids divorcing at a time when emotions or desires may change after intercourse and allows clearer judgment.

f: 18. To which type of wife does the Sunnah timing of divorce specifically apply?
b: The consummated wife.

f: 19. What is the Sunnah method of divorcing a woman who does not menstruate, such as a minor or post-menopausal woman?
b: The divorces should be separated by one month each.

f: 20. Why are months used instead of menstrual cycles for women who do not menstruate?
b: Because the month functions as a substitute measure for the menstrual cycle (qur'a).

f: 21. May a man divorce a wife with whom he has not consummated the marriage during menstruation?
b: Yes. Since there is no concern of confusion regarding the 'Iddah through pregnancy, divorce may occur at any time.

f: 22. Why may an unconsummated wife be divorced during menstruation according to the Hanafi school?
b: Because pregnancy cannot result from an unconsummated marriage, so there is no ambiguity regarding the waiting period.

f: 23. May a pregnant woman be divorced immediately after intercourse?
b: Yes. Pregnancy removes uncertainty regarding the waiting period, so divorce may occur immediately.

f: 24. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how may a pregnant woman be divorced according to the Sunnah method?
b: The three divorces may be spaced by one month each.

f: 25. According to Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Zufar, how should a pregnant woman be divorced?
b: She should only be divorced once, because the month is not considered a formal division of her waiting period.

f: 26. Does divorce during menstruation take effect according to the Hanafi school?
b: Yes. The divorce is valid, although the husband is sinful for issuing it at that time.

f: 27. Is the husband recommended or required to retract a divorce issued during menstruation?
b: It is highly recommended, and according to the more accurate Hanafi view, obligatory.

f: 28. Why should a husband retract a divorce issued during menstruation?
b: To reduce the sin of violating the Sunnah method and to prevent unnecessarily extending the wife's waiting period.

f: 29. What is the scholarly disagreement regarding a single irrevocable (ba'in) divorce?
b: Some scholars consider it contrary to the Sunnah because irrevocability was unnecessary, while others consider it permissible because it fulfills the need for separation.

f: 30. What is the Sunnah method if a husband intends to issue three divorces over three periods of purity?
b: He issues one divorce, waits through the required period, and then issues another divorce in the next period of purity.

f: 31. If a husband divorces his wife during menstruation and then retracts the divorce, does the waiting period continue?
b: Yes. The waiting period continues, and later divorces follow the Sunnah sequence.

f: 32. If a man says to his consummated wife, "You are divorced three times according to the Sunnah," without specifying an intention, how do the divorces occur?
b: They occur one per cycle of purity, following the Sunnah method.

f: 33. If a man says, "You are divorced three times according to the Sunnah," and intends all three immediately, is his intention considered?
b: Yes. His specific intention is honored.

f: 34. If a man says, "You are divorced three times according to the Sunnah," and intends one divorce at the beginning of each month, is this valid?
b: Yes. His intention is considered.

f: 35. If a man says only, "You are divorced according to the Sunnah," without mentioning three divorces, can he intend three immediate divorces?
b: No. The phrase requires following the Sunnah method and does not allow an immediate triple divorce intention.

f: 36. Who has the legal capacity to issue divorce according to Hanafi law?
b: A sane, adult husband.

f: 37. Is divorce valid if issued by a child?
b: No.

f: 38. Is divorce valid if issued by an insane person?
b: No.

f: 39. Is divorce valid if issued by a sleeping person?
b: No.

f: 40. Why is divorce from a sleeping person invalid?
b: Because a sleeping person lacks conscious intention and legal capacity at the time of the statement.

f: 41. Is a divorce pronounced under coercion (ikrah) valid according to the Hanafi school?
b: Yes.

f: 42. Why do the Hanafis consider a coerced divorce valid?
b: Because the husband retains legal capacity and chose the lesser harm by uttering the divorce words even though he did not desire the consequence.

f: 43. Is divorce pronounced by an intoxicated person valid according to the Hanafi school?
b: Yes.

f: 44. Why is divorce by an intoxicated person considered valid?
b: Because the intoxication resulted from his own sinful action, so the law holds him responsible as a deterrent (zajr).

f: 45. Is divorce by someone who lost mental capacity due to illness or medication treated like divorce by an intoxicated person?
b: No. Loss of intellect caused by illness or medication does not carry the same ruling.

f: 46. Can a mute husband issue a valid divorce?
b: Yes.

f: 47. How does a mute husband issue divorce?
b: Through established and understood gestures that clearly communicate divorce.

f: 48. How many divorces may a husband pronounce regarding a free woman before the marriage is completely dissolved?
b: Three divorces.

f: 49. How many divorces may a husband pronounce regarding a slave woman before the marriage is completely dissolved?
b: Two divorces.

f: 50. Does the number of divorces allowed for a slave woman depend on whether the husband is free or enslaved?
b: No. A slave woman receives only two divorces regardless of the husband's status.

f: 51. What evidence is used for the ruling that a slave woman's divorce limit is two?
b: The prophetic tradition: "The divorce of a slave-girl is two, and her waiting period is two menstrual cycles."

f: 52. If a slave marries with his master's permission, who possesses the right to issue divorce?
b: The slave husband possesses the right to divorce.

f: 53. Can the master divorce the wife of his slave?
b: No. The marital bond belongs to the slave, not the master.

f: 54. What are examples of explicit (sarih) divorce expressions?
b: "You are divorced" (Anti taliq), "Divorced" (mutallaqah), and "I have divorced you" (tallaqtuki).

f: 55. Does an explicit (sarih) divorce require the husband's intention (niyyah) to be valid?
b: No. The words themselves establish the divorce.

f: 56. What type of divorce results from an explicit divorce expression?
b: A revocable (raj'i) divorce.

f: 57. If a husband uses an explicit divorce phrase but claims he meant something else, such as freeing the wife from service, is his claim accepted in court?
b: No. It is not accepted in judicial judgment (qada) because it contradicts the apparent meaning of the words.

f: 58. Can a husband who used an explicit divorce phrase be considered truthful before Allah if he intended another meaning?
b: Yes. He may be truthful in his private religious accountability (diyanatan).

f: 59. Is the phrase "You are mutlaqah" considered an explicit divorce expression?
b: No. It is ambiguous and requires intention to cause divorce.

f: 60. If a husband says "You are divorced" and intends three divorces, how many divorces occur?
b: One divorce occurs.

f: 61. Why does "You are divorced" only result in one divorce even if multiple divorces are intended?
b: Because the explicit verb form inherently indicates a single occurrence.

f: 62. Can the phrase "You are the divorce" (Anti al-talaq) carry the intention of three divorces?
b: Yes. The husband's intention of three divorces is accepted.

f: 63. Can the phrase "You are divorced [a] divorce" (Anti taliq talaqan) be intended as three divorces?
b: Yes. The noun form (masdar) can indicate plurality or totality.

f: 64. Why may the noun form of divorce indicate three divorces?
b: Because it can refer to the complete category or totality of divorce.

f: 65. Can a husband intend exactly two divorces using the phrase "You are the divorce"?
b: No. Two is a specific number that is not naturally represented by this form in the same way as totality (three).

f: 66. Is divorce valid if a husband attributes divorce to his wife's neck (raqabatuki)?
b: Yes.

f: 67. Is divorce valid if a husband attributes divorce to his wife's head (ra'suki)?
b: Yes.

f: 68. Is divorce valid if a husband attributes divorce to his wife's soul/self (ruhuki)?
b: Yes.

f: 69. Is divorce valid if a husband attributes divorce to his wife's body (badanki/jasaduki)?
b: Yes.

f: 70. Is divorce valid if a husband attributes divorce to his wife's private part (farjuki)?
b: Yes.

f: 71. Is divorce valid if a husband attributes divorce to his wife's face (wajhuki)?
b: Yes.

f: 72. Why do these expressions cause divorce even though they refer only to parts or descriptions of the woman?
b: Because these terms are commonly used to represent the whole person.

f: 73. If a husband says "Half of you is divorced," does divorce occur?
b: Yes. The divorce applies to the entire person.

f: 74. If a husband says "A third of you is divorced," does divorce occur?
b: Yes. The divorce applies to the entire person.

f: 75. Why does attributing divorce to a fraction of the wife's body result in divorce of the whole person?
b: Because divorce is indivisible and cannot apply to only part of the marital person.

f: 76. Does attributing divorce to the wife's hand (yad) constitute a valid divorce?
b: No.

f: 77. Why does saying "your hand is divorced" not cause divorce?
b: Because the hand does not represent the wife as a whole person and is not a valid place for the legal attachment of divorce.

f: 78. Does attributing divorce to the wife's foot (rijl) constitute a valid divorce?
b: No.

f: 79. Why does attributing divorce to a hand or foot differ from attributing it to the face or neck?
b: The face and neck are expressions commonly used to represent the whole person, while hands and feet are merely individual body parts.

f: 80. If a husband says "half a divorce," how many divorces occur?
b: One complete divorce occurs.

f: 81. If a husband says "a third of a divorce," how many divorces occur?
b: One complete divorce occurs.

f: 82. Why does a fractional divorce result in a complete divorce?
b: Because divorce is legally indivisible and cannot be divided into partial units.

f: 83. If a husband says "three halves of a divorce," how many divorces occur?
b: Three divorces occur because three halves equal three complete units of divorce.

f: 84. If a husband says "from one to two divorces," how many divorces occur?
b: One divorce occurs.

f: 85. If a husband says "between one and two divorces," how many divorces occur?
b: One divorce occurs.

f: 86. If a husband says "from one to three divorces," how many divorces occur?
b: Two divorces occur.

f: 87. If a husband says "between one and three divorces," how many divorces occur?
b: Two divorces occur.

f: 88. Why does "from one to three" result in two divorces rather than three?
b: Because the starting number counts as the first unit, while the upper limit is not included in this legal interpretation of ranges.

f: 89. If a husband says "You are divorced one multiplied by two" (wahidah fi ithnatayn), how many divorces occur?
b: One divorce occurs.

f: 90. Why does multiplication not increase the legal number of divorces?
b: Because multiplication affects the parts or wording of the expression, not the legal count of divorce itself.

f: 91. If a husband says "one in two" (wahidah fi ithnatayn), what possible interpretation may lead to three divorces?
b: If interpreted as "one with two," it may total three divorces.

f: 92. If a husband intends "one multiplied by two," how many divorces occur?
b: One divorce occurs.

f: 93. If a husband says, "You are divorced in Makkah," when does the divorce occur?
b: Immediately.

f: 94. If a husband says, "You are divorced at home," when does the divorce occur?
b: Immediately.

f: 95. Why does saying "You are divorced in Makkah" not delay the divorce until she reaches Makkah?
b: Because divorce is not restricted by physical location.

f: 96. If a husband internally intends that divorce should occur when his wife enters Makkah, is that intention legally effective?
b: It is only recognized between him and Allah (diyanatan), not in court (qada).

f: 97. Why is a private intention of delaying divorce until entering a location not accepted in court?
b: Because it contradicts the apparent meaning of the spoken declaration.

f: 98. What is the ruling of saying, "You are divorced when you enter Makkah"?
b: It is a conditional divorce and takes effect only when she enters Makkah.

f: 99. What type of divorce is "You are divorced when you enter Makkah"?
b: Conditional divorce (talaq mu‘allaq).

f: 100. If a husband says, "You are divorced tomorrow," when does the divorce occur?
b: At the break of dawn (tulu‘ al-fajr) of the next day.

f: 101. Why does "tomorrow" begin at dawn for divorce purposes?
b: Because dawn is considered the first moment of the following day.

f: 102. If a husband intends the end of tomorrow when saying "You are divorced tomorrow," is his interpretation accepted?
b: It is accepted only in his private accountability before Allah, not in court.

f: 103. Why is the husband's intention of "end of the day" not accepted judicially?
b: Because it contradicts the outward meaning of the statement.

f: 104. If a husband says, "You are divorced today, tomorrow," when does the divorce take effect?
b: It takes effect at the earliest time mentioned: today.

f: 105. If a husband says, "You are divorced tomorrow, today," when does the divorce take effect?
b: It takes effect at the earliest time mentioned: today.

f: 106. Why does divorce take effect at the earliest mentioned time in contradictory timing statements?
b: Because the first timing creates an immediate legal effect (tanjiz), and a later addition cannot modify a divorce that has already occurred.

f: 107. What happens to the second time expression in statements like "today, tomorrow"?
b: It becomes legally redundant and has no effect.

f: 108. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can a husband who says "You are divorced in tomorrow" claim that he meant the end of the day?
b: Yes. His claim may be accepted in court.

f: 109. Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ allow the interpretation of "in tomorrow" as the end of the day?
b: Because the preposition "in" (fi) indicates a container or timeframe and does not necessarily include the whole duration.

f: 110. If a husband says, "You are divorced tomorrow," when does the divorce take effect?
b: It takes effect at the first moment of tomorrow.

f: 111. Why does "You are divorced tomorrow" take effect at the beginning of the day rather than the end?
b: Because "tomorrow" refers to the entire upcoming timeframe beginning from its first moment.

f: 112. If a man marries a woman today and says, "You are divorced yesterday," does divorce occur?
b: No.

f: 113. Why does "You are divorced yesterday" not cause divorce when the marriage began today?
b: Because divorce is being attributed to a time when the woman was not his wife and he had no ownership of divorce over her.

f: 114. If a husband was married to a woman the day before yesterday and says, "You are divorced yesterday," does divorce occur?
b: Yes. It takes effect immediately.

f: 115. How is a past-tense divorce expression understood when the marriage already existed?
b: It is interpreted as a present enactment (insha’) rather than a factual report about the past.

f: 116. If a husband says, "You are divorced before I married you," is the divorce valid?
b: No.

f: 117. Why is "You are divorced before I married you" invalid?
b: Because it attributes divorce to a time when the marital relationship did not exist, making the condition impossible.

f: 118. If a husband says, "You are divorced as long as I do not divorce you," and then remains silent, does divorce occur?
b: Yes. Divorce occurs immediately.

f: 119. Why does "as long as I do not divorce you" cause immediate divorce upon silence?
b: Because the condition of not divorcing her is fulfilled by his silence at that moment.

f: 120. If a husband says, "You are divorced if I do not divorce you," when does divorce occur?
b: It does not occur until his death.

f: 121. Why does "if I do not divorce you" delay divorce until death?
b: Because not divorcing is a continuous condition that is only finalized when his life ends.

f: 122. What is the Hanafi disagreement regarding the phrase "You are divorced when I do not divorce you"?
b: Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his disciples differ over whether "when" (idha) indicates a condition or a time.

f: 123. How does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret idha in the phrase "when I do not divorce you"?
b: It may indicate either a condition or a time, so caution is applied.

f: 124. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, if the meaning of idha is ambiguous, does divorce occur immediately?
b: No.

f: 125. Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not apply immediate divorce when idha is ambiguous?
b: Because divorce is a serious consequence, and the conditional interpretation prevents unnecessary immediate effect.

f: 126. How do Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muhammad interpret idha in this context?
b: They interpret it as strictly a temporal marker.

f: 127. According to Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muhammad, when does divorce occur after saying, "You are divorced when I do not divorce you"?
b: It occurs as soon as he remains silent.

f: 128. If the husband explicitly intends idha to mean "time" (waqt), when does divorce occur?
b: Divorce occurs immediately.

f: 129. If the husband explicitly intends idha to mean "condition" (shart), when does divorce occur?
b: Divorce occurs at the end of his life.

f: 130. If a husband says, "You are divorced as long as I do not divorce you," and then immediately says, "You are divorced," by which statement does the divorce occur?
b: The divorce occurs through the second pronouncement.

f: 131. Why does the second divorce statement take effect despite the first condition seemingly preventing it?
b: Because the moment spent pronouncing the statement is excluded from the condition of "not divorcing" through istihsan (juridical preference).

f: 132. What principle allows the time needed to complete a contradictory action to be excluded from a condition?
b: Istihsan (juridical preference).

f: 133. What example is used to explain excluding the moment of action from a condition?
b: A person who swears not to "dwell in this house" is given time to leave the house.

f: 134. If a man says, "The day I marry you, you are divorced," and marries her at night, does divorce occur?
b: Yes.

f: 135. Why does "the day I marry you" include marriage at night?
b: Because yawm (day) can linguistically refer to a period of time in general, not only daylight hours.

f: 136. How is the phrase "The day I marry you, you are divorced" interpreted when connected with divorce?
b: It is interpreted as "at the time I marry you."

f: 137. If the husband claims he intended only daylight hours by the word "day" in "The day I marry you," is his claim accepted?
b: It is accepted only before Allah (diyanatan), not in court (qada).

f: 138. Why is the husband's narrower interpretation of "day" not accepted in court?
b: Because it contradicts the broader accepted linguistic usage of yawm.

f: 139. Is the statement "I am divorced from you" a valid divorce expression?
b: No. It is invalid even if the husband intends divorce.

f: 140. Why is "I am divorced from you" invalid?
b: Because divorce removes the marital bond attached to the wife, not the husband.

f: 141. What is the legal concept removed by divorce?
b: The marital bond (qayd) that binds the wife.

f: 142. Why can the husband not attribute divorce to himself?
b: Because he is not the object upon whom the marital restriction is imposed.

f: 143. Are expressions like "I am detached from you" (ba'in) valid if the husband intends divorce?
b: Yes.

f: 144. Are expressions like "I am forbidden to you" (haram) valid if the husband intends divorce?
b: Yes.

f: 145. Why are "detached" and "forbidden" valid expressions of divorce when "I am divorced from you" is not?
b: Because detachment and prohibition describe the relationship between both spouses rather than only the husband.

f: 146. If a husband says, "You are divorced one or nothing," does divorce occur according to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later view?
b: No divorce occurs.

f: 147. Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later view reject divorce in "You are divorced one or nothing"?
b: Because the wording introduces uncertainty into the actual occurrence of divorce.

f: 148. According to Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ earlier view, what happens with "You are divorced one or nothing"?
b: One revocable divorce occurs.

f: 149. Why do Muhammad and Abu Yusuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ earlier view consider one divorce valid?
b: Because the uncertainty affects only the number, while the statement "You are divorced" remains certain.

f: 150. Is a divorce statement connected to death, such as "You are divorced with my death," valid?
b: No.

f: 151. Is a divorce statement connected to the wife's death, such as "You are divorced with your death," valid?
b: No.

f: 152. Why is divorce linked to death invalid?
b: Because death removes the legal capacity (ahliyyah) and subject matter (mahalliyyah) required for divorce.

f: 153. What two legal requirements for divorce are absent after death?
b: Legal capacity and the existence of a valid subject upon whom divorce can operate.

f: 154. What happens if a husband gains ownership (milk al-yamin) of his wife, even partially?
b: The marriage is automatically dissolved.

f: 155. What happens if a wife gains ownership of her husband?
b: The marriage is automatically dissolved.

f: 156. Why does ownership dissolve the marriage between spouses?
b: Because the relationship of master and slave (mawla/mamluk) is fundamentally incompatible with the marital bond.

f: 157. Why can ownership and marriage not exist together?
b: Because ownership creates a master-servant relationship, while marriage requires reciprocal marital rights.

f: 158. If a husband purchases his wife and then divorces her, is the divorce effective?
b: No. The divorce is ineffective because the marriage already ended when ownership was acquired.

f: 159. Why is a divorce after purchasing one's wife ineffective?
b: Because there is no longer an existing marriage upon which divorce can operate.

f: 160. What view does Muhammad hold regarding divorce after a husband purchases his wife?
b: He suggests the divorce may take effect because of the remaining obligation of the waiting period ('iddah).

f: 161. What is the prevailing Hanafi view regarding divorce after ownership of one's wife?
b: The divorce is ineffective because the marriage no longer exists.

f: 162. If a husband says to his slave-wife, "You are divorced twice upon your master's manumission of you," and the master frees her, when does divorce occur?
b: Divorce occurs after she becomes free.

f: 163. If a slave-wife becomes free before a conditional divorce takes effect, what type of divorce is it?
b: It is a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i).

f: 164. Why is a conditional divorce after manumission considered revocable rather than final?
b: Because she is free when the divorce occurs, and a free woman has a limit of three divorces.

f: 165. What would have happened if the slave-wife were still enslaved when the two divorces occurred?
b: The two divorces would constitute final dissolution (talaq mughallazah).

f: 166. If both manumission and divorce are conditioned upon the same future event, such as "when tomorrow comes," what is the disagreement between the Hanafi scholars?
b: Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ differ from Muhammad regarding whether she is free or still enslaved when divorce takes effect.

f: 167. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, if manumission and divorce occur at the same future time, when does divorce take effect?
b: Divorce takes effect while she is still considered a slave-wife.

f: 168. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how many divorces occur in the simultaneous manumission/divorce case?
b: Two divorces occur, resulting in final dissolution (talaq mughallazah).

f: 169. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can the husband remarry her immediately after the two divorces?
b: No. She is prohibited until she marries another husband and the necessary conditions are fulfilled.

f: 170. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what waiting period ('iddah) does the freed woman observe after this divorce?
b: The waiting period of a free woman (three menstrual cycles), as a precaution.

f: 171. What is Muhammad's position regarding simultaneous manumission and divorce?
b: He argues that the divorce follows the manumission, meaning she is free when divorce occurs.

f: 172. Why does Muhammad believe the woman is free when divorce occurs?
b: Because the divorce condition logically follows the completion of manumission.

f: 173. According to Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what right does the husband retain in the simultaneous manumission/divorce case?
b: The right of revocation (raj'ah).

f: 174. If a husband says, "You are divorced like this," and holds up his thumb, index finger, and middle finger, how many divorces occur?
b: Three divorces occur.

f: 175. If a husband says, "You are divorced like this," and holds up one finger, how many divorces occur?
b: One divorce occurs.

f: 176. If a husband says, "You are divorced like this," and holds up two fingers, how many divorces occur?
b: Two divorces occur.

f: 177. Why do hand gestures determine the number of divorces in this case?
b: Because gestures function as indicators of quantity when accompanying an otherwise ambiguous statement.

f: 178. If a husband later claims he intended a different number than the fingers he displayed, is his claim accepted in court?
b: No.

f: 179. Can the husband’s different intended meaning be accepted privately before Allah (diyanatan)?
b: Yes.

f: 180. Why is a different private intention not accepted in court (qada)?
b: Because it contradicts the customary meaning of the gesture.

f: 181. What type of divorce results from saying, "You are ba'in (irrevocable)"?
b: An irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in).

f: 182. What type of divorce results from the term al-battah (absolutely/severed)?
b: An irrevocable divorce.

f: 183. Why do Hanafi jurists consider terms like ba'in to specify a valid divorce outcome rather than oppose the law?
b: Because irrevocability is one of the legally recognized consequences of divorce.

f: 184. If a husband says an irrevocable divorce term and intends one divorce, what occurs?
b: One irrevocable divorce occurs.

f: 185. If a husband says an irrevocable divorce term and intends two divorces, what occurs?
b: Two divorces occur.

f: 186. If a husband says an irrevocable divorce term and intends three divorces, what occurs?
b: Three divorces occur.

f: 187. Do expressions such as "the most obscene divorce" or "the worst divorce" result in revocable or irrevocable divorce?
b: They result in irrevocable divorce.

f: 188. Why do terms like "most evil divorce" indicate irrevocability?
b: Because they describe the severity and finality of the separation.

f: 189. What is the ruling of the phrase "divorce of the devil" according to the Hanafi treatment?
b: It is treated as an irrevocable divorce.

f: 190. Why is "divorce of the devil" considered irrevocable?
b: Because it is contrasted with Sunnah divorce, which is characterized by revocability.

f: 191. What internal disagreement exists regarding phrases like "divorce of innovation" and "divorce of the devil"?
b: Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muhammad differ over whether these phrases automatically imply irrevocability or require intention.

f: 192. Why might "divorce of innovation" not necessarily indicate irrevocability?
b: Because it could refer to a procedural violation, such as divorcing during menstruation, rather than finality.

f: 193. If a husband says, "You are divorced like the mountain," what type of divorce occurs according to the Hanafi view?
b: An irrevocable divorce occurs.

f: 194. Why does comparing divorce to a mountain result in irrevocability?
b: Because large or heavy objects are understood as emphasizing magnitude and finality.

f: 195. What is Abu Yusuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ alternative interpretation of "You are divorced like the mountain"?
b: He suggests it could mean one revocable divorce.

f: 196. Why does Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret the mountain comparison differently?
b: Because the mountain represents unity or singularity, which may indicate a single divorce.

f: 197. If a husband says, "You are divorced with the severest divorce," what occurs?
b: One irrevocable divorce occurs unless he specifically intends three.

f: 198. If a husband says, "You are divorced like a thousand," what occurs?
b: One irrevocable divorce occurs unless he specifically intends three.

f: 199. If a husband says, "You are divorced filling the house," what occurs?
b: One irrevocable divorce occurs unless he specifically intends three.

f: 200. Why do phrases like "the severest divorce" normally result in one irrevocable divorce?
b: Because they are ambiguous between intensity and quantity, and intensity is interpreted as irrevocability.

f: 201. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why is irrevocability preferred when interpreting intense descriptions?
b: Because describing intensity naturally indicates ba'in (difficulty of reconciliation).

f: 202. Can a husband’s intention of three divorces be accepted when using phrases like "the severest divorce"?
b: Yes.

f: 203. Why can the intention of three divorces be accepted in these expressions?
b: Because the noun form (masdar) can indicate a larger quantity when intended.

f: 204. Do all Hanafi scholars agree that every comparison (tashbih) automatically implies irrevocability?
b: No.

f: 205. What is Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view regarding comparisons in divorce expressions?
b: Any comparison adds intensity and therefore implies irrevocability.

f: 206. What do other scholars require before a comparison implies irrevocability?
b: They require an explicit indication of greatness or magnitude.

f: 207. What is the ruling of descriptive adjectives such as "severe," "broad," or "long" when used for divorce?
b: They result in an irrevocable divorce.

f: 208. Why do adjectives like "severe" or "long" indicate irrevocability?
b: Because they metaphorically describe difficulty of reconciliation and final separation.

f: 209. What is the legal characteristic associated with irrevocable divorce (bainunah)?
b: The difficulty or inability of immediate reconciliation (istidrak).

f: 210. If a husband says to an unconsummated wife, "You are divorced three times," do all three divorces take effect?
b: Yes, all three take effect immediately.

f: 211. Why do three divorces pronounced at once to an unconsummated wife all take effect?
b: Because divorce before consummation is irrevocable (ba'in) from the beginning, so the marriage ends only after the complete pronouncement.

f: 212. If a husband says to an unconsummated wife, "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," how many divorces take effect?
b: Only the first divorce takes effect.

f: 213. Why do later pronouncements not take effect in sequential divorce of an unconsummated wife?
b: Because the first divorce immediately dissolves the marriage, leaving no marital bond for later divorces to affect.

f: 214. If a husband says to an unconsummated wife, "You are divorced one and one," how many divorces occur?
b: Only one divorce occurs.

f: 215. Why does "one and one" result in only one divorce for an unconsummated wife?
b: Because the first divorce ends the marriage, making the second ineffective.

f: 216. If a husband begins saying, "You are divorced..." but the wife dies before he completes the statement, is the divorce valid?
b: No, the divorce is invalid.

f: 217. Why is a divorce invalid if the wife dies before the pronouncement is completed?
b: Because the legal subject (mahall) of divorce no longer exists when the statement becomes complete.

f: 218. What legal requirement must exist for divorce to take effect?
b: The wife must have legal capacity as the subject of divorce.

f: 219. In the phrase "You are divorced one before one" or "one after one," what determines the legal effect?
b: The grammatical placement of the pronoun suffix (ha) in the phrase.

f: 220. If the pronoun suffix is attached, such as qabliha ("before it"), how is the phrase understood?
b: It acts as an adjective for the second divorce, causing both divorces to occur together.

f: 221. If there is no pronoun, such as qabla wahidatin ("before one"), how is the phrase understood?
b: It describes the first divorce, resulting in only one divorce.

f: 222. What effect does the word ma'a ("with") have in divorce expressions?
b: It indicates simultaneity.

f: 223. If a husband says "You are divorced with one" to a consummated wife, how many divorces occur?
b: Two divorces occur.

f: 224. If a husband says, "If you enter, you are divorced one and one," what is Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view?
b: Only one divorce occurs.

f: 225. Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider only one divorce in "If you enter, you are divorced one and one"?
b: Because the conjunction wa ("and") is ambiguous, and divorce is restricted to the minimum when uncertainty exists.

f: 226. What is the view of Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disciples regarding "If you enter, you are divorced one and one"?
b: They hold that two divorces occur.

f: 227. If a husband says, "You are divorced one and one if you enter," how many divorces occur when she enters?
b: Both divorces occur by consensus.

f: 228. Why do both divorces occur when the condition comes at the end of the statement?
b: Because the condition governs the entire preceding statement.

f: 229. If a husband says, "If you enter, you are divorced one then one," how many divorces occur?
b: Only one divorce occurs.

f: 230. Why does "one then one" result in only one divorce?
b: Because fa indicates sequence, and the first divorce dissolves the marriage before the second can take effect.

f: 231. What linguistic principle affects many divorce rulings involving words like wa, fa, and ma'a?
b: The grammatical function and meaning of the connecting words determine whether divorces occur together, separately, or sequentially.

f: 232. What is kinayah (implicit/metaphorical divorce)?
b: Expressions that do not inherently mean divorce but can imply divorce depending on intention or circumstances.

f: 233. Does a kinayah expression cause divorce automatically?
b: No. It requires the husband's intention of divorce or a contextual situation that indicates divorce.

f: 234. Why do kinayah expressions require intention?
b: Because these words are not exclusively used for divorce and can have other meanings.

f: 235. What happens if a husband says, "Observe your waiting period" (I'taddi) and intends divorce?
b: A revocable divorce (talaq raj'i) occurs.

f: 236. Why is "Observe your waiting period" considered a kinayah expression?
b: Because it could mean observing a waiting period after divorce or could have another meaning, such as counting blessings.

f: 237. What happens if a husband says, "Purify your womb" (Istabri'i rahimaki) and intends divorce?
b: A revocable divorce occurs.

f: 238. Why does "Purify your womb" imply divorce?
b: Because it relates to determining whether pregnancy exists so divorce can proceed.

f: 239. If a husband says, "You are one" (Anti wahidah) intending divorce, what occurs?
b: One revocable divorce occurs.

f: 240. Can "You are one" be intended as three divorces?
b: No. The explicit mention of "one" limits the numerical count.

f: 241. Why can "You are one" not mean three divorces even with intention?
b: Because the stated number restricts the interpretation.

f: 242. What type of divorce generally results from kinayah expressions?
b: A revocable divorce (raj'i) for certain implicit expressions, while stronger kinayah terms may result in an irrevocable divorce depending on intention.

f: 243. How many divorces result from kinayah expressions if the husband intends more than one?
b: The wording and type of expression determine the result; many kinayah forms are limited to one unless three is specifically intended.

f: 244. What happens if the husband intends one divorce using strong kinayah terms like "You are detached" (ba'in)?
b: One irrevocable divorce (ba'inah) occurs.

f: 245. What happens if the husband intends three divorces using kinayah?
b: Three divorces occur.

f: 246. What happens if the husband intends two divorces using kinayah?
b: Only one irrevocable divorce occurs.

f: 247. Why does intending two divorces through kinayah result in only one?
b: Because kinayah expressions support the concept of totality (three) but do not properly convey the specific number two.

f: 248. Give examples of strong kinayah divorce expressions.
b: "You are detached" (ba'in), "absolutely/severed" (battah), "forbidden" (haram), "Go join your family," "I have gifted you to your family," and "Choose" (ikhtari).

f: 249. What is the ruling if kinayah is spoken in a normal or neutral situation?
b: No divorce occurs unless the husband explicitly intended divorce.

f: 250. If the husband denies intending divorce in a neutral situation, is his statement accepted?
b: Yes.

f: 251. What is the state of mudhakarah in divorce law?
b: A situation where divorce is being discussed or negotiated.

f: 252. During divorce discussions, which kinayah expressions are treated as divorce in court even if intent is denied?
b: Expressions that function specifically as divorce or rejection, such as "You are detached" or "Choose."

f: 253. Why is a husband not believed if he denies intent with expressions like "Choose" during divorce negotiations?
b: Because the context indicates that divorce is the intended meaning.

f: 254. During divorce negotiations, which expressions may still be interpreted as ordinary dismissal rather than divorce?
b: Expressions like "Go," "Get up," or "Cover yourself."

f: 255. If a husband uses expressions like "Go" or "Get up" during divorce negotiations and denies intending divorce, is he believed?
b: Yes.

f: 256. Why are expressions like "Go" or "Get up" treated differently from "Choose"?
b: Because they can naturally mean dismissal or instruction rather than marital dissolution.

f: 257. What is the ruling of kinayah expressions spoken in anger (ghadab)?
b: The husband is generally believed if he denies intending divorce.

f: 258. Why is a husband generally believed when denying divorce intent during anger?
b: Because anger often causes harsh speech without necessarily intending legal divorce.

f: 259. What is the exception to the rule regarding anger and kinayah?
b: Expressions exclusively connected with ending marriage remain binding.

f: 260. Give examples of kinayah expressions that remain binding during anger.
b: "Choose" (ikhtari) and "The matter is in your hands."

f: 261. Why do expressions like "Choose" remain binding during anger?
b: Because these expressions are specifically associated with transferring the decision of divorce or ending the marriage.

f: 262. According to the Hanafi school, are implicit divorces (kinayah) revocable or irrevocable?
b: They are generally considered irrevocable (ba'inah).

f: 263. Why do Hanafis consider implicit divorces irrevocable?
b: Because these expressions are acts of separation (ibanah) rather than technical synonyms for divorce (talaq), so they immediately sever the marital bond.

f: 264. What is the Shafi'i position regarding implicit divorce?
b: Shafi'is consider implicit divorce revocable, treating it like explicit divorce.

f: 265. If a husband repeats "Observe your waiting period" (I'taddi) three times but intends divorce only with the first, is his claim accepted?
b: Yes, his claim is accepted in court.

f: 266. Why is the husband's claim regarding his intention accepted in repeated kinayah expressions?
b: Because he is considered the trustee (amin) regarding his own internal intention.

f: 267. What additional requirement may be required when the husband claims he intended only the first kinayah expression?
b: He must take an oath (yamin) to support his claim.

f: 268. Why is an oath required in disputes over repeated kinayah expressions?
b: Because the husband's internal intention is known only to him when the wording is ambiguous.

f: 269. What is tafwid in divorce law?
b: Delegating the power of divorce to the wife.

f: 270. What happens if a husband tells his wife "Choose" (ikhtari) intending divorce?
b: He delegates to her the authority to initiate divorce.

f: 271. What happens if a husband tells his wife "Divorce yourself"?
b: She receives the delegated authority to divorce herself.

f: 272. How long does the wife's delegated authority (tafwid) remain valid?
b: Only during the same session (majlis) in which the delegation was given.

f: 273. What invalidates the wife's authority after being told "Choose"?
b: Leaving the session, standing up, or engaging in another activity that indicates turning away from the matter.

f: 274. Why does leaving the session invalidate delegated divorce authority?
b: Because the session is treated as one continuous unit, and changing activity indicates abandonment of the matter.

f: 275. If a wife chooses herself (ikhtartu nafsi) after being given the choice, what occurs?
b: One irrevocable divorce (ba'inah) occurs.

f: 276. Can choosing herself result in three divorces if the husband intended three?
b: No. It results only in one irrevocable divorce.

f: 277. Why does choosing herself result in only one divorce?
b: Because the act of choosing is inherently a single action.

f: 278. What wording must be present for the wife's choice to be valid?
b: There must be a clear reference to the self (nafs).

f: 279. If the husband says "Choose" and the wife says "I have chosen" without mentioning herself, is it valid?
b: No, because the object of the choice remains ambiguous.

f: 280. If the husband says "Choose yourself" and she says "I have chosen," is the divorce valid?
b: Yes, because the husband specified the object of choice.

f: 281. If the husband says "Choose a choice" (ikhtari ikhtiyaran) and she says "I have chosen," is it valid?
b: Yes, because the wording indicates a singular choice referring to herself.

f: 282. If the husband says "Choose" and she says "I choose myself" (ana akhtaru nafsi), what occurs?
b: A valid irrevocable divorce occurs.

f: 283. Why is "I choose myself" treated as an immediate divorce despite being grammatically present tense?
b: Because it is interpreted as a declaration of a current state of action rather than merely a future statement.

f: 284. What precedent supports accepting "I choose myself" as an immediate choice?
b: The statement of Aisha رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا) choosing Allah and His Messenger, which was accepted as a definitive choice.

f: 285. How is "I will divorce myself" treated differently from "I choose myself"?
b: It is treated as a future promise rather than an immediate act of divorce.

f: 286. What linguistic distinction separates "I choose myself" from "I will divorce myself"?
b: The first reports a present action, while the second expresses a future intention.

f: 287. If a husband says "Choose, choose, choose" and the wife selects the first choice, what is Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ ruling?
b: Three divorces take effect.

f: 288. Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider "Choose, choose, choose" to result in three divorces?
b: Because the repetition indicates three separate delegations of the power of choice.

f: 289. What is the view of Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disciples regarding "Choose, choose, choose"?
b: They hold that only one divorce occurs.

f: 290. Why do the disciples consider repeated "Choose" to result in only one divorce?
b: Because the repetition is considered unnecessary emphasis, while the marital bond is only one.

f: 291. If the wife says, "I have chosen a choice" (ikhtiyartu ikhtiyaran), how many divorces occur?
b: Three divorces occur.

f: 292. Why does "I have chosen a choice" result in three divorces?
b: Because it is interpreted as a complete confirmation of the delegated authority to fully dissolve the marriage.

f: 293. If a wife says, "I have divorced myself with one," what occurs?
b: One revocable divorce occurs.

f: 294. Why does "I have divorced myself with one" result in one divorce?
b: Because the qualifier "with one" limits the divorce itself to a single instance.

f: 295. If the husband says "Choose one" or "Your matter is in your hand for one," what happens when she chooses?
b: One revocable divorce occurs.

f: 296. Why does adding "one" to the husband's delegation change the effect?
b: Because the numerical restriction overrides the normal finality associated with delegated divorce.

f: 297. If a husband says "Your matter is in your hand" intending three divorces, and she says "I have chosen myself with one," how many divorces occur?
b: Three divorces occur according to Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ analysis.

f: 298. Why does "I have chosen myself with one" not limit the divorce to one in the case of "Your matter is in your hand"?
b: Because the qualifier "with one" is connected to the delegated authority (matter), not the actual divorce act.

f: 299. What is the difference between "I have chosen myself with one" and "I have divorced myself with one"?
b: The first qualifies the delegated authority, while the second qualifies the divorce itself.

f: 300. If a husband delegates authority by saying "Your matter is in your hand today and the day after tomorrow," are these two separate delegations?
b: Yes, they are treated as two separate delegations.

f: 301. If the wife rejects the delegation today in "today and the day after tomorrow," does she still have authority the day after tomorrow?
b: Yes.

f: 302. Why does rejecting the delegation today not remove the authority for the day after tomorrow?
b: Because the two time periods represent separate delegations.

f: 303. If a husband says "Your matter is in your hand today and tomorrow," are these separate or one continuous delegation?
b: It is treated as one continuous delegation.

f: 304. If the wife rejects the delegation today in "today and tomorrow," does she retain the option tomorrow?
b: No, she loses the option for tomorrow as well.

f: 305. Why is "today and tomorrow" treated as one continuous delegation?
b: Because the consultation/session is considered uninterrupted across the connected timeframe.

f: 306. If a husband says, "Your matter is in your hand the day so-and-so arrives," when must the wife exercise the option?
b: She must exercise it during that day.

f: 307. If the person arrives during daylight and the wife knows about it, but she waits until night, can she still exercise the option?
b: No, the option has expired.

f: 308. If the wife only learns of the person's arrival at night, does she still have the option?
b: No, because the specified time has already ended.

f: 309. Why is "day" (yawm) interpreted as daylight hours in the conditional delegation example?
b: Because the legal interpretation of yawm in this context refers to the daytime period.

f: 310. How long does a wife retain delegated authority of divorce (tafwid/ikhtiyar) after the husband gives it to her?
b: She retains it as long as she remains in the same session (majlis) and does not do something indicating that she has turned away from the matter.

f: 311. When does the session (majlis) begin if the wife directly hears the husband's delegation?
b: It begins immediately when she hears it.

f: 312. When does the session begin if the wife is absent when the husband delegates divorce authority?
b: It begins when the information of the delegation reaches her.

f: 313. What causes the delegated authority of divorce to be lost?
b: Leaving the session, standing up in a way that indicates turning away, engaging in a separate activity, or otherwise showing abandonment of the choice.

f: 314. Does changing posture, such as sitting, reclining, or standing briefly, invalidate the session?
b: No. Such changes generally do not end the session because they do not necessarily indicate abandonment of the choice.

f: 315. Why do ordinary posture changes not invalidate the session?
b: Because they are not considered a turning away from the decision-making process.

f: 316. If a wife asks to consult her father after receiving delegated divorce authority, does she lose her authority?
b: No.

f: 317. Why does consulting her father not invalidate the session?
b: Because it shows she is seeking careful advice rather than abandoning the decision.

f: 318. If a wife requests witnesses before making her decision, does her authority remain?
b: Yes.

f: 319. Why does calling witnesses preserve the session?
b: Because it demonstrates seriousness and preparation rather than rejection of the choice.

f: 320. If a woman receives delegated divorce authority while riding an animal, what maintains her session?
b: Keeping the animal stopped maintains the session.

f: 321. If the animal moves forward while she is riding it, what happens to her delegated authority?
b: The authority ends.

f: 322. Why does movement of the animal terminate the session?
b: Because the movement is under her control and indicates she has moved away from the matter.

f: 323. If a woman is on a boat when she receives delegated divorce authority, does the boat's movement end the session?
b: No.

f: 324. Why does movement of a boat not terminate the session?
b: Because the movement of the boat is not under her control, so it does not indicate abandonment.

f: 325. What does the phrase "Divorce yourself" (Tallaqi nafsaki) mean legally?
b: It is a delegation of the act of divorce to the wife.

f: 326. Why can "Divorce yourself" include up to three divorces?
b: Because "divorce" (talaq) is a generic noun (ism jins) that includes the minimum and can include the maximum if intended.

f: 327. If the husband says "Divorce yourself" without specifying a number, how many divorces occur?
b: One revocable divorce occurs.

f: 328. Why does "Divorce yourself" without a specified number result in one divorce?
b: Because the default form of divorce is one revocable divorce.

f: 329. Is the wife's statement "I have divorced myself" (Tallaqtu nafsi) a valid response to "Divorce yourself"?
b: Yes.

f: 330. Why is "I have divorced myself" valid after "Divorce yourself"?
b: Because it directly corresponds to the delegated act.

f: 331. Is "I have made myself detached" (Abantu nafsi) accepted as a response to "Divorce yourself"?
b: There is scholarly disagreement.

f: 332. Why do some scholars accept "I have made myself detached" as valid?
b: Because ibanah (separation) is a recognized form of ending the marital bond.

f: 333. Why did Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ historically question the validity of "I have made myself detached"?
b: Because detachment (ibanah) is not exactly the same linguistic act as the specific divorce (talaq) that was delegated.

f: 334. Is "I have chosen myself" (Ikhtartu nafsi) valid after the husband says "Divorce yourself"?
b: Generally, no.

f: 335. When is "I have chosen myself" a valid response?
b: When the husband specifically delegated using the word "Choose" (Ikhtari).

f: 336. Why is "I have chosen myself" invalid after "Divorce yourself"?
b: Because it responds to a different linguistic act and does not match the delegated authority given.

f: 337. What is the difference between "Divorce yourself" and "Choose yourself"?
b: "Divorce yourself" delegates the act of divorce, while "Choose yourself" delegates the power of choice.

f: 338. What is the difference between tafwid (delegation) and wakalah (agency) in divorce?
b: Tafwid transfers the power of divorce to the wife, while wakalah appoints another person merely as an agent to carry out the husband's divorce.

f: 339. When a husband tells his wife "Divorce yourself," what type of authority is created?
b: Delegation (tafwid/tamlik) of the power of divorce.

f: 340. Why is delegation to the wife called tamlik?
b: Because the husband transfers ownership/control of the legal act of divorce to her.

f: 341. Can a husband retract the authority he delegated to his wife through "Divorce yourself"?
b: No.

f: 342. Why can the husband not retract delegated authority given to his wife?
b: Because delegation is a transfer of power, not merely permission to act.

f: 343. Is a wife's delegated divorce authority limited to the session (majlis)?
b: Yes, unless another wording extends it.

f: 344. When a husband tells another person "Divorce my wife," what type of authority is this?
b: Agency (wakalah).

f: 345. Can a husband revoke an agency to divorce given to a third party?
b: Yes.

f: 346. Why can agency be revoked but delegation cannot?
b: Because an agent assists the husband, while a delegated person receives authority over the act itself.

f: 347. Is an agent's authority normally limited to the session in which it was granted?
b: No.

f: 348. Why is agency not normally limited to the session?
b: Because it is assistance in performing the husband's act rather than transferring ownership of the act.

f: 349. If a husband tells an agent "Divorce her if you wish," is the agency unrestricted?
b: No. It is limited to the session.

f: 350. Why does "if you wish" restrict an agent's authority to the session?
b: Because it makes the decision dependent on immediate personal choice rather than a permanent agency.

f: 351. If a husband tells his wife "Divorce yourself three times" and she divorces herself once, is it valid?
b: Yes. One divorce occurs.

f: 352. Why can the wife choose fewer divorces than the husband authorized?
b: Because authority for the greater number includes the ability to choose a lesser amount.

f: 353. If a husband says "Divorce yourself once" and the wife divorces herself three times, what is the ruling according to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The divorce is invalid.

f: 354. Why is divorcing herself three times invalid when only one was authorized?
b: Because she exceeded the specific authority granted to her.

f: 355. If the husband orders his wife to divorce herself revocably (raj'i) but she says irrevocably (ba'in), what occurs?
b: A revocable divorce occurs.

f: 356. Why does the divorce remain revocable in this case?
b: Because the added irrevocable description is considered an unnecessary addition and does not override the husband's command.

f: 357. If the husband orders an irrevocable divorce and the wife says revocable, what occurs?
b: An irrevocable divorce occurs.

f: 358. Why does the husband's description control when he specifies irrevocability?
b: Because he designated the legal quality of the delegated act.

f: 359. If a husband says "Divorce yourself three times if you wish" and she divorces herself only once, what happens?
b: Nothing occurs.

f: 360. Why does no divorce occur when she chooses only one in this case?
b: Because the condition was wishing for three divorces, which was not fulfilled.

f: 361. What does "You are divorced if you wish" grant to the wife?
b: The power of choice to bring about her own divorce.

f: 362. If a wife responds "I wish if something else happens," after being told "You are divorced if you wish," is the divorce valid?
b: Generally no.

f: 363. Why is "I wish if something else happens" invalid after "You are divorced if you wish"?
b: Because she added a new condition that was not included in the original delegation.

f: 364. If a wife says "I wish [divorce] if something happened in the past," what is the ruling?
b: The divorce takes effect immediately.

f: 365. Why does a past condition not delay the divorce?
b: Because the condition is already fulfilled, making the statement an immediate enactment (tanjiz).

f: 366. What effect do the words mata (whenever) and idha (when/if) have in delegated divorce?
b: They grant the wife the ability to exercise the choice at any future time.

f: 367. If the wife rejects the offer after being given authority with mata or idha, does she lose the right permanently?
b: No.

f: 368. Why does rejecting the offer not cancel authority granted with mata or idha?
b: Because these words create a continuing right of choice rather than a one-time session-based option.

f: 369. Can the wife use a delegation containing mata or idha to divorce herself multiple times?
b: No.

f: 370. Why is only one divorce possible through this delegation?
b: Because the delegation extends the timing of the act, not a repeated right to perform multiple divorces.

f: 371. What authority does a wife receive when a husband tells her, "You are divorced whenever you wish" (Kullama shi'ti)?
b: She receives the authority to divorce herself one divorce at a time, up to three divorces.

f: 372. How many times may a wife exercise the divorce authority given through the phrase "You are divorced whenever you wish" (Kullama shi'ti)?
b: She may exercise it up to three times.

f: 373. Can a wife who has been given the authority "You are divorced whenever you wish" pronounce all three divorces together in one statement?
b: No. She must activate them sequentially, one after another.

f: 374. Why must the divorces under "You are divorced whenever you wish" (Kullama shi'ti) be exercised sequentially rather than simultaneously?
b: Because each divorce requires a separate activation of the delegated authority.

f: 375. Does the delegation "You are divorced whenever you wish" remain valid if the wife divorces herself, marries another man, and later returns to the first husband?
b: No.

f: 376. Why does the delegation "You are divorced whenever you wish" not carry over after the wife returns to her first husband?
b: Because it was attached only to the original marriage contract.

f: 377. How are phrases such as "Wherever you wish" (haythu shi'ti or ayna shi'ti) treated in divorce delegation?
b: They are treated as spatial expressions that have no effect and are interpreted like "if you wish."

f: 378. Why are expressions like "Wherever you wish" ineffective in divorce delegation?
b: Because divorce can be connected to time but not to location.

f: 379. What happens if "Wherever you wish" (haythu shi'ti) is interpreted as "If you wish" in divorce delegation?
b: The authority becomes limited to the current session (majlis).

f: 380. Why are temporal expressions such as mata ("whenever") effective in divorce delegation?
b: Because divorce can legally be connected to time.

f: 381. What does the phrase "How you wish" (Kayfa shi'ti) relate to in divorce delegation?
b: It relates to the description or quality of the divorce.

f: 382. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens when a husband says "How you wish" (Kayfa shi'ti) to his wife?
b: The divorce itself is established, and the wife determines its quality.

f: 383. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens if a husband says "How you wish" (Kayfa shi'ti) without specifying an intention?
b: It results in one revocable divorce.

f: 384. What types of qualities may a wife choose when given authority through "How you wish" (Kayfa shi'ti)?
b: She may choose qualities such as revocable, irrevocable, or three divorces.

f: 385. What is the position of Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disciples regarding "How you wish" (Kayfa shi'ti)?
b: They hold that no divorce occurs until the wife specifies the type of divorce.

f: 386. What do phrases such as "As many as you wish" (Kam shi'ti) relate to in divorce delegation?
b: They relate to the number of divorces.

f: 387. How many divorces can a wife choose when given authority through "As many as you wish" (Kam shi'ti)?
b: She can choose any number up to three.

f: 388. Is the authority granted through "As many as you wish" (Kam shi'ti) permanent?
b: No.

f: 389. When must a wife exercise the authority given through "As many as you wish" (Kam shi'ti)?
b: She must exercise it during the same session (majlis).

f: 390. What happens if a wife leaves the session after receiving the authority "As many as you wish" (Kam shi'ti)?
b: The authority expires.

f: 391. Why does the authority from "As many as you wish" expire when the session ends?
b: Because it is considered a single delegation connected to that session.

f: 392. If a husband says, "Divorce yourself from three as you wish," how many divorces may the wife choose according to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: She may choose one or two divorces, but not three.

f: 393. Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ prevent choosing three divorces from the phrase "from three as you wish"?
b: Because the phrase "from three" (min thalath) indicates taking a portion from a whole, excluding the complete amount.

f: 394. What is the opinion of Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disciples regarding "Divorce yourself from three as you wish"?
b: They allow the wife to choose up to three divorces.

f: 395. Why do Abu Hanifah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disciples allow three divorces in "Divorce yourself from three as you wish"?
b: Because they interpret "from three" as including the whole number.

f: 396. If a husband says, "If I marry you, you are divorced," when does the divorce occur?
b: The divorce occurs immediately when the marriage contract is completed.

f: 397. If a husband says, "Every woman I marry is divorced," what happens when he marries a woman?
b: She becomes divorced immediately upon the completion of the marriage contract.

f: 398. What is the Shafi'i school's ruling on saying, "If I marry you, you are divorced"?
b: They consider it invalid.

f: 399. Why does the Shafi'i school reject conditional divorce statements made before marriage?
b: Because of the hadith: "There is no divorce before marriage."

f: 400. How does the Hanafi school respond to the argument that there is no divorce before marriage?
b: They argue that this is not divorce before marriage, but a condition attached to the marriage itself.

f: 401. According to the Hanafi school, why is divorce valid in the statement "If I marry you, you are divorced"?
b: Because the divorce takes effect at the exact moment the marriage becomes valid.

f: 402. According to the Hanafi school, does the divorce in "If I marry you, you are divorced" occur before or after the marriage?
b: It occurs simultaneously with the establishment of the marriage.

f: 403. According to the Hanafi school, is it valid for a husband to say, "If I marry you, you are divorced"?
b: Yes. It is valid.

f: 404. According to the Hanafi school, what legal category does divorce linked to a future marriage fall under?
b: It functions as an oath (yamin) rather than an immediate divorce enactment (tanjiz).

f: 405. According to the Hanafi school, when does divorce occur in the statement "If I marry you, you are divorced"?
b: The divorce takes effect immediately when the marriage contract is concluded.

f: 406. How does the Hanafi school interpret the hadith "There is no divorce before marriage" regarding conditional divorce?
b: They interpret it as prohibiting immediate divorce before ownership, not attaching divorce to a future marriage.

f: 407. Which early scholars are cited in support of the Hanafi interpretation of conditional divorce before marriage?
b: Sha'bi and Zuhri.

f: 408. According to the Hanafi school, why is "If I marry you, you are divorced" not considered divorce before marriage?
b: Because the divorce only takes effect after the marriage creates ownership of the marital bond.

f: 409. Is divorce linked to a future condition such as "If you enter the house, you are divorced" valid?
b: Yes. It is valid by consensus.

f: 410. Why is divorce linked to a future condition valid when the husband says "If you enter the house, you are divorced"?
b: Because the marriage bond currently exists and is expected to continue until the condition occurs.

f: 411. What requirement must exist for a divorce oath (yamin) to be valid?
b: The husband must currently possess the marriage bond or connect the divorce to a future cause of ownership, such as a future marriage.

f: 412. Is the statement "If a random woman enters the house, she is divorced" valid as a divorce oath?
b: No.

f: 413. Why is a divorce oath concerning an unrelated stranger invalid?
b: Because there is no current or future ownership connecting the husband to the woman.

f: 414. What role do conditional particles such as in, idha, mata, and kullama play in divorce statements?
b: They act as markers indicating that the divorce is conditional upon an event.

f: 415. How are the conditional particles in ("if"), idha ("when"), and mata ("whenever") generally interpreted regarding repetition?
b: They are generally interpreted as applying only once.

f: 416. What happens to a conditional divorce oath using in, idha, or mata after the condition occurs once?
b: The oath is fulfilled and expires.

f: 417. What special meaning does the particle kullama ("every time") have in conditional divorce?
b: It indicates repetition, so the divorce occurs every time the condition is fulfilled.

f: 418. How does "Every time I marry a woman, she is divorced" differ from other conditional divorce statements?
b: The divorce is triggered each time the condition of marriage occurs.

f: 419. What happens if a husband exhausts all three divorces through a repeated oath such as "Every time I marry a woman, she is divorced"?
b: The oath's legal effect is exhausted.

f: 420. If a woman divorces three times through a repeated conditional divorce oath and later returns to the husband after marrying another man, does the oath revive?
b: No.

f: 421. Why does a repeated divorce oath not revive after a woman returns following another marriage?
b: Because the three divorces granted by the oath have already been consumed.

f: 422. What happens if the condition of a divorce oath occurs after the marriage has already ended?
b: The oath is dissolved, but no divorce occurs.

f: 423. Why does a divorce oath not cause divorce after the marriage has ended?
b: Because there is no longer a legal subject (mahall) to receive the divorce.

f: 424. What does it mean that an oath is "dissolved" (inhallat) when its condition occurs after divorce?
b: The condition has been fulfilled, but the legal consequence cannot occur because the marriage no longer exists.

f: 425. Does the dissolution of a marriage automatically cancel every existing divorce oath?
b: No.

f: 426. If a husband divorces his wife separately and later remarries her, can an earlier conditional divorce oath still remain active?
b: Yes, if its condition was never previously fulfilled.

f: 427. Why can a divorce oath survive after a separate divorce and become effective after remarriage?
b: Because the oath itself was not invalidated; only the marriage bond temporarily ended.

f: 428. If a husband and wife dispute whether a condition for divorce has occurred, whose statement is accepted according to Hanafi law?
b: The husband's statement is accepted unless the wife provides evidence.

f: 429. Why is the husband's statement accepted when there is a dispute about whether a divorce condition occurred?
b: Because the original legal status is that the marriage continues, and the husband holds that established status.

f: 430. If a divorce condition depends on something only the wife knows, such as menstruation, whose statement is accepted?
b: The wife's statement is accepted.

f: 431. Why is a wife's statement accepted regarding a private condition such as menstruation?
b: Because she is considered the trustee (aminah) regarding her own hidden personal state.

f: 432. Can a wife testify against her co-wife regarding a condition of divorce?
b: No.

f: 433. Why is a wife's claim against her co-wife not accepted regarding a divorce condition?
b: Because her claim is considered suspicious and does not serve as valid proof against another person's marital status.

f: 434. If a husband says, "If you love X, you are divorced," and the wife admits that she loves X, does divorce occur?
b: Yes.

f: 435. Why does the wife's statement about her love trigger the divorce in "If you love X, you are divorced"?
b: Because she is the authority regarding her own internal emotional state.

f: 436. Does the wife's statement that she loves X cause divorce for another woman mentioned in the same oath?
b: No.

f: 437. Why does the wife's statement about her feelings not affect another woman mentioned in the oath?
b: Because she cannot provide legal proof regarding another person's internal state.

f: 438. If divorce is conditional upon menstruation (hayd), when does the divorce become effective?
b: After the bleeding continues for at least three days.

f: 439. Why must menstruation last three days before conditional divorce takes effect?
b: Because three days is the minimum legally recognized duration of menstruation.

f: 440. If menstruation reaches three days in a conditional divorce statement, from when is the divorce counted?
b: It is backdated to the beginning of the bleeding.

f: 441. If a husband says, "If you have a menstruation, you are divorced," when does divorce occur?
b: It occurs after the menstrual cycle ends and purification begins.

f: 442. Why does "a menstruation" (haydah) require completion of the cycle before divorce occurs?
b: Because the suffix -ah indicates the complete cycle rather than the beginning of bleeding.

f: 443. If divorce is conditional upon "fasting a day," when does the divorce occur?
b: At sunset.
