f: 752. How did the Sharīʿah modify the pre-Islamic practice of īlāʾ?
b: The Sharīʿah delayed its effect until the completion of a four-month period.

f: 753. If a husband swears that he will not approach his wife for four months, what happens when the four months end?
b: The oath ends because it was limited to that period.

f: 754. If a husband swears that he will never approach his wife, what is the ruling of his oath?
b: The oath remains because it is unrestricted and not limited by a time period.

f: 755. Why does an unlimited oath of īlāʾ remain in effect?
b: Because it has not been broken through intercourse, and therefore the oath-ending consequence has not occurred.

f: 756. Why does repeated divorce not occur when an unlimited oath of īlāʾ remains after separation?
b: Because after irrevocable separation, the wife's right of intercourse is no longer being prevented, so the reason for repeated divorce no longer exists.

f: 757. If a man who made an unrestricted oath of īlāʾ divorces his wife irrevocably, then marries her again, does the īlāʾ return?
b: Yes. The īlāʾ returns because the unrestricted oath remains, and the wife's right of intercourse becomes established again through the new marriage.

f: 758. Why does the īlāʾ return after a man remarries the same wife?
b: Because the oath was unrestricted and never ended through breaking it, and the wrongdoing of preventing her marital right returns once the marriage exists again.

f: 759. From when is the four-month period of īlāʾ counted after a husband remarries his divorced wife?
b: The beginning of the īlāʾ period is counted from the time of the new marriage.

f: 760. What happens if a man remarries his wife after an irrevocable divorce and has intercourse with her?
b: Nothing occurs because he has broken his oath and the īlāʾ ends, although expiation is required.

f: 761. What happens if a man remarries his wife after an irrevocable divorce and does not approach her for four months?
b: Another divorce occurs after the completion of four months.

f: 762. If a man divorces his wife three times, then marries her again after she married another husband, does the previous īlāʾ cause another divorce?
b: No. No divorce occurs through that previous īlāʾ.

f: 763. Why does the previous īlāʾ not cause divorce after the woman marries another husband and returns to the first husband?
b: Because the oath was connected to the ownership of the original marriage, which ended.

f: 764. Why does the oath itself remain after the original marriage ends?
b: Because the oath was unrestricted and it was not broken through intercourse.

f: 765. What principle is the issue of īlāʾ after remarriage connected to?
b: It is connected to the disputed issue of immediate divorce, which was discussed previously.

f: 766. If a husband breaks his oath of īlāʾ by having intercourse with his wife, what becomes obligatory upon him?
b: Expiation for breaking the oath becomes obligatory upon him.

f: 767. Why is expiation required when intercourse occurs after īlāʾ?
b: Because the oath has been broken.

f: 768. If a husband swears not to approach his wife for less than four months, is he considered to have made īlāʾ?
b: No. He is not considered one who has made īlāʾ.

f: 769. What is the evidence of Ibn ʿAbbās regarding īlāʾ for less than four months?
b: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "There is no īlāʾ for less than four months."

f: 770. Why is abstaining from intercourse for less than four months not considered īlāʾ?
b: Because avoiding intercourse for a shorter period is normally possible without causing harm, so the ruling of divorce is not established.

f: 771. If a man says, "By Allah, I will not approach you for two months, and two months after these two months," is this considered īlāʾ?
b: Yes. He is considered to have made īlāʾ because the two periods are joined together by a conjunction and treated as one continuous period.

f: 772. Why are two consecutive two-month periods treated as one period for īlāʾ?
b: Because the conjunction connects them, making the total period four months.

f: 773. If a man waits one day after his first oath and then says, "By Allah, I will not approach you for two months after the first two months," is he considered to have made īlāʾ?
b: No. He is not considered to have made īlāʾ.

f: 774. Why is a second two-month oath after a one-day gap not considered īlāʾ?
b: Because a new period begins after the second oath, and the total period of prevention does not reach four complete months.

f: 775. How is the period of prevention calculated when there is a gap between two īlāʾ oaths?
b: The first oath prevents intercourse for two months, and the second oath prevents intercourse for two months after that, except for the one day gap, so four continuous months of prevention are not completed.

f: 776. If a man says, "By Allah, I will not approach you for a year except one day," is he considered to have made īlāʾ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, no. He is not considered to have made īlāʾ.

f: 777. What was Zufar's opinion regarding the statement, "I will not approach you for a year except one day"?
b: Zufar held that he is considered to have made īlāʾ because the exception applies to the end of the period, allowing the period of prevention to be complete.

f: 778. What analogy did Zufar use to support his view on exceptions in īlāʾ?
b: He compared it to hiring contracts (ijārah), where an exception at the end does not prevent the completion of the contracted period.

f: 779. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not consider "a year except one day" to be īlāʾ?
b: Because the period of abstention is not a complete four months due to the exception, so the required continuous period of prevention is not established.

f: 780. What is the Ḥanafī evidence that an oath of "a year except one day" is not considered īlāʾ?
b: The person who makes īlāʾ is one who cannot approach his wife for four months except by doing something that becomes binding upon him. In this case, he can approach her because the excluded day is unknown and indefinite.

f: 781. Why does an indefinite excluded day prevent an oath from being considered īlāʾ?
b: Because it is possible that the excluded day could occur at any point, meaning he is not certainly prevented from approaching her for four complete months.

f: 782. Why is the ruling different between exceptions in oaths and exceptions in hiring contracts (ijārah)?
b: In hiring contracts, applying the exception to the end is needed to validate the contract because an indefinite exception makes the contract invalid. This reasoning does not apply to oaths.

f: 783. If a husband who made an oath of "a year except one day" approaches his wife during the excluded day, and the remaining period is four months or more, does he become one who has made īlāʾ?
b: Yes. He becomes one who has made īlāʾ because the exception has fallen away.

f: 784. Why does approaching his wife during the excluded day cause the exception to fall away?
b: Because by using the excluded day, he can no longer rely on that exception to avoid completing the period of abstention.

f: 785. If a man in Basrah swears, "By Allah, I will not enter Kūfah," while his wife is in Kūfah, is this considered īlāʾ?
b: No. He is not considered to have made īlāʾ.

f: 786. Why is a man's oath not to enter a city where his wife is located not considered īlāʾ?
b: Because he can still approach his wife without breaking his oath by bringing her out of that city.

f: 787. What types of oaths can make a person one who has made īlāʾ besides swearing by Allah?
b: Swearing through pilgrimage, fasting, charity, emancipation of a slave, or divorce can also establish īlāʾ.

f: 788. Why do oaths involving pilgrimage, fasting, charity, emancipation, or divorce establish īlāʾ?
b: Because the prevention of intercourse is realized through the oath, as these consequences involve hardship that prevents him from approaching her.

f: 789. What are the two components of an oath according to the discussion of īlāʾ?
b: An oath consists of mentioning a condition and a consequence that results from that condition.

f: 790. How does an oath involving emancipation prevent intercourse?
b: The husband makes intercourse with his wife the cause for freeing his slave, so approaching her causes a binding consequence upon him.

f: 791. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disagreement regarding an oath involving emancipation?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that it does not establish īlāʾ because the husband could sell the slave before intercourse, preventing the consequence from occurring.

f: 792. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad reject Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument regarding selling the slave?
b: They argued that the possibility of selling the slave is merely hypothetical and does not remove the preventative nature of the oath.

f: 793. How does an oath involving divorce establish īlāʾ?
b: It is when the husband makes intercourse with his wife the cause for divorcing her or divorcing another woman.

f: 794. Why does an oath involving divorce prevent the husband from intercourse?
b: Because intercourse would cause the binding consequence of divorce, which acts as a deterrent.

f: 795. If a man makes īlāʾ from a woman divorced with a revocable divorce (ṭalāq rajʿī), is he considered to have made īlāʾ?
b: Yes. He is considered to have made īlāʾ because the marriage still exists.

f: 796. If a man makes īlāʾ from a woman divorced with an irrevocable divorce (ṭalāq bāʾin), is he considered to have made īlāʾ?
b: No. He is not considered to have made īlāʾ because the marriage no longer exists.

f: 797. Why does īlāʾ apply to a revocably divorced woman but not an irrevocably divorced woman?
b: Because the marriage remains in the case of revocable divorce but does not remain in the case of irrevocable divorce.

f: 798. What is the subject of īlāʾ according to the Qur'anic wording?
b: The subject of īlāʾ is the woman included among "our wives."

f: 799. What happens if the waiting period of a revocably divorced woman ends before the period of īlāʾ ends?
b: The īlāʾ falls away because the marital relationship and eligibility have ended.

f: 800. Why does īlāʾ disappear when the waiting period ends before the four-month period is completed?
b: Because the marital eligibility upon which īlāʾ depends no longer exists.

f: 801. If a man says to a woman who is not his wife, "By Allah, I will not approach you," then marries her afterwards, is he considered to have made īlāʾ?
b: No. He is not considered to have made īlāʾ because the statement was originally invalid due to the absence of a marital relationship.

f: 802. If a man says to a non-wife, "You are to me like my mother's back," then marries her afterwards, is he considered to have made ẓihār?
b: No. He is not considered to have made ẓihār because the statement was invalid when made and does not become valid after marriage.

f: 803. Why does an oath of īlāʾ made before marriage not become valid after the marriage occurs?
b: Because the statement was originally made without the legal relationship upon which īlāʾ depends, so it cannot become effective later.

f: 804. If a man makes an oath before marriage and then approaches the woman after marrying her, does he owe expiation?
b: Yes. He must perform expiation because the oath is considered established regarding him and he has broken it.

f: 805. What is the period of īlāʾ for a slave woman?
b: The period of īlāʾ for a slave woman is two months.

f: 806. Why is the īlāʾ period for a slave woman two months instead of four months?
b: Because the separation period is halved due to slavery, just as the waiting period (ʿiddah) is halved for a slave woman.

f: 807. If the husband making īlāʾ is unable to have intercourse due to illness, how does he end the īlāʾ?
b: His return (fayʾ) is through verbally saying during the period of īlāʾ: "I have returned to her."

f: 808. If the wife is sick and unable to have intercourse, how does the husband end the īlāʾ?
b: His return is through verbally declaring his return during the period of īlāʾ.

f: 809. If the wife is physically incapable of intercourse or is a young girl unable to be approached, how does the husband's return from īlāʾ occur?
b: His return occurs through a verbal declaration of returning to her during the period of īlāʾ.

f: 810. If the husband and wife are separated by a distance that prevents intercourse during the īlāʾ period, how does he perform fayʾ (return)?
b: He performs fayʾ by verbally stating that he has returned to her during the period of īlāʾ.

f: 811. What was Al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding the return (fayʾ) of a person making īlāʾ?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī held that there is no return except through intercourse.

f: 812. What was al-Ṭaḥāwī's position regarding fayʾ in īlāʾ?
b: Al-Ṭaḥāwī also held that return is only through intercourse.

f: 813. What was the reasoning of those who required intercourse for fayʾ?
b: They argued that if verbal return counted as breaking the oath, then it would be treated as a violation of the oath itself.

f: 814. What is the Ḥanafī evidence that verbal return is sufficient for someone unable to have intercourse?
b: They argue that the husband harmed his wife by expressing his intention to prevent intercourse, so removing that harm through a verbal promise is sufficient.

f: 815. Why is divorce not imposed when a husband verbally returns from īlāʾ while unable to have intercourse?
b: Because the injustice that caused the ruling has been removed, so he is not punished with divorce.

f: 816. If a husband becomes capable of intercourse during the īlāʾ period after verbally returning, is his verbal return still valid?
b: No. His verbal return becomes invalid, and his return must occur through intercourse.

f: 817. Why does verbal return become invalid if the husband becomes capable of intercourse during the īlāʾ period?
b: Because he became capable of performing the original act before the purpose of the oath was achieved.

f: 818. If a husband says to his wife, "You are forbidden for me," what does the judge ask him about?
b: He is asked about his intention.

f: 819. If a husband says, "I intended merely a lie" when he said "You are forbidden for me," what is the ruling?
b: According to the text, his statement is accepted because he intended only the literal meaning of his words.

f: 820. Is a husband's claim that he intended only a lie accepted in court when he says, "You are forbidden for me"?
b: There is a view that it is not accepted in court because the outward meaning appears to be an oath.

f: 821. If a husband says, "You are forbidden for me," and intends divorce, what is the ruling?
b: It is one irrevocable divorce (ṭalāq bāʾin), unless he intends three divorces.

f: 822. Where was the ruling regarding indirect expressions (kināyāt) of divorce previously discussed?
b: It was discussed in the chapter of indirect expressions (kināyāt).

f: 823. If a husband says, "You are forbidden for me," and intends ẓihār, is it considered ẓihār according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, it is considered ẓihār.

f: 824. What was Muḥammad's opinion regarding a husband who says, "You are forbidden for me," intending ẓihār?
b: Muḥammad held that it is not ẓihār because the essential element of ẓihār, comparing the wife to a permanently forbidden woman, is absent.

f: 825. What is the reasoning of Muḥammad that "You are forbidden for me" is not ẓihār?
b: He argued that ẓihār requires a specific comparison to a permanently unmarriageable woman, and that element is missing.

f: 826. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to Muḥammad's argument regarding ẓihār?
b: They argued that the husband expressed unrestricted prohibition, and ẓihār contains a form of prohibition, so the unrestricted expression can include the restricted meaning of ẓihār.

f: 827. If a husband says, "You are forbidden for me," and intends prohibition, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It is considered an oath through which he becomes one who has made īlāʾ.

f: 828. If a husband says, "You are forbidden for me," and has no intention, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It is considered an oath of īlāʾ.

f: 829. Why does intending prohibition or having no intention make "You are forbidden for me" an oath of īlāʾ according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because the original ruling of declaring something lawful as prohibited is that it is treated as an oath.

f: 830. Where will the discussion of making something lawful prohibited be mentioned in detail?
b: It will be discussed in the chapter of oaths (Aymān), if Allah wills.

f: 831. What do some scholars say regarding the phrase "You are forbidden for me"?
b: Some scholars say that the word "prohibition" is interpreted as divorce according to common usage, even without considering the husband's intention.

f: 832. What is khulʿ?
b: Khulʿ is a separation between husband and wife where the wife gives compensation in exchange for the husband divorcing her.

f: 833. What is the basis for khulʿ being permitted when the spouses fear they cannot maintain Allah's limits?
b: The basis is the verse: "There is no blame upon them concerning that by which she ransoms herself" (Qur'an 2:229).

f: 834. When a husband and wife perform khulʿ, what type of divorce occurs according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: One irrevocable divorce (ṭalāq bāʾin) occurs through khulʿ.

f: 835. Why does khulʿ result in an irrevocable divorce?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Khulʿ is an irrevocable divorce."

f: 836. Why is khulʿ considered among indirect expressions (kināyāt) of divorce?
b: Because khulʿ can carry the meaning of divorce and separation.

f: 837. Why does khulʿ not require the husband's intention for divorce when compensation is mentioned?
b: Because the wife only gives wealth in order to receive release from the marriage, and that release occurs through separation.

f: 838. What becomes obligatory upon the wife when khulʿ occurs?
b: She becomes responsible for paying the agreed compensation.

f: 839. If the wife's rebellion (nushūz) is the cause of separation, may the husband take compensation through khulʿ?
b: Yes. If the wife is the source of conflict, compensation through khulʿ is permitted.

f: 840. If the husband's rebellion (nushūz) is the cause of separation, what is the ruling on him taking compensation through khulʿ?
b: It is disliked for him to take compensation from her.

f: 841. What Qur'anic evidence is used to show that a husband should not take compensation when he is the wrongdoer?
b: The verse: "And if you wish to replace one wife with another... then do not take anything from it" (Qur'an 4:20).

f: 842. Why is it disliked for a husband whose nushūz caused separation to take compensation?
b: Because he has already caused her harm by replacing her, so he should not increase her harm by taking her wealth.

f: 843. What moral principle is mentioned regarding a husband taking wealth in khulʿ when he is at fault?
b: A person who causes harm should not increase that harm by taking compensation from the harmed party.

f: 844. If the wife's rebellion (nushūz) causes the khulʿ, what amount of compensation does the Ḥanafī position dislike the husband taking?
b: It is disliked for him to take more compensation than the amount he originally gave her.

f: 845. According to the narration of al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, is it permissible for a husband to take more compensation than he gave when the wife's rebellion caused khulʿ?
b: Yes. According to that narration, the excess compensation is also permissible.

f: 846. What is the evidence that allows a husband to take excess compensation in khulʿ when the wife is rebellious?
b: The unrestricted nature of the Qur'anic verse: "There is no blame upon them concerning that by which she ransoms herself" (Qur'an 2:229).

f: 847. What evidence is used by those who dislike taking more than the original amount in khulʿ compensation?
b: They use the statement of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the wife of Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammas: "As for the increase, then no."

f: 848. In the case of Thābit ibn Qays, from whom was the rebellion (nushūz)?
b: The rebellion was from the wife.

f: 849. If a husband takes excess compensation in khulʿ despite it being disliked, is the transaction legally valid in court?
b: Yes. The khulʿ is valid in court.

f: 850. If the husband takes compensation in khulʿ even though the rebellion was from him, is it legally valid?
b: Yes. It is legally valid in court, even though it is disliked.

f: 851. Why is khulʿ valid in court even when taking compensation is disliked?
b: Because the evidence for khulʿ establishes both legal validity and permissibility. The permissibility ruling is affected by another factor, but the validity remains.

f: 852. If a husband divorces his wife in exchange for wealth and she accepts, does the divorce occur?
b: Yes. The divorce occurs and she becomes obligated to pay the agreed wealth.

f: 853. Why does divorce occur when the husband offers divorce in exchange for wealth and the wife accepts?
b: Because the husband has independent authority to issue divorce immediately or conditionally, and he made it conditional upon her acceptance.

f: 854. Why can the wife obligate herself to pay compensation in exchange for divorce?
b: Because she has authority over herself and can assume financial obligations.

f: 855. Why is compensation allowed in exchange for the marital bond even though marriage itself is not wealth?
b: Because the marital relationship is something for which compensation can be exchanged, similar to how retaliation (qiṣāṣ) can be exchanged for compensation.

f: 856. Is divorce through exchange for compensation irrevocable or revocable?
b: It is irrevocable (ṭalāq bāʾin).

f: 857. Why is divorce in exchange for compensation irrevocable?
b: Because it is an exchange of wealth for the wife's release from the marriage. Since the husband acquires one side of the exchange, she acquires the other side, namely her freedom from the marital bond.

f: 858. If khulʿ compensation becomes invalid, such as when a Muslim gives wine, pork, or carrion as compensation, what happens?
b: The husband receives nothing, but the separation remains irrevocable.

f: 859. If compensation in a normal divorce becomes invalid, what type of divorce occurs?
b: The divorce is revocable.

f: 860. Does the divorce itself occur when the compensation in khulʿ or divorce becomes invalid?
b: Yes. The divorce occurs in both cases because it was made conditional upon the wife's acceptance.

f: 861. Why is invalid compensation in khulʿ different from invalid compensation in ordinary divorce?
b: Because in khulʿ the effective element is the wording of khulʿ, which is an indirect expression (kināyah), while in ordinary divorce the effective element is explicit divorce wording, which carries the right of rajʿah.

f: 862. Why does khulʿ remain irrevocable even when the compensation is invalid?
b: Because khulʿ itself is an indirect expression that establishes separation without the right of taking her back.

f: 863. Why does ordinary divorce with invalid compensation remain revocable?
b: Because explicit divorce wording establishes a divorce that normally includes the husband's right of rajʿah.

f: 864. If a woman performs khulʿ in exchange for something that has no legally recognized value, does the husband receive compensation?
b: No. The husband receives nothing because she did not specify something of recognized value and did not commit herself to any compensation.

f: 865. Why does the husband receive nothing when a woman performs khulʿ with invalid compensation such as wine or pork?
b: Because Islam prohibits the specified compensation, and there is no basis for obligating another compensation since she did not commit herself to anything.

f: 866. Why is a woman who offers invalid compensation in khulʿ not considered to have deceived the husband?
b: Because she did not name something that is considered legally valuable, so she did not mislead him regarding valid wealth.

f: 867. If a woman performs khulʿ in exchange for vinegar, but it is later discovered to be wine, does the husband receive compensation?
b: Yes, because she specified a form of wealth, so she deceived him.

f: 868. Why is khulʿ in exchange for falsely specified vinegar treated differently from khulʿ in exchange for wine?
b: Because vinegar is normally recognized as wealth, so specifying it creates the possibility of deception, whereas wine has no legal value in Islam.

f: 869. Why is compensation required when a slave is freed through kitābah or emancipation in exchange for wine?
b: Because the value of the slave remains considered property, and the master did not consent to losing that valuable ownership without compensation.

f: 870. Why is the marital relationship during separation not treated as valuable property requiring compensation?
b: Because ownership of the marital relationship at the time of separation is not considered something with monetary value.

f: 871. Why is marriage itself different from separation regarding value?
b: Because after consummation, the marital relationship is considered valuable, while releasing oneself from the marriage is itself a noble act and does not require compensation to establish its worth.

f: 872. Why was compensation legislated for entering marriage?
b: Because marriage is a noble relationship, and requiring compensation demonstrates its value and importance.

f: 873. Why is compensation not required when ending the marriage through khulʿ?
b: Because separation itself is a noble act of release, so there is no need to make wealth obligatory in exchange for it.

f: 874. What is the ruling regarding what can serve as khulʿ compensation?
b: Whatever is valid to be a dowry (mahr) is valid to be compensation in khulʿ.

f: 875. Why is anything valid as a dowry also valid as khulʿ compensation?
b: Because something suitable as compensation for a valuable matter is even more suitable as compensation for something that is not itself considered monetary property.

f: 876. If a woman says to her husband, "Perform khulʿ with me for whatever is in my hand," and he accepts, but there is nothing in her hand, what does the husband receive?
b: He receives nothing.

f: 877. Why does the husband receive nothing when she says, "Whatever is in my hand," but there is nothing there?
b: Because she did not deceive him by specifying wealth.

f: 878. If a woman says, "Perform khulʿ with me for whatever wealth is in my hand," and there is no wealth in her hand, what does she owe the husband according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: She returns the dowry that he gave her.

f: 879. Why does a woman who specifies "whatever wealth is in my hand" owe the husband her dowry if nothing exists?
b: Because the husband only agreed to end the marriage in exchange for compensation, but the specified compensation is unknown and cannot be made obligatory.

f: 880. Why is the equivalent dowry (mahr al-mithl) not required when the specified khulʿ compensation is unknown?
b: Because the marital relationship at separation is not considered something having monetary value.

f: 881. Why is the original dowry returned when unspecified wealth does not exist in khulʿ?
b: To remove harm from the husband, since he gave up the marital bond believing he would receive compensation.

f: 882. If a woman performs khulʿ in exchange for "whatever dirhams are in my hand," but there are no dirhams, what does she owe according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: She owes three dirhams.

f: 883. Why does a woman owe three dirhams when she says "whatever dirhams are in my hand" but has none?
b: Because she used the plural form of dirhams, and the minimum plural in Arabic is three.

f: 884. What is the function of the word "min" (from) in the phrase "whatever of the dirhams are in my hand"?
b: It is for connection and emphasis, not for indicating partiality or a portion.

f: 885. Why is "min" in this context not interpreted as meaning "some of"?
b: Because the statement would be incomplete without it, so it serves to connect and emphasize the meaning.

f: 886. If a woman performs khulʿ in exchange for one of her runaway slaves on the condition that she is free from liability for the slave, is she released from responsibility?
b: No. She is not free from liability for the slave.

f: 887. If the slave given as khulʿ compensation is a runaway slave and the woman is not freed from liability, what must she provide?
b: If she can deliver the slave itself, she must hand over the slave. If she cannot, she must provide the slave's value.

f: 888. Why is the condition of being free from liability for a runaway slave invalid in khulʿ?
b: Because khulʿ is an exchange contract, and exchange contracts require the compensation to be sound and properly defined.

f: 889. Why does an invalid condition not invalidate khulʿ itself?
b: Because invalid conditions are cancelled while the underlying contract remains valid.

f: 890. What other contract is mentioned as having the same ruling regarding invalid conditions?
b: Marriage.

f: 891. If a woman says, "Divorce me three times for one thousand," and the husband divorces her once, how much does she owe according to the first view?
b: She owes one-third of the thousand.

f: 892. Why does one divorce out of three requested divorces correspond to one-third of the compensation?
b: Because the compensation is divided according to the things being exchanged, and each divorce represents one portion of the requested exchange.

f: 893. Why is the divorce irrevocable when the woman owes one-third of the compensation?
b: Because the payment of money becomes obligatory, making it a khulʿ-type separation.

f: 894. If a woman says, "Divorce me three times for one thousand," and the husband gives only one divorce, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, she owes nothing and the husband retains the right of taking her back (rajʿah).

f: 895. If a woman says, "Divorce me three times for one thousand," and the husband gives one divorce, what is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: They hold that it is one irrevocable divorce and she owes one-third of the thousand.

f: 896. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad consider one divorce to require one-third of the compensation?
b: Because they consider the word "ʿalā" (upon/on) to function like the letter bāʾ in exchange contracts.

f: 897. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not treat "ʿalā" like bāʾ in this case?
b: Because he considers "ʿalā" to be a word of condition rather than a word indicating compensation.

f: 898. What example is given showing that "ʿalā" can indicate a condition?
b: The verse: "They pledge allegiance to you on the condition that they will not associate anything with Allah" (Qur'an 60:12).

f: 899. How is "ʿalā" used in divorce expressions according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It indicates that the divorce is attached to a condition, such as saying: "You are divorced on condition that you enter the house."

f: 900. Why was the word "ʿalā" borrowed to indicate conditions?
b: Because it originally indicates obligation, and the condition remains attached to the consequence.

f: 901. Why is a condition not divided according to parts of what it is attached to?
b: Because a condition is a single attached requirement, unlike compensation which is divided according to the exchanged items.

f: 902. What is the difference between bāʾ and ʿalā in exchange-based divorce expressions?
b: Bāʾ indicates compensation, so the amount is divided according to the parts exchanged, while ʿalā indicates a condition, so it is not divided.

f: 903. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens when no compensation becomes obligatory in "Divorce me three times for one thousand"?
b: It becomes a simple divorce statement, so the divorce occurs and the husband retains the right of taking her back.

f: 904. If a husband says to his wife, "Divorce yourself three times for one thousand," and she divorces herself once, does the divorce occur?
b: No. Nothing occurs.

f: 905. If a husband says, "Divorce yourself three times upon one thousand," and she divorces herself once, does the divorce occur?
b: No. Nothing occurs.

f: 906. Why does nothing occur when the husband tells his wife to divorce herself three times for one thousand and she does it once?
b: Because the husband only agreed to separation in exchange for receiving the entire thousand, not part of it.

f: 907. Why is this different from when the wife says, "Divorce me three times for one thousand"?
b: Because when she requests divorce for one thousand, she is also satisfied with part of that amount being exchanged for one divorce.

f: 908. If a husband says, "You are divorced for one thousand," and the wife accepts, what is the ruling?
b: She is divorced and owes the husband one thousand.

f: 909. Why does "You are divorced for one thousand" require the wife's acceptance?
b: Because compensation does not become obligatory without her acceptance.

f: 910. What is the meaning of the phrase "You are divorced for one thousand"?
b: It means: "You are divorced in exchange for one thousand which you owe me."

f: 911. What is the meaning of the phrase "You are divorced upon one thousand"?
b: It means: "You are divorced on the condition that one thousand becomes owed to me by you."

f: 912. Why does "upon one thousand" also require the wife's acceptance?
b: Because something attached to a condition does not occur before the condition exists, and the condition is her acceptance.

f: 913. Is divorce through "You are divorced for one thousand" irrevocable or revocable?
b: It is irrevocable (ṭalāq bāʾin).

f: 914. Why is divorce through compensation irrevocable?
b: Because it is an exchange in which the husband receives compensation and the wife receives separation from the marriage.

f: 915. If a husband says, "You are divorced, and upon you is one thousand," and the wife accepts, what happens according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The divorce occurs, but she does not owe the one thousand.

f: 916. If a master says to his slave, "You are free, and upon you is one thousand," and the slave accepts, what happens according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The slave is freed, but the slave owes nothing.

f: 917. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, does acceptance or rejection affect the ruling of "You are divorced, and upon you is one thousand"?
b: No. Whether she accepts or not, the divorce occurs and no payment is owed.

f: 918. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what is the ruling when a husband says, "You are divorced, and upon you is one thousand," and the wife accepts?
b: The wife owes the one thousand.

f: 919. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what happens if the wife does not accept "You are divorced, and upon you is one thousand"?
b: The divorce does not occur.

f: 920. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what happens if a master says, "You are free, and upon you is one thousand," and the slave accepts?
b: The slave owes the one thousand.

f: 921. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what happens if the slave does not accept the emancipation with payment?
b: The emancipation does not occur.

f: 922. What is the evidence of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad that "upon you is one thousand" creates an exchange?
b: They argue that this wording is used for exchange, similar to saying: "Carry this item and you will have a dirham," which means "Carry this item for a dirham."

f: 923. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that "You are divorced, and upon you is one thousand" does not create an exchange?
b: He argues that it is a complete sentence by itself, so it does not automatically connect to the previous statement.

f: 924. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say the sentence should be treated independently?
b: Because the default is that complete sentences stand independently unless there is an indication connecting them.

f: 925. Why is there no indication connecting "upon you is one thousand" to the divorce according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because divorce and emancipation can exist without compensation.

f: 926. Why are sale and hiring contracts different from divorce and emancipation regarding compensation?
b: Because sale and hiring cannot exist without compensation, whereas divorce and emancipation can exist without wealth.

f: 927. If a husband says, "You are divorced for one thousand, on the condition that I have the option (khiyār) to cancel," and the wife accepts, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The option is invalid because it belongs to the husband, but the divorce occurs.

f: 928. If a husband says, "You are divorced for one thousand, on the condition that you have the option for three days," and the wife accepts, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The woman's option is valid.

f: 929. If the wife rejects her option during the three days in a khulʿ agreement where she has the option, what happens?
b: The option is cancelled and the divorce does not occur.

f: 930. If the wife does not reject her option within the three days in a khulʿ agreement, what happens?
b: The divorce occurs and the thousand dirhams become obligatory upon her.

f: 931. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding adding an option (khiyār) to divorce in exchange for wealth?
b: They held that the option is invalid whether it belongs to the husband or the wife, and the divorce occurs with the wife owing one thousand dirhams.

f: 932. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad consider the option invalid in both cases?
b: Because an option is for cancelling a contract after it has been concluded, not for preventing the contract from coming into existence.

f: 933. Why does khiyār not apply from the husband's side in divorce for compensation according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: Because from his side it is an oath, and oaths do not accept cancellation options.

f: 934. Why does khiyār not apply from the wife's side according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: Because from her side it is merely a condition attached to the divorce.

f: 935. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that a woman's option is valid in khulʿ?
b: He argues that khulʿ from her side resembles a sale transaction, because her withdrawal from the offer is valid and the agreement can remain pending beyond the session.

f: 936. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ compare khulʿ from the woman's side to sale?
b: Because both involve an exchange where acceptance and withdrawal are relevant.

f: 937. Why is the husband's option invalid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because his side is considered an oath, and withdrawal from an oath is not valid through an option.

f: 938. Why is there no option in oaths according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because an oath is binding by its nature and does not operate like an exchange contract.

f: 939. In emancipation in exchange for payment, whose side is compared to the woman's side in divorce?
b: The slave's side is compared to the woman's side in divorce.

f: 940. If a husband says, "I divorced you yesterday for one thousand dirhams," but she did not accept at that time and later says, "I accept," whose statement is accepted?
b: The husband's statement is accepted.

f: 941. Why is the husband's statement accepted when he claims he divorced her yesterday for one thousand dirhams?
b: Because divorce in exchange for wealth is considered an oath from his side, and his admission is not an admission of a condition requiring acceptance.

f: 942. Why does admitting a divorce for compensation not require admitting acceptance?
b: Because the divorce can be valid from the husband's side even without her acceptance.

f: 943. If a person says, "I sold you this slave yesterday for one thousand dirhams," but the buyer did not accept, then later says, "I accept," whose statement is accepted?
b: The buyer's statement is accepted.

f: 944. Why is the buyer's statement accepted in the sale example?
b: Because sale cannot be completed without acceptance, so admitting the sale is admitting something that necessarily requires acceptance.

f: 945. Why is denying acceptance in the sale example considered a withdrawal?
b: Because the sale cannot exist without acceptance, so denying acceptance means denying the completion of the contract.

f: 946. What is the fundamental difference between divorce for compensation and sale regarding acceptance?
b: Divorce for compensation can exist from the husband's side without acceptance, whereas sale cannot exist without acceptance from both parties.

f: 947. What is mubāraʾah?
b: Mubāraʾah is a type of mutual separation between husband and wife, similar to khulʿ.

f: 948. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the effect of khulʿ and mubāraʾah regarding rights connected to marriage?
b: They remove every right belonging to either spouse against the other that is connected to marriage.

f: 949. According to Muḥammad, what rights are removed through khulʿ and mubāraʾah?
b: Only the rights specifically mentioned in the agreement are removed.

f: 950. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position regarding khulʿ and mubāraʾah?
b: He agreed with Muḥammad regarding khulʿ, but agreed with Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding mubāraʾah.

f: 951. What is Muḥammad's reasoning that only specifically mentioned rights are removed in khulʿ and mubāraʾah?
b: Because they are exchange transactions, and in exchange transactions only the stipulated matter is considered.

f: 952. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning regarding mubāraʾah removing rights from both sides?
b: Mubāraʾah comes from barāʾah (freedom from responsibility), which indicates mutual release from both sides.

f: 953. Why does Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ restrict the unrestricted meaning of mubāraʾah?
b: Because the purpose of mubāraʾah is separation, so it is restricted to rights connected with marriage.

f: 954. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why is khulʿ different from mubāraʾah?
b: Because khulʿ means separation from the marriage bond itself, which occurs by ending the marriage, and there is no necessity to remove all legal consequences.

f: 955. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning that khulʿ removes all marriage-related rights?
b: Because khulʿ indicates separation, similar to removing a shoe or removing work/service, and its unrestricted meaning applies to the marriage, its rulings, and its rights.

f: 956. What happens if a father performs khulʿ on behalf of his young daughter using her wealth?
b: The khulʿ is not valid against her.

f: 957. Why is a father's khulʿ on behalf of his young daughter using her wealth invalid?
b: Because there is no benefit for her, and the marital relationship at separation is not considered valuable while the compensation is valuable.

f: 958. Why is khulʿ different from marriage regarding the value of the marital relationship?
b: Because the marital relationship after consummation is considered valuable, whereas ending the relationship through khulʿ is not itself considered valuable property.

f: 959. How is the khulʿ of a sick woman treated regarding her wealth?
b: It is considered from one-third of her wealth because it involves giving away valuable compensation.

f: 960. How is the marriage of a sick man treated regarding the dowry?
b: It is considered according to the equivalent dowry (mahr al-mithl) from all his wealth.

f: 961. If a young girl's khulʿ performed by her father is invalid, does her dowry fall away?
b: No. Her dowry does not fall away.

f: 962. If a father's khulʿ on behalf of his young daughter is invalid, does he gain entitlement to her wealth?
b: No. He does not gain entitlement to her wealth.

f: 963. If a father's khulʿ on behalf of his young daughter is invalid, does divorce occur according to one narration?
b: Yes. According to one narration, divorce occurs.

f: 964. If a father's khulʿ on behalf of his young daughter is invalid, does divorce occur according to another narration?
b: According to another narration, divorce does not occur.

f: 965. Which narration regarding invalid khulʿ by a father is considered more correct?
b: The narration that divorce occurs is considered more correct.

f: 966. Why is the narration that divorce occurs considered stronger in the case of invalid khulʿ?
b: Because the divorce was made conditional upon acceptance, so it is treated like making divorce conditional upon other conditions.

f: 967. If a father performs khulʿ with his daughter for one thousand on the condition that he guarantees the payment, what happens?
b: The khulʿ occurs and the thousand becomes the father's responsibility.

f: 968. Why can a father guarantee the compensation in khulʿ?
b: Because making a third party responsible for khulʿ compensation is valid, and the father is even more suitable for this responsibility.

f: 969. Does the daughter's dowry fall away when her father guarantees the khulʿ compensation?
b: No. Her dowry does not fall away because it was not under the father's authority.

f: 970. If the father makes the thousand compensation the daughter's responsibility instead of guaranteeing it himself, what is required?
b: It depends on her acceptance if she is capable of accepting.

f: 971. If the daughter accepts responsibility for the thousand compensation in khulʿ, what occurs?
b: The divorce occurs because the condition has been fulfilled.

f: 972. If the daughter accepts responsibility for the thousand compensation in khulʿ, does the wealth become obligatory upon her?
b: No. The wealth does not become obligatory because she is not legally capable of financial liability.

f: 973. If the father accepts the khulʿ compensation on behalf of his daughter, how many narrations exist?
b: There are two narrations regarding this issue.

f: 974. If a man performs khulʿ with his wife for her dowry and the father does not guarantee the dowry, what is the ruling?
b: It depends upon her acceptance. If she accepts, she is divorced, but the dowry does not fall away.

f: 975. If the father accepts the khulʿ agreement on behalf of his daughter when the compensation is her dowry, what is the ruling?
b: The ruling follows the two narrations mentioned regarding the father's acceptance on behalf of his daughter.

f: 976. If a father guarantees his daughter's dowry of one thousand dirhams as khulʿ compensation, what is the ruling?
b: The daughter is divorced because his acceptance exists, which fulfills the condition.

f: 977. How much is the father responsible for when he guarantees his daughter's one thousand dirham dowry as khulʿ compensation?
b: According to istiḥsān, he is responsible for five hundred dirhams.

f: 978. According to analogy (qiyās), how much would the father owe when guaranteeing his daughter's one thousand dirham dowry as khulʿ compensation?
b: According to analogy, he would owe the full one thousand dirhams.

f: 979. What is the basis for the ruling that the father only owes five hundred dirhams by istiḥsān?
b: It is based on the case of an adult woman who performs khulʿ before consummation for one thousand while her dowry is one thousand.

f: 980. According to analogy, what would an adult woman owe if she performed khulʿ before consummation for one thousand while her dowry was one thousand?
b: She would owe an additional five hundred dirhams.

f: 981. According to istiḥsān, what would an adult woman owe if she performed khulʿ before consummation for one thousand while her dowry was one thousand?
b: She would owe nothing because the purpose normally is the amount actually owed to her.

f: 982. What is ẓihār?
b: Ẓihār is when a man compares his wife to the back of his mother or another permanently prohibited relative, making her temporarily prohibited until expiation is performed.

f: 983. What happens if a man says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother"?
b: She becomes prohibited for him, and he may not have intercourse with her, touch her, or kiss her until he performs expiation for ẓihār.

f: 984. What evidence establishes the prohibition of ẓihār until expiation?
b: The verse: "Those who make ẓihār from their wives... then the freeing of a slave before they touch one another." (Qur'an 58:3)

f: 985. What was ẓihār considered during the time of ignorance?
b: It was considered a form of divorce.

f: 986. How did the Sharīʿah change the ruling of ẓihār?
b: The Sharīʿah affirmed its basic concept but changed its consequence into temporary prohibition removed by expiation, without ending the marriage.

f: 987. Why is ẓihār treated as a temporary prohibition rather than divorce?
b: Because ẓihār is a sinful and false statement, so its punishment is prohibition rather than removal of the marriage bond.

f: 988. Why are the causes and preliminaries of intercourse also prohibited in ẓihār?
b: So that the person does not fall into the prohibited act of intercourse.

f: 989. What is the analogy used to explain why preliminaries are prohibited in ẓihār?
b: It is compared to iḥrām, where acts leading toward prohibited actions are also restricted.

f: 990. Why are preliminaries not prohibited during menstruation and fasting in the same way as ẓihār?
b: Because menstruation and fasting occur frequently, and prohibiting preliminaries would create hardship.

f: 991. What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with his wife before performing expiation for ẓihār?
b: He seeks Allah's forgiveness, and only the original expiation remains obligatory. He cannot return to intercourse until he performs expiation.

f: 992. What evidence shows that no additional expiation is required for intercourse before the first expiation?
b: The Prophet ﷺ told the man who did so: "Seek Allah's forgiveness and do not return until you perform expiation." If another obligation existed, he would have mentioned it.

f: 993. If a man says "You are to me like the back of my mother," what legal category does this expression fall under?
b: It is an explicit expression of ẓihār.

f: 994. If a man intends divorce when saying "You are to me like the back of my mother," does divorce occur?
b: No. The divorce meaning is not valid because that meaning was abrogated and cannot be brought into effect.

f: 995. If a man says to his wife "You are to me like my mother's stomach," does ẓihār occur?
b: Yes.

f: 996. If a man says to his wife "You are to me like my mother's thigh," does ẓihār occur?
b: Yes.

f: 997. If a man says to his wife "You are to me like my mother's private part," does ẓihār occur?
b: Yes.

f: 998. Why do comparisons such as the mother's stomach, thigh, or private part constitute ẓihār?
b: Because ẓihār is comparing something permissible to something prohibited, and this meaning exists through comparison with a limb that is impermissible to look at.

f: 999. If a man compares his wife to a permanently unmarriageable female relative (maḥram) such as his sister, paternal aunt, or foster mother, what is the ruling?
b: It is ẓihār because these women are permanently prohibited like one's mother.

f: 1000. Why does comparing one's wife to his sister, paternal aunt, or foster mother constitute ẓihār?
b: Because they are permanently forbidden to him, just like his mother.

f: 1001. If a man says: "Your head is like my mother's back to me," does ẓihār occur?
b: Yes, because such expressions refer to the whole body.

f: 1002. If a man says: "Your private part, face, neck, half, third, or body is like my mother's back," does ẓihār occur?
b: Yes, because these expressions are commonly understood to refer to the whole body.

f: 1003. Why do expressions involving a part of the wife's body extend to the ruling of the whole body in ẓihār?
b: Because legal rulings are established according to common usage, and the meaning extends to the rest of the body, similar to indirect divorce expressions.

f: 1004. If a man says: "You are to me like my mother," or "like my mother," what determines the ruling?
b: It depends upon his intention.

f: 1005. If a man says: "You are like my mother," and intends honouring her, what is the ruling?
b: It is as he intended, and no ẓihār occurs.

f: 1006. Why can "You are like my mother" be interpreted as honouring?
b: Because honouring someone through comparison is common in speech.

f: 1007. If a man says: "You are like my mother," and intends ẓihār, what is the ruling?
b: It is ẓihār.

f: 1008. Why does intending ẓihār make the statement "You are like my mother" into ẓihār?
b: Because it is a comparison to her entire being and also contains an implied comparison to a limb, though it is not explicit.

f: 1009. If a man says: "You are like my mother," and intends divorce, what is the ruling?
b: It is one irrevocable divorce.

f: 1010. Why does intending divorce in "You are like my mother" result in an irrevocable divorce?
b: Because he compared her to his mother regarding prohibition, making it similar to saying "You are forbidden to me" while intending divorce.

f: 1011. If a man says: "You are like my mother" without any intention, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Nothing occurs because the statement could be interpreted as honouring.

f: 1012. What is Muḥammad's view if a man says: "You are like my mother" without intention?
b: It is ẓihār.

f: 1013. What is Muḥammad's reasoning that "You are like my mother" without intention is ẓihār?
b: Since comparing her to a limb of her mother is ẓihār, comparing her to her entire mother is even more deserving of being ẓihār.

f: 1014. If a man intends only prohibition when saying "You are like my mother," what is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view?
b: It is īlāʾ, so that the lesser prohibition becomes established.

f: 1015. If a man intends only prohibition when saying "You are like my mother," what is Muḥammad's view?
b: It is ẓihār because the letter kāf of comparison is specifically connected to ẓihār.

f: 1016. If a man says: "You are forbidden to me like my mother," and intends ẓihār or divorce, what is the ruling?
b: It follows his intention.

f: 1017. Why can "You are forbidden to me like my mother" carry either ẓihār or divorce?
b: Because both meanings are possible: ẓihār due to the comparison, and divorce due to the prohibition.

f: 1018. If a man says: "You are forbidden to me like my mother" without intention, what is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view?
b: It is īlāʾ.

f: 1019. If a man says: "You are forbidden to me like my mother" without intention, what is Muḥammad's view?
b: It is ẓihār.

f: 1020. If a man says: "You are forbidden to me like the back of my mother," and intends divorce or īlāʾ, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view?
b: It is only ẓihār.

f: 1021. If a man says: "You are forbidden to me like the back of my mother," and intends divorce or īlāʾ, what is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: It follows his intention.

f: 1022. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad allow intention to determine the meaning of "You are forbidden to me like the back of my mother"?
b: Because the word "prohibition" can carry multiple meanings, including ẓihār, divorce, and īlāʾ.

f: 1023. According to Muḥammad, if a man intends divorce when saying "You are forbidden to me like the back of my mother," does it become ẓihār?
b: No, because his intention is divorce.

f: 1024. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, if a man intends divorce when saying "You are forbidden to me like the back of my mother," what happens?
b: Both meanings apply together.

f: 1025. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that "You are forbidden to me like the back of my mother" is only ẓihār?
b: Because it is explicit for ẓihār, cannot carry another meaning, and the prohibition is referred back to the explicit wording.

f: 1026. From whom does ẓihār occur?
b: Ẓihār only occurs from a wife.

f: 1027. If a man makes ẓihār from his slave woman, does ẓihār occur?
b: No, he is not considered to have made ẓihār.

f: 1028. What is the evidence that ẓihār only applies to wives and not slave women?
b: The statement of Allah: "From their wives..." (Qur'an 58:2).

f: 1029. Why does ẓihār not apply to a slave woman?
b: Because permissibility regarding a slave woman is secondary, so she does not have the same status as a wife.

f: 1030. Why else does ẓihār not apply to a slave woman?
b: Because ẓihār was transferred from divorce, and divorce does not apply to a slave woman.

f: 1031. If a man marries a woman without her permission, makes ẓihār from her, and then she approves the marriage, what is the ruling of the ẓihār?
b: The ẓihār is invalid.

f: 1032. Why is ẓihār invalid if a man makes it before his unauthorized marriage is approved?
b: Because at the time of his statement, his comparison was truthful and therefore it was not an evil statement.

f: 1033. Why can ẓihār not remain suspended until a marriage is approved?
b: Because ẓihār is not one of his rights that can remain suspended.

f: 1034. What is the difference between suspended ẓihār and freeing a slave purchased from a usurper?
b: The emancipation relates to ownership rights, whereas ẓihār does not relate to a right that can remain pending.

f: 1035. If a man says to his wives: "You are all to me like the back of my mother," what is the ruling?
b: He has made ẓihār from all of them.

f: 1036. Why does saying "You are all to me like the back of my mother" result in ẓihār for all wives?
b: Because he attached the ẓihār to all of them, similar to attaching divorce to all of them.

f: 1037. If a man makes ẓihār from multiple wives in one statement, how many expiations does he owe?
b: He owes one expiation for each wife.

f: 1038. Why does expiation multiply according to the number of wives in ẓihār?
b: Because the prohibition is established separately for each wife, and expiation removes the prohibition.

f: 1039. Why is ẓihār different from īlāʾ involving multiple wives regarding expiation?
b: Because īlāʾ expiation is for preserving the sanctity of the oath, and the mention of the oath is not repeated.

f: 1040. What is the expiation (kaffārah) for ẓihār?
b: The expiation for ẓihār is, in order: freeing a slave; if unable, fasting two consecutive months; and if unable, feeding sixty poor people.

f: 1041. What is the evidence for the order of the expiation of ẓihār?
b: The revealed text concerning ẓihār establishes the expiation in this order.

f: 1042. Must the expiation for ẓihār be completed before intercourse?
b: Yes. All forms of expiation must occur before intercourse.

f: 1043. Why must freeing a slave and fasting occur before intercourse in ẓihār?
b: Because this is explicitly stated in the revealed text.

f: 1044. Why must feeding sixty poor people occur before intercourse in ẓihār?
b: Because the purpose of expiation is to remove the prohibition, so it must precede intercourse in order for intercourse to become permissible.

f: 1045. What type of slave is sufficient for the expiation of ẓihār according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Any completely owned slave is sufficient, whether disbeliever or Muslim, male or female, young or old.

f: 1046. Why is a disbelieving slave valid for the expiation of ẓihār according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the text only requires freeing a slave, and that requirement has been fulfilled.

f: 1047. What is al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding freeing a disbelieving slave for ẓihār expiation?
b: He says it is not valid because expiation is a right of Allah and should not be directed toward an enemy of Allah, similar to zakāh.

f: 1048. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to al-Shāfiʿī's argument about a disbelieving slave?
b: The purpose of freeing is enabling obedience, and if the freed person later sins, that is due to his own choice.

f: 1049. Is a blind slave sufficient for the expiation of ẓihār?
b: No, a blind slave is not sufficient.

f: 1050. Why is a blind slave not sufficient for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because an entire category of benefit, namely sight, has been lost.

f: 1051. Is a slave missing both hands or both feet sufficient for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, such a slave is not sufficient.

f: 1052. Why is a slave missing both hands or both feet not sufficient for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the entire categories of grasping or walking benefit have been lost.

f: 1053. Is a one-eyed slave valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Yes, a one-eyed slave is valid.

f: 1054. Is a slave missing one hand valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Yes, a slave missing one hand is valid.

f: 1055. Is a slave missing one foot valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Yes, a slave missing one foot is valid.

f: 1056. Why are slaves missing one eye, one hand, or one foot valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the type of benefit remains, although it is weakened.

f: 1057. Why is a slave whose limbs are cut from the same side invalid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the type of walking benefit is lost, making walking impossible.

f: 1058. Is a deaf slave valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Yes, a deaf slave is valid according to istiḥsān.

f: 1059. Why would analogy suggest that a deaf slave is not valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because hearing is an entire category of benefit that has been lost.

f: 1060. Why is a deaf slave nevertheless valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the foundation of hearing remains; if someone shouts at him, he can hear.

f: 1061. Is a person born completely deaf and mute valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, such a person is not sufficient.

f: 1062. Why is a completely deaf and mute person not valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because he is completely unable to hear at all.

f: 1063. Is a slave whose two thumbs are cut off valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, such a slave is not valid.

f: 1064. Why are missing thumbs a preventing factor in ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the strength of grasping depends upon the thumbs, and losing them removes the entire category of grasping benefit.

f: 1065. Is a completely insane slave who has no understanding valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, such a slave is not valid.

f: 1066. Why is a completely insane person without understanding not valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because benefiting from the limbs only occurs through intellect, and therefore the benefits are absent.

f: 1067. Is a person who becomes insane but later recovers valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Yes, such a person is valid.

f: 1068. Why is a person who recovers from insanity valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the benefit was only impaired temporarily, not completely lost.

f: 1069. Is freeing a mudabbar slave valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, it is not valid.

f: 1070. Why is freeing a mudabbar slave invalid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because the slave has already acquired a right to freedom through another means, so his slavery is incomplete.

f: 1071. Is freeing an umm walad valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, it is not valid.

f: 1072. Why is freeing an umm walad invalid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because she already has a right to freedom through another means, making her slavery incomplete.

f: 1073. Is freeing a mukātab slave who has paid part of his agreed amount valid for ẓihār expiation?
b: No, it is not valid.

f: 1074. Why is freeing a partially paid mukātab slave invalid for ẓihār expiation?
b: Because freeing him involves compensation due to the remaining amount of the contract.

f: 1075. What is the narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding freeing a mukātab slave who has paid part of his contract?
b: It is narrated that it is valid.

f: 1076. Why does the narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ allow freeing a partially paid mukātab slave for expiation?
b: Because complete ownership of slavery still exists, and the mukātabah contract can be cancelled.

f: 1077. Why is a mukātab slave different from an umm walad and mudabbar slave regarding emancipation?
b: Because the status of an umm walad and mudabbar slave cannot be cancelled, while mukātabah can be cancelled.

f: 1078. Is freeing a mukātab slave who has paid nothing valid for ẓihār expiation according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes, it is valid.

f: 1079. What is al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding freeing a mukātab slave who has paid nothing for expiation?
b: He says it is not valid.

f: 1080. What is al-Shāfiʿī's reasoning that freeing a mukātab slave is invalid for expiation?
b: Because the mukātab has already acquired a right to freedom through the contract, resembling a mudabbar slave.

f: 1081. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that freeing a mukātab slave who has paid nothing is valid?
b: Slavery remains complete, as indicated by the statement that a mukātab remains a slave as long as he owes even one dirham.

f: 1082. Does the mukātabah contract contradict slavery?
b: No, it does not contradict slavery.

f: 1083. How is the mukātabah contract compared to a restriction on ownership?
b: It is like removing a restriction, similar to giving a slave permission to conduct business.

f: 1084. Why does the mukātabah contract remain binding despite not removing slavery?
b: Because it involves compensation and remains binding upon the slave's side.

f: 1085. If mukātabah were a barrier to emancipation, what would happen after freeing the mukātab?
b: It would be cancelled because it is something capable of cancellation.

f: 1086. After freeing a mukātab slave, do his earnings and children remain his?
b: Yes, his earnings and children remain his.

f: 1087. Why do the earnings and children of a freed mukātab remain his?
b: Either because emancipation occurred through the mukātabah contract, or because cancellation is only a necessary consequence and does not extend to offspring and earnings.

f: 1088. If a person buys his father or son intending the purchase as ẓihār expiation, is it valid?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ it is valid.

f: 1089. What is al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding buying one's father or son for expiation?
b: He says it is not valid.

f: 1090. Does the disagreement regarding buying one's father or son for expiation also apply to oath expiation?
b: Yes, the same disagreement applies regarding the expiation of an oath.

f: 1091. If someone frees half of a jointly-owned slave while wealthy and compensates the partner for the remaining half, is it valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, it is not valid as expiation.

f: 1092. If someone frees half of a jointly-owned slave while wealthy and compensates the partner for the remaining half, is it valid according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: Yes, it is valid according to them.

f: 1093. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad consider freeing half of a jointly-owned slave valid for expiation?
b: Because the person acquires his partner's share through compensation, becomes the owner of the entire slave, and then frees the entire slave.

f: 1094. Why is freeing half of a jointly-owned slave different when the person freeing is poor according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: Because he becomes obligated to pay for the partner's share, making the emancipation one performed through compensation.

f: 1095. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that freeing half of a jointly-owned slave while wealthy is invalid for expiation?
b: Because the partner's share first decreases while remaining in the partner's ownership, then transfers through compensation, and this prevents it from being valid as expiation.

f: 1096. If a person frees half of his slave for ẓihār expiation and later frees the remaining half for the same expiation, is it valid?
b: Yes, it is valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 1097. Why is freeing half of a slave and then the remaining half for the same expiation valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because he freed the slave through two separate statements, and the deficiency occurred while the ownership was entirely his.

f: 1098. What analogy does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to support the validity of freeing half of a slave and then the other half?
b: It is like a person who prepares a sheep for sacrifice and the knife accidentally cuts its eye; an accidental deficiency does not prevent validity.

f: 1099. Why is freeing half of a slave different from the earlier case of a jointly-owned slave according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because in the earlier case the deficiency occurred regarding the ownership of a partner, whereas here the deficiency occurred while all ownership belonged to him.

f: 1100. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding freeing half of a slave and then the remaining half?
b: They say it is not considered two emancipations because emancipation is not divisible.

f: 1101. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad consider freeing half equivalent to freeing the whole?
b: Because emancipation is indivisible, so freeing half is treated as freeing the entire slave.

f: 1102. If a person frees half of his slave for ẓihār expiation, has intercourse with the woman from whom he made ẓihār, and then frees the remaining half, is it valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, it is not valid.

f: 1103. Why is freeing the remaining half after intercourse invalid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because emancipation is divisible according to him, and the condition is that emancipation must occur before intercourse.

f: 1104. Why does the second half of emancipation not complete the expiation according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the emancipation of that half occurred after intercourse, violating the condition established by the text.

f: 1105. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding freeing half before intercourse and half after intercourse?
b: They consider it valid because freeing half is equivalent to freeing the whole.

f: 1106. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad consider the expiation completed before intercourse?
b: Because, according to them, emancipation is indivisible, so the complete emancipation occurred when the first half was freed.

f: 1107. If a person who made ẓihār cannot find a slave to free, what is his next form of expiation?
b: He must fast two consecutive months.

f: 1108. Which days cannot be included within the two consecutive months of ẓihār expiation fasting?
b: Ramaḍān, the day of Fiṭr, the day of Naḥr (ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā), and the days of tashrīq.

f: 1109. Why must the fasting for ẓihār expiation be consecutive?
b: Because continuity is explicitly required by the revealed text.

f: 1110. Why does fasting during Ramaḍān not count as ẓihār expiation?
b: Because it would invalidate the specific obligation Allah placed upon the person.

f: 1111. Why do the prohibited festival days not count toward ẓihār expiation fasting?
b: Because fasting on those days cannot replace a complete obligatory fast.

f: 1112. If a person making ẓihār has intercourse during the two months of expiation fasting, must he restart according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: Yes, he must restart the fast.

f: 1113. Does it matter whether intercourse during the ẓihār expiation fast occurs intentionally at night or forgetfully during the day according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: No, in both cases he must restart the fast.

f: 1114. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view if intercourse occurs during the two months of ẓihār expiation fasting?
b: He does not have to restart because the continuity of the fast has not been broken.

f: 1115. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning that intercourse does not require restarting the ẓihār expiation fast?
b: Because the fast itself is not invalidated, and the required condition is only continuity.

f: 1116. What is the reasoning of Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad that intercourse requires restarting the ẓihār expiation fast?
b: Because the fast must occur before intercourse and remain free from intercourse, as indicated by the text.

f: 1117. If a person breaks the ẓihār expiation fast during the two months, must he restart?
b: Yes, whether he breaks it with an excuse or without an excuse.

f: 1118. Why must the ẓihār expiation fast be restarted after breaking it?
b: Because continuity has been lost while he normally has the ability to maintain it.

f: 1119. If a slave makes ẓihār, which type of expiation is valid for him?
b: Only fasting is valid as his expiation.

f: 1120. Why can a slave only perform fasting as ẓihār expiation?
b: Because he does not own wealth and therefore cannot perform financial forms of expiation.

f: 1121. If a slave makes ẓihār, can his master perform the financial kaffārah on his behalf by freeing a slave or feeding poor people?
b: No. It does not suffice because the slave is not legally capable of ownership, and he does not become an owner merely through someone giving him ownership.

f: 1122. What does the person who made ẓihār do if he is unable to fast?
b: He feeds sixty poor people, based on Allah's statement: "Whoever is unable, then feeding sixty poor people." (Qur'an 58:4)

f: 1123. How much food is given to each poor person in ẓihār kaffārah?
b: Each poor person receives half a ṣāʿ of wheat, or one ṣāʿ of dates/barley, or the value of that according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 1124. Why is ẓihār kaffārah measured according to ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Because the purpose is fulfilling the daily need of each poor person.

f: 1125. Is giving the monetary value of the food valid for ẓihār kaffārah?
b: Yes, according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 1126. If someone gives one mann of wheat, or two manns of dates/barley, is the kaffārah valid?
b: Yes, because the objective of feeding the poor has been achieved. The exact type of food is not required.

f: 1127. Can someone appoint another person to distribute his ẓihār kaffārah on his behalf?
b: Yes, it is sufficient.

f: 1128. How is appointing someone else to give ẓihār kaffārah understood?
b: It is like borrowing: the poor person first receives ownership as a recipient, then ownership is transferred through the representative.

f: 1129. Is it valid to gather sixty poor people and feed them lunch and dinner instead of transferring ownership of food?
b: Yes, according to the Ḥanafīs, whether the amount eaten is little or much.

f: 1130. What is al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding feeding sixty poor people for ẓihār kaffārah?
b: He says it is not valid except through transferring ownership, comparing it to zakāh and ṣadaqat al-fiṭr.

f: 1131. What is the Ḥanafī response to al-Shāfiʿī regarding feeding rather than transferring ownership?
b: The Qur’an requires "feeding," and the literal meaning of feeding is enabling someone to eat. This occurs both through allowing someone to eat and through transferring ownership.

f: 1132. Why do zakāh and ṣadaqat al-fiṭr require ownership transfer according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because zakāh requires "giving" and ṣadaqat al-fiṭr requires "delivering," both of which imply ownership transfer.

f: 1133. Does feeding a weaned child count among the sixty poor people for ẓihār kaffārah?
b: No. It does not suffice because the child cannot fully consume the food in the required manner.

f: 1134. Why does barley bread require accompaniment while wheat bread does not?
b: Because barley bread normally requires additional food so that a person can become satisfied, whereas wheat bread can suffice by itself.

f: 1135. If someone feeds one poor person for sixty days, is it sufficient for ẓihār kaffārah?
b: Yes, because the objective is relieving the poor person's need, and the need renews each day.

f: 1136. If someone gives food to one poor person on only one day, how much does it count for?
b: It only counts for that one day, because each day's need is considered separate.

f: 1137. Is there disagreement regarding feeding one poor person repeatedly through permission to eat?
b: No. It is sufficient because the person's need renews each day.

f: 1138. Is there disagreement regarding giving ownership to the same poor person multiple times in one day?
b: Yes. It has been said that it is not sufficient, and it has also been said that it is sufficient because the need for ownership renews during the same day.

f: 1139. Why is giving the entire kaffārah amount in one payment different from repeated giving during one day?
b: Because the text requires distribution among the poor, so giving everything at once does not fulfil the requirement.

f: 1140. If the person who made ẓihār has intercourse during the feeding stage of kaffārah, must he restart?
b: No. He does not restart because Allah did not stipulate that feeding must occur before intercourse.

f: 1141. Why is intercourse prohibited before completing feeding kaffārah even though it does not invalidate the feeding?
b: Because he may later become capable of freeing a slave or fasting, which would then become the required kaffārah. The prohibition is due to an external reason, not because the feeding itself is invalid.

f: 1142. If someone feeds sixty poor people for two ẓihār kaffārahs, giving each person one ṣāʿ of wheat, does it count for both according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. It only counts for one kaffārah.

f: 1143. What is Muḥammad's view regarding feeding sixty poor people for two ẓihār kaffārahs?
b: He says it counts for both kaffārahs because the amount given fulfils both obligations and the recipients are suitable for both.

f: 1144. What is Muḥammad's reasoning for counting one payment for two kaffārahs?
b: The amount given fulfils both obligations, and the recipients are eligible for both, similar to when causes differ or when payments are separated.

f: 1145. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say it only counts for one kaffārah?
b: Because intention within the same category is not meaningful. Since half a ṣāʿ is the minimum amount for one person, the extra amount becomes surplus and only applies to one kaffārah.

f: 1146. Why does separating the payments make a difference according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because with a second separate payment, the recipient is treated like another poor person receiving a new obligation.

f: 1147. If a person has two obligations of ẓihār kaffārah and frees two slaves without specifying which slave is for which obligation, is it valid?
b: Yes, it is valid for both obligations because the type of kaffārah is the same, so a specific intention is unnecessary.

f: 1148. If a person has two obligations of ẓihār kaffārah and fasts four months, does it suffice for both?
b: Yes, it suffices because the type of obligation is the same and a specific assignment is unnecessary.

f: 1149. If a person has two obligations of ẓihār kaffārah and feeds one hundred and twenty poor people, does it suffice for both?
b: Yes, it suffices because the two obligations are of the same category.

f: 1150. If a person frees one slave for two ẓihār kaffārahs, can it fulfil both simultaneously?
