f: 1517. Why would analogy (qiyās) suggest that the woman in the case of a man acknowledging a son should not inherit?
b: Analogy suggests she should not inherit because lineage can be established through means other than a valid marriage, such as an invalid marriage, intercourse due to a mistaken assumption (waṭʾ bi-shubha), or ownership of a slave woman. Therefore, his acknowledgment of the child does not necessarily prove that a marriage existed.

f: 1518. What is the basis of istiḥsān in the case where a man acknowledges a son and the mother claims to be his wife?
b: The basis is that the woman is known to be free and known to be the mother of the child. In customary practice and according to the legal situation, a valid marriage is the only apparent explanation for this relationship, so she is treated as his wife.

f: 1519. If it is unknown whether the mother of the acknowledged child was free, and the heirs claim that she was his slave woman, does she inherit?
b: No, she does not inherit because the presumption of freedom from living in Muslim lands removes the assumption of slavery, but it does not establish the right of inheritance.

f: 1520. Who has the greatest right to custody of a child when separation occurs between the parents according to the Hanafi scholars?
b: The mother has the greatest right to custody of the child after separation because she is generally more compassionate and more capable of caring for the child. Giving the child to her is considered more beneficial for the child.

f: 1521. What evidence is used to establish that the mother has priority in custody of her child after separation?
b: The evidence is the report of a woman who said to the Prophet ﷺ: “My womb was a vessel for him, my lap was a shelter for him, and my breast was his source of nourishment. His father wants to take him away from me.” The Prophet ﷺ replied: “You have more right to him as long as you do not marry.”

f: 1522. Why is the mother given priority over the father regarding custody of a young child?
b: The mother is given priority because she has greater compassion, affection, and ability to provide the daily care that a young child requires.

f: 1523. What did Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ say to ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ regarding custody of a child?
b: Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ said: “Her saliva is better for him than your honey,” meaning that the mother's care, affection, and nurturing are more beneficial for the child than the care of another person.

f: 1524. Who is responsible for the maintenance of the child after separation?
b: The father is responsible for the child's maintenance, even though the mother may have the right of custody.

f: 1525. Is the mother forced to accept custody of her child?
b: No, the mother is not forced to take custody because she may become unable to fulfil the responsibilities and requirements of custody.

f: 1526. If the child has no mother, who has priority in custody: the maternal grandmother or the paternal grandmother?
b: The maternal grandmother has priority over the paternal grandmother, even if she is more distant in lineage, because custody follows the maternal line and because of her greater connection and compassion.

f: 1527. Why does the maternal grandmother have priority over the paternal grandmother in custody?
b: She has priority because custody is inherited through the maternal line, and the maternal grandmother is generally closer in care and affection to the child.

f: 1528. If there is no maternal grandmother, who has priority in custody: the paternal grandmother or the sisters?
b: The paternal grandmother has priority over the sisters because she is from the category of mothers and because she has greater compassion toward children.

f: 1529. If there is no grandmother, who has priority in custody: sisters or aunts?
b: The sisters have priority over paternal and maternal aunts because they are the daughters of the parents and are closer relatives, similar to their precedence in inheritance.

f: 1530. According to one narration, which relative may have priority over others among the sisters and aunts?
b: According to one narration, the maternal aunt has priority over the paternal sister based on the statement of the Prophet ﷺ: “The maternal aunt is like a mother.”

f: 1531. How are the sisters ranked in priority for custody?
b: The full sister (same father and mother) comes first because she has greater compassion, followed by the maternal sister, then the paternal sister.

f: 1532. Why does the full sister have priority over the maternal and paternal sisters in custody?
b: The full sister has priority because she is related through both parents, giving her a stronger relationship and greater compassion toward the child.

f: 1533. How are maternal aunts ranked in priority for custody?
b: Maternal aunts are arranged similarly to sisters: preference is first given to those with a stronger relationship, especially those connected through both sides, followed by those related through the mother.

f: 1534. How are paternal aunts ranked in priority for custody?
b: Paternal aunts are arranged according to the same principle used for sisters and maternal aunts, giving priority based on the strength of the relationship.

f: 1535. What happens to a woman's right of custody if she marries another man?
b: A woman loses her right of custody if she marries another man because her new husband is a stranger to the child and may not provide the same care, affection, and attention that the child needs.

f: 1536. Why does marriage to another man cause a woman to lose custody rights?
b: The reason is that the new husband may view the child unfavorably and may not care for him properly, so giving custody to the mother in that situation may no longer serve the child's benefit.

f: 1537. Does a grandmother lose her right to custody if she marries, even if her husband is the child's grandfather?
b: No. The grandmother does not lose custody if her husband is the child's grandfather because he takes the position of the child's father and will care for the child.

f: 1538. Why does a woman not lose custody if her new husband is a close unmarriageable relative (maḥram) of the child?
b: She does not lose custody because affection and care remain due to the close family relationship between the husband and the child.

f: 1539. If a woman loses custody because of marriage, can she regain custody after the marriage ends?
b: Yes. She regains her right to custody once the marriage ends because the preventing factor has disappeared.

f: 1540. If a boy has no female relatives who can take custody and male relatives dispute custody, who has priority?
b: The male relative with the closest agnatic relationship (ʿaṣabah) has priority because guardianship belongs to the closest relative according to the known order of agnatic relatives.

f: 1541. Why is a young girl not given custody to a non-maḥram agnatic relative such as a paternal cousin or freedman's patron (mawlā al-ʿitāqah)?
b: She is not given to such relatives because they are not unmarriageable relatives, and giving custody to them may lead to temptation or harm.

f: 1542. Until what age do the mother and grandmother have greater right to custody of a boy?
b: The mother and grandmother have greater right to custody of a boy until he becomes independent in basic personal matters: eating alone, drinking alone, dressing himself alone, and cleaning himself after using the toilet.

f: 1543. What does it mean when the scholars say a boy remains with his mother or grandmother until he becomes independent?
b: It means until he can manage his basic personal needs by himself, including eating, drinking, dressing, and cleaning himself after using the toilet.

f: 1544. Why does custody of a boy transfer from the mother to the father after he becomes independent?
b: After independence, the boy needs education, discipline, and training in masculine manners and character, and the father is considered more capable of providing this.

f: 1545. At what age did al-Khaṣṣāf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ estimate that a boy usually becomes independent for custody purposes?
b: Al-Khaṣṣāf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ estimated independence at seven years old based on what is commonly observed among children.

f: 1546. Until what age do the mother and grandmother have greater right to custody of a girl?
b: The mother and grandmother have greater right to custody of a girl until she menstruates.

f: 1547. Why does custody of a girl transfer after menstruation?
b: After menstruation, the girl requires protection and safeguarding, and the father is considered stronger and more suitable for protecting her. She also needs instruction in women's matters before that stage, which women are more capable of providing.

f: 1548. What is another narration from Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding when a girl is transferred to her father?
b: Another narration from Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ states that the girl is given to her father when she reaches the age of sexual maturity because the need for protection becomes established at that point.

f: 1549. Until what age do women other than the mother and grandmother have greater right to custody of a girl?
b: Women other than the mother and grandmother have greater right to custody until the girl reaches an age where she becomes desired for marriage.

f: 1550. What wording is found in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr regarding custody of a girl by women other than her mother and grandmother?
b: Al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr states that they have custody until she becomes independent.

f: 1551. Why do women other than the mother and grandmother lose custody of a girl when she becomes independent?
b: They lose custody because they are unable to properly use and train her for service. The purpose of custody is therefore not achieved through them, unlike the mother and grandmother who have the legal ability and closer relationship to train her.

f: 1552. Are a freed female slave and a freed umm walad treated like free women regarding custody of children?
b: Yes. A female slave who has been freed and an umm walad who has been freed are treated like free women regarding custody because they have become free women, or because their right to custody has already been established.

f: 1553. Does a female slave have the right to custody of her child before being freed?
b: No. Before being freed, she does not have the right to custody because her obligation to serve her master prevents her from properly caring for the child.

f: 1554. Why does a freed female slave gain the same custody rights as a free woman?
b: She gains the same rights because freedom removes the obstacle that prevented her from caring for the child, and custody is based on her ability to provide care.

f: 1555. Does a non-Muslim woman living under Muslim rule have the right to custody of her Muslim child?
b: Yes. A non-Muslim woman under Muslim rule has greater right to custody of her Muslim child as long as there is no fear that she will influence his religion or cause him to become accustomed to disbelief.

f: 1556. Why is a non-Muslim mother allowed custody of her Muslim child under certain conditions?
b: Because consideration is first given to the child's immediate benefit, and custody remains with her unless there is a real fear of religious harm.

f: 1557. Can a Muslim child choose between his parents regarding custody?
b: No. According to the Hanafi position, neither the boy nor the girl has a choice in deciding custody.

f: 1558. What is the position of al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding a child's choice in custody?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that the child does have a choice, based on the report that the Prophet ﷺ gave a child the option between his parents.

f: 1559. Why do the Hanafi scholars reject giving a child the choice regarding custody?
b: They argue that a child's intellect is incomplete, so he will usually choose whoever gives him comfort, ease, and permission to play rather than what is genuinely beneficial for him. Therefore, his choice cannot reliably determine his welfare.

f: 1560. What evidence do the Hanafi scholars use that children were not given a choice regarding custody?
b: They rely on reports that the Companions رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ did not give children the choice between parents in custody matters.

f: 1561. How do the Hanafi scholars respond to the hadith where the Prophet ﷺ gave a child a choice?
b: They respond that the Prophet ﷺ supplicated: “O Allah, guide him,” and Allah granted the child the ability to choose what was most beneficial due to the Prophet’s ﷺ supplication. Alternatively, they interpret the hadith as referring to a child who had reached adulthood.

f: 1562. Does a divorced woman have the right to leave the city with her child?
b: No. If a divorced woman wishes to leave the city with her child, she does not have the right to do so because this would harm the father by preventing him from seeing and caring for his child.

f: 1563. When does a divorced woman have the right to leave the city with her child?
b: She has the right if she leaves with him to her homeland and the husband had married her there, because by marrying her there he is considered to have accepted remaining in that place.

f: 1564. What evidence is used for the ruling that settling in a place creates attachment to it?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever settles in a town becomes one of its people.” This indicates that residence in a place creates a legal connection to it.

f: 1565. Does a woman have the right to move with her child to a city that is not her homeland if the marriage took place there?
b: According to the narration in Kitāb al-Ṭalāq, she does not have this right. However, it is mentioned in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr that she does have this right.

f: 1566. What is the reasoning of those who say she may move to a city where the marriage took place?
b: Their reasoning is that when a contract occurs in a place, its legal consequences apply there, just as a sale contract requires delivery at the place of sale. The right to retain custody of children is among those consequences.

f: 1567. What is the reasoning of those who say she may not move to a city where the marriage took place?
b: Their reasoning is that marrying in a foreign place does not create a customary commitment to remain there. This is the more correct position.

f: 1568. What are the two conditions required for a divorced woman to move with her child?
b: 1. The destination must be her homeland. 2. The marriage must have existed there.

f: 1569. Does this ruling apply when the two cities are close to each other?
b: No. If the cities are close enough that the father can visit his child and spend the night in his own home, then there is no harm in her moving.

f: 1570. Does the same custody ruling apply to villages?
b: Yes. The same principles apply to villages as they do to cities.

f: 1571. Can a divorced woman move from a village to a city with her child?
b: Yes. There is no harm in this because it benefits the child by allowing him to develop the manners and qualities of city people, while it does not harm the father.

f: 1572. Can a divorced woman move from a city to a village with her child?
b: No. This is different because it harms the child by causing him to adopt the manners and characteristics of rural people. Therefore, she does not have the right to do this.

f: 1573. Is maintenance (nafaqah) obligatory upon the husband for his wife?
b: Yes. Maintenance is obligatory upon the husband for his wife if she makes herself available to him by coming to his residence. He must provide her maintenance, clothing, and housing.

f: 1574. Does the obligation of maintenance apply only to Muslim wives?
b: No. Maintenance is obligatory for both Muslim and non-Muslim wives because the evidences do not differentiate between them.

f: 1575. What is the evidence that maintenance is obligatory upon the husband?
b: The evidence includes Allah’s statements: “Let the wealthy person spend according to his wealth” (Qur’an 65:7), and “Upon the father is their provision and clothing according to what is acceptable” (Qur’an 2:233). Also, the Prophet ﷺ said in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon that women have the right to food and clothing in a proper manner.

f: 1576. Why is maintenance obligatory upon the husband from a legal perspective?
b: Maintenance is considered compensation for being confined for the husband’s benefit. Whoever is confined for another person’s intended benefit has their maintenance upon that person, similar to a judge or workers collecting charity.

f: 1577. What is the relied-upon position regarding how the amount of maintenance is determined?
b: The condition of both husband and wife is considered. This is the choice of al-Khaṣṣāf and the relied-upon fatwā.

f: 1578. How is maintenance determined when both husband and wife are wealthy?
b: Wealthy-level maintenance is obligatory.

f: 1579. How is maintenance determined when both husband and wife are poor?
b: Poor-level maintenance is obligatory.

f: 1580. How is maintenance determined when the wife is poor and the husband is wealthy?
b: Her maintenance is below that of wealthy women but above that of poor women.

f: 1581. What was the view of al-Karkhī regarding maintenance?
b: Al-Karkhī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that only the husband’s condition is considered. This is also the view of al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 1582. What evidence does al-Shāfiʿī use for considering only the husband’s condition?
b: He uses Allah’s statement: “Let the wealthy person spend according to his wealth” (Qur’an 65:7), arguing that spending is based on the husband’s ability.

f: 1583. What is the evidence for considering both the husband’s and wife’s conditions?
b: The evidence is the statement of the Prophet ﷺ to Hind, the wife of Abū Sufyān: “Take from your husband’s wealth what is sufficient for you and your child according to what is acceptable.” This shows that the wife’s condition is also considered.

f: 1584. Why is considering the wife’s condition more correct according to this view?
b: Because maintenance is obligatory according to sufficiency. A poor woman does not require the same amount as a wealthy woman, so there is no reason to require extra payment beyond what fulfills her needs.

f: 1585. How is the verse “Let the wealthy person spend according to his wealth” understood according to this view?
b: The husband is commanded to spend according to his ability, and whatever remains unpaid becomes a debt upon him. The verse does not mean that only his condition determines the exact amount.

f: 1586. What does “according to what is acceptable” (bil-maʿrūf) mean regarding maintenance?
b: It means the moderate amount that fulfills the need, and this is what is obligatory.

f: 1587. Is there a fixed legal amount for maintenance?
b: No. There is no fixed amount because maintenance is based on sufficiency, and sufficiency differs according to circumstances.

f: 1588. What fixed amounts did al-Shāfiʿī propose for maintenance?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī held that the wealthy person must give two mudd, the poor person one mudd, and the middle class one and a half mudd.

f: 1589. Why do the Hanafis reject fixed amounts of maintenance?
b: Because maintenance is intended to fulfil a need, and something whose purpose is sufficiency cannot be fixed in itself since needs differ between people.

f: 1590. Does a wife receive maintenance if she refuses to make herself available until she receives her dowry?
b: Yes. She is still entitled to maintenance because she is refusing with a legitimate reason. The loss of marital availability is attributed to the husband, so legally it is treated as though it has not been lost.

f: 1591. Why does a wife who refuses intimacy until receiving her dowry still receive maintenance?
b: Because her refusal is considered justified. Since the husband caused the situation by not giving the dowry, the lack of availability is considered to be from his side.

f: 1592. Does a disobedient wife (nāshiz) receive maintenance?
b: No. A disobedient wife does not receive maintenance until she returns to her husband's home because the loss of marital availability came from her side.

f: 1593. Why does a disobedient wife lose her maintenance?
b: Because she has removed herself from the marital relationship without a valid reason. When she returns, availability returns, and the husband regains the ability to benefit from her.

f: 1594. Does a young girl who cannot yet be enjoyed receive maintenance?
b: No. She does not receive maintenance because the inability to benefit from her comes from something within herself, and the legally recognized confinement of marriage does not exist in this case.

f: 1595. Why is a young girl who cannot be enjoyed different from a sick woman regarding maintenance?
b: A sick woman will be discussed separately because her inability is temporary and not due to the absence of the marital purpose itself.

f: 1596. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding maintenance for a young girl who cannot be enjoyed?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says she receives maintenance because he considers maintenance to be compensation for ownership, similar to a slave woman owned by possession.

f: 1597. How do the Hanafis respond to al-Shāfiʿī’s reasoning regarding a young girl?
b: They respond that the dowry is already compensation for ownership, and two compensations cannot apply to the same compensated thing. Therefore, she receives dowry but not maintenance.

f: 1598. Does a wife receive maintenance if the husband is young and unable to have intercourse while she is mature?
b: Yes. She receives maintenance from his wealth because she has made herself available, and the inability comes from his side.

f: 1599. What case is the young husband unable to have intercourse compared to?
b: It is compared to the case of a husband who is castrated or impotent, because the inability is from the husband's side.

f: 1600. Does a wife receive maintenance if she is imprisoned due to a debt?
b: No. She does not receive maintenance because the loss of availability resulted from her delaying payment of the debt.

f: 1601. If a woman is imprisoned for a reason beyond her control, does she lose maintenance?
b: No. If the imprisonment is not caused by her, such as when she is unable to pay the debt, it is not considered to be from her side.

f: 1602. Does a woman lose maintenance if she is forcibly abducted?
b: No. If a man forcibly abducts her, she does not lose her maintenance because the loss of availability was not caused by her.

f: 1603. What was narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding an abducted woman’s maintenance?
b: It is narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ that she does receive maintenance.

f: 1604. What is the relied-upon fatwā regarding an abducted woman’s maintenance?
b: The fatwā follows the first opinion: she does not receive maintenance because the loss of availability was not from the husband and therefore cannot be legally assumed to remain.

f: 1605. Does a wife receive maintenance if she performs pilgrimage with a maḥram?
b: According to the first view, she does not receive maintenance because the loss of marital availability came from her choice.

f: 1606. What is Abū Yūsuf’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view regarding a wife who leaves for pilgrimage with a maḥram?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says she receives maintenance because performing an obligatory duty is considered an excuse.

f: 1607. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what type of maintenance does a woman receive while travelling for pilgrimage?
b: She receives only the maintenance of residence, not travel expenses, because she chose the travel herself.

f: 1608. If the husband travels with his wife, does she receive maintenance?
b: Yes. Maintenance is obligatory by agreement because her marital availability remains since the husband is accompanying her.

f: 1609. If the husband travels with his wife, what expenses is he required to provide?
b: He must provide residence maintenance, but transportation expenses are not obligatory because the travel was chosen by her and not part of the required maintenance.

f: 1610. Does a wife receive maintenance if she becomes ill while in her husband's home?
b: Yes. She still receives maintenance even if her illness prevents intercourse.

f: 1611. What would analogy (qiyās) suggest regarding a wife who becomes ill and cannot have intercourse?
b: Qiyās would suggest that she does not receive maintenance because the marital availability for enjoyment has been lost due to illness.

f: 1612. Why does istiḥsān establish maintenance for an ill wife?
b: Because her marital availability still exists. The husband can still find comfort with her, touch her, and benefit from her presence in maintaining the household. The illness only prevents one aspect of benefit, similar to menstruation.

f: 1613. How is illness compared to menstruation regarding maintenance?
b: Both prevent intercourse temporarily but do not remove the overall marital relationship or availability, so maintenance remains obligatory.

f: 1614. What is narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding a wife who becomes ill?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that if she made herself available to her husband and then became ill, maintenance becomes obligatory because her submission had already occurred.

f: 1615. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what if the wife became ill before making herself available?
b: If she became ill first and then offered herself, maintenance is not obligatory because her submission is not considered valid in that situation.

f: 1616. How did the scholars view Abū Yūsuf’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position regarding illness?
b: They considered it a good position, and the wording of the book indicates this view.

f: 1617. Is the husband required to provide maintenance for his wife's servant?
b: Yes, if the husband is wealthy, he must provide maintenance for her servant.

f: 1618. Why is the husband required to provide maintenance for the wife's servant?
b: Because her sufficiency is obligatory upon him, and having a servant is part of her sufficiency when she requires one.

f: 1619. Is maintenance required for more than one servant?
b: No. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, maintenance is not imposed for more than one servant.

f: 1620. What is Abū Yūsuf’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view regarding the number of servants whose maintenance is required?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says maintenance for two servants is imposed because she needs one for household matters and another for outside matters.

f: 1621. What is the Hanafi response to the view that two servants are required?
b: They argue that one servant can perform both internal and external tasks, so there is no necessity for two servants.

f: 1622. Why is one servant considered sufficient according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: Because if the husband himself were to fulfil her needs, that would suffice; similarly, one servant can take his place.

f: 1623. To what extent is a wealthy husband required to provide servant maintenance?
b: He is required to provide servant maintenance only to the extent of basic sufficiency, similar to the minimum maintenance required from a poor husband for his wife.

f: 1624. Does a poor husband have to provide maintenance for his wife's servant?
b: According to the narration of al-Ḥasan from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, which is the correct view, a poor husband is not required to provide servant maintenance.

f: 1625. Why is servant maintenance not obligatory upon a poor husband?
b: Because the obligation upon a poor man is only the minimum level of sufficiency, and the wife can fulfil her needs by serving herself.

f: 1626. What is the position of Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding servant maintenance for a poor husband?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held a different view, but the correct position according to the text is that it is not obligatory for a poor husband.

f: 1627. What happens if a husband becomes unable to provide his wife's maintenance?
b: According to the Hanafis, they are not separated. Rather, the wife is instructed to borrow against him.

f: 1628. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding a husband who cannot provide maintenance?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that they should be separated because the husband is unable to maintain the marriage properly. The judge takes his place in separating them, similar to the case of castration or impotence.

f: 1629. Why does al-Shāfiʿī argue for separation when the husband cannot provide maintenance?
b: Because maintenance is a necessary part of marriage, and inability to provide it causes harm to the wife. He argues that the need for maintenance is even stronger than the need for intercourse.

f: 1630. What is the Hanafi response to al-Shāfiʿī’s position on separation due to lack of maintenance?
b: They argue that separation would cancel the husband's right, whereas delaying her maintenance only delays her right. The harm of cancelling his right is greater.

f: 1631. Why do the Hanafis consider the husband's right greater in this case?
b: Because maintenance becomes a debt through the judge's ruling and can be collected later, while separation permanently removes the marital relationship.

f: 1632. Why is inability to provide wealth different from inability to have intercourse?
b: Because wealth is a secondary matter in marriage, while reproduction and marital relations are among the primary purposes of marriage.

f: 1633. What is the benefit of ordering the wife to borrow after the judge imposes maintenance?
b: It allows her to make the creditor's claim against the husband because the maintenance has been established through the judge's ruling.

f: 1634. What happens if the wife borrows money without the judge ordering maintenance?
b: The debt is against her personally, not against the husband.

f: 1635. If the judge previously ruled that the wife receives hardship-level maintenance, and the husband later becomes wealthy, what happens?
b: He must increase her maintenance to the level of wealthy people because maintenance changes according to wealth and poverty.

f: 1636. Why does the wife receive increased maintenance when the husband's financial condition improves?
b: Because the earlier ruling was only an estimation based on his previous condition, not a permanently fixed amount. When his circumstances change, she can demand the completion of her entitlement.

f: 1637. Does a wife receive unpaid maintenance from previous periods if the husband failed to provide it?
b: Generally, no. She does not receive maintenance for past periods unless the judge had imposed maintenance upon him or she had made a settlement with him regarding the amount.

f: 1638. Why does a wife not receive past maintenance according to the Hanafi view?
b: Because maintenance is considered a gift (ṣilah), not compensation. Therefore, the obligation does not become firmly established until there is a judicial ruling.

f: 1639. When does maintenance become an established obligation according to the Hanafis?
b: It becomes established through a judicial ruling, because the ruling creates the obligation.

f: 1640. Why does a judicial ruling require a confirming factor before establishing ownership?
b: Because ownership is not established merely by the ruling; it requires receipt (qabḍ) as the confirming factor.

f: 1641. Why is a settlement between husband and wife treated like a judicial ruling regarding past maintenance?
b: Because a person's authority over himself is stronger than the authority of a judge. Therefore, his agreement establishes the obligation.

f: 1642. Why is past maintenance different from dowry?
b: Because dowry is compensation, while maintenance is considered a gift. Compensation becomes established differently from a voluntary provision.

f: 1643. What happens to unpaid maintenance if the husband dies after the judge ruled that he must provide it?
b: The maintenance falls away, even if several months had passed after the ruling.

f: 1644. Does the same ruling apply if the wife dies after maintenance was imposed?
b: Yes. If the wife dies, the unpaid maintenance also falls away.

f: 1645. Why does unpaid maintenance fall away after the death of either spouse?
b: Because maintenance is considered a gift (ṣilah), and gifts are cancelled by death, just as a gift becomes invalid if the giver dies before delivery.

f: 1646. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding maintenance after death?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that maintenance becomes a debt before the ruling, so it does not fall away through death because he considers it compensation like other debts.

f: 1647. How do the Hanafis respond to al-Shāfiʿī’s argument regarding maintenance as a debt?
b: They respond that maintenance is not compensation but rather a gift, and therefore it does not become a binding debt before the ruling.

f: 1648. If a husband gives his wife one year's maintenance in advance and then dies, does she return any of it?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, she does not return anything.

f: 1649. What is Muḥammad’s view regarding advance maintenance if the husband dies?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that she keeps the maintenance for the period that has already passed, but whatever remains belongs to the husband’s estate.

f: 1650. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding advance maintenance after the husband’s death?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ agrees with Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ that the remaining amount should be returned.

f: 1651. Does the same disagreement apply to clothing given in advance?
b: Yes. The same disagreement applies regarding clothing.

f: 1652. What is the reasoning of those who say remaining advance maintenance must be returned?
b: They argue that it was given as compensation for the wife's future marital availability. When the marriage ends through death, the compensation should end proportionally, similar to the salary of a judge or the allowance of soldiers.

f: 1653. What is the Hanafi evidence that advance maintenance is not returned?
b: They argue that maintenance is a gift, and possession has already occurred. Gifts are not returned after death, just as a gift is not reclaimed.

f: 1654. What happens if the advance maintenance is destroyed without negligence?
b: Nothing is recovered from it by agreement because possession occurred and it is treated like a gift.

f: 1655. What is narrated from Muḥammad regarding small amounts of advance maintenance?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ narrated that if she received the maintenance of one month or less, nothing is taken back because it is a small amount and is treated as current maintenance.

f: 1656. What happens if a slave marries a free woman with his master's permission?
b: Her maintenance becomes a debt upon him, and he may be sold because of this debt.

f: 1657. Why does the wife's maintenance become a debt upon a slave husband?
b: Because the cause requiring maintenance exists, and its obligation becomes attached to the slave himself, similar to a business debt owed by a merchant-slave.

f: 1658. Why can the slave be sold because of his wife's maintenance debt?
b: Because the obligation is connected to his person (raqabah), and the debt must be fulfilled.

f: 1659. Does the master have an option regarding the sale of the slave for maintenance debt?
b: Yes. The master may ransom him and prevent his sale because the wife's right is maintenance, not ownership of the slave's person.

f: 1660. What happens to the maintenance debt if the slave husband dies?
b: The maintenance debt falls away.

f: 1661. What happens to the maintenance debt if the slave husband is killed?
b: According to the correct view, it falls away because maintenance is considered a gift.

f: 1662. If a free man marries a slave woman and her master gives her a residence with her husband, is the husband required to provide maintenance?
b: Yes. He must provide her maintenance because marital availability has been established.

f: 1663. Why does a slave woman receive maintenance when she is given residence with her husband?
b: Because she has become available for the purposes of marriage, so the husband is responsible for her maintenance.

f: 1664. Does a slave woman receive maintenance if her master does not place her with her husband?
b: No. She does not receive maintenance because marital availability has not occurred.

f: 1665. What does it mean for the master to give a slave woman residence with her husband?
b: It means allowing her to live with her husband in his home and not using her as a servant.

f: 1666. What happens if the master gives the slave woman residence but then uses her as a servant?
b: Her maintenance falls away because marital availability has been removed.

f: 1667. Is giving a slave woman residence with her husband obligatory upon the master?
b: No. Giving her residence is not obligatory, as previously explained in the chapter of marriage.

f: 1668. If a slave woman serves occasionally without the master treating her as a servant, does her maintenance fall away?
b: No. Her maintenance does not fall away because this does not indicate that the permission for marital residence has been withdrawn.

f: 1669. Do a mudabbarah and an umm walad have the same maintenance ruling as a slave woman?
b: Yes. A mudabbarah (a slave woman promised freedom after her master's death) and an umm walad (a slave woman who bore her master a child) have the same ruling as a slave woman.

f: 1670. Must a husband provide his wife with separate housing?
b: Yes. The husband must provide her with a separate residence in which none of his family members live, unless she chooses otherwise.

f: 1671. Why is separate housing obligatory for the wife?
b: Because housing is part of her necessities (kifāyah), just like maintenance. Allah mentioned housing together with maintenance as an obligation.

f: 1672. Why cannot the husband force his wife to share her residence with his family?
b: Because when Allah grants her a right, the husband cannot share that right with others if it causes her harm.

f: 1673. What harm can occur if the wife shares housing with the husband's family?
b: She may not feel secure regarding her belongings, and it may prevent normal marital relations and enjoyment between husband and wife.

f: 1674. When can the wife agree to shared housing?
b: She may choose to do so because she has the right to waive or reduce her own entitlement.

f: 1675. Can a husband house his child from another woman with his wife?
b: No. He does not have the right to house a child from another woman with her because this contradicts her right to separate housing.

f: 1676. Is a separate locked room within the husband's house sufficient housing for the wife?
b: Yes. If she has a separate room with its own lock, this is sufficient because the purpose of separate housing has been achieved.

f: 1677. Can a husband prevent his wife's parents, children from another husband, and relatives from entering her?
b: Yes. Since the house belongs to him, he has the right to prevent people from entering his property.

f: 1678. Can a husband prevent his wife's relatives from speaking with her or seeing her?
b: No. He cannot prevent them from seeing her and speaking with her whenever they wish because this would lead to severing family ties, and there is no harm to him in this.

f: 1679. What restriction can a husband place on his wife's relatives visiting her?
b: He may prevent them from staying permanently or prolonging conversations because temptation may arise through extended visits and interaction.

f: 1680. Can a wife visit her parents according to this ruling?
b: Yes. It has been said that he does not prevent her from going out to visit her parents.

f: 1681. How often may her parents visit her?
b: It has been said that they may enter upon her once every week.

f: 1682. How often may other unmarriageable relatives (maḥārim) visit her?
b: According to the correct view, other maḥārim may visit her once every year.

f: 1683. If an absent husband has wealth held by another person who acknowledges both the wealth and the marriage, can the judge assign maintenance from that wealth for his wife, minor children, and parents?
b: Yes. The judge assigns maintenance from that wealth for the absent man's wife, minor children, and parents. The same applies if the judge himself knows that the wealth exists, even if the person holding it does not acknowledge it.

f: 1684. Why can maintenance be taken from the wealth held by another person when he acknowledges the wealth and marriage?
b: Because by acknowledging the marriage and the property, he has acknowledged that she has a right to take from it. The wife has the right to take what is due to her from her husband's wealth without his permission.

f: 1685. Why is the acknowledgment of the person holding the property accepted?
b: Because his acknowledgment is accepted regarding matters connected to himself. Also, if he denied the marriage or the property, the wife's evidence would not be accepted against him because he is not the opponent in establishing the marriage, and she is not the opponent in establishing the absent husband's rights. Therefore, once the matter is established against him, it extends to the absent husband.

f: 1686. Does this ruling also apply if the wealth is held by someone as a business partner (muḍārib)?
b: Yes, the same ruling applies if the wealth is held by him as a muḍārib.

f: 1687. Does this ruling apply to debts owed to the absent husband?
b: Yes, the same ruling applies to debts owed to him.

f: 1688. What type of wealth can maintenance be taken from directly?
b: Wealth of the same type as the obligation: money (dirhams and dinars), food, or clothing of the same type.

f: 1689. Why is maintenance not assigned from wealth of a different type?
b: Because it would require selling the property, and the property of an absent person is not sold by agreement.

f: 1690. What is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that the property of an absent person cannot be sold?
b: He argues that property cannot be sold on behalf of an absent person, just as it cannot be sold on behalf of a present person.

f: 1691. What do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad say regarding selling the property of an absent person?
b: They argue that if a ruling can be issued against a present person because his refusal is known, it cannot be issued against an absent person because his refusal is unknown.

f: 1692. Why does the judge take a guarantor from the wife before giving her maintenance?
b: This is out of consideration for the absent husband, because it is possible that she already received the maintenance, or that he divorced her and her waiting period ended.

f: 1693. Why is a guarantor not taken from heirs when distributing inheritance according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because in inheritance the person who would reclaim the property is unknown, whereas in the case of maintenance the person entitled to the guarantee is known: the absent husband.

f: 1694. What additional requirement is placed upon the wife when receiving maintenance from her absent husband's wealth?
b: She must swear by Allah that her husband did not already give her the maintenance. This is out of consideration for the absent husband.

f: 1695. For whom can a judge issue a ruling for maintenance from the wealth of an absent person?
b: A ruling for maintenance from the wealth of an absent person is only issued for the wife, minor children, and parents.

f: 1696. Why are the wife, minor children, and parents treated differently from other relatives regarding maintenance from absent wealth?
b: Because their maintenance is already obligatory before the judge’s ruling. Therefore, they already have the right to take it, and the judge’s ruling only assists them in obtaining it.

f: 1697. Why are other relatives not given maintenance from the wealth of an absent person?
b: Because their maintenance only becomes obligatory through a judicial ruling, as it is a matter of juristic disagreement (ijtihād). A ruling cannot be issued against an absent person in such cases.

f: 1698. If the judge does not know that the absent husband has wealth, and the person holding the wealth does not acknowledge it, can the judge assign maintenance from it?
b: No. The judge does not issue such a ruling because this would amount to judging against an absent person.

f: 1699. If the absent husband left no wealth, and the wife presents evidence of marriage so that the judge would order maintenance or allow her to borrow, does the judge issue this ruling?
b: No. The judge does not issue this ruling because it would be a judgment against an absent person.

f: 1700. What was Zufar’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding issuing maintenance rulings against absent husbands?
b: Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ said that a ruling should be issued because it benefits the wife and causes no harm to the absent husband.

f: 1701. What happens if the absent husband returns and confirms the wife's claim?
b: Her claim is confirmed, and the maintenance she received was her rightful due.

f: 1702. What happens if the absent husband returns and denies the wife's claim?
b: He takes an oath. If he swears, his denial is accepted. If he refuses to swear, his refusal confirms the wife's claim.

f: 1703. If the wife presents evidence regarding her maintenance claim, what happens?
b: Her right is established through the evidence.

f: 1704. If the wife cannot provide evidence, who bears responsibility for the maintenance taken?
b: The guarantor or the woman herself bears responsibility, depending on the circumstances.

f: 1705. What is the current practice of judges regarding maintenance for absent husbands?
b: Judges today issue rulings for maintenance against absent husbands due to people's need. This is based on juristic reasoning (ijtihād).

f: 1706. Why are other opinions regarding this issue not mentioned?
b: Because they have been abandoned and are no longer relied upon.

f: 1707. If a man divorces his wife, is she entitled to maintenance and housing during her waiting period (ʿiddah)?
b: Yes. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, she receives maintenance and housing during her waiting period whether the divorce is revocable or irrevocable.

f: 1708. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position regarding maintenance after irrevocable divorce?
b: He says that a woman divorced irrevocably does not receive maintenance unless she is pregnant.

f: 1709. Why does al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say a woman in revocable divorce receives maintenance?
b: Because the marriage remains after revocable divorce, especially according to the Ḥanafīs, since intercourse remains permissible for the husband.

f: 1710. What evidence does al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to deny maintenance after irrevocable divorce?
b: He uses the narration of Fāṭimah bint Qays رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا: “My husband divorced me three times, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not assign for me housing or maintenance.”

f: 1711. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s reasoning that maintenance is not due after irrevocable divorce?
b: He argues that the husband no longer has ownership over her, and maintenance is based upon ownership. Therefore, it is also not due for a widow because that basis no longer exists.

f: 1712. Why does al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ make an exception for a pregnant divorced woman?
b: Because Allah says: “And if they are pregnant, then spend upon them until they give birth.” (Qur’an 65:6).

f: 1713. What is the Ḥanafī evidence that an irrevocably divorced woman receives maintenance?
b: Maintenance is compensation for marital availability (iḥtisāb), and that availability remains regarding the purpose of marriage, namely preserving the child. Therefore, maintenance remains obligatory.

f: 1714. Why does an irrevocably divorced woman receive housing according to the scholars?
b: Because she is still required to remain in the waiting period, and housing is established for her by agreement. Therefore, her case resembles that of a pregnant woman.

f: 1715. How did ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ respond to the narration of Fāṭimah bint Qays رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا?
b: He rejected it, saying: “We will not abandon the Book of our Lord and the Sunnah of our Prophet because of the statement of a woman whose truthfulness or falsehood we do not know, and whose memory or forgetfulness we do not know.”

f: 1716. What narration did ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ mention regarding a woman divorced three times?
b: He said that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “The woman divorced three times is entitled to maintenance and housing as long as she remains in her waiting period.”

f: 1717. Which Companions also rejected the narration of Fāṭimah bint Qays رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا?
b: Zayd ibn Thābit رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Usāmah ibn Zayd رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Jābir رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and ʿĀʾishah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا.

f: 1718. Why is there no maintenance for a widow during her waiting period?
b: Because her waiting period is not for the husband’s right, but rather for the right of Allah. It is an act of worship, and after death the husband no longer has ownership over her.

f: 1719. Why can maintenance not be made obligatory upon the heirs after the husband's death?
b: Because maintenance becomes obligatory gradually, and after death the husband’s ownership has ended, so it cannot be transferred as an obligation upon the inheritance.

f: 1720. Does the widow’s waiting period function like the divorced woman’s waiting period in terms of determining pregnancy?
b: No. The consideration of determining whether the womb is free is not applied in the same way, since menstruation is not required as a condition for the widow’s waiting period.

f: 1721. If separation occurs because of a sin committed by the woman, does she receive maintenance?
b: No. If separation occurs because of her sin, such as apostasy or allowing the husband’s son to have intercourse with her, she does not receive maintenance.

f: 1722. Why does a woman who causes sinful separation lose maintenance?
b: Because she has caused herself to be withheld from the husband without a valid right, so she is treated like a disobedient wife (nāshiz).

f: 1723. Why does sinful separation differ from the dowry after consummation?
b: Because in the dowry case, her surrender of herself was already realized through intercourse, so the dowry remains due.

f: 1724. Does a woman lose maintenance if separation occurs through a valid right from her side?
b: No. If separation occurs through a legitimate right, such as the option of a freed slave woman (khiyār al-ʿitq), the option upon maturity (khiyār al-bulūgh), or separation due to lack of compatibility (kafāʾah), she still receives maintenance.

f: 1725. Why does a woman seeking her dowry not lose maintenance even though she withholds herself?
b: Because she is withholding herself due to a legitimate right, not through disobedience.

f: 1726. If a man divorces his wife three times and she later apostatizes, what happens to her maintenance?
b: Her maintenance falls because she becomes imprisoned due to apostasy, and a woman who is imprisoned does not receive maintenance.

f: 1727. If a man divorces his wife three times and she later allows the husband's son to have intercourse with her, does she lose maintenance?
b: No. She still receives maintenance because the separation had already occurred through the three divorces, and this later act does not change the existing separation.

f: 1728. Why is there a difference between apostasy and allowing the husband's son to have intercourse after three divorces?
b: The apostate woman is imprisoned until she repents, so she loses maintenance due to imprisonment. The woman who allows the husband's son is not imprisoned, so she continues to receive maintenance.

f: 1729. Who is responsible for the maintenance of young children?
b: The father alone is responsible for the maintenance of young children. No one shares this obligation with him, just as no one shares the obligation of maintaining his wife.

f: 1730. What is the evidence that the father is responsible for his children’s maintenance?
b: Allah says: “And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing according to what is acceptable.” (Qur’an 2:233). The phrase “father of the child” refers to the father.

f: 1731. Is the mother required to breastfeed her child?
b: No. The mother is not required to breastfeed if another person can be found to do so.

f: 1732. Why is the mother not forced to breastfeed her child?
b: Because providing sufficiency for the child is the father’s responsibility, and the payment for breastfeeding is treated like maintenance. Also, the mother may have an excuse preventing her from breastfeeding.

f: 1733. How is the verse “No mother should be harmed because of her child” (Qur’an 2:233) understood regarding breastfeeding?
b: It means that the mother should not be harmed by being forced to breastfeed when she does not wish to do so.

f: 1734. When can the mother be compelled to breastfeed?
b: If no other woman can be found to breastfeed the child, she is compelled to breastfeed in order to protect the child from harm.

f: 1735. Who pays for breastfeeding the child?
b: The father pays for breastfeeding because the child’s sufficiency is his responsibility.

f: 1736. If the mother wants the child to remain with her, can the father hire someone to breastfeed the child while the child is with her?
b: Yes. The father may hire someone to breastfeed the child while the child remains with the mother, because custody belongs to her.

f: 1737. Can the father hire his wife to breastfeed their child?
b: No. He cannot hire his wife to breastfeed their child because breastfeeding is already a religious obligation upon her.

f: 1738. Why can the wife not take payment for breastfeeding her own child?
b: Because Allah says: “And mothers shall breastfeed their children.” (Qur’an 2:233). She was only excused because of possible inability, but accepting payment shows that she is able, so she cannot charge for an obligation.

f: 1739. Does this ruling apply to a woman divorced by revocable divorce who is still in her waiting period?
b: Yes. There is agreement that she cannot be hired to breastfeed her child because the marriage still remains.

f: 1740. Can a permanently divorced woman be hired to breastfeed her own child?
b: There are two narrations. One says she cannot be hired because some rulings of marriage remain. Another allows it because the marriage has ended completely.

f: 1741. Can a wife be hired to breastfeed a child of the husband from another woman?
b: Yes. This is permissible because breastfeeding that child is not an obligation upon her.

f: 1742. Can a divorced woman whose waiting period has ended be hired to breastfeed her own child?
b: Yes. Once her waiting period ends, the marriage has completely ended and she is treated like a stranger.

f: 1743. If the father refuses to hire the mother and brings another woman to breastfeed, but the mother accepts the same payment as the other woman or agrees to do it for free, who has more right?
b: The mother has more right because she is more compassionate toward the child, and giving the child to her is more beneficial.

f: 1744. If the mother demands more payment than another woman would receive, must the father pay it?
b: No. The father is not compelled to pay extra because this would harm him.

f: 1745. What is the evidence that the father cannot be forced to pay excessive breastfeeding costs?
b: Allah says: “No mother should be harmed through her child, nor the father through his child.” (Qur’an 2:233). This means he should not be forced to pay more than the normal wage.

f: 1746. Is the father responsible for maintaining a child who differs from him in religion?
b: Yes. The father must maintain his child even if the child has a different religion.

f: 1747. Why is the father responsible for maintaining a child who differs from him in religion?
b: Because the Qur’anic verses establishing maintenance are general, and because the child is part of the father, so the child is treated like an extension of himself.

f: 1748. Why is maintenance of a non-Muslim wife obligatory upon a Muslim husband?
b: Because the cause of maintenance is the valid marriage contract, which creates marital availability in exchange for maintenance. A valid marriage between a Muslim man and a non-Muslim woman establishes this obligation.

f: 1749. Is the father always responsible for the child’s maintenance even if the child has wealth?
b: No. The father is only responsible if the child has no wealth. If the child possesses wealth, the basic principle is that a person's maintenance comes from his own wealth, whether young or old.

f: 1750. When is a man required to provide maintenance for his parents, grandparents, and grandmothers?
b: He must provide maintenance for them if they are poor, even if they differ from him in religion.

f: 1751. What is the evidence that a person must maintain his parents?
b: Allah says: “And accompany them in this world with kindness.” (Qur’an 31:15). This verse was revealed regarding unbelieving parents, showing that kindness toward parents remains obligatory even if they are not Muslim.

f: 1752. Why does kindness toward unbelieving parents include providing maintenance?
b: Because it is not considered kindness for a person to enjoy Allah’s blessings while allowing his parents to die from hunger.

f: 1753. Why must a person maintain grandparents and grandmothers?
b: Because they are included in the category of fathers and mothers. The grandfather takes the position of the father when the father is absent, and grandparents were also a cause of his existence, so they deserve preservation of their lives.

f: 1754. Why is poverty a condition for the maintenance of parents and grandparents?
b: Because if they possess wealth, their own wealth takes priority for their maintenance rather than making their maintenance obligatory upon someone else.

f: 1755. Does difference of religion prevent maintenance of parents, grandparents, and children?
b: No. Difference of religion does not prevent maintenance because of the evidence regarding kindness and family connection.

f: 1756. Is maintenance obligatory for the wife, parents, grandparents, children, and grandchildren even if they differ in religion?
b: Yes, difference of religion does not prevent maintenance for these relatives, except in the case of those actively at war against Muslims (ḥarbīs).

f: 1757. Why is maintenance of a non-Muslim wife connected to religion?
b: Because her maintenance becomes obligatory through the marriage contract, as she is being kept for a purpose intended by the husband, and this depends upon unity of religion according to this discussion.

f: 1758. Why does disbelief not remove the obligation of maintaining parents and children?
b: Because their relationship as a part of oneself remains established. A person's own maintenance does not cease because of disbelief, and likewise the maintenance of those connected to him by this relationship does not cease.

f: 1759. Are the maintenance rights of ḥarbīs obligatory upon Muslims?
b: No. Their maintenance is not obligatory, even if they have been granted temporary protection (mustaʾmins), because Muslims have been prohibited from showing support and kindness to those who fight them regarding religion.

f: 1760. Is a Christian required to maintain his Muslim brother?
b: No. A Christian is not required to maintain his Muslim brother.

f: 1761. Is a Muslim required to maintain his Christian brother?
b: No. A Muslim is not required to maintain his Christian brother.

f: 1762. Why is maintenance between siblings connected to religion?
b: Because maintenance is connected to inheritance according to textual evidence. Unlike emancipation through ownership, which is connected to kinship and close unmarriageable relationship (maḥram).

f: 1763. Why does inheritance affect the ruling of maintenance between siblings?
b: Because inheritance indicates a financial relationship recognized by the Sharīʿah, and maintenance follows this connection.

f: 1764. Why is emancipation through ownership different from maintenance between siblings?
b: Because emancipation is based on kinship and being a maḥram, while maintenance is connected to inheritance. Ownership of a slave involves a greater severing of ties than merely not receiving maintenance.

f: 1765. Does anyone share responsibility with a child in maintaining his parents?
b: No. The child alone bears this responsibility and no one shares it with him.

f: 1766. Why does no one share with the child in maintaining his parents?
b: Because parents have a recognized claim upon their child's wealth through textual evidence, but they do not have such a claim upon the wealth of others. Also, the child is the closest person to them and therefore most deserving of maintaining them.

f: 1767. Does the obligation of maintaining parents apply only to sons?
b: No. According to the apparent narration, it applies equally to males and females. This is the correct view because the reasoning applies to both.

f: 1768. When is maintenance (nafaqah) obligatory upon close unmarriageable relatives (dhū raḥim maḥram)?
b: Maintenance is obligatory upon close unmarriageable relatives when the relative is in need and falls into one of the categories indicating inability to earn: a poor minor, a poor adult woman, or a poor adult man who is chronically ill or blind.

f: 1769. What type of relatives are included in the obligation of maintenance?
b: The obligation applies to close blood relatives who are permanently unmarriageable (maḥram) to one another, unlike distant relatives who do not fall under this ruling.

f: 1770. What is the evidence for obligating maintenance upon close relatives?
b: The evidence is Allah’s statement: “And upon the heir is a similar obligation.” (Qur’an 2:233). It is also reported in the recitation attributed to ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: “And upon the heir who is a close unmarriageable relative is a similar obligation.”

f: 1771. Why are childhood, femininity, chronic illness, and blindness considered signs of need?
b: Because these conditions generally indicate inability to earn. A person who cannot support himself is considered needy and therefore entitled to maintenance from those responsible for him.

f: 1772. Why does an adult man who is capable of earning not receive maintenance from relatives?
b: Because his ability to earn makes him legally self-sufficient. His ability to work removes the need that would require others to support him.

f: 1773. Why are parents different from other relatives regarding the ability to earn?
b: Parents must be supported even if they are capable of earning, because requiring them to work may cause hardship. The child is commanded to remove harm from his parents and treat them with kindness.

f: 1774. How is the amount of maintenance divided among relatives?
b: The maintenance obligation is divided according to inheritance shares. The relative who would receive a greater share of inheritance bears a greater portion of the maintenance responsibility.

f: 1775. Why is maintenance divided according to inheritance shares?
b: Because Allah mentioned the heir in the verse, indicating that responsibility corresponds to inheritance entitlement. Also, liability corresponds to benefit: whoever receives greater benefit from inheritance carries greater responsibility.

f: 1776. Can a judge force a relative to provide maintenance?
b: Yes. Since the maintenance is an established right, the judge can compel the responsible relative to fulfil this obligation.

f: 1777. How is the maintenance of an adult daughter or a chronically ill son divided between the parents according to the narration of al-Khaṣṣāf and al-Ḥasan رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The maintenance is divided between the parents in thirds: two-thirds upon the father and one-third upon the mother, because inheritance between them is divided in this same proportion.

f: 1778. What is the apparent narration regarding who is responsible for the maintenance of an adult daughter or chronically ill son?
b: According to the apparent narration, the entire maintenance is upon the father, based on Allah’s statement: “And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing.” (Qur’an 2:233).

f: 1779. Why does the first narration make the mother share responsibility for an adult child’s maintenance?
b: Because the father’s exclusive responsibility for a young child is due to him having both guardianship (wilāyah) and financial responsibility. Once the child becomes an adult, guardianship ends, so the mother shares responsibility.

f: 1780. Why is the maintenance of a young child specifically upon the father?
b: Because the father has guardianship over the child and is responsible for his financial needs, similar to his obligation regarding zakāt al-fiṭr.

f: 1781. How is the maintenance of relatives other than parents and children divided?
b: It is divided according to inheritance shares. Each relative contributes according to the share by which they would inherit from that person.

f: 1782. How is the maintenance of a poor child divided if the responsible relatives are the mother and grandfather?
b: According to inheritance proportions, the mother and grandfather divide the responsibility in thirds.

f: 1783. How is the maintenance of a poor brother divided among wealthy maternal sisters?
b: It is divided according to their inheritance shares, in this case according to fifths.

f: 1784. Is actual inheritance considered when assigning maintenance responsibility?
b: No. What is considered is general eligibility for inheritance, not whether the person would actually inherit in that specific case.

f: 1785. If a poor person has a maternal uncle and a paternal cousin, who is responsible for his maintenance?
b: The maternal uncle is responsible for his maintenance because he is a close unmarriageable relative (dhū raḥim maḥram), even though the paternal cousin may inherit from him.

f: 1786. Is maintenance between relatives obligatory when there is a difference of religion?
b: No. Maintenance between relatives is not obligatory when there is a difference of religion because inheritance eligibility is absent, and inheritance connection is the basis for this obligation.

f: 1787. Why is maintenance not obligatory upon a poor relative?
b: Because this type of maintenance is a form of kindness (ṣilah), and the poor person himself is someone who requires kindness. Therefore, it cannot be required from him.

f: 1788. Why is maintenance of a wife and young child different from maintenance of relatives?
b: Because the husband’s obligation toward his wife comes from the marriage contract, and the father’s obligation toward a young child is connected to preserving society and family structure. Poverty does not remove obligations of this type.

f: 1789. How is wealth measured when determining whether someone is financially responsible for relatives’ maintenance?
b: According to a narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, wealth is measured according to the niṣāb threshold.

f: 1790. What is the view attributed to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding financial ability for maintenance?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considered a person capable if, after covering his own maintenance and the maintenance of his dependents for a month, or after his regular daily earnings, something remains.

f: 1791. What is the principle regarding financial ability in people’s rights?
b: The principle is that ability to pay is considered, not merely the niṣāb amount. Niṣāb is only used as an easier legal measurement.

f: 1792. Which view is the relied-upon fatwā regarding wealth for maintenance obligations?
b: The fatwā follows the first view, using the niṣāb that prevents a person from receiving charity as the measure of financial ability.

f: 1793. If an absent son has wealth, can maintenance for his parents be taken from his wealth?
b: Yes. A judgment may be issued to take the parents’ maintenance from the wealth of their absent son, because their maintenance is already an established obligation upon him.

f: 1794. Can a father sell his absent adult son's belongings to obtain his maintenance according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, this is permitted as an exception based on juristic preference (istiḥsān), although the normal analogy would not allow it.

f: 1795. Can a father sell his absent adult son's real estate to obtain maintenance according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ only permits selling movable property, not real estate, because real estate itself preserves wealth and does not require disposal for preservation.

f: 1796. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding a father selling his absent adult son's property for maintenance?
b: They hold that neither movable property nor real estate may be sold. They follow the analogy that a father has no guardianship over the wealth of an adult child.

f: 1797. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say the father cannot sell his adult son's property?
b: Because once the child reaches adulthood, the father's guardianship ends. Therefore, he cannot dispose of the son's wealth while he is absent, just as he could not dispose of it while he is present except with permission.

f: 1798. What is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence for allowing the father to sell movable property?
b: He argues that the father has a type of guardianship for preserving the absent son’s wealth. A trustee (waṣī) has this authority, and the father is even more deserving because of his greater compassion and concern.

f: 1799. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish between movable property and real estate?
b: Because selling movable property can be considered preservation of wealth when needed, whereas real estate preserves itself and does not require disposal.

f: 1800. Why do other relatives not have the same authority as the father over an absent person's property?
b: Because other relatives do not possess guardianship over the person's wealth during childhood nor preservation authority after adulthood.

f: 1801. If the father sells the absent son's property and the sale price is the same type as the maintenance owed, may he take from it?
b: Yes. He may take his maintenance from it as fulfilment of his right, similar to taking from the property of a minor child under complete guardianship.

f: 1802. If absent son's wealth is in the possession of his parents and they spend from it for their maintenance, are they liable to repay it?
b: No. They are not liable because they took something that was already their right, since their maintenance obligation existed before any judicial ruling.

f: 1803. If a stranger has an absent son's wealth and spends from it on the son's parents without the judge's permission, is the stranger liable?
b: Yes. The stranger acted upon another person's property without authorization. He only had the role of a custodian, not someone permitted to dispose of the property.

f: 1804. Why is a person not liable if he spends from absent son's wealth after the judge orders him to do so?
b: Because the judge's command is binding due to his general authority. The person's action becomes authorized by the judge's ruling.

f: 1805. If the stranger becomes liable for spending without permission, can he demand repayment from the parents?
b: No. Since liability caused ownership to transfer to him, it becomes as though he gave them the money voluntarily, so he cannot reclaim it.

f: 1806. Does maintenance granted by a judge for children, parents, or relatives remain as a debt after time passes?
b: No. It falls away after the period passes because their maintenance is based on need, and the need of that period has already been fulfilled.

f: 1807. Why does maintenance granted for relatives fall away after time passes, unlike a wife's maintenance?
b: Because relatives receive maintenance due to need. If time has passed, that specific need has ended. A wife's maintenance is different because it remains obligatory regardless of her wealth.

f: 1808. What happens if the judge permits someone to borrow on behalf of the person responsible for maintenance?
b: The maintenance becomes a debt upon the responsible person's liability and does not disappear with the passing of time, because the judge's permission functions like authorization from the absent person himself.

f: 1. What is the ruling regarding a master's maintenance of his male and female slaves?
b: The master must provide maintenance for his male and female slaves.

f: 2. What evidence is mentioned for the obligation of maintaining slaves?
b: The statement of the Prophet ﷺ regarding slaves: "They are your brothers whom Allah has placed under your authority. Feed them from what you eat, clothe them from what you wear, and do not punish the servants of Allah."

f: 3. If a master refuses to provide maintenance and the slave can earn, what should the slave do?
b: The slave should earn and spend upon himself.

f: 4. Why is a slave allowed to earn his own maintenance if the master refuses to provide it?
b: Because it preserves the welfare of both parties: the slave remains alive and remains under the ownership of the master.

f: 5. If a slave cannot earn enough for his maintenance, what is the ruling?
b: The master is compelled to sell the slave.

f: 6. What are examples of slaves who may be unable to earn their maintenance?
b: A male slave who is chronically ill or a female slave who is not suitable for being hired out.

f: 7. Why is a master compelled to sell a slave who cannot earn and whom he does not maintain?
b: Because the slave is a person who possesses a right to maintenance.

f: 8. How does the sale of an unmaintained slave fulfill the rights of both the slave and the master?
b: The slave's right to maintenance is fulfilled through the sale, and the master's right is fulfilled because he receives the slave's price.

f: 9. How does the maintenance of a slave differ from the maintenance of a wife?
b: The maintenance of a wife becomes a debt that may be delayed, whereas the maintenance of a slave does not become a debt.

f: 10. Why does abandoning a slave's maintenance cancel their right?
b: Because slave maintenance is not a debt that remains owed; neglecting it means abandoning an immediate right.

f: 11. Why is a master not compelled to spend on animals according to the stronger view?
b: Because animals are not recipients of legal rights, unlike slaves who are human beings with legal rights.

f: 12. What is the owner's responsibility toward animals despite not being legally compelled to maintain them?
b: He is instructed to care for them between himself and Allah.

f: 13. Why is neglecting animals blameworthy even though their maintenance is not legally compulsory?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited tormenting animals, and neglecting them contains harm and torment.

f: 14. Why is neglecting animals also considered a form of wasting wealth?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited wasting wealth, and allowing animals to perish through neglect wastes property.

f: 15. What view regarding spending on animals is narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ narrated that the owner is compelled to spend on animals.

f: 16. What is the more correct view regarding compelling owners to maintain animals?
b: The more correct view is that owners are not compelled to spend on animals.

f: 17. What is the ruling of manumission (freeing slaves) according to Al-Hidayah?
b: Manumission is an encouraged act.

f: 18. What hadith is mentioned regarding the virtue of freeing a believing slave?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Any Muslim who frees a believing person, Allah will free from the Fire a limb of his for every limb of that person."

f: 19. Why did scholars recommend that a man free a male slave and a woman free a female slave?
b: Because they considered it preferable for there to be correspondence between the limbs of the one freed and the one who frees.

f: 20. What is the reasoning behind freeing a slave with corresponding gender according to the scholars?
b: It is based on the hadith mentioning Allah freeing a limb of the person who frees a slave for every limb of the freed person, so matching genders creates correspondence between the limbs.

f: 21. From whom is manumission (freeing a slave) valid according to Al-Hidayah?
b: Manumission is valid from a free, adult, sane person regarding his property.

f: 22. Why is being free a condition for the validity of manumission?
b: Because manumission can only occur over ownership, and a slave does not possess ownership.

f: 23. Why is a slave unable to perform manumission?
b: Because a slave does not possess ownership over property, and manumission requires ownership.

f: 24. Why is adulthood a condition for valid manumission?
b: Because a child is not qualified for manumission due to the obvious harm involved, and therefore his guardian cannot perform it on his behalf.

f: 25. Why is sanity a condition for valid manumission?
b: Because an insane person is not legally capable of performing transactions.

f: 26. If an adult says, "I freed him while I was a child," is his statement accepted?
b: Yes, his statement is accepted because he attributed the action to a state in which manumission would not be valid.

f: 27. If someone who freed a slave says, "I freed him while I was insane," is his statement accepted?
b: Yes, if his insanity was apparent, his statement is accepted because he attributed the action to a state that prevents validity.

f: 28. Is it valid for a child to say, "Every slave I own is free when I reach puberty"?
b: No, it is not valid because a child is not qualified to make a binding legal statement.

f: 29. What condition must exist regarding the slave for manumission to be valid?
b: The slave must be owned by the person freeing him.

f: 30. What is the ruling if someone frees another person's slave?
b: The manumission does not take effect.

f: 31. What hadith is used to prove that a person cannot free a slave he does not own?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no manumission regarding that which the son of Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ does not own."

f: 32. What happens if a master says to his slave, "You are free"?
b: The slave becomes free, whether the master intended manumission or not.

f: 33. What explicit phrases cause a slave to become free according to Al-Hidayah?
b: Phrases such as "You are free," "you are emancipated," "you are freed," "you are liberated," "I have liberated you," and "I have freed you."

f: 34. Why do explicit words of manumission not require intention?
b: Because they are clear expressions used for manumission both legally and customarily.

f: 35. Why are some phrases treated as legal declarations even if they can originally be statements of information?
b: Because in legal transactions they are treated as effective declarations due to necessity, similar to divorce, sales, and other matters.

f: 36. If someone says after freeing a slave, "I only intended that he was already free," is he believed?
b: He is believed religiously, but not judicially.
