f: 37. Why is a person not believed in court if he claims he intended a false report rather than manumission?
b: Because his claim contradicts the apparent meaning of the explicit words.

f: 38. What is the ruling if someone says to his slave, "O free one!" or "O freed one!"?
b: The slave becomes free.

f: 39. Why does calling someone "O free one" result in manumission?
b: Because it is a phrase explicit for manumission, and calling someone by a quality implies that the described attribute exists in him.

f: 40. How is the statement "O free one" treated legally?
b: It is treated as establishing the attribute of freedom, and judgment is made according to that apparent meaning.

f: 41. What is the exception to the ruling of calling a slave "O free one"?
b: If the master had already named the slave "Free" and is merely using that proper name, then the slave does not become free.

f: 42. If a person named his slave "Free" and later says "O Free one!", why does manumission not occur?
b: Because he intends only to call him by his established name, not to declare the attribute of freedom.

f: 43. If someone calls his slave "O Āzād (free one)" in Persian and had given him that title, does the slave become free?
b: According to the scholars, yes, because it is not merely a known personal name and is treated as a statement about the attribute.

f: 44. Why does the Persian case differ from the case where "Free" was given as a personal name?
b: Because the phrase is not merely being used as a known name, so it is understood as a declaration of the attribute of freedom.

f: 45. Which body-part expressions cause manumission to occur when a master attributes freedom to them, and why?
b: Expressions such as "Your head is free," "your face is free," "your neck is free," "your body is free," or for a female slave, "your private part is free," cause manumission to occur because these expressions are understood to refer to the entire body.

f: 46. If a master attributes freedom to an unspecified shared part of a slave, what is the ruling?
b: Freedom occurs in that part. The detailed disagreement regarding this issue is discussed later.

f: 47. If a master attributes freedom to a specific body part that does not represent the whole body, such as the hand or foot, does manumission occur according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his companions, manumission does not occur. This differs from al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, and the discussion is similar to the issue of divorce.

f: 48. If a master says, "I have no ownership over you," what is the ruling?
b: If he intends manumission, the slave becomes free; if he does not intend manumission, the slave does not become free.

f: 49. Why does the statement "I have no ownership over you" require intention?
b: Because it can mean either that ownership ended through sale or that ownership ended through manumission. The intended meaning is only determined through intention.

f: 50. What are the indirect expressions (kināyāt) of manumission mentioned in Al-Hidayah?
b: Examples include: "You have left my ownership," "I have no authority over you," "You are no longer my slave," and "I have released your way."

f: 51. Why do indirect expressions of manumission require intention?
b: Because these expressions can indicate different meanings, such as removal from ownership through sale, freeing through manumission, or release through another contract. Therefore, intention is required to determine that manumission was intended.

f: 52. If a master says to his female slave, "I have released you," what is the ruling according to the narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: She becomes free if the statement is intended as "I have released your way."

f: 53. Why is "I have released you" considered an indirect expression of manumission for a female slave?
b: Because it is understood as equivalent to "I have released your way," which can carry meanings other than manumission and therefore requires intention.

f: 54. How does the statement "I have released you" differ from the statement "I have divorced you"?
b: The distinction between these expressions is discussed later in the chapter of divorce.

f: 55. If a master says, "I have no authority over you" and intends emancipation, does the slave become free?
b: No, the slave does not become free.

f: 56. Why does the statement "I have no authority over you" not cause emancipation even if the master intends it?
b: Because authority (sulṭān) refers to control (yad), not ownership itself. A person may still own something even if he lacks control over it, as seen with a mukātab slave.

f: 57. What is the difference between ownership (milk) and authority/control (sulṭān)?
b: Ownership can remain even when control is absent, whereas authority refers specifically to having control over something.

f: 58. Why does the statement "I have no path over you" (lā sabīla lī ʿalayka) cause emancipation according to Al-Hidayah?
b: Because completely negating a path over someone implies negating ownership, and the master still has a path over a mukātab slave. Therefore, the statement can carry the meaning of emancipation.

f: 59. If a master says about his slave, "This is my son," what is the ruling if this claim is established?
b: The slave becomes free.

f: 60. What condition applies when a master claims that his slave is his son?
b: The slave must be someone who could biologically be his son, meaning their ages and circumstances make this possible.

f: 61. If a slave has no known lineage and his master says, "This is my son," why is the lineage established from the master?
b: Because the right to claim lineage (wilāyat al-daʿwah) exists due to ownership, and the slave is in need of lineage.

f: 62. When does the lineage of a slave become traced back to the master?
b: When the slave has no known lineage and the master claims him as his son in a situation where biological parentage is possible.

f: 63. Why does establishing lineage from the master result in the slave becoming free?
b: Because lineage is traced back to the time of conception, meaning the slave was considered the master's son from the beginning.

f: 64. If a slave already has a known lineage, is his lineage established from the master who claims him as his son?
b: No, because that is impossible due to the existing known lineage.

f: 65. If a slave has known lineage and the master says, "This is my son," why does the slave still become free?
b: The statement is interpreted metaphorically because applying the literal meaning is impossible, and the metaphorical explanation is discussed later.

f: 66. If a master says, "This is my master" (hādhā mawlāya) regarding his slave, what is the ruling?
b: The slave becomes free.

f: 67. If a master says to his slave, "O my master" (yā mawlāya), what is the ruling?
b: The slave becomes free.

f: 68. Why does calling a slave "my master" result in emancipation despite the word mawlā having multiple meanings?
b: Because in this context the meaning becomes specifically the freed slave (the inferior mawlā), making it equivalent to an explicit expression of manumission.

f: 69. What are the possible meanings of the word mawlā?
b: It can mean a helper, a cousin/relative, a religious ally, the superior in a manumission relationship (the one who freed the slave), or the inferior (the freed slave).

f: 70. Why is the meaning of mawlā as "helper" excluded when a master calls his slave "my mawlā"?
b: Because normally a master does not seek help from his slave.

f: 71. Why is the meaning of mawlā as a relative excluded in this context?
b: Because the slave already has a known lineage, so this meaning does not apply.

f: 72. Why are meanings such as religious ally not preferred for the word mawlā in this situation?
b: Because they would be metaphorical meanings, while speech is interpreted according to the literal meaning unless there is a reason otherwise.

f: 73. Why does attributing the word mawlā to the slave indicate the meaning of the freed slave rather than the person who freed the slave?
b: Because calling the slave a mawlā contradicts the meaning of the master as the muʿtiq (the one who grants freedom), so the remaining applicable meaning is the freed slave.

f: 74. If a master says to his female slave, "This is my mistress (mawlātī)," what is the ruling?
b: The female slave becomes free for the same reasoning as the male slave case.

f: 75. If a master says "This is my mawlā" but claims he intended religious allyship or that he was lying, is he believed?
b: He is believed between himself and Allah, but he is not believed in legal judgment (qaḍāʾ).

f: 76. Why is a person not believed in court if he claims he intended another meaning of mawlā?
b: Because his claim contradicts the apparent meaning of the statement.

f: 77. Why does saying "O my master" (yā mawlāya) to a slave cause emancipation according to Al-Hidayah?
b: Because once the meaning of mawlā as the freed slave (the inferior mawlā) is established, the expression becomes equivalent to an explicit expression of manumission.

f: 78. Why is calling a slave "O my master" treated like calling him "O free one" or "O freed one"?
b: Because both expressions are explicit indications of the attribute of freedom, and calling someone by an explicit expression of emancipation causes freedom to occur.

f: 79. What was Imām Zufar's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ objection regarding saying "O my master" to a slave?
b: He said the slave does not become free because the master may intend it as a form of honour, similar to saying "O my lord" or "O my owner."

f: 80. How is Imām Zufar's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ objection answered?
b: Speech is interpreted according to its true meaning when possible. This differs from expressions like "O my lord" because those do not specifically indicate emancipation and are only expressions of honour.

f: 81. If a master says to his slave, "O my son" or "O my brother," does the slave become free?
b: No, the slave does not become free.

f: 82. Why does saying "O my son" or "O my brother" not cause emancipation?
b: Because these expressions are only used to identify the person being addressed, not to establish the attribute mentioned.

f: 83. What is the difference between calling someone "O free one" and "O my son" regarding legal effect?
b: "O free one" establishes an attribute that can be legally created by the speaker, while "O my son" only identifies someone because sonship cannot be established merely through speech.

f: 84. Why does calling a slave "O free one" establish freedom but calling him "O my son" does not establish sonship?
b: Because freedom is an attribute that can be created through the speaker's declaration, whereas biological sonship cannot be created by a statement if the child was created from another man's lineage.

f: 85. Why does saying "O my son" not establish sonship even if the master says it?
b: Because if the child was created from another man's fluid, he does not become the speaker's son merely by the statement.

f: 86. What is the unusual narration reported from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding saying "O my son" or "O my brother"?
b: It is narrated that the slave becomes free in both cases, but reliance is placed upon the apparent narration that he does not become free.

f: 87. What is the ruling if a master says to his slave, "O son" (yā ibn)?
b: The slave does not become free.

f: 88. Why does saying "O son" not cause emancipation?
b: Because the statement is understood according to its actual meaning: he is the son of his own father, not the master's son.

f: 89. What is the ruling if a master says, "O my little son" (yā bunayya) or "O my little daughter" (yā bunayyah)?
b: The slave does not become free.

f: 90. Why do the diminutive forms "bunayya" and "bunayyah" not cause emancipation?
b: Because they are merely diminutive forms of son and daughter without attribution, so they do not establish a legal relationship.

f: 91. If a master says about a slave who could not possibly be his biological child, "This is my son," does the slave become free according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the slave becomes free.

f: 92. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding a master saying "This is my son" about a slave who could not be his child?
b: They said the slave does not become free, and this is also the opinion of al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 93. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Muḥammad, and al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say that the slave does not become free in this case?
b: Because the statement is literally impossible, so it is rejected and treated as meaningless, similar to saying "I freed you before I existed" or "I freed you before you existed."

f: 94. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to the argument that the statement is literally impossible?
b: He says that although the literal meaning is impossible, the statement can carry a valid metaphorical meaning, so it should not be made meaningless.

f: 95. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret the statement "This is my son" when literal sonship is impossible?
b: He interprets it as an announcement that the slave is free from the time he entered the master's ownership.

f: 96. Why can "This is my son" metaphorically indicate freedom according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because sonship in a slave is a cause of freedom, either by consensus or due to the connection of kinship, and mentioning a cause while intending its consequence is a recognized metaphor in language.

f: 97. How is sonship a cause of freedom for a slave?
b: Because a slave who becomes the child of his owner becomes free, either by scholarly agreement or due to the legal effect of kinship.

f: 98. What linguistic principle does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to support his interpretation?
b: A cause may be mentioned while intending its consequence, which is an accepted form of metaphor in language.

f: 99. Why can freedom be metaphorically understood from sonship in the case of a slave?
b: Because freedom accompanies sonship in a slave, and an inseparable attribute can be used metaphorically to indicate another inseparable attribute.

f: 100. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ prefer a metaphorical interpretation instead of rejecting the statement?
b: To avoid making the statement meaningless when a valid interpretation is possible.

f: 101. Why is the example "I cut off your hand" not interpreted metaphorically as an admission of financial liability?
b: Because although cutting a hand causes financial liability, it specifically causes a particular type of compensation (arsh), which differs from general wealth in its nature and legal rulings.

f: 102. How does compensation (arsh) differ from unrestricted wealth?
b: Compensation may be paid by the clan (ʿāqilah) in certain cases and may be paid over two years, so it cannot be established without the actual cutting.

f: 103. Why can freedom be treated metaphorically as equivalent to sonship, unlike compensation in the example of cutting?
b: Because the essence and legal consequence of freedom do not differ from the cause that brings it about, whereas compensation has separate rules and conditions.

f: 104. If a master says about his slave, "This is my father" or "This is my mother," when such parentage is impossible, does the same disagreement apply?
b: Yes, the same disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his companions applies.

f: 105. Why does the disagreement regarding "This is my father" or "This is my mother" follow the same reasoning as "This is my son"?
b: Because it is based on whether an impossible literal statement can be interpreted metaphorically as an announcement of freedom.

f: 106. If a master says to a small child, "This is my grandfather," does the slave become free?
b: There are two opinions: some scholars applied the same disagreement, while others said the child does not become free by agreement.

f: 107. Why did some scholars say that "This is my grandfather" does not cause freedom by agreement?
b: Because grandfatherhood only affects ownership through an intermediary, namely the father, and that intermediary is not established by the statement.

f: 108. Why does grandfatherhood differ from fatherhood and sonship regarding metaphorical interpretation?
b: Because fatherhood and sonship directly affect ownership and freedom without an intermediary, whereas grandfatherhood requires the existence of the father as an intermediary.

f: 109. If a master says about his slave, "This is my brother," does the slave become free according to the apparent narration?
b: No, according to the apparent narration, the slave does not become free.

f: 110. What other narration is reported from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding saying "This is my brother" about a slave?
b: It is narrated from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ that the slave becomes free.

f: 111. What is the basis of the disagreement regarding saying "This is my brother" to a slave?
b: The disagreement is based on whether such a statement can be interpreted metaphorically as establishing freedom, similar to the earlier discussion of impossible lineage claims.

f: 112. If a master says about his slave, "This is my daughter," does the slave become free?
b: Some scholars applied the same disagreement as in the case of "my brother," while others said by agreement that the slave does not become free.

f: 113. Why did some scholars say that saying "This is my daughter" does not cause freedom by agreement?
b: Because the person being pointed to is not from the same category as the name mentioned, so the ruling would attach to something nonexistent and is therefore disregarded.

f: 114. Why can statements of emancipation and freeing serve as metaphors in other legal matters?
b: Because legal rulings are based on the prior existence of legal responsibility (taklīf), allowing one legal action to be metaphorically compared with another in some cases.

f: 115. Why did some scholars argue that emancipation (ʿitq) and divorce could be metaphors for each other?
b: Because both involve changing a person's legal state: emancipation removes slavery and divorce removes marriage restrictions.

f: 116. Why is emancipation not a valid metaphor for divorce according to the response?
b: Because the wording of emancipation does not carry the meaning of divorce; linguistically, emancipation means establishing strength and ability, while divorce means removing a restriction.

f: 117. What is the linguistic meaning of emancipation (ʿitq)?
b: It means establishing strength, ability, and independence.

f: 118. Why is a slave described as being given ability through emancipation?
b: Because a slave is treated like an inanimate object in terms of legal control, and emancipation brings him into a state of freedom and ability.

f: 119. Why does divorce differ from emancipation regarding ability?
b: A married woman already possesses ability, but marriage restricts her exercise of it; divorce removes that restriction.

f: 120. Why is emancipation considered stronger than divorce?
b: Because emancipation creates ability and removes slavery, whereas divorce only removes a restriction from someone who already possesses ability.

f: 121. Why can a word be used metaphorically for something below its literal meaning but not something above it?
b: Because metaphorical usage can transfer a term to something weaker or lesser, but not to something stronger or greater than its original meaning.

f: 122. Why is the metaphor between emancipation and divorce invalid in the disputed case?
b: Because divorce is not equivalent to emancipation in strength or meaning, so the wording cannot properly carry that interpretation.

f: 123. If a master says to his slave, "You are like a free person," does the slave become free?
b: No, the slave does not become free.

f: 124. Why does saying "You are like a free person" not cause emancipation?
b: Because the word "like" (mithl) usually indicates similarity in only some qualities, leaving uncertainty about whether actual freedom is intended.

f: 125. If a master says, "You are nothing except free," does the slave become free?
b: Yes, the slave becomes free.

f: 126. Why does the statement "You are nothing except free" cause emancipation?
b: Because exclusion after negation (istithnāʾ min al-nafy) establishes affirmation with emphasis, similar to the wording of the testimony of faith.

f: 127. If a master says, "Your head is the head of a free person," does the slave become free?
b: No, the slave does not become free.

f: 128. Why does saying "Your head is the head of a free person" not cause emancipation?
b: Because it is merely a comparison, with the word of comparison being omitted.

f: 129. If a master says, "Your head is a free head," does the slave become free?
b: Yes, the slave becomes free.

f: 130. Why does saying "Your head is a free head" cause emancipation?
b: Because it establishes the attribute of freedom in him, and the word "head" can refer to the entire body.

f: 131. What is the ruling if a person owns a close relative whom he is permanently prohibited from marrying (maḥram)?
b: The relative becomes free automatically because of his ownership.

f: 132. What hadith is used as evidence that owning a maḥram relative causes emancipation?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever owns a relative whom he is prohibited from marrying, then that person is free."

f: 133. Which relatives are included in the rule of automatic emancipation according to the general wording?
b: Every relative whose marriage is permanently prohibited due to kinship, whether through descendants or other relatives.

f: 134. Does automatic emancipation of relatives apply only to descendants according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No, it applies to all permanently prohibited relatives through kinship, not only descendants.

f: 135. What is the position of Imām al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding relatives other than descendants?
b: He disagrees and does not consider relatives other than descendants to become free automatically.

f: 136. What is Imām al-Shāfiʿī's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument against automatic emancipation of relatives other than descendants?
b: He argues that emancipation without the owner's consent is rejected by analogy because analogy does not require it, and siblings and similar relatives are lower in status than descendants.

f: 137. Why does Imām al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not compare siblings and similar relatives to descendants?
b: Because direct descendants have a higher status and cannot be used as the basis for extending the ruling to other relatives.

f: 138. What example does Imām al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use regarding a mukātab and his relatives?
b: He argues that a mukātab cannot enter into another emancipation contract with relatives other than descendants, while this is not prevented with descendants.

f: 139. What is the Ḥanafī response to Imām al-Shāfiʿī's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument?
b: They rely upon the hadith and argue that the effective cause is not merely direct descent, but any relationship that establishes permanent prohibition (maḥramiyyah).

f: 140. What is the effective cause for automatic emancipation of relatives according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Owning a relative whose relationship creates permanent marriage prohibition (maḥramiyyah).

f: 141. Why is direct descent (walad) not considered the actual cause of automatic emancipation?
b: Because the true cause is the type of relationship that Allah commanded people to maintain and prohibited them from severing.

f: 142. What legal effects result from the relationship that causes automatic emancipation?
b: Maintenance (nafaqah) becomes obligatory and marriage becomes permanently prohibited.

f: 143. Does automatic emancipation of a maḥram relative apply only when the owner is Muslim?
b: No, it applies whether the owner is Muslim or a non-Muslim living under Islamic rule, because the effective cause is general.

f: 144. If a mukātab purchases his brother or another similar relative, does that relative become free through the emancipation contract?
b: No, the relative does not become subject to emancipation through the contract.

f: 145. Why does a mukātab not cause emancipation of his brother or similar relative through ownership?
b: Because a mukātab does not possess complete ownership that enables him to emancipate, and the assumption of such ability does not apply.

f: 146. Why does this ruling differ in the case of descendants owned by a mukātab?
b: Because freeing descendants is one of the objectives of the emancipation contract, so selling them is prevented to achieve the purpose of the contract.

f: 147. What narration is reported from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding a mukātab purchasing his brother?
b: It is narrated that even a brother becomes subject to emancipation through the contract.

f: 148. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding a mukātab purchasing his brother?
b: They also held that the brother becomes subject to emancipation through the contract.

f: 149. What is the Ḥanafī response to the narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: They reject this position.

f: 150. If someone owns his paternal cousin who is also his sister through breastfeeding (raḍāʿah), does automatic emancipation occur?
b: No, because the prohibition of marriage in this case is not established through blood relationship.

f: 151. Why does a breastfeeding relationship not cause automatic emancipation like a blood relationship?
b: Because the rule applies to relationships that establish permanent prohibition through kinship, and breastfeeding does not establish the same blood relationship.

f: 152. Do a child and an insane person cause automatic emancipation when they acquire ownership of a maḥram relative?
b: Yes, both a child and an insane person cause the relative to become free upon ownership.

f: 153. Why does a child or insane person cause emancipation of a maḥram relative despite lacking full legal capacity?
b: Because the slave's right to freedom is attached to the ownership itself, making it similar to maintenance (nafaqah), which can also become obligatory without full legal capacity.

f: 154. If someone frees a slave for Allah, for Satan, or for an idol, does emancipation occur?
b: Yes, the slave becomes free in all these cases.

f: 155. Why does emancipation remain valid if someone frees a slave for Satan or an idol?
b: Because the essential element (rukn) of emancipation exists: a qualified person performs emancipation over an appropriate slave. The intention of worship and seeking reward is only an additional description.

f: 156. Does the absence of intending worship invalidate manumission?
b: No, because the essential act of emancipation remains valid even if the additional intention is absent or corrupt.

f: 157. Is the emancipation of a person who is forced valid according to Al-Hidayah?
b: Yes, the emancipation of a person who is forced is valid.

f: 158. Is the emancipation of an intoxicated person valid?
b: Yes, the emancipation of an intoxicated person is valid.

f: 159. Why is the emancipation of a forced or intoxicated person valid?
b: Because the essential element of emancipation came from a person considered qualified and was directed toward a proper object, similar to the ruling in divorce.

f: 160. Can emancipation be attached to ownership or a future condition?
b: Yes, emancipation can be attached to ownership or made conditional upon something.

f: 161. What is the ruling if someone attaches emancipation to future ownership?
b: It is valid, although there is disagreement with al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, as discussed in the Book of Divorce.

f: 162. Why can emancipation be made conditional upon a future event?
b: Because emancipation is a relinquishment (isqāṭ), and relinquishments can be made conditional.

f: 163. Why can emancipation be conditional while ownership transfers (tamlikāt) generally cannot?
b: Because emancipation removes a right, whereas ownership transfers create or transfer ownership, and the two have different legal principles.

f: 164. If the slave of a non-Muslim in enemy territory enters Muslim lands as a Muslim, what is the ruling?
b: The slave becomes free.

f: 165. What hadith is used regarding slaves of al-Ṭāʾif who accepted Islam and came to the Prophet ﷺ?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "They are the freed ones of Allah."

f: 166. Why does a slave of a non-Muslim become free upon coming as a Muslim?
b: Because he has protected himself through Islam, and a Muslim cannot initially be enslaved.

f: 167. If a master frees a pregnant female slave, what is the ruling regarding her child?
b: The child is also freed along with her.

f: 168. Why is the child of a freed pregnant slave also free?
b: Because the child is connected to the mother.

f: 169. If a master frees only the fetus in a slave woman's womb, does the mother become free?
b: No, only the fetus becomes free and the mother does not.

f: 170. Why does freeing only the fetus not free the mother?
b: Because the statement was not directed toward the mother, and she does not become free as a consequence of the child because that would reverse the proper order.

f: 171. Is emancipation of a fetus itself valid?
b: Yes, the emancipation of the fetus is valid.

f: 172. Can a fetus that has been freed be sold?
b: No, selling the fetus is not valid.

f: 173. Can a fetus that has been freed be gifted?
b: No, gifting the fetus is not valid.

f: 174. Why can a fetus not be sold or gifted?
b: Because delivery (taslīm) is required for gifting and the ability to deliver is required for selling, and neither is possible with a fetus.

f: 175. Why is emancipation of a fetus valid even though selling and gifting it are invalid?
b: Because emancipation does not require delivery or the ability to deliver, unlike selling and gifting.

f: 176. If a master frees a fetus in exchange for wealth, is the emancipation valid?
b: Yes, the emancipation is valid, but the payment is not obligatory.

f: 177. Why is the payment not obligatory when freeing a fetus in exchange for wealth?
b: Because there is no legal basis for obligating payment upon the fetus, as it has no independent legal authority or responsibility.

f: 178. Can the payment for freeing a fetus be imposed upon the mother?
b: No, because in matters of emancipation the fetus is considered an independent person separate from the mother.

f: 179. Why cannot compensation for emancipation be stipulated upon someone other than the person being freed?
b: Because making emancipation compensation binding upon someone else is impermissible, similar to the ruling mentioned regarding khulʿ.

f: 180. How is the existence of the fetus at the time of emancipation determined?
b: It is known if the woman gives birth within less than six months after the emancipation, because six months is the minimum duration of pregnancy.

f: 181. What is the ruling regarding the child of a female slave from her master?
b: The child is free.

f: 182. Why is the child of a female slave from her master free?
b: Because the child was created from the master's fluid, so the child becomes free through him.

f: 183. What is the original principle regarding the child of a female slave and her master?
b: The child follows the master in freedom and becomes free.

f: 184. Why is there no opposing factor preventing the freedom of a child born from a female slave and her master?
b: Because the child of a female slave belongs to her master, so there is no conflicting claim preventing freedom.

f: 185. What is the ruling regarding the child of a female slave from her husband?
b: The child is owned by the woman's master.

f: 186. Why does the child of a female slave from her husband follow the mother rather than the father?
b: Because the mother's side is given preference due to custody (ḥaḍānah), and because the husband's fluid is considered mixed with hers, creating a conflict between following the father and following the mother.

f: 187. Why is the husband's consent considered when determining the status of the child of a female slave and her husband?
b: Because the husband willingly accepted the situation of having a child with a slave woman.

f: 188. How does the child of a female slave from her husband differ from the child of a maghrūr (a man deceived into marrying a slave woman thinking she was free)?
b: In the case of the maghrūr, the father did not consent to the situation, unlike the husband of the slave woman.

f: 189. What is the ruling regarding the child of a free woman?
b: The child is free in every circumstance.

f: 190. Why does the child of a free woman always follow her status of freedom?
b: Because the mother's side is stronger, so the child follows her in the quality of freedom.

f: 191. In which other matters does the child follow the mother according to Al-Hidayah?
b: The child follows the mother regarding ownership, slavery, being under a contract of manumission, being an umm walad, and being a mukātab.

f: 192. What principle explains why children follow the mother in these rulings?
b: The mother's side is stronger in these matters, so the child's legal status follows hers.

f: 193. If a master frees only part of his slave, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The freed portion becomes free, and the slave must perform sāʿayah (work to pay the remaining value) for his master.

f: 194. If a master frees only part of his slave, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The entire slave becomes free.

f: 195. What is the basis of the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his companions regarding freeing part of a slave?
b: The disagreement is whether emancipation can be divided (yatajazzaʾ) or whether freeing part of a slave applies to the entire slave.

f: 196. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider emancipation divisible?
b: Because emancipation is the removal of ownership, and ownership itself can be divided. Therefore, the master's action only affects the portion over which he exercised emancipation.

f: 197. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ consider emancipation indivisible?
b: Because emancipation establishes freedom, and freedom is a legal quality that cannot be divided; therefore, freeing part of a slave is treated like freeing the whole slave.

f: 198. What is the argument of those who say emancipation cannot be divided?
b: They argue that emancipation establishes freedom by removing slavery, and neither freedom nor slavery can be divided. Therefore, emancipation is indivisible.

f: 199. Which legal matters are compared to emancipation by those who say it cannot be divided?
b: Divorce, pardoning retaliation (qiṣāṣ), and making a slave woman an umm walad (istīlād).

f: 200. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the nature of emancipation?
b: It is the establishment of freedom through removing ownership, or the removal of ownership itself.

f: 201. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does emancipation only affect the portion of the slave that was freed?
b: Because a person's legal action only affects what is under his authority, and the master only has authority over removing his own ownership, not the right of slavery itself.

f: 202. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, who owns the right of ownership and who owns the right of slavery?
b: The master owns the right of ownership, while slavery is a right belonging to the Sharīʿah or the general public.

f: 203. What is the general principle regarding the scope of a person's legal action according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: A legal action is restricted to the thing to which it is directly attributed and only extends beyond it when necessity requires it because the matter cannot be divided.

f: 204. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say ownership can be divided?
b: Because ownership is divisible, as shown by transactions such as sales and gifts.

f: 205. Why does the partially freed slave have to perform sāʿayah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the remaining financial value of the master's ownership is still attached to the slave.

f: 206. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explain the status of a partially freed slave?
b: The slave is treated like a mukātab: he has possession and control over himself but does not have complete ownership of himself.

f: 207. Why is a partially freed slave compared to a mukātab according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because emancipation has established freedom in one respect, but the continuation of ownership over part of him prevents complete freedom.

f: 208. What is the sāʿayah payment of a partially freed slave compared to?
b: It is compared to the compensation paid in a contract of manumission (kitābah).

f: 209. Can a master require a partially freed slave to perform sāʿayah?
b: Yes, the master may require him to work and pay the remaining value.

f: 210. Does a master have the option to completely free a partially emancipated slave?
b: Yes, the master may choose to free him completely.

f: 211. Why can a master completely free a partially emancipated slave?
b: Because a mukātab can be freed, and the partially freed slave is treated similarly to a mukātab.

f: 212. If a partially freed slave becomes unable to complete his sāʿayah payments, does he return to slavery?
b: No, he does not return to slavery.

f: 213. Why does a partially freed slave not return to slavery if he becomes unable to pay?
b: Because emancipation is a relinquishment (isqāṭ), and a relinquishment does not return once it has occurred.

f: 214. How does partial emancipation differ from a normal contract of emancipation (kitābah)?
b: Kitābah is a contract that can be concluded and cancelled, whereas emancipation is a relinquishment that cannot be reversed.

f: 215. Why does partial emancipation differ from divorce and pardoning retaliation (qiṣāṣ) regarding whether the ruling applies to the whole?
b: Because unlike divorce and pardoning retaliation, partial emancipation has an intermediate state where part of the slave is free and part remains under ownership, so the ruling is not necessarily applied to the whole.

f: 216. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can istīlād (making a slave woman an umm walad) be divided?
b: Yes, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, istīlād can be divided.

f: 217. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens if someone makes his share of a mudabbar slave into an umm walad?
b: The istīlād only applies to his share of the slave.

f: 218. In the case of an ordinary slave woman (qinnah), why can istīlād become complete after compensation?
b: Because when the owner compensates his partner for the partner's share due to causing damage, he acquires that share, causing the istīlād to become complete.

f: 219. If a slave is owned by two partners and one partner frees his share, what happens according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The freed partner's share becomes free, while the remaining share requires further action according to the circumstances of the partners.

f: 220. If one partner frees his share of a jointly owned slave and the emancipating partner is wealthy, what options does the other partner have according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The other partner may: (1) free his own share, (2) demand compensation from the emancipating partner for the value of his share, or (3) require the slave to perform sāʿayah.

f: 221. If the non-emancipating partner demands compensation from the wealthy partner who freed his share, who owns the right of walāʾ?
b: The walāʾ belongs to the emancipating partner.

f: 222. If the non-emancipating partner chooses to free his own share or require sāʿayah from the slave, who owns the walāʾ?
b: The walāʾ belongs to both partners.

f: 223. If one partner frees his share of a jointly owned slave and the emancipating partner is poor, what options does the other partner have according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: He may either free the slave or require the slave to perform sāʿayah.

f: 224. If the emancipating partner is poor and the other partner frees the slave or requires sāʿayah, who owns the walāʾ?
b: The walāʾ belongs to both partners in both cases.

f: 225. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ when one partner frees his share of a jointly owned slave?
b: They say the other partner has no choice except compensation if the emancipator is wealthy and sāʿayah if the emancipator is poor.

f: 226. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, can the emancipating partner recover the compensation he paid from the slave?
b: No, he cannot recover anything from the slave.

f: 227. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, who receives the walāʾ when one partner frees his share?
b: The walāʾ belongs only to the emancipating partner.

f: 228. What are the two principles upon which the ruling of a jointly owned slave being partially freed is based?
b: The two principles are: (1) whether emancipation can be divided, and (2) whether the wealth of the emancipator prevents requiring sāʿayah.

f: 229. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view the wealth of the emancipator regarding requiring sāʿayah?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the emancipator's wealth does not prevent requiring sāʿayah.

f: 230. How do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ view the wealth of the emancipator regarding requiring sāʿayah?
b: They hold that if the emancipator is wealthy, sāʿayah is not required; instead, compensation must be paid.

f: 231. What hadith do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ use regarding freeing a share of a jointly owned slave?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said regarding a person who frees his share: "If he is wealthy, he compensates; and if he is poor, the slave works for the share of the other."

f: 232. How do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ argue that emancipation cannot be divided in the case of a jointly owned slave?
b: They argue that division contradicts the reality of partnership, because a slave jointly owned by two people cannot properly be divided into separate states of freedom and slavery.

f: 233. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the non-emancipating partner have the right to demand compensation when one partner frees his share of a jointly owned slave?
b: Because the financial value of the partner's remaining share has become attached to the slave, so the partner has the right to demand its value.

f: 234. What example does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to explain why compensation becomes necessary?
b: He compares it to a person's garment being blown into another person's dye, causing it to absorb the dye; the garment owner must pay for the value of the dye regardless of whether he is wealthy or poor.

f: 235. Why does the slave perform sāʿayah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ after one partner frees his share?
b: Because the slave himself is poor, so he works to provide the compensation for the remaining share.

f: 236. What type of wealth is considered when determining whether the emancipator is wealthy according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Wealth of ability (yusār al-taysīr), meaning that he owns property equal to the value of the other partner's share.

f: 237. Why is wealth of ability considered the relevant type of wealth in this issue?
b: Because true wealth is that which allows the interests of both sides to be balanced: fulfilling the emancipator's intention of worship and compensating the silent partner for his right.

f: 238. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why does the emancipator not recover compensation from the slave?
b: Because they do not require sāʿayah when the emancipator is wealthy, so there is no basis for the emancipator recovering payment from the slave.

f: 239. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why does the walāʾ belong only to the emancipator?
b: Because they hold that emancipation is not divisible, so all freedom came through the emancipator.

f: 240. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the other partner have the option to free his remaining share?
b: Because the other partner's ownership remains over his share, since Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considers emancipation divisible.

f: 241. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the other partner have the option to demand compensation from the emancipator?
b: Because the emancipator harmed his partner by preventing him from benefiting from his share through selling, gifting, and similar actions, except for emancipation and its consequences.

f: 242. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the other partner have the option of requiring sāʿayah?
b: Because the slave must provide compensation for the remaining ownership attached to him.

f: 243. Why can the emancipator recover the compensation he paid from the slave according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the emancipator takes the position of the silent partner by paying the compensation, and the silent partner originally had the right to receive payment through sāʿayah.

f: 244. How does the emancipator indirectly acquire ownership of the remaining share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: By paying compensation for his partner's share, he acquires the partner's right indirectly, making it as though the entire slave belongs to him.

f: 245. After the emancipator acquires the remaining share through compensation, what options does he have according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: He may either free the remaining share completely or require the slave to perform sāʿayah.

f: 246. Why does the walāʾ belong to the emancipator when he acquires the remaining share through compensation?
b: Because all freedom came through him after he acquired the remaining share by paying compensation.

f: 247. If one partner frees his share of a jointly owned slave and the emancipator is poor, what options does he have according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: He may either free the slave completely because his ownership remains, or require the slave to perform sāʿayah.

f: 248. If the emancipator is poor and chooses to free the slave completely, who receives the walāʾ according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The walāʾ belongs to the emancipator because the emancipation came from him.

f: 249. If the emancipator is poor and requires sāʿayah from the slave, who receives the walāʾ according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The walāʾ still belongs to the emancipator because the emancipation originated from him.

f: 250. If a slave performs sāʿayah after partial emancipation, can he recover the amount he paid from the emancipator?
b: No, according to the agreement of the scholars, he cannot recover what he paid from the emancipator.

f: 251. Why does a slave performing sāʿayah not recover his payments from the emancipator?
b: Because he is working to free himself, not to repay a debt owed by the emancipator.

f: 252. Why is the emancipator not responsible for the slave's sāʿayah payments when he is poor?
b: Because his poverty means there is no obligation upon him to compensate the other partner.

f: 253. How does this differ from the case of a mortgaged slave (rahn) whose debtor frees him while insolvent?
b: In the case of the mortgaged slave, the person works either to free a slave whose freedom has already been established or to repay a debt owed by the debtor, so he has a right of recovery.

f: 254. What is al-Shāfiʿī's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position regarding the wealthy partner who frees his share of a jointly owned slave?
b: His position regarding the wealthy person is similar to the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ.

f: 255. What is al-Shāfiʿī's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position regarding the insolvent partner who frees his share of a jointly owned slave?
b: He holds that the remaining share of the silent partner remains under his ownership and may be sold or gifted.

f: 256. Why does al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argue that the remaining share should remain owned by the silent partner when the emancipator is insolvent?
b: Because the partner cannot be forced to compensate due to insolvency, the slave cannot be made to work because he is not responsible for what occurred, and freeing the entire slave would harm the silent partner.

f: 257. How does the Ḥanafī response answer al-Shāfiʿī's argument that the slave cannot be required to work?
b: They argue that there is a way to make the slave work toward freedom because this obligation is not based on wrongdoing but on the financial value of ownership becoming attached to him.

f: 258. Why is it incorrect to leave the partially freed slave in both a state of ownership and a state of being unable to gain freedom according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because one person cannot simultaneously possess the strength that establishes ownership and the weakness that removes it.

f: 259. If two partners each testify that the other partner freed the jointly owned slave, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The slave must perform sāʿayah to pay the value of each partner's share, whether both partners are wealthy or poor.

f: 260. Does the ruling of sāʿayah change if one partner is wealthy and the other is poor in the case where both testify against each other?
b: No, the same ruling applies whether both are wealthy, both are poor, or one is wealthy and the other is poor.

f: 261. Why does each partner's testimony that the other freed the slave make the slave like a mukātab according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because each partner is making a claim that his partner freed his share, so the slave becomes like a mukātab regarding that partner's claim.

f: 262. Why can a partner not enslave the slave again after claiming that his partner freed him?
b: Because a person is believed regarding his own rights, so the partner's claim prevents him from returning the slave to slavery.

f: 263. Why does each partner require the slave to work toward freedom whether the claim of emancipation is true or false?
b: Because the slave has a right to work toward freedom in either case: if the claim is true, he is a mukātab; if false, he remains a slave whose freedom is still being pursued.

f: 264. Why does the wealth of the partners not affect the obligation of sāʿayah in the case where each partner testifies against the other?
b: Because the slave's right can only be fulfilled in one of two ways: compensation from the wealthy partner or sāʿayah by the slave. Since compensation is impossible due to the denial of the other partner, sāʿayah remains.

f: 265. Who receives the walāʾ when both partners testify against each other that the other freed the slave?
b: The walāʾ belongs to both partners.

f: 266. Why does each partner receive a share of the walāʾ in this case?
b: Because each partner claims that the other's share became free through the other's emancipation, while his own share became free through the slave's payments toward freedom.

f: 267. If two partners both claim that the other freed his share of a jointly owned slave and both partners are wealthy, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The slave is not required to perform sāʿayah (work toward freedom) for either partner.

f: 268. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that a slave does not perform sāʿayah when both partners who claim emancipation are wealthy?
b: Because each partner rejects responsibility for the slave's payment by claiming that the other partner freed his share, and according to them the wealth of the emancipator removes the need for sāʿayah.

f: 269. In the case where two wealthy partners deny responsibility for freeing a slave, why is the obligation of sāʿayah removed according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: Because each partner's own admission establishes the removal of the sāʿayah obligation from himself, even though the actual emancipation is not established due to the other partner's denial.

f: 270. If two partners both claim that the other freed his share of a jointly owned slave and both partners are poor, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The slave performs sāʿayah for both partners.

f: 271. Why does a slave perform sāʿayah for both poor partners when each claims the other freed the slave?
b: Because each partner claims that the slave must work toward freedom for him, and this remains true whether the claim is correct or mistaken.

f: 272. If two partners both claim that the other freed his share of a jointly owned slave, and one partner is wealthy while the other is poor, for whom does the slave perform sāʿayah according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The slave performs sāʿayah for the wealthy partner only.

f: 273. Why does the slave perform sāʿayah for the wealthy partner but not the poor partner according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The wealthy partner does not claim compensation from his partner due to his poverty, so he maintains the obligation of sāʿayah. The poor partner claims compensation from the wealthy partner, so he removes the obligation of sāʿayah.

f: 274. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what happens to the walāʾ when two partners dispute who freed the slave?
b: The walāʾ remains suspended until they agree upon who actually caused the emancipation.

f: 275. Why does the walāʾ remain suspended according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ when both partners attribute emancipation to each other?
b: Because each partner attributes the emancipation to the other while the other denies responsibility, so the cause of walāʾ is uncertain.

f: 276. If one partner says, "If a person does not enter this house tomorrow, then the slave is free," and the other partner says, "If he enters, then the slave is free," and it becomes unknown whether the person entered, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: Half of the slave becomes free, and the slave performs sāʿayah for the value of the remaining half.

f: 277. If two partners attach emancipation to opposite conditions and it becomes unknown whether the condition occurred, what is the ruling according to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The slave must perform sāʿayah for his entire value.

f: 278. Why does Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say that the slave must perform sāʿayah for his entire value when it is unknown which condition occurred?
b: Because the person from whom the obligation of sāʿayah was removed is unknown, and a judgment cannot be issued regarding an unknown matter.

f: 279. What example does Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to support his argument that judgment cannot be based on an unknown matter?
b: He compares it to a person saying: "You owe one thousand dirhams to one of us," where no judgment can be issued because the creditor is unknown.

f: 280. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ respond to Muḥammad's argument regarding uncertainty?
b: They argue that half of the obligation of sāʿayah is certainly removed because one of the two conditions must have occurred, so it is incorrect to judge that the entire obligation remains.

f: 281. How is the uncertainty in this issue resolved according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: It is resolved through division and distribution, similar to freeing one of two slaves without specifying which one, or forgetting which specified slave was freed before death.

f: 282. What previous disagreement affects the ruling of whether sāʿayah is required in this conditional emancipation case?
b: The disagreement over whether the wealth of the emancipator prevents the slave from performing sāʿayah or not.

f: 283. If two partners swear oaths concerning two separate slaves, with each slave belonging exclusively to one partner, does either slave become free?
b: No, neither slave becomes free.

f: 284. Why does no slave become free when two partners swear oaths concerning two different slaves?
b: Because both the slave upon whom freedom would be judged and the person receiving the judgment are unknown, causing excessive uncertainty that prevents a legal ruling.

f: 285. How does the case of two slaves differ from the case of one slave where the partners dispute emancipation?
b: In the case of one slave, the person receiving freedom and the subject of the judgment are known, so the known aspect outweighs the uncertainty.

f: 286. If two men purchase a slave who is the son of one of them, what happens to the father's share according to Al-Hidayah?
b: The father's share becomes free because purchasing a close relative functions as emancipation.

f: 287. If a father and another partner purchase the father's son as a slave, is compensation due from the father for the other partner's share?
b: No, there is no compensation due from the father.

f: 288. Does it matter whether the other partner knew that the purchased slave was the father's son when determining whether compensation is due?
b: No, compensation is not due whether the partner knew or did not know.

f: 289. If two men inherit a slave who is the close relative of one of them, what options does the relative owner have according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: He may either free his share or require the slave to perform sāʿayah.

f: 290. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what happens when two men purchase a slave who is the son of one of them?
b: The father must compensate for half of the slave's value if he is wealthy; if he is poor, the son must perform sāʿayah to pay half his value to the father's partner.

f: 291. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what other forms of acquiring ownership have the same ruling as purchasing a relative?
b: Gifts, charity, and bequests have the same disagreement.

f: 292. If two men purchase a slave and one partner had sworn, "If I purchase him, he is free," what happens according to the ruling of Al-Hidayah?
b: His purchase causes emancipation, and the other partner's share is affected because purchasing a close relative functions as emancipation.

f: 293. What previous case is the purchase of a relative compared to when one partner's purchase causes emancipation of a jointly owned slave?
b: It is compared to the case where two unrelated partners own a slave and one partner frees his share.

f: 294. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning that no compensation is due when a father acquires his son's share through purchase?
b: The other partner accepted the destruction of his own share because he entered into a partnership in the very cause that produces emancipation: purchasing the relative.

f: 295. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ compare this case to someone permitting another person to free his share of a slave?
b: Because in both cases the partner has effectively accepted the loss of his ownership, so compensation is not required.

f: 296. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider purchasing a close relative to be a cause of emancipation?
b: Because purchasing a permanently unmarriageable relative (maḥram) causes automatic emancipation according to the established ruling.

f: 297. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why is compensation required in the case of purchasing a relative?
b: Because they view the compensation as payment for damage caused to the other partner's ownership.

f: 298. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why does the amount of compensation differ depending on whether the person is wealthy or poor?
b: Because compensation for damage depends upon the person's financial ability.

f: 299. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, when can compensation for the partner's share fall away?
b: It falls away if the partner consented to the loss of his share.

f: 300. Why does the ruling not change whether the partner knew or did not know that the purchased slave was the father's son?
b: Because the ruling is attached to the cause itself (purchasing the relative), not to the person's knowledge of the cause.

f: 301. What example does Al-Hidayah give to show that a ruling can apply even when the person is unaware of the relevant cause?
b: If someone tells another person, "Eat this food," while not knowing that the food actually belongs to him, the permission still applies because the ruling is attached to the cause itself.

f: 302. If an outsider first purchases half of a slave who is the son of another person, and then the father purchases the remaining half while wealthy, what options does the outsider have according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The outsider may either demand compensation from the father for his share or require the son to perform sāʿayah to pay half his value.

f: 303. Why can the outsider demand compensation when the father purchases the remaining half of his son according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the outsider did not consent to the destruction of his ownership share.

f: 304. Why can the outsider require the son to perform sāʿayah when the father purchases the remaining half according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the financial value of his ownership share has become attached to the slave due to the father's action.

f: 305. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ allow sāʿayah even though the father who caused emancipation is wealthy?
b: Because according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the wealth of the person who frees a share does not prevent the slave from performing sāʿayah.

f: 306. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what happens if an outsider owns half of a slave and the father purchases the remaining half while wealthy?
b: The outsider has no choice, and the father must compensate for half the slave's value.

f: 307. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ require compensation from the father in this case?
b: Because they hold that the wealth of the person who causes emancipation prevents the slave from performing sāʿayah.

f: 308. If a man purchases half of his son while wealthy from someone who owns the entire slave, does he owe compensation according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, he does not owe compensation.

f: 309. If a man purchases half of his son while wealthy, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: He must compensate the seller for the value of the share he acquired.

f: 310. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say that a father who purchases half of his son does not owe compensation to the seller?
b: Because the reasoning is based on the principle that the partner accepted the consequence of emancipation occurring through the purchase of the relative.

f: 311. If a slave is jointly owned by three people and one partner makes his share a mudabbar while wealthy, then another partner frees his share while wealthy, what may the silent partner demand according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The silent partner may demand from the mudabbir one-third of the slave's value as an ordinary slave (qinn), but he cannot demand anything from the partner who freed his share.

f: 312. In the three-partner case where one partner made his share a mudabbar and another freed his share, why can the silent partner demand compensation from the mudabbir but not from the emancipating partner according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the mudabbir's action affected the silent partner's share while the other partner's emancipation did not create a claim against him in the same way.

f: 313. In the three-partner case according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what can the mudabbir demand from the partner who freed his share?
b: The mudabbir may demand one-third of the slave's value calculated as a mudabbar.

f: 314. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can the mudabbir demand from the emancipating partner the amount that the mudabbir himself paid as compensation?
b: No, the mudabbir cannot demand from him the third that he himself compensated.

f: 315. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if one of three partners makes his share a mudabbar and another partner frees his share?
b: The entire slave belongs to the first partner who made him a mudabbar, and he must compensate both partners for two-thirds of the slave's value.

f: 316. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, does the mudabbir's wealth affect his obligation to compensate the other partners?
b: No, he must compensate whether he is wealthy or poor.

f: 317. What is the basis of the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding making a slave a mudabbar?
b: The disagreement is whether tadbīr (making a slave free after the owner's death) is divisible (yatajazzaʾ). Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ holds that it is divisible, while Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad hold that it is not.

f: 318. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider tadbīr divisible?
b: Because tadbīr is a branch of emancipation (iʿtāq), and emancipation is divisible according to him, so tadbīr follows the same ruling.

f: 319. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what portion of a jointly owned slave becomes mudabbar when one partner makes him a mudabbar?
b: Only the share of the partner who made him a mudabbar becomes mudabbar.

f: 320. If one partner makes his share of a jointly owned slave a mudabbar according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why do the other partners have rights over their shares?
b: Because their ownership remains, although it has been damaged by the first partner's action.

f: 321. How does making a jointly owned slave a mudabbar damage the other partners' ownership according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It prevents them from benefiting from their shares through sale, gifting, and similar transactions.

f: 322. What options do the other partners have if one partner makes his share of a jointly owned slave a mudabbar according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: They may make their share a mudabbar, free it, enter into a kitābah contract with the slave, demand compensation from the mudabbir, require the slave to perform istisʿāʾ (work toward freedom), or leave him as he is.

f: 323. If one partner chooses to free his share after another partner has made his share a mudabbar, what happens to the choices of the other partners?
b: Once one partner chooses emancipation, his right becomes established in the slave and the other partners' options fall away.

f: 324. What two possible causes of compensation exist for the silent partner when one partner makes his share a mudabbar and another later frees his share?
b: The two causes are: (1) the first partner's tadbīr, and (2) the second partner's emancipation.

f: 325. Why may the silent partner demand compensation from the mudabbir rather than the partner who freed his share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because compensation from the mudabbir is considered compensation in exchange (ḍamān muʿāwaḍah), which is the original type of compensation.

f: 326. Why is compensation from the mudabbir possible in the case of tadbīr?
b: Because at the time tadbīr occurs, the slave can still be transferred from one ownership to another.

f: 327. Why is compensation from the emancipator not possible after emancipation according to this explanation?
b: Because after emancipation the slave has become either a mukātab or free, and a mukātab cannot be returned from his status without his consent, so ownership transfer is no longer possible.

f: 328. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does compensation come from the mudabbir rather than the emancipator?
b: Because ownership transfer was still possible when tadbīr occurred, allowing compensation to be treated as an exchange for the damaged ownership.

f: 329. After compensating the silent partner, how much can the mudabbir demand from the partner who freed his share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The mudabbir may demand one-third of the slave's value calculated as a mudabbar.

f: 330. Why can the mudabbir demand compensation from the partner who freed his share?
b: Because the emancipator damaged the mudabbir's share while it was still in the state of tadbīr.

f: 331. How is compensation measured when a mudabbar's share is damaged?
b: Compensation is measured according to the value of the thing damaged, and the value of a mudabbar is considered two-thirds of the value of an ordinary slave (qinn) according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ.

f: 332. Why does the mudabbir not demand from the emancipator the value of the share acquired through compensation from the silent partner?
b: Because that ownership is established retroactively (mustanad) and only from one perspective, so it does not become effective for matters of compensation.

f: 333. How is the walāʾ divided when a slave becomes free after being partly owned by a mudabbir and partly by an emancipator?
b: Two-thirds of the walāʾ belongs to the mudabbir and one-third belongs to the emancipator.

f: 334. Why does the walāʾ belong two-thirds to the mudabbir and one-third to the emancipator?
b: Because the slave became free while owned by both of them in those proportions.

f: 335. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what happens if tadbīr is not considered divisible and one partner makes his share of a jointly owned slave a mudabbar?
b: The entire slave becomes a mudabbar belonging to the partner who made him a mudabbar.

f: 336. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why must the mudabbir compensate the other partners if tadbīr is indivisible?
b: Because his action affected and damaged the shares of his partners by making the entire slave a mudabbar.

f: 337. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, does the mudabbir's wealth affect whether he must compensate the other partners?
b: No, compensation is required whether he is wealthy or poor.

f: 338. Why is compensation required from the mudabbir according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, regardless of wealth?
b: Because it is compensation for acquiring ownership (ḍamān tamalluk), not compensation for causing damage (ḍamān jināyah).

f: 339. What case is compensation for a mudabbir compared to according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: It is compared to istīlād, where a man makes his slave woman the mother of his child.

f: 340. How does compensation for tadbīr differ from compensation for emancipation according to this discussion?
b: Compensation in tadbīr is compensation for acquiring ownership (ḍamān tamalluk), while compensation in emancipation is compensation for causing damage (ḍamān jināyah).

f: 341. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, who receives the entire walāʾ when one partner makes a jointly owned slave a mudabbar and tadbīr is indivisible?
b: The entire walāʾ belongs to the mudabbir.

f: 342. If a slave woman is jointly owned by two men and one partner claims that she is an Umm Walad of his partner while the other partner denies it, what is her status according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: She is suspended between them: one day she serves one partner and the next day she serves the partner who denies the claim.

f: 343. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what can the denying partner do if his partner claims that the slave woman is his Umm Walad?
b: He may require the slave woman to perform istisʿāʾ (work toward paying half her value), after which she becomes free and no one has authority over her.

f: 344. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say the slave woman should perform istisʿāʾ when one partner claims she is an Umm Walad and the other denies it?
b: Because the denial means the claimant's acknowledgment does not establish the status of Umm Walad for the other partner, so the remaining share is treated like ownership that must be compensated through work.

f: 345. What analogy do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ use for treating the claimant as if he caused the slave woman to become an Umm Walad?
b: They compare it to a purchaser admitting that the item he bought had already been freed before the sale, where the purchaser is treated as though he himself freed it.

f: 346. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why should the slave woman's service stop after she is treated as an Umm Walad?
b: Because the claimant's acknowledgment establishes the status of Umm Walad, while the denying partner's remaining ownership is dealt with through istisʿāʾ.

f: 347. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to the argument that the claimant's statement should make the woman an Umm Walad completely?
b: He argues that the claimant's statement cannot be treated like an actual act of making her an Umm Walad because the claimant is only reporting a status, not creating it.

f: 348. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what amount of service is certainly established when one partner claims a slave woman is an Umm Walad and the other denies it?
b: Half of the service is certainly established.

f: 349. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say only half the service is certain in the dispute over whether a slave woman is an Umm Walad?
b: Because if the claimant is truthful, all service belongs to the denying partner, and if he is not believed, half the service belongs to the claimant; therefore, the certain amount is half.

f: 350. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the claimant partner not receive service rights or require istisʿāʾ?
b: Because his claim that she is an Umm Walad removes those rights by acknowledging her status and accepting the consequences of that acknowledgment.

f: 351. Why does acknowledging a slave woman as an Umm Walad also acknowledge the child's lineage according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because establishing her as an Umm Walad necessarily includes accepting the lineage of the child.

f: 352. Why can the claimant partner not be treated like someone who actually made the slave woman an Umm Walad according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because he is only making an acknowledgment of an existing status, and he cannot create the same legal consequences as the actual act of making her an Umm Walad.

f: 353. If an Umm Walad jointly belongs to two people and one partner frees her while wealthy, is compensation due according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, no compensation is due from him.

f: 354. If an Umm Walad jointly belongs to two people and one partner frees her while wealthy, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: He must compensate his partner for half her value.

f: 355. What is the basis of the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding compensation for a jointly owned Umm Walad?
b: The disagreement is whether the financial value (mālīyyah) of an Umm Walad is legally recognized. Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ does not recognize it, while Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad do.

f: 356. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ consider an Umm Walad to have financial value?
b: Because she has valuable benefits, such as sexual use, being hired out, and being employed.

f: 357. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why does the inability to sell an Umm Walad not remove her financial value?
b: Because loss of the ability to sell does not necessarily remove financial value, just as a mudabbar still has financial value despite restrictions on sale.

f: 358. What example do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ give as evidence that an Umm Walad has financial value?
b: The case where the son of a Christian Umm Walad becomes Muslim and she is required to work toward freedom (istisʿāʾ).

f: 359. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what is the estimated value of an Umm Walad compared to an ordinary slave woman?
b: Her value is considered one-third of the value of an ordinary slave woman.

f: 360. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ consider the value of an Umm Walad to be only one-third of an ordinary slave woman's value?
b: Because the benefit of selling her is lost, although the benefits of service and working toward freedom remain.

f: 361. How do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ distinguish an Umm Walad from a mudabbar regarding financial value?
b: In an Umm Walad, the benefit of sale is lost permanently, while in a mudabbar only the benefit of sale is restricted until the owner's death.

f: 362. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how is financial value established?
b: Financial value is established through preservation (iḥrāz).

f: 363. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why is an Umm Walad preserved?
b: She is preserved because of lineage and the relationship created through her child, not because she has financial value.

f: 364. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does preservation due to lineage not establish financial value for an Umm Walad?
b: Because preservation for financial value is secondary, whereas her preservation occurs because of lineage.

f: 365. What evidence does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ give that an Umm Walad does not have recognized financial value?
b: She does not work toward repayment for a creditor or heir, unlike a mudabbar.

f: 366. Why does an Umm Walad not work toward repayment of a creditor or heir according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because the cause removing her financial value already exists during her owner's lifetime due to the relationship established through the child.

f: 367. How does the child relationship of an Umm Walad affect her ownership status according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The relationship functions to remove her financial value, similar to how kinship creates permanent marriage prohibition.

f: 368. Why does the effect of the cause of lineage not completely appear regarding ownership of an Umm Walad?
