b: Because there remains a necessity to benefit from her during the owner's lifetime.

f: 369. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish an Umm Walad from a mudabbar regarding the timing of the cause affecting ownership?
b: In an Umm Walad, the cause exists immediately through the child, while in a mudabbar the effect only occurs after death.

f: 370. Why is sale prevented for a mudabbar according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because preventing sale fulfills the purpose of tadbīr (the promise of freedom after death).

f: 371. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explain the case of a Christian Umm Walad whose son becomes Muslim?
b: He explains that she enters into a form of kitābah with her master to remove harm from both sides.

f: 372. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, does the payment required in kitābah for a Christian Umm Walad who becomes Muslim depend upon her having recognized financial value?
b: No, kitābah payment does not require her financial value to be legally recognized.

f: 373. If a man owns three slaves, says "One of you two is free" to two slaves present, then one leaves, another enters, and he again says "One of you two is free," what happens if he dies without clarifying according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: The slave present in both declarations becomes three-quarters free, while each of the other two slaves becomes half free.

f: 374. In the case where a master makes two statements of "One of you two is free" among three slaves and dies without clarification, what is the ruling according to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The continuing slave becomes three-quarters free, the first slave becomes half free, and the later entering slave becomes one-quarter free.

f: 375. Why does the slave who was present in the first declaration become half free?
b: Because the first declaration was between him and the slave who remained, and since both were equally possible recipients, the emancipation is divided equally between them.

f: 376. Why does the slave who remained present in both declarations become three-quarters free according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: Because he receives half freedom from the first declaration and an additional quarter from the second declaration.

f: 377. How is the additional quarter of freedom for the continuing slave calculated from the second declaration?
b: The second declaration is divided equally between him and the newly entered slave, giving each half; however, part of his share overlaps with his already existing half-freedom, so only one-quarter remains effective.

f: 378. Why does the second declaration not give the continuing slave a full additional half according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: Because part of that half overlaps with the freedom he already received from the first declaration, so the overlapping portion is disregarded.

f: 379. Why does Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say the later entering slave receives only one-quarter freedom?
b: Because the second declaration is between him and the continuing slave, and since the continuing slave receives one-quarter from that declaration, the later slave should also receive one-quarter.

f: 380. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ disagree with Muḥammad regarding the later entering slave?
b: They say the second declaration is originally divided equally between the two slaves; the continuing slave receives only one-quarter because of his previous half-freedom, while this does not apply to the new slave, so he receives half.

f: 381. If a master makes these emancipation statements during his terminal illness, how is the emancipation treated?
b: It is treated like a bequest, so only one-third of the estate can be used for emancipation.

f: 382. In the terminal illness case, why is emancipation limited to one-third?
b: Because emancipation during terminal illness has the ruling of a bequest, and a bequest cannot exceed one-third without the heirs' consent.

f: 383. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, how are the freedom shares calculated among the three slaves?
b: The continuing slave has 3 shares of freedom, and each of the other two slaves has 2 shares, making 7 total freedom shares.

f: 384. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, how is the one-third emancipation limit calculated in the terminal illness case?
b: The estate is divided into 21 shares so that 7 shares of freedom equal one-third of the total.

f: 385. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, how much freedom does the continuing slave receive in the terminal illness calculation?
b: He receives 3 shares of freedom and must work to pay for the remaining 4 shares.

f: 386. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, how much freedom do the other two slaves receive in the terminal illness calculation?
b: Each receives 2 shares of freedom and must work to pay for the remaining 5 shares.

f: 387. In the terminal illness case according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, what portion remains for the heirs?
b: Two-thirds of the estate remains for the heirs after one-third is used for emancipation.

f: 388. Why does the calculation differ according to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ in the terminal illness case?
b: Because he assigns the later entering slave one-quarter freedom rather than one-half, which changes the total shares.

f: 389. If a master makes an ambiguous emancipation statement regarding two slaves and dies without clarification, how are the shares treated differently if the case is divorce instead of emancipation?
b: The case is treated through reduction of dowries rather than division of freedom shares.

f: 390. If a husband says regarding two women "One of you is divorced," the women were not consummated with, and he dies before clarification, how much is the dowry of the woman who left reduced according to the discussion?
b: Her dowry is reduced by one-quarter.

f: 391. If a husband says regarding two women "One of you is divorced," the women were not consummated with, and he dies before clarification, how much is the dowry of the woman who remained reduced?
b: Her dowry is reduced by three-eighths.

f: 392. If a husband says regarding two women "One of you is divorced," the women were not consummated with, and he dies before clarification, how much is the dowry of the later entering woman reduced?
b: Her dowry is reduced by one-eighth.

f: 393. Is the division of dowry reductions in the ambiguous divorce case attributed only to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Some scholars attribute it specifically to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, while others say it is also the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ.

f: 394. If a person says to two slaves "One of you is free," and one slave is later sold, who becomes free?
b: The remaining slave becomes free.

f: 395. If a person says to two slaves "One of you is free," and one slave dies before clarification, who becomes free?
b: The remaining slave becomes free.

f: 396. If a person says to two slaves "One of you is free," then makes one of them a mudabbar, who becomes free immediately?
b: The other remaining slave becomes free.

f: 397. Why does the remaining slave become identified when one of two slaves mentioned in an ambiguous emancipation statement dies, is sold, or becomes a mudabbar?
b: Because the other slave is the only remaining person capable of receiving the emancipation.

f: 398. Why does death remove a slave from being a possible recipient of emancipation?
b: Because the deceased is no longer a living legal subject who can become free.

f: 399. Why does sale remove a slave from being a possible recipient of emancipation?
b: Because ownership has ended, and emancipation can only occur over something owned.

f: 400. Why does making one slave a mudabbar remove him from immediate emancipation?
b: Because his freedom has been attached to a future condition rather than immediate emancipation.

f: 401. Does the same principle apply if a man says regarding two wives "One of you is divorced" and one wife dies?
b: Yes, the remaining wife becomes identified as the one divorced.

f: 402. If a man says to two female slaves "One of you is free" and then has intercourse with one of them, do both Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his companions agree on the ruling?
b: No. Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says the other slave does not become free, while Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say she becomes free.

f: 403. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why does the other female slave become free when the master has intercourse with one of two slaves after saying "One of you is free"?
b: Because intercourse is only lawful with a slave whom he still owns, so the one he had intercourse with must have remained his slave, meaning the other one must have been freed.

f: 404. What analogy do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ use for the case where intercourse clarifies which slave remained owned?
b: They compare it to divorce, where intercourse can indicate the continuation of marriage.

f: 405. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the other female slave not become free when the master has intercourse with one of two slaves after saying "One of you is free"?
b: Because the emancipation was attached to an unspecified individual, and intercourse does not necessarily identify which slave remained in ownership.

f: 406. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does intercourse clarify the matter in divorce but not in emancipation of female slaves?
b: Because intercourse with wives is primarily connected to preserving marriage and producing children, whereas intercourse with female slaves is primarily for fulfilling desire and does not indicate preservation of ownership.

f: 407. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does the original uncertainty remain after intercourse with one of two female slaves?
b: Because intercourse only proves that the person was treated as a slave, but it does not prove that she was the one excluded from the original emancipation statement.

f: 408. If a master says to his female slave, "If the first child you give birth to is a boy, then you are free," and she gives birth to a boy and a girl but it is unknown which was born first, what is the ruling?
b: The mother becomes half free, the girl becomes half free, and the boy remains a slave.

f: 409. Why does the mother become half free in the case where the condition is "If your first child is a boy, you are free" but the order of birth is unknown?
b: Because she has two possible states: she is free if the boy was born first and remains a slave if the girl was born first, so half of her freedom is established.

f: 410. Why does the daughter become half free in the case where the order of birth is unknown?
b: Because if the boy was born first, the mother became free before the girl's birth and the girl was born to a free woman; if the girl was born first, she remains a slave. Therefore, half of her status is freedom.

f: 411. Why does the boy remain a slave when the order of birth is unknown in the conditional emancipation case?
b: Because in both certain possibilities he is not established as free: if he is first, he causes the mother's freedom but is not born to a free woman; if he is second, his freedom depends on a doubtful matter that is not established.

f: 412. What principle explains why the mother and daughter receive half freedom while the son remains a slave in the case of uncertain birth order?
b: The mother and daughter each have two possible states (free and slave), while the son remains enslaved in both established possibilities.

f: 413. If two witnesses testify that a man freed one of his two slaves but do not specify which slave, is the testimony accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, the testimony is invalid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, except if it concerns a bequest (waṣiyyah).

f: 414. Why is testimony regarding an unspecified emancipated slave invalid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because according to him, testimony of emancipation requires a claim (daʿwā) from the slave, and an unknown slave cannot make such a claim.

f: 415. Why is the exception of a bequest (waṣiyyah) mentioned in the ruling of testimony for unspecified emancipation according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because it is an exceptional ruling established through istiḥsān (juristic preference).

f: 416. If two witnesses testify that a man divorced one of his wives without specifying which wife, is their testimony accepted?
b: Yes, the testimony is accepted, and the husband is compelled to divorce one of them.

f: 417. Do the three Imams agree that testimony regarding an unspecified divorced wife is accepted?
b: Yes, this is agreed upon by Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ.

f: 418. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, how is testimony regarding an unspecified emancipated slave treated?
b: They treat it like testimony regarding an unspecified divorced wife, so it is accepted even without a claim from the slave.

f: 419. What is the basis of the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his two companions regarding testimony of an unspecified emancipated slave?
b: The disagreement is whether a claim from the slave is a condition for accepting testimony of emancipation.

f: 420. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, when is testimony that a slave has been emancipated accepted?
b: It is accepted only when the slave himself makes a claim (daʿwā).

f: 421. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, is a claim from the slave required before accepting testimony of emancipation?
b: No, they hold that testimony is accepted even without a claim from the slave.

f: 422. Are there cases where testimony of emancipation is accepted without a claim according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes, testimony regarding the emancipation of a female slave is accepted without a claim.

f: 423. Is testimony regarding divorce accepted without the wife's claim according to all three Imams?
b: Yes, all three Imams agree that testimony regarding divorce is accepted without a claim from the wife.

f: 424. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reject testimony regarding one unspecified emancipated slave among two slaves?
b: Because the required claim cannot exist, since the person who would make the claim is unknown.

f: 425. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ accept testimony regarding one unspecified emancipated slave among two slaves?
b: Because they do not consider the slave's claim to be a condition for accepting testimony of emancipation.

f: 426. Why does the absence of a claim not prevent testimony regarding divorce according to the Hanafi scholars?
b: Because a claim is not a requirement for establishing divorce.

f: 427. Why is a claim not required in the case of a female slave's emancipation according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because emancipation of a female slave makes sexual relations unlawful, so it resembles divorce.

f: 428. If witnesses testify that a man emancipated one of his two female slaves without specifying which one, is the testimony accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, the testimony is not accepted.

f: 429. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not accept testimony regarding one unspecified female slave being emancipated?
b: Because ambiguous emancipation does not make sexual relations unlawful according to him, so it is treated like the emancipation of one of two unspecified male slaves.

f: 430. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the difference between the emancipation of a specified female slave and an unspecified female slave regarding testimony?
b: The emancipation of a specified female slave resembles divorce because it prohibits relations, but emancipation of an unspecified female slave does not establish that prohibition because the person freed is unknown.

f: 431. What situation is being discussed when testimony regarding emancipation is generally not accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: When witnesses testify during the master's lifetime and health that he emancipated one of his two slaves without specifying which one.

f: 432. If witnesses testify that a man emancipated one of his slaves during his terminal illness, and the testimony is given during his illness or after his death, is the testimony accepted?
b: Yes, it is accepted through istiḥsān (juristic preference).

f: 433. If witnesses testify that a man made one of his slaves a mudabbar during his health or illness, and the testimony is given during his illness or after his death, is the testimony accepted?
b: Yes, it is accepted through istiḥsān.

f: 434. Why is testimony accepted for emancipation during terminal illness or tadbīr according to istiḥsān?
b: Because both emancipation during terminal illness and tadbīr are treated like bequests.

f: 435. Why does the fact that emancipation during terminal illness is treated like a bequest allow testimony to be accepted?
b: Because the opposing party in a bequest is known: first the testator, then the executor or heirs after his death.

f: 436. Why is an unspecified slave in a terminal illness emancipation case considered identifiable after death?
b: Because the emancipation is distributed among the slaves upon death, making each person's share of freedom identifiable.

f: 437. If witnesses testify after a man's death that he said during his lifetime, "One of you is free," is their testimony accepted?
b: The correct view is that it is accepted, although some scholars said it is not accepted.

f: 438. Why did some scholars reject testimony after death regarding the statement "One of you is free"?
b: Because it was not originally a bequest, so they did not apply the ruling of bequests to it.

f: 439. Why is the correct view that testimony after death regarding "One of you is free" is accepted?
b: Because after death the emancipation becomes distributed and each slave's share of freedom becomes identifiable.

f: 440. What is the reason that tadbīr and emancipation during terminal illness are treated similarly in testimony rulings?
b: Both are connected to future freedom after death and therefore take the ruling of a bequest.

f: 441. If a person says, "If I enter the house, every slave I own on that day is free," owns no slave at the time of the oath, then buys a slave and enters the house, does the slave become free?
b: Yes, the slave becomes free.

f: 442. Why does a slave purchased after making the oath become free when the oath says "every slave I own on that day"?
b: Because "on that day" refers to the day of entering the house, so the relevant ownership is the ownership at the time of entering.

f: 443. How is the phrase "on that day" understood in the oath "If I enter the house, every slave I own on that day is free"?
b: It means "on the day when I enter," because the verb has been omitted and replaced by the tanwīn.

f: 444. If a person owns a slave when making the oath "If I enter the house, every slave I own on that day is free," and the slave remains his property until he enters, what is the ruling?
b: The slave becomes free when he enters.

f: 445. If a person says, "If I enter the house, every slave of mine is free," without saying "on that day," and later buys a slave before entering, does the newly purchased slave become free?
b: No, the newly purchased slave does not become free.

f: 446. Why do slaves purchased after making an oath without the phrase "on that day" not become free?
b: Because "every slave of mine" normally refers to slaves already owned at the time of making the oath, while the consequence is only delayed until the condition occurs.

f: 447. In the oath "If I enter the house, every slave of mine is free," which slaves are included according to the normal meaning of the wording?
b: Only slaves who were already owned when the oath was made.

f: 448. If a person says, "Every male slave I own is free," and he owns a pregnant female slave who later gives birth to a male child, does the child become free?
b: No, the child does not become free.

f: 449. Does the ruling change if the pregnant female slave gives birth before six months after the oath?
b: No, the child still does not become free.

f: 450. Does the ruling change if the pregnant female slave gives birth six months or more after the oath?
b: No, the child still does not become free.

f: 451. Why does a male child born from a pregnant female slave not become free when the master says, "Every male slave I own is free"?
b: Because the wording applies to an existing slave, and it is uncertain whether the fetus existed at the time of the oath.

f: 452. Even if the fetus existed at the time of the oath, why does it not become free according to this ruling?
b: Because the fetus is only a slave indirectly through its mother and is not an independent slave.

f: 453. Why is a fetus not considered an independent slave for the purpose of an emancipation oath?
b: Because it is like a limb in one respect, and the term "slave" applies to persons, not body parts.

f: 454. What legal example shows that a fetus is not treated as an independent person regarding ownership?
b: A fetus cannot be sold separately from its mother.

f: 455. Why does mentioning the condition "male" in the oath "Every male slave I own is free" prevent the fetus from being included?
b: Because the wording specifically applies to existing male slaves, and the fetus is not independently considered a slave.

f: 456. If a person instead says, "Every slave of mine is free," would the fetus of his pregnant slave be included according to the explanation?
b: Yes, the fetus would be included indirectly because the mother is included.

f: 457. Why would a fetus be included in the oath "Every slave of mine is free" but not in "Every male slave of mine is free"?
b: Because the general wording includes the mother and the fetus follows her indirectly, while the specific wording of "male slave" does not include a fetus that is not independently classified as a male slave.

f: 458. If a person says, "Every slave I own will be free the day after tomorrow," owns a slave at the time of the statement, then buys another slave before the day arrives, which slaves become free?
b: Only the slave he owned when he made the statement becomes free. The newly purchased slave does not become free.

f: 459. Why does a slave purchased after the statement "Every slave I own will be free the day after tomorrow" not become free?
b: Because the phrase "I own" normally refers to present ownership, not future ownership, unless a future marker such as "I will own" is used.

f: 460. What wording would be needed for future ownership to be included in an oath or statement about ownership?
b: A marker of future tense, such as "I will own" or "I shall own."

f: 461. If a person says, "Every slave I own is free after my death," owns a slave, then buys another slave before his death, what happens to the first slave?
b: The first slave becomes a mudabbar (a slave promised freedom after the master's death).

f: 462. If a person says, "Every slave I own is free after my death," does a slave purchased after making the statement become included?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, yes. The later-purchased slave becomes free after death from one-third of the estate.

f: 463. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ in al-Nawādir, which slaves become free from the statement "Every slave I own is free after my death"?
b: Only slaves owned at the time of making the statement become free. A slave purchased later is not included.

f: 464. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, why does the statement "Every slave I own is free after my death" include slaves purchased later?
b: Because the statement contains two legal aspects: emancipation (ʿitq) and bequest (waṣiyyah). The emancipation aspect applies to current slaves, while the bequest aspect includes future ownership.

f: 465. From the perspective of emancipation (ʿitq), which slaves are included in the statement "Every slave I own is free after my death"?
b: Only slaves owned when the statement was made are included, and they become mudabbars.

f: 466. What happens to a slave who becomes a mudabbar due to the statement "Every slave I own is free after my death"?
b: He cannot be sold and becomes free after the master's death.

f: 467. From the perspective of bequest (waṣiyyah), why are slaves purchased after making the statement "Every slave I own is free after my death" included?
b: Because future situations are considered in bequests.

f: 468. What examples demonstrate that future ownership is considered in bequests?
b: A bequest of wealth includes wealth acquired after the bequest, and a bequest to "the children of so-and-so" includes children born after the bequest.

f: 469. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ answer the objection that they are combining present and future ownership in one statement?
b: They say the two rulings operate through different legal mechanisms: immediate emancipation applies to the current slave, while bequest applies to the future slave.

f: 470. Why can the statement "Every slave of mine is free after tomorrow" not be treated like "Every slave of mine is free after my death"?
b: Because the first statement contains only emancipation, while the second contains both emancipation and bequest.

f: 471. Why does the presence of a bequest element allow future slaves to be included after death but not in ordinary delayed emancipation?
b: Because bequests legally consider future circumstances, while ordinary emancipation applies only to the ownership existing when the emancipation statement is made.

f: 472. What is the ruling if a master emancipates his slave in exchange for wealth and the slave accepts the exchange?
b: The slave becomes free, and the wealth becomes a debt upon the slave.

f: 473. What are examples of emancipation in exchange for compensation?
b: Saying: "You are free in exchange for one thousand dirhams" or "You are free for one thousand dirhams."

f: 474. Why does a slave only become free after accepting an emancipation agreement in exchange for wealth?
b: Because it is an exchange contract where wealth is exchanged for something other than wealth, so the ruling takes effect when the counter-value is accepted, similar to a sale.

f: 475. Why is acceptance required in emancipation in exchange for wealth but not in ordinary emancipation?
b: Because emancipation in exchange for wealth is treated as an exchange contract, while ordinary emancipation is a unilateral act.

f: 476. When does the slave become free in an emancipation agreement involving compensation?
b: The slave becomes free when he accepts the agreement.

f: 477. What becomes of the compensation owed by a slave who accepts emancipation in exchange for wealth?
b: It becomes a debt upon the slave.

f: 478. Can a guarantee (kafālah) be made for the payment owed in emancipation in exchange for compensation?
b: Yes, because the payment becomes an established debt upon the slave.

f: 479. How does emancipation in exchange for compensation differ from kitābah?
b: In kitābah, the payment obligation is established while the obstacle of slavery still remains, whereas in emancipation for compensation the slave becomes free upon acceptance and the payment becomes a debt.

f: 480. What types of things are included under the term "wealth" (māl) in emancipation for compensation?
b: Cash, goods, and animals are included under the term wealth.

f: 481. Is emancipation in exchange for compensation valid if the specific item of wealth is not identified?
b: Yes, it is valid even if the exact item is not specified.

f: 482. Why is uncertainty tolerated regarding the compensation in emancipation for wealth?
b: Because it resembles other contracts where minor uncertainty is overlooked, such as marriage, khulʿ, and settlement for intentional homicide.

f: 483. Are food items and measured or weighed goods valid forms of compensation in emancipation agreements?
b: Yes, as long as their type is known.

f: 484. Why does a lack of detailed description of the compensation not invalidate emancipation in exchange for wealth?
b: Because the uncertainty is minor and does not prevent the validity of the exchange.

f: 485. What is the ruling if a master makes emancipation dependent upon the slave paying a certain amount of wealth?
b: The condition is valid, and the slave becomes free when he makes the payment.

f: 486. What is an example of conditional emancipation based upon payment?
b: The master says: "If you pay me one thousand dirhams, then you are free."

f: 487. Does a slave who becomes free through payment-based conditional emancipation become a mukātab?
b: No, he becomes free directly upon making the payment and does not become a mukātab.

f: 488. Why does conditional emancipation upon payment not make the slave a mukātab?
b: Because the wording explicitly makes freedom dependent upon payment rather than establishing a contract of kitābah.

f: 489. Why does the slave become authorized (maʾdhūn) when emancipation is made conditional upon payment?
b: Because the master has encouraged him to earn money in order to make the payment, implying permission to engage in business and earning.

f: 490. What type of activity is implied by the master's permission in conditional emancipation for payment?
b: Trade and earning, not begging.

f: 491. Why is permission for business implied when a master says, "If you pay me, you are free"?
b: Because the slave must be able to earn the money needed for payment, and the intended means is lawful earning.

f: 492. If a slave brings the required payment in a conditional emancipation agreement, what is the ruling?
b: The judge forces the master to accept the payment, and the slave becomes free.

f: 493. What does it mean that the judge "forces" the master to accept the payment in conditional emancipation?
b: It means that the judge treats the master as having accepted by making the payment available (takhliyah).

f: 494. According to Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, is the master forced to accept the payment when a slave brings the money for conditional emancipation?
b: No, according to Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ the master is not forced to accept it.

f: 495. Why does Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argue that the master cannot be forced to accept payment in conditional emancipation?
b: Because he views it as a conditional oath-like statement rather than an exchange contract.

f: 496. What similarities does Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ see between conditional emancipation and an oath?
b: Freedom is verbally connected to a condition, it does not require acceptance, it cannot be cancelled, and people cannot be forced to fulfil the conditions of oaths.

f: 497. How does conditional emancipation differ from kitābah according to Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Kitābah is a genuine exchange contract where payment becomes an obligation, while conditional emancipation is not treated as an exchange.

f: 498. How do the scholars respond to Zufar's analogy between conditional emancipation and an oath?
b: They say it is conditional in wording but an exchange in purpose.

f: 499. Why is conditional emancipation considered an exchange in purpose?
b: Because the master only attached freedom to payment in order to encourage the slave to pay wealth, giving the slave freedom and giving the master compensation.

f: 500. What contract does conditional emancipation most closely resemble according to the response to Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It resembles kitābah because both involve freedom in exchange for wealth.

f: 501. What evidence shows that statements of this type can function as exchanges rather than only conditions?
b: In divorce, similar wording makes compensation valid and causes an irrevocable (bāʾin) divorce.

f: 502. Why is conditional emancipation treated as a condition at the beginning of the agreement?
b: To protect the master's rights.

f: 503. What rights of the master are protected by treating conditional emancipation as a condition at the beginning?
b: The master may sell the slave, the slave does not automatically gain ownership of his earnings, and children born before payment do not automatically become free.

f: 504. Why is conditional emancipation treated as an exchange when payment actually occurs?
b: To protect the slave's rights by allowing the judge to force the master to accept the payment.

f: 505. What is the main principle underlying the entire discussion of conditional emancipation for payment?
b: It is treated as a condition at the beginning to protect the master, and as an exchange at the end to protect the slave.

f: 506. What type of transaction is conditional emancipation in exchange for payment similar to?
b: It is similar to a gift with a condition of compensation.

f: 507. If a slave pays only part of the required amount in a conditional emancipation agreement, does he become free?
b: No, he does not become free until the full amount is paid.

f: 508. If a slave pays part of the payment for conditional emancipation, what must the master do?
b: The master is forced to accept the partial payment, but freedom does not occur until the complete payment is made.

f: 509. Why does a slave not become free after paying only part of the amount in conditional emancipation?
b: Because the condition for freedom has not yet been fulfilled.

f: 510. If the master reduces the required payment and the slave pays the remaining amount, does the slave become free?
b: Yes, because the full agreed amount after reduction has been paid and the condition has been fulfilled.

f: 511. If a slave pays the payment using money he earned before the condition of emancipation was made, can the master reclaim that money?
b: Yes, the master can reclaim it.

f: 512. Why can the master reclaim money earned by the slave before the emancipation condition was made?
b: Because the slave was not yet authorized to earn and pay from his own earnings.

f: 513. If a slave earns the money after the emancipation condition was made and pays it, can the master reclaim it?
b: No, the master cannot reclaim it.

f: 514. Why can the master not reclaim money earned after the emancipation condition was made?
b: Because the master's permission for the slave to earn money is implied by the condition requiring payment.

f: 515. What is the ruling difference between the words "if" (in) and "when" (idhā) in conditional emancipation statements?
b: "If" (in) is restricted to the same sitting because it indicates a choice, while "when" (idhā) is not restricted to the sitting because it indicates a time.

f: 516. If a master says, "If you pay me one thousand dirhams, you are free," when must the slave pay according to the wording of "if" (in)?
b: The payment must occur in the same sitting.

f: 517. If a master says, "When you pay me one thousand dirhams, you are free," when may the slave pay according to the wording of "when" (idhā)?
b: The payment may occur later, because "when" indicates a future time.

f: 518. If a master says to his slave, "You are free after my death in exchange for one thousand dirhams," when does acceptance of the emancipation occur?
b: Acceptance occurs after the master's death.

f: 519. Why does acceptance occur after death in the statement "You are free after my death in exchange for one thousand dirhams"?
b: Because the offer of emancipation is attached to the time after death.

f: 520. What example is similar to saying, "You are free after my death in exchange for one thousand dirhams"?
b: Saying, "You are free tomorrow for one thousand dirhams."

f: 521. How does "You are free after my death in exchange for one thousand dirhams" differ from "You are a mudabbar for one thousand dirhams"?
b: In the first statement, the offer of emancipation only takes effect after death, while in tadbīr the slave becomes a mudabbar immediately even though freedom is delayed.

f: 522. Does payment become binding immediately when a slave is made a mudabbar in exchange for payment?
b: No, the payment does not become binding because slavery still remains.

f: 523. Why does payment not become binding when a slave is made a mudabbar for compensation?
b: Because the slave remains enslaved, and the obligation of payment is not established while the obstacle of slavery remains.

f: 524. In the case where a slave accepts emancipation in exchange for payment after the master's death, does the slave become free merely through acceptance?
b: No, according to the discussion, the slave does not become free merely through acceptance after death unless the heirs emancipate him.

f: 525. Why does a slave not become free merely through acceptance after the master's death?
b: Because the deceased is no longer legally capable of performing emancipation.

f: 526. What is the ruling if a master emancipates his slave in exchange for the slave serving him for four years and the slave accepts?
b: The slave becomes free, and the four years of service become the compensation owed by the slave.

f: 527. Why is service for a known period valid as compensation for emancipation?
b: Because service for a known period has recognized value and can function as compensation, similar to a payment of one thousand dirhams.

f: 528. If a slave is emancipated in exchange for four years of service and dies immediately after acceptance, what does he owe according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: He owes the value of himself from his estate.

f: 529. If a slave is emancipated in exchange for four years of service and dies immediately after acceptance, what does he owe according to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: He owes the value of his four years of service.

f: 530. What disagreement forms the basis for the difference between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ on one side and Muḥammad on the other regarding failed compensation?
b: The disagreement over what is reclaimed when a slave is sold in exchange for a specific female slave who later cannot be delivered.

f: 531. If someone sells a slave to himself in exchange for a specific female slave, and that female slave dies or is found not to belong to the seller, what does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say is reclaimed?
b: They say the value of the original slave is reclaimed.

f: 532. If someone sells a slave to himself in exchange for a specific female slave, and that female slave dies or is found not to belong to the seller, what does Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say is reclaimed?
b: He says the value of the female slave is reclaimed.

f: 533. Why is the disagreement over failed service compensation connected to the disagreement over exchanging a slave for another slave?
b: Because just as the female slave cannot be delivered due to death or loss of ownership, service cannot be obtained after the slave dies or the master dies.

f: 534. If a person asks another to free his female slave for one thousand dirhams on the condition that he marries her, and the owner frees her but she refuses marriage, is the emancipation valid?
b: Yes, the emancipation is valid.

f: 535. If someone requests another person to free his slave for payment and promises to pay the compensation, does the requester owe the payment?
b: No, the requester does not owe the payment.

f: 536. Why does a person who requests another to emancipate his slave not become liable for the payment?
b: Because compensation in emancipation cannot be made payable by someone other than the slave being freed.

f: 537. How does requesting emancipation differ from requesting divorce in exchange for compensation?
b: In divorce, making compensation payable by a third party is valid, while in emancipation it is not valid.

f: 538. If a person says to another, "Divorce your wife for one thousand dirhams which I will pay," and the husband divorces her, does the requester owe the payment?
b: Yes, the payment becomes binding upon the requester.

f: 539. Why is third-party payment valid in divorce but not in emancipation?
b: Because compensation in divorce (khulʿ) can be assigned to a third party, while compensation in emancipation must be owed by the slave being freed.

f: 540. What is the ruling if a person emancipates his slave in exchange for wealth and the slave accepts?
b: The slave becomes free, and the compensation becomes a debt upon him.

f: 541. What are examples of emancipation in exchange for wealth (ʿitq ʿalā jaʿl)?
b: Saying: "You are free in exchange for one thousand dirhams" or "You are free for one thousand dirhams."

f: 542. Why does a slave only become free after accepting emancipation in exchange for wealth?
b: Because it is an exchange of wealth for something other than wealth, so the ruling takes effect when the compensation is accepted, similar to a sale.

f: 543. Why is acceptance necessary in emancipation in exchange for wealth?
b: Because the slave does not own himself, so the transaction only takes effect when the counter-value is accepted.

f: 544. When does the compensation become a debt in emancipation in exchange for wealth?
b: It becomes a debt once the slave accepts the emancipation.

f: 545. How does emancipation in exchange for wealth differ from kitābah?
b: In emancipation for wealth, the slave becomes free upon acceptance and owes the payment, whereas in kitābah the payment obligation exists while slavery remains.

f: 546. What does the term "wealth" (māl) include in emancipation in exchange for compensation?
b: It includes cash, goods, animals, and other types of property.

f: 547. Is emancipation in exchange for wealth valid if the specific item of compensation is not identified?
b: Yes, it is valid even if a specific item is not designated.

f: 548. Why is unspecified wealth accepted as compensation in emancipation?
b: Because it resembles transactions such as marriage, khulʿ, and settlement for intentional homicide where minor uncertainty is tolerated.

f: 549. Are food items and measured or weighed commodities valid as compensation in emancipation?
b: Yes, as long as their type is known.

f: 550. Why does a lack of detailed description of the compensation not invalidate emancipation?
b: Because the uncertainty involved is minor.

f: 551. What is the ruling if a master makes emancipation dependent upon the slave paying a specified amount?
b: The arrangement is valid, and the slave becomes free when he makes the payment.

f: 552. What is an example of conditional emancipation upon payment?
b: The master says: "If you pay me one thousand dirhams, you are free."

f: 553. Does conditional emancipation upon payment make the slave a mukātab?
b: No, the slave becomes free upon payment without becoming a mukātab.

f: 554. Why does conditional emancipation upon payment not create a kitābah contract?
b: Because the wording explicitly suspends freedom upon payment rather than establishing a contract of emancipation.

f: 555. Why does a slave become authorised (maʾdhūn) when emancipation is conditional upon payment?
b: Because the master has encouraged him to earn money in order to make the required payment.

f: 556. What type of activity is intended by the permission given to a slave in conditional emancipation?
b: Trade and earning, not begging.

f: 557. If a slave brings the required payment in conditional emancipation, what must the judge do?
b: The judge forces the master to accept the payment, and the slave becomes free.

f: 558. What does it mean that the judge "forces" the master to accept payment?
b: It means the judge treats the master as having accepted by the slave making the payment available (takhliyah).

f: 559. According to Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can the master be forced to accept payment in conditional emancipation?
b: No, according to Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ the master cannot be forced to accept.

f: 560. Why does Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say the master cannot be forced to accept payment?
b: Because he views the arrangement as similar to an oath, where freedom is attached to a condition and people cannot be forced to fulfil oath conditions.

f: 561. How does Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish conditional emancipation from kitābah?
b: Kitābah is a true exchange contract with an obligatory payment, while conditional emancipation resembles an oath.

f: 562. How do the Hanafis respond to Zufar's analogy between conditional emancipation and an oath?
b: They say the wording is conditional, but the purpose is an exchange because the master seeks payment in return for freedom.

f: 563. Why is conditional emancipation considered an exchange in purpose?
b: Because the master intends for the slave to gain freedom while receiving wealth in return.

f: 564. What contract does conditional emancipation resemble according to the Hanafi explanation?
b: It resembles kitābah.

f: 565. Why is conditional emancipation treated as a condition at the beginning?
b: To protect the master's rights before payment occurs.

f: 566. What rights of the master are protected by treating conditional emancipation as a condition before payment?
b: The master may sell the slave, the slave does not become entitled to his earnings, and a child born before payment does not become free.

f: 567. Why is conditional emancipation treated as an exchange after payment occurs?
b: To protect the slave's right by allowing the master to be forced to accept the payment.

f: 568. What principle explains the legal rulings of conditional emancipation upon payment?
b: At the beginning it is treated as a condition to protect the master, and at the end it is treated as an exchange to protect the slave.

f: 569. In ʿitq ʿalā jaʿl (emancipation in exchange for compensation), when does a slave become free?
b: When the master emancipates him in exchange for wealth and the slave accepts, he becomes free. This is because it is an exchange contract: wealth is exchanged for freedom, similar to a sale where the ruling takes effect upon acceptance.

f: 570. Why does emancipation in exchange for compensation require the slave’s acceptance, unlike ordinary emancipation?
b: Because it is not merely a unilateral relinquishment; it is an exchange of compensation for freedom. Since the slave does not yet own himself, the exchange only becomes effective after his acceptance.

f: 571. What types of property are included under the term māl (wealth) in emancipation for compensation?
b: It includes cash, goods, animals, foodstuffs, measured commodities, and weighed commodities, provided the type is known. Minor uncertainty does not invalidate it, similar to marriage, khulʿ, and settlement agreements.

f: 572. What is the ruling if a master says: “If you pay me one thousand dirhams, you are free”?
b: The arrangement is valid. The slave becomes free once he pays the amount, but he does not become a mukātab.

f: 573. Why does a slave become authorised to trade when emancipation is made conditional upon payment?
b: Because the master has encouraged him to earn money in order to achieve freedom. Permission for earning and trading is therefore implied.

f: 574. Why did Zufar say that a master cannot be forced to accept payment in conditional emancipation?
b: Because he viewed it as an oath-like condition: freedom was verbally attached to payment, so acceptance is not required and the master cannot be forced to fulfil an oath condition.

f: 575. How do the Hanafis respond to Zufar’s argument regarding conditional emancipation?
b: They say it is treated as a condition in wording but as an exchange in purpose. The master intended to receive compensation while giving freedom, so it resembles kitābah.

f: 576. Why is conditional emancipation treated as a condition at the beginning but as an exchange at the end?
b: At the beginning it protects the master: he may sell the slave, the slave does not own his earnings, and children born before payment are not automatically free. After payment it protects the slave: the master can be forced to accept the payment.

f: 577. What happens if the slave pays only part of the compensation in conditional emancipation?
b: The master must accept the partial payment, but the slave does not become free until the entire amount is paid because the condition has not been fulfilled.

f: 578. If the master reduces the required compensation and the slave pays the remainder, does emancipation occur?
b: Yes. Since the full reduced amount has been paid, the condition is fulfilled and the slave becomes free.

f: 579. If a slave pays the compensation using money earned before the emancipation condition, can the master reclaim it?
b: Yes. The slave was not yet authorised to earn for this purpose, so the master may reclaim it.

f: 580. If a slave pays compensation using money earned after the emancipation condition, can the master reclaim it?
b: No. The master implicitly authorised him to earn and pay for his freedom.

f: 581. What is the difference between “If you pay me…” and “When you pay me…” in conditional emancipation?
b: “If you pay” is restricted to the same sitting because it indicates a choice (takhyīr). “When you pay” is not restricted because it indicates a future time.

f: 582. If a master says: “You are free after my death in exchange for one thousand dirhams,” when does acceptance occur?
b: Acceptance occurs after death because the offer of emancipation is attached to the period after death.

f: 583. Why is “You are free after my death for one thousand dirhams” different from “You are a mudabbar for one thousand dirhams”?
b: Tadbīr is established immediately, even though freedom is delayed until death. In the first statement, the emancipation itself is delayed until after death.

f: 584. Does a slave become free merely by accepting after the master’s death in the statement “You are free after my death for one thousand dirhams”?
b: No. The deceased no longer has legal ability to emancipate. The heirs must emancipate him.

f: 585. Is emancipation in exchange for a fixed period of service valid?
b: Yes. If the master says: “You are free in exchange for serving me for four years,” and the slave accepts, the emancipation is valid because a known period of service can serve as compensation.

f: 586. If a slave emancipated in exchange for four years of service dies immediately, what does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say he owes?
b: He owes the value of himself from his estate.

f: 587. If a slave emancipated in exchange for four years of service dies immediately, what does Muḥammad say he owes?
b: He owes the value of the four years of service.

f: 588. What earlier disagreement explains the difference between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ/Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding compensation for lost service?
b: It is based on the issue of selling a slave in exchange for another slave who is later unavailable: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ compensate according to the value of the original slave, while Muḥammad compensates according to the value of the missing counter-value.

f: 589. If someone tells another person: “Free your slave for one thousand dirhams which I will pay,” and he does so, is the person who ordered it liable for the payment?
b: No. Nothing is owed by the person who ordered it, and the emancipation belongs to the one who performed it.

f: 590. Why is compensation not made obligatory upon a third party in emancipation, unlike divorce?
b: Because in divorce, making compensation obligatory upon someone other than the spouse is valid. In emancipation, compensation cannot be imposed upon someone other than the slave being freed.

f: 591. If someone says: “Free your slave-girl on my behalf for one thousand dirhams,” how is the payment divided?
b: The thousand is divided between the value of the slave-girl and the dowry of her equivalent (mahr al-mithl). The portion corresponding to her value is owed, while the portion corresponding to the dowry is cancelled if the marriage does not occur.

f: 592. Why does the phrase “Free your slave-girl on my behalf” imply purchasing her?
b: Because the phrase “on my behalf” indicates that the person is acting as though he is acquiring her, so the payment relates partly to her value and partly to the intended marital relationship.

f: 593. What expressions establish tadbīr (freedom after the master's death)?
b: Expressions such as: “When I die you are free,” “You are free after me,” “You are a mudabbar,” or “I have made you mudabbar.” These are explicit expressions of tadbīr.

f: 594. What is the meaning of tadbīr?
b: Tadbīr means establishing a slave’s emancipation after the death of the master.

f: 595. Can a mudabbar slave be sold, gifted, or transferred according to the Hanafi school?
b: No. A mudabbar cannot be sold, gifted, or removed from ownership except in a way that leads to his freedom.

f: 596. Why did Imām al-Shāfiʿī allow the sale of a mudabbar?
b: Because he viewed tadbīr as merely attaching freedom to a future condition, and therefore the slave remains ordinary property until that condition occurs.

f: 597. What is the Hanafi proof that a mudabbar cannot be sold?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said that the mudabbar is not sold, gifted, or inherited, but becomes free from one-third of the estate.

f: 598. Why do the Hanafis consider tadbīr established immediately even though freedom occurs after death?
b: Because tadbīr itself is the cause of freedom. Since the cause exists now, it is preferable to consider its legal effects established now.

f: 599. How does tadbīr differ from ordinary conditional emancipation?
b: In ordinary conditional emancipation, the cause of freedom cannot exist before the condition because the condition is the barrier preventing freedom. In tadbīr, the cause already exists because the master's statement itself establishes the future freedom.

f: 600. What rights does the master retain over a mudabbar slave during his lifetime?
b: The master may use him, hire him out, have intercourse with a female mudabbar, and marry her, because ownership remains with the master.

f: 601. Why does the master retain ownership rights over a mudabbar during his lifetime?
b: Because tadbīr does not immediately remove ownership. It only establishes freedom after the master's death.

f: 602. When does a mudabbar become free?
b: A mudabbar becomes free after the master's death from one-third of the master's wealth.

f: 603. Why is a mudabbar freed only from one-third of the master's wealth?
b: Because tadbīr is treated as a bequest (waṣiyyah): it is a donation connected to death and does not take effect during the master's lifetime.

f: 604. Why is tadbīr considered similar to a bequest?
b: Because both are voluntary donations whose effects begin after death, so they are restricted to one-third of the estate.

f: 605. If the master dies owning no other wealth besides the mudabbar, what happens?
b: The mudabbar becomes free to the extent of one-third of his value and must work (sāʿayah) to pay the remaining two-thirds of his value.

f: 606. If the master dies while having debts, what happens to the mudabbar?
b: The mudabbar must work to pay his entire value because debts take priority over bequests.

f: 607. What is the ruling if a master says: “If I die from this illness, or this journey, or this specific illness, then you are free”?
b: This is not considered tadbīr, and selling the slave is permitted.

f: 608. Why is conditional tadbīr not treated as normal tadbīr?
b: Because the cause of freedom has not been fully established due to uncertainty regarding the description of death.

f: 609. What is the difference between unrestricted tadbīr and conditional tadbīr?
b: Unrestricted tadbīr is based on certain death, so the cause of freedom is established. Conditional tadbīr depends on a specific uncertain manner of death, so the cause is not established until that condition occurs.

f: 610. If the master dies in the manner specified in conditional tadbīr, what is the ruling?
b: The slave becomes free like an ordinary mudabbar, from one-third of the master's wealth.

f: 611. What is the ruling when a female slave gives birth to a child from her master?
b: She becomes an Umm Walad, and selling her or transferring ownership of her becomes prohibited.

f: 612. What is the meaning of the hadith “Her child has freed her” regarding an Umm Walad?
b: It means that the child causes certain consequences of freedom, especially the prohibition of selling her, even though complete freedom is delayed until the master's death.

f: 613. Why does giving birth to her master's child make a slave woman an Umm Walad?
b: Because a connection exists between the father and mother through the child. The mixing of bodily fluids creates a legal connection of lineage, causing the mother's freedom-related rulings.

f: 614. Why does an Umm Walad not become immediately free during the master's lifetime?
b: Because her freedom is connected to the master's death, like a bequest. However, the right of freedom exists immediately, so selling her is prohibited.

f: 615. If a master owns only part of a female slave and she gives birth to his child, does she become an Umm Walad?
b: Yes. The ruling applies even to partial ownership because istīlād (making a slave woman an Umm Walad) cannot be divided.

f: 616. What rights does a master retain over an Umm Walad during his lifetime?
b: He may have intercourse with her, use her, hire her out, and marry her, because ownership remains with him.

f: 617. Why can the master continue to benefit from an Umm Walad during his lifetime?
b: Because she remains his property until his death, similar to a mudabbar slave.

f: 618. Is the lineage of a child born from a slave woman automatically established from the master?
b: No. The master must acknowledge the child’s lineage.

f: 619. Why did Imām al-Shāfiʿī say that the child's lineage is established without acknowledgement?
b: Because intercourse is more likely to produce a child than marriage, so lineage should be established from it.

f: 620. Why do the Hanafis require acknowledgement for the lineage of a child born from a slave woman?
b: Because intercourse with a slave woman is normally for pleasure rather than producing children, and there is a barrier preventing automatic lineage. Therefore acknowledgement is required.

f: 621. Why is marriage different from intercourse with a slave woman regarding lineage?
b: Because having children is an intended purpose of marriage, whereas intercourse with a slave woman is not normally intended for lineage.

f: 622. If a master acknowledges one child from an Umm Walad, is acknowledgement required for later children?
b: No. Later children’s lineage is established automatically because the first acknowledgement makes her like a marital bed (firāsh).

f: 623. If the master denies the lineage of a later child after acknowledging the first, is his denial accepted?
b: Yes. Her status as a marital bed is weaker than that of a free wife, so his denial is accepted.

f: 624. When does an Umm Walad become free?
b: She becomes free when the master dies.

f: 625. How is the freedom of an Umm Walad different from the freedom of a mudabbar?
b: An Umm Walad is freed from the entire estate before the heirs receive their shares, while a mudabbar is freed only from one-third of the estate.

f: 626. Why does an Umm Walad receive freedom before the heirs take their shares?
b: Because the right connected to the child and lineage takes precedence over the heirs’ rights.

f: 627. Is an Umm Walad required to work to pay the master's debts according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. She is not required to work for creditors because she is not considered legally valuable property (māl mutaqawwam) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 628. Why can creditors not claim an Umm Walad according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because her financial value is not legally recognised, so creditors cannot demand payment from her value.

f: 629. How does an Umm Walad differ from a mudabbar regarding debts?
b: A mudabbar retains recognised financial value, whereas an Umm Walad does not according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 630. What happens if a Christian master's Umm Walad becomes Muslim?
b: She must work to pay her value and is treated like a mukātabah. She does not become free until the payment is completed.

f: 631. When does the disagreement occur regarding a Christian master's Umm Walad who becomes Muslim?
b: The disagreement occurs when the Christian master is invited to accept Islam but refuses. If he accepts Islam, she remains in her original status.

f: 632. What was Zufar's opinion regarding a Christian master's Umm Walad who becomes Muslim?
b: She becomes free immediately, and the payment for her value becomes a debt upon her.

f: 633. Why did Zufar say that a Muslim Umm Walad of a Christian master should be freed immediately?
b: Because after becoming Muslim, removing her humiliation becomes obligatory. Since she can no longer be sold, emancipation becomes necessary.

f: 634. What are the two possible ways to remove the humiliation of a Muslim slave woman owned by a non-Muslim?
b: Either selling her or freeing her. Since selling her is no longer possible, emancipation becomes necessary.

f: 635. What is the Hanafi solution for a Christian master's Umm Walad who becomes Muslim?
b: She is made like a mukātabah: she works toward her freedom by paying her value.

f: 636. How does making her a mukātabah protect the slave woman?
b: She gains control over her earnings and becomes free in terms of possession (ḥurrah yad-an), removing the humiliation of slavery.

f: 637. How does making her a mukātabah protect the Christian master?
b: He eventually receives compensation for the financial value of his property, while she is encouraged to work toward freedom.

f: 638. Why did the Hanafis not simply free her immediately if she becomes Muslim?
b: Because if she has no wealth and is immediately freed, she may become inactive in earning. The mukātabah system encourages her to work and achieve freedom.

f: 639. Why do the Hanafis preserve the Christian master's claim to compensation?
b: Because the Christian considers the financial value of an Umm Walad to be recognised, so his consideration of her value is preserved.

f: 640. Even if an Umm Walad’s value is not legally recognised, why can compensation still become obligatory?
b: Because she remains protected property/personhood, and this protection is sufficient to establish compensation, similar to financial compensation in shared qiṣāṣ when one heir pardons.

f: 641. How is the case of a Muslim Umm Walad owned by a Christian similar to shared retaliation (qiṣāṣ)?
b: In both cases, even if one aspect removes the original right, compensation may still become due to protect the rights of the remaining party.

f: 642. What happens to an Umm Walad when her master dies?
b: She becomes free without needing to perform siyāyah (working to pay her value).

f: 643. Why does an Umm Walad become free immediately upon her master's death?
b: Because she already has the status of Umm Walad, whose freedom is connected directly to the master's death.

f: 644. If a Christian master's Umm Walad who became Muslim was unable to complete her payments during his lifetime, does she return to being an ordinary slave?
b: No. She does not return to ordinary slavery because the reason requiring her mukātabah status remains.

f: 645. If a man has a child with another person's slave woman through marriage and later acquires ownership of her, does she become an Umm Walad according to the Hanafis?
b: Yes. Once he owns her, she becomes an Umm Walad because the child’s lineage is established from him.

f: 646. What was Imām al-Shāfiʿī’s position regarding a man who had a child with another person's slave woman through marriage and later acquired her?
b: He said she does not become an Umm Walad.

f: 647. What is the issue of walad al-maghūr (the child of the deceived person) mentioned in this discussion?
b: It refers to the case where a man has a child with a slave woman through a relationship where ownership or status is later disputed, and whether she becomes an Umm Walad when he acquires her.

f: 648. What is the argument against making such a woman an Umm Walad?
b: She conceived while the child was connected to a slave status, so she should not become an Umm Walad, similar to a woman who conceived through adultery and later becomes owned by the adulterer.

f: 649. How do the Hanafis respond to the argument against making her an Umm Walad?
b: They say the effective cause is the connection (juzʾiyyah) created through the child, and this exists because the child’s lineage is legally established from both parents.

f: 650. Why does adultery differ from a valid marriage regarding Umm Walad status?
b: Because adultery does not establish legally recognised lineage, whereas marriage establishes lineage and creates the connection between parent and child.

f: 651. Why does an adulterer who later owns his child free the child according to the Hanafis?
b: Because the child is literally considered a part of him, without the need for established lineage.

f: 652. Why does a person not free his brother born from adultery if he purchases him?
b: Because the relationship of brotherhood depends on lineage, and lineage is not established in the case of adultery.

f: 653. If a father has intercourse with his son's slave woman and she gives birth, what happens if he acknowledges the child?
b: The child's lineage is established from him, and the woman becomes his Umm Walad.

f: 654. What financial obligations apply when a father has intercourse with his son's slave woman and acknowledges the child?
b: He must pay her value, but he does not pay compensation for intercourse (ʿuqr) and does not pay the value of the child.

f: 655. Why does the father not pay compensation for the child when he has intercourse with his son's slave woman?
b: Because the child was originally free: the father's ownership is considered to extend back before conception.

f: 656. Why does the father have to pay the value of the slave woman in this case?
b: Because he benefited from her despite not originally owning her, so compensation for her value becomes due.

f: 657. What is the ruling if a Christian master's Umm Walad becomes Muslim?
b: If the Umm Walad of a Christian becomes Muslim, she must work to pay her value. She is treated like a mukātabah and does not become free until she completes the payment.

f: 658. What was Zufar's opinion regarding a Christian master's Umm Walad who becomes Muslim?
b: Zufar said that she becomes free immediately, and the payment (siyāyah) becomes a debt upon her.

f: 659. When does the disagreement regarding a Christian master's Umm Walad becoming Muslim apply?
b: It applies when the master is offered Islam but refuses. If he accepts Islam, then she remains as she is.

f: 660. Why did the Hanafis require a Christian master's Umm Walad who became Muslim to work toward freedom?
b: After she becomes Muslim, removing humiliation from her becomes obligatory. This can happen either by selling her or freeing her. Since selling her is no longer possible, emancipation must occur.

f: 661. Why did the Hanafis not immediately free a Christian master's Umm Walad who became Muslim?
b: They considered making her a mukātabah a better solution because it removes her humiliation while also preserving the master's financial interest. She gains control of her earnings and eventually reaches freedom while the master receives compensation.

f: 662. Why would immediate emancipation harm the Christian master according to the Hanafi reasoning?
b: If she were simply freed while having no wealth, she might become lazy in earning. Making her work encourages her to attain freedom while compensating the master.

f: 663. If a Christian considers the financial value of an Umm Walad recognised, how do the Hanafis respond?
b: They preserve that consideration and require compensation. Even if her value is not legally recognised according to Islamic law, she is still protected, which is sufficient for compensation to become obligatory.

f: 664. What happens when the master of an Umm Walad dies?
b: She becomes free without having to perform siyāyah because she is his Umm Walad.

f: 665. Does an Umm Walad return to slavery if she becomes unable to pay during her master's lifetime?
b: No. She does not return to being an ordinary slave because the reason requiring her status as a mukātabah remains.

f: 666. What happens if someone has a child with another person's slave woman through marriage and later acquires ownership of her?
b: She becomes an Umm Walad for him according to the Hanafis.

f: 667. What was Imam al-Shafi'i's opinion regarding someone who had a child with another person's slave woman through marriage and later acquired her?
b: Imam al-Shafi'i disagreed and said that she does not become an Umm Walad.

f: 668. What is the argument against making the slave woman of the deceived man (walad al-maghūr case) an Umm Walad?
b: She became pregnant while the child was connected to slavery, so she should not become an Umm Walad, similar to a woman who becomes pregnant through adultery and is later acquired by the adulterer.

f: 669. How do the Hanafis respond to the argument against making the deceived man's slave woman an Umm Walad?
b: They say the effective cause is the connection created by the child. This connection exists because lineage is legally established between the child and both parents, unlike adultery where lineage is not established.

f: 670. Why does a child born through adultery not create the same ruling of Umm Walad?
b: Because there is no legally recognised lineage between the adulterer and the child.

f: 671. Why does an adulterer free his child if he later acquires ownership of him?
b: Because the child is literally his part without an intermediary, unlike a relationship based on unrecognised lineage.

f: 672. What happens if a man purchases his brother born from adultery?
b: The brother does not become free because the relationship depends upon lineage, and lineage is not established.

f: 673. What happens if a man has intercourse with his son's slave woman and she gives birth, and he acknowledges the child?
b: The child's lineage is established from him, and she becomes his Umm Walad. He must pay her value.

f: 674. What payments are not required from a father who has intercourse with his son's slave woman and acknowledges the child?
b: He does not pay compensation for the intercourse (ʿuqr), nor does he pay the value of the child.

f: 675. Why does a father who has intercourse with his son's slave woman not pay the value of the child?
b: Because the child was originally free, since the father's ownership is considered to extend back before conception.

f: 676. What happens if the grandfather has intercourse with his son's slave woman while the son is alive?
b: Lineage is not established because the grandfather has no legal authority while the father exists.

f: 677. What happens if the grandfather has intercourse with his son's slave woman after the son has died?
b: Lineage is established from the grandfather because his authority appears when the father is absent.

f: 678. Why is the father's disbelief or slavery treated like death regarding the grandfather's intercourse with the son's slave woman?
b: Because disbelief or slavery removes the father's legal authority, allowing the grandfather's authority to appear.

f: 679. What happens if a shared slave woman owned by two partners gives birth and one partner acknowledges the child?
b: The child's lineage is established from him because once lineage is established regarding his share, it extends to the other share.

f: 680. Why can the cause of lineage not be divided in the case of a shared slave woman?
b: Because conception is a single event and a child cannot be created from two separate legal causes.

f: 681. According to Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muhammad, does a shared slave woman become an Umm Walad when one partner acknowledges the child?
b: Yes. They hold that istīlād (making a slave woman an Umm Walad) is not divisible.

f: 682. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens when one partner in a shared slave woman acknowledges the child?
b: His portion becomes Umm Walad for him. Then he acquires his partner's share because it is capable of ownership, and he must compensate for half her value.

f: 683. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what payments are due when one partner acknowledges the child of a shared slave woman?
b: He owes half of her value because he acquired his partner's share, and half of the compensation for intercourse (ʿuqr) because he had intercourse with a jointly-owned slave woman.

f: 684. Why does the case of a shared slave woman differ from a father having intercourse with his son's slave woman?
b: In the son's slave woman case, ownership is established before intercourse as a condition of permissibility. In the shared slave woman case, ownership of the remaining share is established after intercourse as a consequence of the legal ruling.

f: 685. Why does a man who has intercourse with a shared slave woman and acknowledges the child not owe the value of the child?
b: Because the child's lineage goes back to the time of conception, and nothing of the child's creation occurred while the partner owned part of the slave woman.

f: 686. What happens if both owners of a shared slave woman claim the child?
b: The child's lineage is established from both of them if she became pregnant while owned by both partners.

f: 687. What was Imam al-Shafi'i's opinion when both owners claim the child of a shared slave woman?
b: He said the matter should be referred to a qāʾif (a person skilled in recognising lineage through physical resemblance), because a child cannot come from two men's sperm.

f: 688. Why did Imam al-Shafi'i use the judgement of a qāʾif as evidence?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ accepted the judgement of a lineage expert regarding Usāmah ibn Zayd, which refuted accusations against his lineage.

f: 689. What is the Hanafi evidence for establishing lineage from both owners when both claim the child?
b: They rely on the letter of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ to Shurayḥ regarding a similar case, where he stated that they should be treated as both being related to the child, with inheritance flowing between them.

f: 690. What similar opinion is attributed to ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ regarding two men claiming the same child?
b: A similar judgement is attributed to ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ that the child is attributed to both claimants.

f: 691. What is the Hanafi reasoning for establishing lineage from both owners?
b: Both men have equal entitlement to claim the child, so they are equal regarding the ruling. Although lineage itself cannot be divided, the legal consequences attached to lineage can be divided.

f: 692. How do the Hanafis apply the principle that legal consequences of lineage can be divided?
b: Matters capable of division apply to both according to division, while matters that cannot be divided apply fully to each man, as though each had no partner.

f: 693. Why can lineage itself not be divided between two men?
b: Because a child cannot physically originate from two separate fathers.

f: 694. What are the exceptions where lineage is not established equally from both owners?
b: The exceptions are when one owner is the father of the other, or when one owner is Muslim and the other is a protected non-Muslim.

f: 695. Why does Islam give preference to one claimant over another in the case of shared ownership?
b: Because Islam gives preference to the Muslim over the non-Muslim claimant.

f: 696. Why does being the father give preference in the case of two claimants?
b: Because the father has a special right connected to the child's lineage and share.

f: 697. Why does a shared slave woman become an Umm Walad for both owners when both claim the child?
b: Because each man's claim is valid regarding his share of the child. Therefore, his share of her becomes Umm Walad due to her connection with the child.

f: 698. When two owners both claim the child of a shared slave woman, what compensation (ʿuqr) is due from each of them?
b: Each owes half of the intercourse compensation (ʿuqr), but these obligations cancel against each other because each owes the other the same amount.

f: 699. Why does the son of two men who both claim him inherit from each of them as a complete son?
b: Because each man acknowledges the child's complete right of inheritance, and a person's acknowledgement is evidence against himself.

f: 700. How do the two men who both claim the same child inherit from him?
b: They inherit from him as one father because they are equal regarding the established lineage.

f: 701. What analogy is given for two men inheriting from a child they both claim?
b: It is compared to two people both presenting evidence claiming the same child.

f: 702. What happens if a master has intercourse with the slave woman of his mukātib and she gives birth, and he claims the child?
b: If the mukātib confirms him, the child's lineage is established from the master.

f: 703. What was narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding a mukātib confirming his master's claim of lineage?
b: It is narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ that the mukātib's confirmation is not considered, by analogy with the case of a father claiming the child of his son's slave woman.

f: 704. Why is the mukātib's confirmation considered in the apparent ruling but not in Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ analogy?
b: The distinction is that the master does not have the right to dispose of the mukātib's earnings or property, whereas a father does possess the right to take ownership from his son. Therefore, the son's confirmation has no legal consideration.

f: 705. Why must the master pay ʿuqr when he has intercourse with the slave woman of his mukātib?
b: Because his ownership does not exist before the intercourse. The right he possesses over her is sufficient for the validity of istīlād, but not enough to remove the obligation of compensation.

f: 706. Why must the master pay the value of the child born from his mukātib's slave woman?
b: Because he resembles the case of the maghrūr (a person who was deceived). He relied upon an indication that the child came from his own slave's property, so he did not consent to the child being enslaved. Therefore, the child is free, but compensation for the child's value is required.

f: 707. Why does the master's child from the mukātib's slave woman become free?
b: Because the master did not consent to the child being enslaved, and the child is attributed to him through established lineage.

f: 708. Why does the slave woman of the mukātib not become an Umm Walad for the master?
b: Because he does not actually own her, similar to the case of the child of the maghrūr.
