f: 709. What happens if the mukātib denies the master's claim of lineage?
b: The child's lineage is not established because the mukātib's confirmation is necessary.

f: 710. What happens if the master later acquires ownership of the mukātib's slave woman, even for one day?
b: The child's lineage becomes established from him because the cause for lineage remains, while the obstacle — the mukātib's right over her — has disappeared.

f: 1. What are the three types of oaths mentioned in Kitāb al-Aymān?
b: Oaths are of three types: the yamīn ghamūs (immersing oath), the binding oath, and the vain/accidental oath (laghw).

f: 2. What is a yamīn ghamūs (immersing oath)?
b: It is an oath taken regarding a past matter while deliberately lying in it.

f: 3. Why is the yamīn ghamūs called "ghamūs" (immersing)?
b: It is called ghamūs because it immerses a person into sin due to deliberately swearing falsely by Allah's Name.

f: 4. What is the ruling of a person who takes a yamīn ghamūs?
b: The person sins because he has deliberately lied while swearing by Allah.

f: 5. What evidence is mentioned regarding the sin of a false oath?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears falsely, Allah will enter him into the Fire."

f: 6. Is kaffārah required for a yamīn ghamūs according to the Hanafis?
b: No. According to the Hanafis, there is no kaffārah for a yamīn ghamūs. The required action is repentance and seeking forgiveness from Allah.

f: 7. What was Imam al-Shafi'i's opinion regarding kaffārah for a yamīn ghamūs?
b: Imam al-Shafi'i said that kaffārah is required because the sanctity of Allah's Name was violated through the false oath.

f: 8. Why did Imam al-Shafi'i consider a yamīn ghamūs similar to a binding oath?
b: Because kaffārah was legislated to remove the sin of violating Allah's Name, and that violation occurs in both cases.

f: 9. What is the Hanafi response to the argument that kaffārah should apply to a yamīn ghamūs?
b: The Hanafis argue that a yamīn ghamūs is purely sinful, while kaffārah is an act of worship involving fasting and requiring intention, so it cannot be attached to this type of oath.

f: 10. Why is kaffārah not attached to a yamīn ghamūs according to the Hanafis?
b: Because kaffārah is a worship act that requires intention, whereas the yamīn ghamūs is sinful by its very nature and has no aspect of lawful origin.

f: 11. How does a binding oath differ from a yamīn ghamūs according to the Hanafis?
b: A binding oath is originally permissible, and sin only occurs later if the person chooses to violate it. A yamīn ghamūs is sinful from the beginning because it is based on deliberate falsehood.

f: 12. Why is a binding oath suitable for kaffārah while a yamīn ghamūs is not?
b: Because a binding oath contains an originally permissible act followed by a possible violation, whereas a yamīn ghamūs is an inherently sinful act.

f: 13. What is the yamīn al-munʿaqidah (binding oath)?
b: It is an oath regarding a future matter, where a person swears that he will do something or will not do something.

f: 14. When does kaffārah become necessary for a binding oath?
b: Kaffārah becomes necessary when a person breaks the binding oath.

f: 15. What is the evidence for kaffārah being required for a broken binding oath?
b: The evidence is the verse: "Allah does not take you to account for your unintentional oaths, but He takes you to account for the oaths which you have bound firmly." (Qur'an 5:89)

f: 16. What does the verse regarding firmly bound oaths refer to according to the Hanafis?
b: It refers to the yamīn al-munʿaqidah, an oath concerning a future matter which a person intentionally binds himself to.

f: 17. What is a laghw oath?
b: It is an oath concerning a past matter where the person believes his statement to be true, but the reality is contrary.

f: 18. What is the ruling of a laghw oath according to the Hanafis?
b: They hope that Allah will not hold the person accountable for it.

f: 19. What is an example of a laghw oath?
b: A person says: "By Allah, this is Zayd," believing it is Zayd, but in reality it is ʿAmr.

f: 20. What verse is the basis for the ruling of laghw oaths?
b: The verse: "Allah does not take you to account for your vain oaths, but He takes you to account..." (Qur'an 5:89).

f: 21. Why does the author say "we hope" regarding the forgiveness of laghw oaths?
b: Because scholars differ regarding the exact interpretation and scope of what constitutes a laghw oath.

f: 22. According to the author, are the intentional oath, the coerced oath, and the forgotten oath treated the same?
b: Yes. Kaffārah becomes obligatory upon all three according to the author.

f: 23. What is the evidence that intentional, coerced, and forgotten oaths are treated the same?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Three matters: their seriousness is serious and their joking is serious: marriage, divorce, and oaths."

f: 24. What was Imam al-Shafi'i's position regarding coerced oaths?
b: Imam al-Shafi'i disagreed with the Hanafis regarding this issue, and the detailed discussion of coercion comes later.

f: 25. What is the ruling if a person does what he swore not to do while being forced?
b: According to the Hanafis, kaffārah becomes necessary because the action that breaks the oath still occurred.

f: 26. Why does coercion not prevent the breaking of an oath?
b: Because coercion does not remove the reality of the act, and the occurrence of the act is the legal condition for breaking the oath.

f: 27. What is the ruling if a person breaks his oath while forgetting?
b: It is the same as if he did it intentionally: kaffārah becomes necessary because the action itself occurred.

f: 28. What is the ruling if a person breaks his oath while unconscious or insane?
b: The ruling is the same because the condition for breaking the oath — the action itself — occurred.

f: 29. Why does kaffārah remain necessary even when there is no sin, such as in coercion or forgetfulness?
b: Because the legal ruling is connected to the legal cause (the breaking of the oath), not to the actual presence of sin.

f: 30. What is the Hanafi principle regarding the relationship between kaffārah and sin?
b: Although kaffārah removes sin, its obligation is connected to the occurrence of the oath violation, not necessarily to sinful intention.

f: 31. What is the ruling of saying "By the right of Allah" (wa ḥaqq Allāh) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It is not considered an oath according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 32. Who agreed with Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ that saying "By the right of Allah" is not an oath?
b: Muḥammad agreed, and it is also one narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 33. What was the other narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding "By the right of Allah"?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ narrated that it is an oath because "the right" is among the attributes of Allah.

f: 34. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider "By the right of Allah" to be an oath?
b: Because "the right" can mean Allah's true reality and truth, making the phrase equivalent to "By Allah, the Truth." Swearing by this meaning is customary.

f: 35. What is the argument of Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad that "By the right of Allah" is not an oath?
b: They argue that the phrase is normally understood as referring to Allah's rights upon His servants, meaning acts of obedience. Therefore, it is an oath by something other than Allah.

f: 36. Why is "By the Truth" (wa al-Ḥaqq) considered an oath according to the Hanafis?
b: Because al-Ḥaqq (the Truth) is one of Allah's Names and Attributes.

f: 37. Why is "truly" (ḥaqqan) not considered an oath?
b: Because the indefinite form is understood as emphasis and confirmation of a statement, not as swearing by Allah's Name.

f: 38. Which expressions constitute an oath according to the Hanafis?
b: Expressions such as "I swear" (أُقْسِمُ), "I swear by Allah" (أُقْسِمُ بِاَللَّهِ), "I take an oath" (أَحْلِفُ), "I take an oath by Allah" (أَحْلِفُ بِاَللَّهِ), "I testify" (أَشْهَدُ), and "I testify by Allah" (أَشْهَدُ بِاَللَّهِ) constitute an oath.

f: 39. Why do expressions such as "I swear" and "I testify" count as oaths?
b: Because these expressions are commonly used and recognised as expressions of oath.

f: 40. Are expressions like "I swear" normally understood as referring to the present or future?
b: They normally refer to the present tense, although they may refer to the future through contextual indication. Therefore, they are treated as an oath immediately.

f: 41. Why can testimony function as an oath?
b: Because Allah described testimony as an oath. Allah says: "They say: We testify that you are surely the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" (Qur'an 63:1), and then described them as taking their oaths as a shield (Qur'an 58:16).

f: 42. How do the Hanafis interpret ambiguous oath expressions?
b: Since swearing by Allah is the recognised and legislated oath, while swearing by other than Him is prohibited, ambiguous expressions are interpreted according to the lawful meaning.

f: 43. Do scholars differ over whether intention is required for expressions like "I testify"?
b: Yes. Some scholars say intention is not required because the wording itself establishes an oath, while others say intention is required because the words could also mean a promise or an oath by something other than Allah.

f: 44. What is the ruling of the Persian expression "Sowgand mīkhuram be khodāy" (I swear by God)?
b: It is considered an oath because it refers to swearing by Allah in the present tense.

f: 45. What is the ruling of the Persian expression "Sowgand khoram" (I swear)?
b: Some scholars said it is not considered an oath because it does not specify what the oath is by.

f: 46. What is the ruling of the Persian expression "Sowgand khoram be ṭalāq-i zanam" (I swear by the divorce of my wife)?
b: It is not considered an oath because this is not a recognised expression of oath.

f: 47. What is the ruling of saying "By the life of Allah" (wa la-ʿumr Allāh)?
b: It is an oath.

f: 48. What is the ruling of saying "By Allah's oath" (wa aym Allāh)?
b: It is an oath.

f: 49. What does "ʿUmr Allah" mean in the phrase "wa la-ʿumr Allāh"?
b: It means Allah's eternity or existence.

f: 50. What does "Aym Allah" mean in the phrase "wa aym Allāh"?
b: One explanation is that it means "the oaths of Allah," being the plural of yamīn.

f: 51. What is another explanation of "Aym Allah"?
b: Another explanation is that it means "By Allah," and the additional word is merely an attached particle similar to the letter wāw.

f: 52. Why are "wa la-ʿumr Allāh" and "wa aym Allāh" considered oaths?
b: Because both expressions are commonly used and recognised as oath formulas.

f: 53. Are the phrases "By the covenant of Allah" and "By the pledge of Allah" considered oaths?
b: Yes. They are considered oaths because a covenant is a form of oath, and a pledge (mīthāq) means a covenant.

f: 54. What evidence is given that a covenant is connected to an oath?
b: Allah says: "Fulfil the covenant of Allah." (Qur'an 16:91)

f: 55. Why is a pledge (mīthāq) considered an oath?
b: Because a mīthāq means a covenant, and a covenant carries the meaning of a binding oath.

f: 56. Is the phrase "Upon me is a vow" (ʿalayya nadhr) considered an oath?
b: Yes. It is considered an oath.

f: 57. Is the phrase "Allah's vow" (nadhr Allāh) considered an oath?
b: Yes. It is considered an oath.

f: 58. What evidence is given that an unspecified vow has the ruling of an oath?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever makes a vow but does not specify it, then its expiation is the expiation of an oath."

f: 59. What is the ruling if someone says: "If I do such-and-such, then I am a Jew"?
b: It is considered an oath.

f: 60. What is the ruling if someone says: "If I do such-and-such, then I am a Christian"?
b: It is considered an oath.

f: 61. What is the ruling if someone says: "If I do such-and-such, then I am a disbeliever"?
b: It is considered an oath.

f: 62. Why are statements such as "If I do this, I am a Jew/Christian/disbeliever" considered oaths?
b: Because the person makes the condition a sign of disbelief, meaning he considers the action something that must absolutely be avoided.

f: 63. How can statements involving disbelief be understood as oaths?
b: They can be understood like an oath used to emphasise the prohibition of an action, similar to making something normally permissible appear forbidden upon oneself.

f: 64. What is the ruling if a person says "If I do this, I am a Jew" after he has already performed the action?
b: It becomes a yamīn ghamūs because he is making a false statement regarding a past matter.

f: 65. Does a person become a disbeliever merely by saying "If I do this, I am a Jew/Christian/disbeliever"?
b: No. According to the correct view, he does not become a disbeliever merely by saying it if he understands it as an oath.

f: 66. What other opinion exists regarding statements like "If I do this, I am a Jew"?
b: Another opinion says that he becomes a disbeliever because the statement carries the meaning of declaring himself a disbeliever.

f: 67. What is the correct Hanafi view regarding a person who says "If I do this, I am a Jew/Christian/disbeliever" while intending an oath?
b: He does not become a disbeliever, whether he said it before or after the action, as long as he knows it is merely an oath expression.

f: 68. When does a person become a disbeliever through such a statement?
b: If he believes that actually becoming a Jew, Christian, or disbeliever would occur through performing the action, then he becomes a disbeliever because he willingly accepted disbelief.

f: 69. What is the ruling of saying "May Allah's anger be upon me" or "Allah's wrath"?
b: If someone says: "If I do this, then upon me is Allah's anger" or "Allah's wrath," he has not sworn an oath. This is because it is a supplication against himself, and such expressions are not customarily used as oaths.

f: 70. What is the ruling if someone says: "If I do this, then I am a fornicator, thief, wine drinker, or consumer of interest"?
b: It is not considered an oath. The reason is that these descriptions are not equivalent to the permanent sanctity of Allah's Name, and such expressions are not customary forms of oath.

f: 71. What is the chapter discussed after this?
b: The chapter of Expiation of Oaths (Kaffārat al-Yamīn).

f: 72. What is the expiation of an oath?
b: The expiation is: freeing a slave who qualifies for freeing in ẓihār; or clothing ten poor people, each with a garment or more, with the minimum being clothing sufficient for prayer; or feeding ten poor people according to the feeding required in ẓihār.

f: 73. What is the evidence for the forms of kaffārah?
b: The evidence is the verse: "Its expiation is feeding ten needy people..." (Qur'an 5:89). The word "or" indicates a choice, meaning one of these three options is obligatory.

f: 74. What happens if a person cannot afford any of the three forms of kaffārah?
b: If he cannot perform any of them, then he fasts three consecutive days.

f: 75. What was the opinion of Imām al-Shāfiʿī regarding fasting for kaffārah?
b: Imām al-Shāfiʿī said that the person has a choice.

f: 76. What is the Hanafi evidence that the fasting must be consecutive?
b: The Hanafis rely on the recitation attributed to Ibn Masʿūd: "Then fasting three consecutive days." This reading is treated like a well-known transmitted report.

f: 77. What is the minimum clothing required for kaffārah according to the narration from Muḥammad?
b: The minimum clothing mentioned in the book is based on a narration from Muḥammad.

f: 78. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding minimum clothing?
b: According to them, the minimum is something that covers most of the body.

f: 79. Why are trousers alone not sufficient for clothing kaffārah?
b: Because a person wearing only trousers is still considered "naked" according to common custom.

f: 80. Can clothing that is insufficient for kaffārah count in another form?
b: Yes. Clothing that does not suffice as clothing may count as feeding if its monetary value is given.

f: 81. Does giving kaffārah before breaking the oath suffice?
b: No. If he gives the expiation before breaking the oath, it does not suffice.

f: 82. What was Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding giving kaffārah before breaking the oath?
b: He said it suffices because the person performed it after the cause existed, namely the oath, similar to expiation after an injury.

f: 83. What is the Hanafi response regarding early kaffārah?
b: Kaffārah is meant to cover an actual violation, and no violation exists yet. The oath itself is not the cause; rather, it is a restraint that may or may not be violated. This differs from injury, which necessarily produces its consequence.

f: 84. Can kaffārah given before breaking the oath be reclaimed?
b: No. Once it has been given to the poor, it cannot be reclaimed because it has become charity.

f: 85. What should someone do if he swears an oath to commit a sin?
b: He should break the oath and perform kaffārah.

f: 86. What are examples of sinful oaths?
b: Examples include: "I will not pray," "I will not speak to my father," or "I will kill so-and-so."

f: 87. What is the evidence for breaking a sinful oath?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him do that which is better and expiate his oath."

f: 88. Why should a person break a sinful oath?
b: By breaking it, he abandons the sinful action and replaces the loss of fulfilling the oath with the remedy of kaffārah. Maintaining the sin has no remedy.

f: 89. What is the ruling of an oath taken by a disbeliever?
b: If a disbeliever swears an oath and breaks it while still a disbeliever, or after accepting Islam, there is no kaffārah due upon him.

f: 90. Why is there no binding oath upon a disbeliever?
b: Because he is not legally capable of an oath. An oath is established through glorifying Allah, and the disbeliever does not glorify Him.

f: 91. Why is kaffārah not required from a disbeliever?
b: Because kaffārah is an act of worship, and he is not eligible for it.

f: 92. What is the ruling if someone declares something he owns unlawful for himself?
b: It does not actually become unlawful, but if he uses it, kaffārah of an oath becomes necessary.

f: 93. What is an example of declaring something unlawful for oneself?
b: Saying: "This food is unlawful for me."

f: 94. What was Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding this statement?
b: He said no kaffārah is due, because declaring something lawful to be unlawful destroys the validity of the oath.

f: 95. What is the Hanafi position regarding declaring something lawful unlawful?
b: The wording indicates establishing a prohibition, and it can be given the legal consequence of an oath. Therefore, it is treated as an oath.

f: 96. If a person uses something he declared unlawful, does the amount matter?
b: No. Whether he uses a little or a lot, he breaks the oath and kaffārah becomes necessary.

f: 97. Why does using any amount require kaffārah?
b: Because once the prohibition is established, it applies to every part of the thing prohibited.

f: 98. What is the ruling if someone says: "Everything lawful is unlawful for me" (كُلُّ حِلٍّ عَلَيَّ حَرَامٌ)?
b: According to the preferred Hanafi ruling, it applies to food and drink unless he intends something else.

f: 99. What was Zufar's opinion regarding "Everything lawful is unlawful for me"?
b: He held according to analogy that the oath is broken by performing any permissible action, such as breathing and other necessary actions.

f: 100. What is the reasoning of the preferred Hanafi ruling (istiḥsān)?
b: The purpose of the statement is piety and abstention (birr). Applying it literally to everything would make that purpose impossible because a person cannot avoid all lawful things. Therefore, it is interpreted according to customary usage.

f: 101. Why is the statement understood as referring to food and drink?
b: Because such expressions are commonly used regarding things that are consumed.

f: 102. Does "Everything lawful is unlawful for me" include one's wife?
b: Not unless he intends her, because including her would require abandoning the customary meaning.

f: 103. What happens if he intends his wife by this statement?
b: It becomes īlāʾ (the oath of abstention from marital relations).

f: 104. Does intending his wife remove the application to food and drink?
b: No. According to the apparent narration, the oath is not diverted away from food and drink.

f: 105. What did some scholars say regarding this statement and divorce?
b: They said that such a statement causes divorce without intention because this is the dominant customary usage. This is the relied-upon fatwā.

f: 106. What is the ruling of saying: "Ḥalāl is unlawful for me"?
b: According to customary usage, it carries the same ruling and causes divorce without intention.

f: 107. What expression in Persian was discussed?
b: The expression: "Har che bar dast-e rāst gīram barū-ye ḥarām" ("Whatever I take in my right hand is unlawful").

f: 108. What was the disagreement regarding the Persian expression?
b: Scholars differed whether intention is required for its effect.

f: 109. What is the stronger view regarding the Persian expression?
b: The stronger view is that it causes divorce without intention because of customary usage.

f: 110. What is the ruling of an unrestricted vow (nadhr)?
b: Whoever makes an unrestricted vow must fulfil it.

f: 111. What is the evidence that a vow must be fulfilled?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever makes a vow and specifies it, then he must fulfil what he specified."

f: 112. What is the ruling of a conditional vow?
b: If someone attaches a vow to a condition and the condition occurs, he must fulfil the vow itself.

f: 113. What is the evidence for fulfilling a conditional vow?
b: The general wording of the hadith, and because something attached to a condition is treated like something immediately enacted.

f: 114. What was Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later position regarding certain conditional vows?
b: He later withdrew from his earlier view and held that the expiation of an oath (kaffārat al-yamīn) is sufficient.

f: 115. Which conditional vows are included in Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later position?
b: Statements such as: "If I do such-and-such, then upon me is pilgrimage," "fasting for a year," or "charity of everything I own."

f: 116. Who also held this later position?
b: Muḥammad (رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) also held this view.

f: 117. Can a person still fulfil the actual vow instead of only giving kaffārah?
b: Yes. He may fulfil the vow itself, and by doing so his obligation is discharged.

f: 118. When does a conditional vow take the ruling of an oath?
b: When the condition is something he does not desire to happen, because the vow then contains the meaning of an oath — preventing himself from something.

f: 119. Why does a conditional vow resemble an oath when the condition is unwanted?
b: Because the purpose is to restrain oneself, which is the meaning of an oath.

f: 120. Why does the ruling differ when the person desires the condition to happen?
b: Because the meaning of an oath is absent. For example: "If Allah cures my sick person, then I will do such-and-such." There is no intention of preventing anything.

f: 121. What is the correct distinction regarding conditional vows?
b: If the condition is unwanted, it carries the meaning of an oath and kaffārah suffices. If the condition is desired, it remains a true vow that must be fulfilled.

f: 122. What is the ruling of saying "if Allah wills" (إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ) immediately after an oath?
b: If it is connected directly to the oath, the person does not break the oath.

f: 123. What is the evidence for saying "if Allah wills" in an oath?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears an oath and says 'if Allah wills,' then he has fulfilled his oath."

f: 124. Does the phrase "if Allah wills" work if said after completing the oath?
b: No. It must be connected immediately. If said afterwards, it is considered a withdrawal, and withdrawal from an oath is not valid.

f: 125. What is the next chapter discussed?
b: The chapter of Oaths Regarding Entering and Residence.

f: 126. If someone swears: "I will not enter a house," what places are included?
b: According to the ruling, entering the Kaʿbah, a mosque, a synagogue, or a church does not break the oath.

f: 127. Why does entering these places not break the oath?
b: Because the word bayt (house) refers to something prepared for sleeping overnight, while these places were not constructed for that purpose.

f: 128. If someone swears not to enter a house and enters a vestibule (dihlīz), does he break his oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath because the vestibule is not normally considered a place prepared for sleeping.

f: 129. What is a ẓullah?
b: It is a covered structure extending over the pathway at the entrance of a house.

f: 130. What is another opinion regarding a vestibule (dihlīz)?
b: If the vestibule is roofed and when the door is closed a person would still be considered inside the house, then he breaks his oath because people normally sleep there.

f: 131. If someone enters a ṣuffah (covered courtyard/veranda), does he break his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because a ṣuffah is sometimes constructed for sleeping.

f: 132. Why is a ṣuffah treated differently from a vestibule?
b: Because it can function as a living and sleeping area, similar to summer and winter rooms.

f: 133. What was said regarding the condition of the ṣuffah?
b: Some scholars said this applies only when the ṣuffah has four walls, because their ṣuffahs were built that way. Others said the ruling is general, and this is the correct view.

f: 134. If someone swears not to enter a house and enters a ruined house, does he break his oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath.

f: 135. If someone swears not to enter a specific house and enters it after it has collapsed and become open land, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath.

f: 136. Why does entering a specific ruined house break the oath?
b: Because the word dār (house) refers to the land or area itself according to Arabic and non-Arab usage. The building is only a description of it.

f: 137. How is the word dār treated when referring to a specific present house?
b: The description of being built or ruined is ignored because the thing itself is known.

f: 138. How is the word dār treated when referring to an absent house?
b: The description may be considered because the identity depends on such descriptions.

f: 139. If someone swears not to enter a house, then it collapses and another building is built in its place, does entering break the oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because the name of the house remains after collapse and rebuilding.

f: 140. If the collapsed house is turned into a mosque, does entering it break the oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath because it is no longer called a house.

f: 141. If the collapsed house is turned into a bathhouse, does entering it break the oath?
b: No. The original name has been replaced by another name.

f: 142. If the collapsed house becomes a garden or another type of building, does entering it break the oath?
b: No. It no longer carries the name of a house.

f: 143. If a bathhouse or similar structure is destroyed and rebuilt, does entering it break the oath?
b: No. The original name does not return after the change of identity.

f: 144. If someone swears not to enter a house and enters it after it collapses and becomes open land, does he break his oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath because the name "house" no longer applies.

f: 145. Why does the word "house" disappear when it becomes open land?
b: Because a house is something prepared for sleeping, and once the structure disappears, it is no longer called a house.

f: 146. If only the roof of the house falls while the walls remain, does entering break the oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because it is still possible to sleep there, and the house still exists.

f: 147. Why does the loss of the roof not remove the status of a house?
b: Because the roof is only an additional description, while the essential identity of the house remains.

f: 148. If someone swears not to enter a house and stands on its roof, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because the roof is considered part of the house.

f: 149. What evidence is given that the roof is part of the house?
b: A person performing iʿtikāf does not invalidate his iʿtikāf by going onto the roof of the mosque.

f: 150. Is there another view regarding standing on the roof?
b: Some scholars said that according to modern local custom he would not break his oath. This was the preference of al-Faqīh Abū al-Layth.

f: 151. If someone enters the vestibule (dihlīz) of the house, does he break his oath?
b: Yes, according to this statement. However, the same distinction mentioned earlier regarding whether it is considered part of the house applies.

f: 152. If someone stands in the doorway, does he break his oath?
b: If he stands in a position where, when the door is closed, he would still be outside, then he does not break his oath.

f: 153. Why does standing in the doorway not count as entering?
b: Because the door exists to protect the house and its contents, so someone outside the door is not considered inside the house.

f: 154. If someone swears not to enter a house while he is already inside it, does remaining there break his oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath merely by staying inside until he leaves and then enters again.

f: 155. What is the basis for this ruling?
b: It is based on istiḥsān (juristic preference).

f: 156. What would analogy (qiyās) say regarding someone already inside?
b: Analogy would say that he breaks his oath because continuing an action has the legal status of beginning it.

f: 157. What is the preferred Hanafi reasoning?
b: Entering specifically means moving from outside to inside. Since the person is already inside, there is no longer an act of "entering." Therefore, remaining there is not considered entry.

f: 158. If a person swears that he will not wear a particular garment while he is already wearing it, and he immediately removes it, has he broken his oath?
b: No. Likewise, if he swears not to ride an animal while already riding it and immediately dismounts, he has not broken his oath. The same applies if he swears not to live in a house while already living there and immediately begins moving out.

f: 159. What is Zufar’s opinion regarding someone who swears not to do something while already doing it?
b: Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that he has broken his oath because the condition of breaking the oath existed, even if only for a short moment.

f: 160. Why do the other Hanafi scholars say the oath is not broken when the person immediately removes himself from the situation?
b: Because an oath is made with the intention of fulfilling it and avoiding the prohibited action. The unavoidable brief moment in which the situation exists is therefore overlooked.

f: 161. If someone remains wearing the garment, riding the animal, or living in the house for an hour after making the oath, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. These actions are considered continuing actions, and remaining in them after the oath breaks it.

f: 162. Why is wearing, riding, and living considered continuing actions while entering is not?
b: People assign durations to these actions, saying things like "I rode for a day" or "I wore clothes for a day." However, one does not say "I entered for a day" to describe a continuing state.

f: 163. If someone claims that he intended only the beginning of wearing, riding, or living when making the oath, is his claim accepted?
b: Yes, because this interpretation is possible in his wording.

f: 164. If someone swears that he will not live in a particular house, then leaves but his family and belongings remain there, has he fulfilled his oath?
b: No. If he does not intend to return but leaves his family and belongings behind, he has still broken his oath because custom considers him to still be living there.

f: 165. Why is someone still considered to be living in a house if his family and possessions remain there?
b: Because residence is understood according to custom. A person may spend much of his day elsewhere but still be considered a resident of his home.

f: 166. If someone swears not to live in a city and leaves it, must he move his family and belongings to fulfil the oath?
b: According to a narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, no. Custom does not consider a person to still be living in a city after leaving it. A village has the same ruling according to the correct position.

f: 167. What is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding moving belongings when leaving a place?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that it is necessary to transfer the belongings. If anything remains, residence may still remain because residence was established through all these things.

f: 168. What is Abū Yūsuf’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding leaving belongings behind?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that the consideration is moving the majority of one's belongings, because moving everything may be difficult or impossible.

f: 169. What is Muḥammad’s opinion regarding what must be moved to end residence?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that the consideration is moving what is essential for residence, such as household arrangements and necessities. Anything beyond this is not considered part of residence.

f: 170. Which opinion regarding moving belongings was considered more suitable for people?
b: The scholars said that Muḥammad’s opinion is better and more accommodating because it takes practical circumstances into account.

f: 171. If someone swears not to live in a place, should he move immediately to fulfil the oath?
b: It is said that he should move to another dwelling without delay.

f: 172. If someone moves only to another part of the same street or to a mosque, has he fulfilled his oath not to live in that place?
b: No. Moving only nearby or temporarily elsewhere does not fulfil the oath.

f: 173. What evidence is mentioned regarding a person who leaves his city with his family but has not yet established another home?
b: In al-Ziyādāt it is mentioned that until he establishes another permanent residence, his first residence remains his home for certain legal rulings, such as those related to travel.

f: 174. If a person swears that he will not leave the mosque and orders someone to carry him out, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He has broken his oath because the action of the person commanded is attributed to the one who commanded him. It is like a person riding an animal: the movement of the animal is attributed to the rider.

f: 175. If a person is removed from the mosque against his will, has he broken his oath not to leave?
b: No. He has not broken his oath because the action cannot be attributed to him, as he neither commanded nor chose it.

f: 176. If someone carries a person out of the mosque with his permission but without him ordering it, has he broken his oath?
b: No. The correct view is that leaving is attributed through command, not merely through permission.

f: 177. If someone swears that he will not leave his house except for a funeral, then leaves for the funeral and afterwards goes to fulfil another need, has he broken his oath?
b: No. The actual leaving occurred for the permitted reason (the funeral). What happens afterwards is not considered a separate act of leaving.

f: 178. If someone swears that he will not go out towards Makkah, then leaves intending Makkah but later returns, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He has broken his oath because the condition occurred: he left while intending to go towards Makkah. Leaving means separating oneself from the inside to the outside.

f: 179. If someone swears that he will not come to a place, when does he break his oath?
b: He does not break his oath until he enters the place, because "coming" refers to reaching something.

f: 180. What evidence shows that "coming" means reaching?
b: Allah says: "So go to Pharaoh and say..." (Qur'an 26:16), meaning: reach Pharaoh.

f: 181. If someone swears not to go somewhere (yadhhab), what is the stronger interpretation?
b: The stronger view is that it is like "leave" rather than "come," because the word indicates movement away from a place.

f: 182. If someone swears that he will come to Basrah but does not come until he is about to die, when does he break his oath?
b: He breaks his oath at the final moment of his life because until then fulfilling the oath remained possible.

f: 183. If someone swears that he will not ride the animal of a certain person and rides an animal owned by that person's authorised slave (ʿabd maʾdhūn), does he break his oath according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, he does not break his oath because the animal is attributed to the slave rather than the master.

f: 184. If an authorised slave has a debt that completely consumes his wealth (dayn mustaghriq), does riding his animal break the oath?
b: No. Even if the person intended that animal to be included, he does not break his oath because according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ the master has no ownership in the slave's property in this case.

f: 185. If the authorised slave has no debt or his debt does not consume all his wealth, when does riding his animal break the oath?
b: He only breaks his oath if he intended the slave's animal to be included.

f: 186. Why is intention required regarding an authorised slave's property when there is no complete debt?
b: Because legally the ownership belongs to the master, but custom attributes the property to the slave. Since both attributions exist, intention is required to determine what was meant.

f: 187. What hadith is used to show that an authorised slave's wealth legally belongs to his master?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sells a slave who has wealth, then his wealth belongs to the seller." This indicates that the slave's wealth is legally connected to the master.

f: 188. Why is ownership of an authorised slave's property considered weakened for the purpose of oaths?
b: Because although the master legally owns the wealth, custom attributes it to the slave. This weakens the attribution to the master, so intention becomes necessary.

f: 189. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, when does a person break his oath regarding the property of an authorised slave (ʿabd maʾdhūn)?
b: In all cases, he breaks his oath if he intended the slave's property to be included, because the attribution of the property to the slave rather than the master is problematic.

f: 190. According to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, when does a person break his oath regarding an authorised slave's property?
b: He breaks his oath even without intention because the consideration is the actual reality of ownership.

f: 191. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, does debt prevent the master from owning the authorised slave's property?
b: No. According to them, debt does not prevent the master from owning the slave's property.

f: 192. If someone swears: "I will not eat from this palm tree," what does the oath refer to?
b: It refers to the fruit of the palm tree, namely the dates.

f: 193. Why does "I will not eat from this palm tree" refer to its fruit rather than the tree itself?
b: Because the oath is attached to something that is not itself eaten, so it is understood metaphorically as referring to what comes from it. The fruit is caused by the tree and can represent it.

f: 194. Does an oath not to eat from a palm tree include products made after processing its fruit?
b: No. It only applies before the fruit undergoes a new transformation.

f: 195. If someone swears not to eat from a palm tree, does drinking wine made from its fruit break the oath?
b: No. Wine made from the fruit is a transformed product and is not included.

f: 196. If someone swears not to eat from a palm tree, does eating vinegar made from its fruit break the oath?
b: No. Vinegar made from the fruit is not included because the fruit has undergone transformation.

f: 197. If someone swears not to eat from a palm tree, does eating cooked date syrup (dibs) break the oath?
b: No. Cooked date syrup is a transformed product and is not included.

f: 198. If someone swears not to eat these unripe dates (busr), then they become ripe dates (rutab) and he eats them, has he broken his oath?
b: No. He has not broken his oath because the oath was connected specifically to the state of being unripe dates.

f: 199. If someone swears not to eat these ripe dates (rutab), then they become ordinary dates (tamr) and he eats them, has he broken his oath?
b: No. The oath was restricted to the state of being ripe dates.

f: 200. If someone swears not to drink this milk and it becomes cheese (shīrāz), then he eats it, has he broken his oath?
b: No. The oath was connected to the original state of milk, not the transformed product.

f: 201. Why are oaths regarding unripe dates, ripe dates, and milk restricted to their original states?
b: Because the specific description was the reason motivating the oath. The fact that they were unripe dates, ripe dates, or milk was the motivating factor, so the oath remains limited to that condition.

f: 202. Why is this different from someone swearing not to speak to a child or young man and then speaking after he becomes old?
b: Because refusing to speak to a Muslim is prohibited in Islamic law, so the motivating factor behind the oath is not recognised when it involves abandoning a Muslim.

f: 203. If someone swears not to speak to a child and later speaks to him after he becomes an old man, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. The change in age does not remove the oath because the reason behind avoiding speech is not legally recognised.

f: 204. If someone swears that he will not eat the meat of a particular lamb, then eats it after it grows into a ram, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He has broken his oath because the young age of the animal was not the reason for the oath. In fact, avoiding the meat of a mature ram would be even more likely.

f: 205. If someone swears that he will not eat unripe dates (busr) and eats ripe dates (rutab), has he broken his oath?
b: No. He has not broken his oath because ripe dates are not called busr.

f: 206. If someone swears not to eat ripe dates or unripe dates and eats a mixed date (mudhanab), what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that he breaks his oath because a mudhanab contains both ripe and unripe portions.

f: 207. What is a mudhanab date?
b: A mudhanab is a date which is partly ripe and partly unripe.

f: 208. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding eating a mudhanab date after swearing not to eat ripe dates?
b: They say he does not break his oath regarding ripe dates because a mudhanab that is considered ripe remains within the category of ripe dates.

f: 209. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad say a mudhanab remains within one category?
b: Because a ripe mudhanab is still called ripe, and an unripe mudhanab is still called unripe. The dominant description determines its category.

f: 210. What is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning that eating a mudhanab breaks the oath?
b: Because the ripe portion and the unripe portion are both present. Whoever eats it has eaten both ripe dates and unripe dates, and each part is independently intended in eating.

f: 211. Why is the ruling of buying mixed dates different from eating them?
b: Buying applies to the whole item as one unit, so the smaller part follows the dominant portion. Eating occurs piece by piece, so each individual part is considered separately intended.

f: 212. If someone swears not to buy ripe dates, then buys a cluster of unripe dates containing some ripe dates, has he broken his oath?
b: No. The purchase applies to the whole cluster, and the small amount of ripe dates follows the majority.

f: 213. If someone swears not to eat ripe dates, then eats a cluster of unripe dates containing some ripe dates, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. Since eating occurs piece by piece, the ripe portion is considered separately and the oath is broken.

f: 214. If someone swears not to buy barley and buys wheat containing some barley grains, has he broken his oath?
b: No. The barley grains are a minor part and are included under the whole purchase of wheat.

f: 215. If someone swears not to eat barley and eats wheat containing some barley grains, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. Eating considers each part separately, so consuming the barley grains breaks the oath.

f: 216. What general principle distinguishes buying and eating in mixed items?
b: In buying, the minor part follows the majority because the transaction applies to the whole item. In eating, each consumed part is considered individually, so the minor part can independently break the oath.

f: 217. If someone swears: "I will not eat meat," and eats fish meat, has he broken his oath?
b: No. According to istiḥsān, he has not broken his oath because calling fish "meat" is considered metaphorical in this context.

f: 218. What would the analogy (qiyās) say regarding eating fish after swearing not to eat meat?
b: The analogy would say that he has broken his oath because the Qur'an refers to fish as "fresh meat": "And from it you eat fresh meat..." (Qur'an 16:14).

f: 219. Why does istiḥsān exclude fish from the oath of not eating meat?
b: Because ordinary meat originates from blood, while fish does not have blood in that sense due to living in water. Therefore, calling it meat is considered figurative.

f: 220. If someone swears not to eat meat and eats pork meat, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because pork is genuinely meat, even though it is prohibited.

f: 221. If someone swears not to eat meat and eats human flesh, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. Human flesh is genuinely meat, and an oath may be intended to prevent oneself from eating something forbidden.

f: 222. If someone swears not to eat meat and eats liver, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes, according to the view that liver is considered meat, because it originates from blood and is used like meat.

f: 223. If someone swears not to eat meat and eats stomach lining (karsh), has he broken his oath?
b: Yes, according to the view that it is considered meat because it shares the characteristics of meat.

f: 224. Is there another view regarding liver and stomach lining when someone swears not to eat meat?
b: Yes. It is also said that according to local custom he would not break his oath because people do not normally call these things "meat."

f: 225. If someone swears not to eat or buy fat (shahm), what type of fat breaks the oath according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, only abdominal fat breaks the oath.

f: 226. What do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad say regarding back fat when someone swears not to eat or buy fat?
b: They say that back fat is also included and eating or buying it breaks the oath.

f: 227. What is meant by back fat?
b: It refers to the fatty tissue found on the back of an animal.

f: 228. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad include back fat under the term fat?
b: Because it has the characteristics of fat, especially that it melts when heated.

f: 229. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not consider back fat to be included under fat?
b: Because he considers it to actually be meat: it originates from blood, is used like meat, and provides nourishment like meat.

f: 230. If someone swears not to eat meat, does eating back fat break the oath according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes. Since Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considers back fat to be meat, eating it breaks an oath not to eat meat.

f: 231. If someone swears not to sell fat, does selling back fat break the oath according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. Although he considers it meat for eating purposes, it is not normally called fat in a sale context.

f: 232. If someone swears not to buy or eat meat or fat, and eats tail fat (aliyah), has he broken his oath?
b: No. Tail fat is considered a separate category that is neither meat nor ordinary fat.

f: 233. Why does tail fat (aliyah) not break an oath against eating meat or fat?
b: Because it is not classified as either meat or ordinary fat, so neither category applies to it.

f: 234. If someone swears: "I will not eat from this wheat," when does he break his oath according to the Hanafi scholars?
b: He breaks his oath when he eats the wheat itself as grains.

f: 235. If someone swears: "I will not eat from this wheat," and eats bread made from that wheat, what is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says he does not break his oath because the literal meaning of wheat refers to the actual grains, not products made from it.

f: 236. If someone swears: "I will not eat from this wheat," and eats bread made from that wheat, what do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad say?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that he does break his oath because custom understands "from this wheat" to include things produced from it.

f: 237. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad include bread made from wheat under the oath not to eat from wheat?
b: Because customary usage understands the phrase broadly, including things made from the original item.

f: 238. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not include bread made from wheat under the oath not to eat wheat?
b: Because wheat has a literal meaning that is actually used. Wheat itself can be roasted, boiled, or eaten directly, so the literal meaning takes precedence over the customary metaphor according to his principle.

f: 239. If someone swears not to eat from wheat and eats the wheat grains themselves, what is the correct view?
b: The correct view is that he breaks his oath, and this is accepted by both Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad.

f: 240. Why do the two companions say eating wheat grains breaks the oath?
b: Because the metaphorical meaning is broad and includes the actual wheat itself.

f: 241. What example is given to show that customary meanings can extend beyond literal wording?
b: The example is someone saying: "I will not put my foot in so-and-so's house," where the intended meaning includes entering the house.

f: 242. If someone swears not to eat from flour and eats bread made from that flour, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because flour is not normally eaten directly, so the oath refers to what is produced from it.

f: 243. If someone swears not to eat from flour and eats the flour itself dry, has he broken his oath?
b: No. This is the correct view because the metaphor has become clearly intended toward the common usage of flour as something used to make food.

f: 244. If someone swears: "I will not eat bread," what type of bread does the oath refer to?
b: It refers to the bread which people of that region customarily call bread.

f: 245. What type of bread is generally intended by the word "bread" (khubz)?
b: In most lands, it refers to wheat and barley bread because these are the common forms of bread.

f: 246. If someone swears not to eat bread and eats qaṭāʾif bread, has he broken his oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath because qaṭāʾif is not generally called "bread" without qualification.

f: 247. If someone intended qaṭāʾif when swearing not to eat bread, does eating it break the oath?
b: Yes. His oath applies because that interpretation is possible in his statement.

f: 248. If someone swears not to eat bread and eats rice bread in Iraq, has he broken his oath?
b: No. Rice bread is not the customary meaning of bread in Iraq.

f: 249. If someone swears not to eat bread and eats rice bread in Ṭabaristān or another region where rice bread is the normal bread, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. Since rice bread is the customary meaning of bread in that region, it is included in the oath.

f: 250. If someone swears: "I will not eat grilled food (shawāʾ)," what does the oath normally refer to?
b: It refers to grilled meat, not grilled vegetables such as eggplant or carrots.

f: 251. Why does "grilled food" (shawāʾ) normally refer to meat?
b: Because when the word is used generally, customary usage understands it as grilled meat.

f: 252. If someone swears not to eat grilled food and intends all grilled items, including eggs or vegetables, is his intention accepted?
b: Yes. His intention is accepted because the literal meaning of the word can include anything grilled.

f: 253. If someone swears: "I will not eat ṭabīkh (cooked food)," what does the oath refer to?
b: It refers to food cooked from meat, based on istiḥsān and customary usage.

f: 254. Why is ṭabīkh restricted to cooked meat rather than all cooked foods?
b: Because applying the word to every cooked item is impractical, so it is restricted to the commonly understood meaning: meat cooked in water.

f: 255. If someone intends a different meaning when swearing not to eat ṭabīkh, is his intention accepted?
b: Yes. His intention is accepted because restricting the meaning further would make the oath stricter than necessary.

f: 256. If someone swears not to eat ṭabīkh and only consumes the broth, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because the broth contains parts of the meat and is itself called ṭabīkh.

f: 257. If someone swears: "I will not eat heads," what does the oath refer to?
b: It refers to the heads that are cooked in ovens (tanūr) and commonly sold in the town.

f: 258. What does the verb yukabbas refer to in relation to heads?
b: It refers to the preparation of animal heads by cooking them in ovens.

f: 259. In al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, if someone swears: "I will not eat a head," what is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that it includes both cattle heads and sheep heads.

f: 260. In al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, if someone swears: "I will not eat a head," what do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad say?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that it refers only to sheep heads.

f: 261. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and the two companions differ regarding the meaning of "head"?
b: Because their customs differed. In Abū Ḥanīfah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ time, both cattle and sheep heads were commonly called "heads," while in the time of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, the term normally referred only to sheep heads.

f: 262. What is the ruling regarding the word "head" in modern times?
b: The fatwā follows local custom, as mentioned in the Mukhtaṣar. The meaning depends on what people normally understand by the word in that region.

f: 263. If someone swears, "I will not eat fruit," which foods are included according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the oath does not include grapes, pomegranates, fresh dates, cucumbers, or snake cucumbers. However, it includes apples, watermelon, apricots, and similar fruits.

f: 264. What is the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding the word "fruit" (fākihah)?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that grapes, fresh dates, and pomegranates are also included in the oath because they are enjoyed as fruits. Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ excludes them because they are also used as food and medicine, so their status as pure enjoyment is weaker.

f: 265. What is the principle behind the term "fruit" (fākihah) in oaths?
b: Fruit refers to things eaten for enjoyment, such as before meals or after meals, as an extra pleasure beyond normal nourishment.

f: 266. Are fresh and dried forms of fruit treated the same in oaths?
b: Yes, fresh and dried forms are treated alike when eating them for enjoyment is customary.

f: 267. Why does dried watermelon not break an oath against eating fruit?
b: Because dried watermelon is not normally considered a fruit eaten for enjoyment; it can function more like a staple food or spice.

f: 268. Why are cucumbers and snake cucumbers not included in the oath against eating fruit?
b: Because they are classified as vegetables (baql), both in buying and eating customs, so they are not considered fruit.

f: 269. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad include grapes, fresh dates, and pomegranates as fruit?
b: They argue that the purpose of fruit is enjoyment, and these items provide enjoyment even more than many other foods because they are prized fruits.

f: 270. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to the argument of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding grapes, dates, and pomegranates?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argues that these items are not only eaten for enjoyment but are also used as food and medicine. Because they fulfil necessary purposes, their classification as pure fruit is weakened.

f: 271. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider grapes, dates, and pomegranates different from apples and similar fruits?
b: Apples and similar fruits are primarily eaten for enjoyment, whereas grapes, dates, and pomegranates can serve additional purposes such as nourishment and medicinal use.

f: 272. Why are dried forms of some fruits treated differently according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because dried fruits may become staple foods or ingredients rather than being consumed merely for enjoyment.

f: 273. If someone swears, "I will not eat idām (food eaten with bread)," what does idām refer to according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, idām refers to anything that is dipped into bread or mixed with it. Grilled meat is not idām, while salt is idām.

f: 274. What is the view of Muḥammad regarding idām?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that anything normally eaten with bread is considered idām, such as meat, eggs, and similar foods. This view is also narrated from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 275. What is Muḥammad's evidence for including meat and eggs as idām?
b: Muḥammad argues that idām comes from muʾādamah, meaning something that accompanies another thing. Anything eaten together with bread accompanies it, so it is considered idām.

f: 276. What is the argument of Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding idām?
b: They argue that idām is something eaten as a supplement to bread, and true supplementation requires actual mixing and dependence upon the bread rather than being an independent food.

f: 277. Why are vinegar and similar liquids considered idām according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because they are not normally eaten alone; they are usually consumed as an accompaniment and become part of the bread, so they are considered subordinate to it.

f: 278. Why is salt considered idām according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because salt is not normally eaten independently and dissolves into the food, making it subordinate to the bread.

f: 279. Why is meat not considered idām according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because meat can be eaten independently and is not dependent upon bread, so it does not meet the definition of idām.

f: 280. Can meat become included in an oath against idām if the person intended it?
b: Yes. If the person specifically intended meat or another independent food, his intention is accepted because it makes the oath stricter.

f: 281. Are grapes and watermelon considered idām?
b: No. The correct view is that grapes and watermelon are not considered idām.

f: 282. If someone swears, "I will not eat lunch," what time period does lunch (taghaddaytu) refer to?
b: Lunch refers to eating from dawn until noon.

f: 283. If someone swears, "I will not eat dinner," what time period does dinner (ʿashāʾ) refer to?
b: Dinner refers to eating from noon until midnight.

f: 284. Why is the noon prayer connected with the two "evening prayers" in the hadith?
b: Because after midday the meal is called dinner (ʿashāʾ), showing that the period after noon is associated with the evening time in certain linguistic usages.

f: 285. What is the time period for the pre-dawn meal (suḥūr)?
b: Suḥūr refers to eating from midnight until dawn because it comes from the word saḥar, meaning the time close to dawn.

f: 286. What determines whether something is considered lunch or dinner in an oath?
b: The consideration is the meal intended to satisfy hunger, and the custom of each locality is taken into account.

f: 287. Is any small amount of food considered lunch or dinner for the purpose of an oath?
b: No. It must be an amount that is more than half of one's normal fullness according to the discussion in the text.

f: 288. If someone says, "If I wear, eat, or drink, then my slave is free," and claims he intended only one specific thing, is his intention accepted?
b: No. His intention is not accepted either in court or privately because intention only affects words that are actually mentioned. The words "clothing," "food," and "drink" were not explicitly stated.

f: 289. Why is intention not accepted when the words "wear," "eat," and "drink" are used without mentioning their objects?
b: Because the implied objects do not have a general scope that can be restricted. An intention cannot restrict something that was not explicitly expressed.

f: 290. If someone says, "If I wear a garment, eat food, or drink a beverage, then my slave is free," is his intention accepted?
b: His intention is accepted privately but not in court.

f: 291. Why is intention accepted privately but not judicially when he mentions "a garment," "food," or "a beverage"?
b: Because these are indefinite nouns (nakirah) used in a conditional sentence, so they carry a general meaning. His intention can restrict them, but because it contradicts the apparent wording, it is not accepted by a judge.

f: 292. If someone swears, "I will not drink from the Tigris," and drinks water from it using a container, does he break his oath according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, he does not break his oath until he drinks directly from the Tigris with his mouth.

f: 293. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding drinking from the Tigris with a container?
b: They say that he breaks his oath because taking water from the Tigris in a container is the commonly understood meaning of drinking from it.

f: 294. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument regarding the phrase "drink from the Tigris"?
b: He argues that the word "from" (min) indicates taking a portion directly from the source. Therefore, the literal meaning is direct drinking from the river itself.

f: 295. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not accept the customary meaning of taking water in a container?
b: Because the literal meaning is established and everyone agrees that direct drinking from the river breaks the oath. A metaphorical meaning is not adopted when the literal meaning is valid.

f: 296. If someone swears, "I will not drink from the water of the Tigris," and drinks it from a container, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. According to the text, he breaks his oath because even after being removed from the river, the water is still attributed to the Tigris.

f: 297. Why does water taken from the Tigris remain connected to the Tigris?
b: Because it is still called "the water of the Tigris," just as water from another river originating from the Tigris would still be attributed to it.

f: 298. If someone says, "If I do not drink the water that is in this jug today, then my wife is divorced," but there is no water in the jug, does divorce occur?
b: No. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, divorce does not occur because fulfilling the oath was impossible.

f: 299. If the jug contained water when the oath was made, but the water was poured away before night, does divorce occur according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: No. Since fulfilment became impossible before the end of the time period, divorce does not occur.

f: 300. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding the oath involving water in the jug?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that the oath takes effect and divorce occurs in all these cases.

f: 301. What is the basis of the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad versus Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The disagreement concerns whether the possibility of fulfilling the oath is a condition for the oath to exist and remain binding.

f: 302. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad require that fulfilment be possible?
b: Because an oath is originally established for the purpose of fulfilling it. Therefore, fulfilment must be possible before the oath can become binding.

f: 303. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument that the oath is still valid even if fulfilment is impossible?
b: He argues that the oath can exist while requiring either fulfilment or, if it is broken, its substitute — expiation (kaffārah).

f: 304. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad respond to Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument?
b: They say that the original obligation (fulfilment of the oath) must first be possible before the substitute (kaffārah) can apply.

f: 305. Why does a yamīn ghamūs (false oath) not require kaffārah according to this reasoning?
b: Because the original fulfilment of the oath is not possible; the oath was sinful from the beginning rather than a valid oath that was later broken.

f: 306. If an oath regarding water in a jug is unrestricted (not time-bound) and no water existed when the oath was made, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, he does not break his oath because the oath was never established due to the impossibility of fulfilment.

f: 307. If an unrestricted oath was made regarding water in a jug that did not contain water, what is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that he breaks his oath immediately because fulfilment was required at once and became impossible.

f: 308. If water existed in the jug when the oath was made but was poured away afterward, what is the ruling according to all three Imams?
b: All three agree that he breaks his oath.

f: 309. Why does Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish between unrestricted oaths and time-limited oaths?
b: He argues that a time limit gives additional allowance, so fulfilment is only required at the end of the period. In an unrestricted oath, fulfilment is required immediately.

f: 310. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does an unrestricted oath break when the object disappears?
b: Because fulfilment was immediately required, and once the object of the oath disappears, fulfilment becomes impossible, so the oath is broken.

f: 311. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad distinguish between unrestricted and time-limited oaths?
b: They say that in an unrestricted oath fulfilment is immediately required, but in a time-limited oath fulfilment is only required at the final moment.

f: 312. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, why does a time-limited oath not break when the water disappears before the deadline?
b: Because the oath only becomes binding at the final time of fulfilment. If fulfilment is impossible then, the oath was never established due to the absence of the condition of possibility.

f: 313. How is the disappearance of the water before the deadline compared?
b: It is compared to making an oath initially in a situation where fulfilment is already impossible; therefore no valid oath is established.

f: 314. If someone swears, "By Allah, I will climb the sky," does the oath become established?
b: Yes. According to the majority of scholars, the oath is established and he breaks it immediately due to inability to fulfil it under normal circumstances.

f: 315. What is Zufar's view regarding an oath to climb the sky or turn a stone into gold?
b: Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that such an oath is not established because these actions are normally impossible and resemble truly impossible matters.

f: 316. What is the majority's response to Zufar regarding impossible actions?
b: They argue that fulfilment is theoretically possible. Climbing to the sky is possible in itself because angels ascend to the heavens, and turning a stone into gold is possible through Allah's power.

f: 317. Why does the majority consider the oath established despite normal inability?
b: Because the action is possible in reality, even if it is beyond ordinary human ability. Therefore, the oath exists, and inability causes the oath to be broken.

f: 318. Why is this compared to a person who dies while under an oath?
b: Because Allah could theoretically restore his life, but legally his death means he can no longer fulfil the oath, so the oath is considered broken.

f: 319. Why is the oath regarding the empty jug different from an oath to climb the sky?
b: In the empty jug case, fulfilment was impossible at the very time the oath was made because there was no water. Therefore, the oath was never established. In the sky example, fulfilment is theoretically possible, so the oath is established.

f: 320. If someone swears, "I will not speak to so-and-so," and then speaks while the person can hear him, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath if the person is able to hear him, even if the person is asleep.

f: 321. Why does speaking to a sleeping person break the oath?
b: Because he spoke to him and the sound reached him, even though the sleeping person did not understand. This is like calling someone who can hear but deliberately ignores the caller.

f: 322. Is it required that the sleeping person be awakened for the oath to be broken?
b: Some narrations from al-Mabsūṭ mention that he must awaken him. Most scholars follow this view because if he does not wake him, it resembles calling someone who is too far away to hear.

f: 323. If someone swears, "I will not speak to him except with his permission," and the person gives permission but he does not know about it and speaks, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. He breaks his oath because the permission did not reach him.

f: 324. Why does permission (idhn) require knowledge of it?
b: Because the word idhn is connected to informing (adhāna) or entering into the ear (udhun), both of which require the permission to be communicated.

f: 325. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view regarding permission that was given but not known?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says he does not break his oath because permission means authorization, and authorization exists even without communication.

f: 326. How do the other scholars respond to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding permission?
b: They say that mere consent is an internal matter of the heart, whereas permission requires communication and reaching the person.

f: 327. If someone swears, "I will not speak for a month," when does the month begin?
b: The month begins from the moment he makes the oath.

f: 328. Why does the month begin immediately in an oath not to speak?
b: Because without mentioning the month, the oath would continue forever. Mentioning the month removes all time beyond it, leaving the period immediately after the oath included.

f: 329. How does "I will not speak for a month" differ from "By Allah, I will fast for a month"?
b: In fasting, mentioning the month specifies the amount of fasting. In not speaking, mentioning the month limits an oath that would otherwise have been permanent.

f: 330. If someone swears, "I will not speak," and recites Qur'an during prayer, does he break his oath?
b: No. According to the Hanafi position, he does not break his oath because Qur'an recitation in prayer is not considered speech.

f: 331. If someone swears, "I will not speak," and recites Qur'an outside prayer, does he break his oath?
b: Yes, according to the discussion in the text, because outside prayer it is considered speech.

f: 332. Does saying subḥān Allāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, or Allāhu akbar break an oath not to speak?
b: According to analogy, yes, because these are literally speech. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 333. Why do the Hanafi scholars say Qur'an recitation in prayer does not break an oath not to speak?
b: Because in prayer it is not considered speech either legally or according to custom. The Prophet ﷺ said: "This prayer of ours is not suitable for any speech of people."

f: 334. Is there another view regarding Qur'an recitation outside prayer?
b: Yes. Some scholars say that according to modern custom, even outside prayer it would not break the oath because a person is called a reciter or one glorifying Allah, not a "speaker."

f: 335. If someone says, "The day I speak to so-and-so, my wife is divorced," does "day" refer only to daytime?
b: No. It refers to both night and day because when "day" is connected to an action that is not continuous, it means any time.

f: 336. Why does "the day I speak to so-and-so" include night as well?
b: Because speaking is a momentary action, so "day" is understood as a general period of time rather than only daylight hours.

f: 337. What Qur'anic example supports the usage of "day" to mean time generally?
b: Allah says: "The day they turn their backs..." (Qur'an 8:16). Turning away is not a continuous action, so "day" refers to the time when it occurs.

f: 338. If someone intends by "the day I speak" only the daytime, is his intention accepted?
b: Yes. His intention is accepted judicially because using "day" for daytime is also a valid linguistic usage.

f: 339. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view regarding intending only daytime in "the day I speak"?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that this intention is not accepted in court because it contradicts the common usage of the expression.

f: 340. If someone says, "The night I speak to him," what does "night" refer to?
b: It refers only to the night.

f: 341. Why does "night" refer only to nighttime while "day" can refer generally to time?
b: Because night literally means darkness, while day literally means brightness.

f: 342. If someone says, "I will not speak to him unless so-and-so arrives," and he speaks before the arrival, what is the ruling?
b: His wife is divorced because the condition ending the oath has not yet occurred.

f: 343. If someone says, "I will not speak to him until so-and-so arrives," and he speaks after the person arrives, what is the ruling?
b: His wife is not divorced because the oath has ended once the endpoint occurred.

f: 344. What is the legal effect of words such as "unless," "until," and similar expressions in oaths?
b: They indicate an endpoint (ghāyah). Before the endpoint, the oath remains effective; after it, the oath ends.

f: 345. If the person whose arrival or permission was mentioned dies, what happens to the oath?
b: According to the majority, the oath falls away because the event that would end the oath is no longer possible.

f: 346. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view if the person mentioned in the exception dies?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says the oath does not fall away because possibility is not a condition. Once the exception disappears, the oath becomes permanent.

f: 347. If someone swears, "I will not speak to the slave of so-and-so," and he does not intend a specific slave, then so-and-so sells the slave and he speaks to him, does he break his oath?
b: No. He does not break his oath because the attribution "the slave of so-and-so" no longer exists.

f: 348. If someone swears, "I will not speak to the wife of so-and-so," and the marriage ends, does he break his oath if he speaks to her?
b: According to the narration of al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, he does not break his oath because the relationship upon which the oath was based has disappeared.

f: 349. What types of attribution are mentioned regarding "the slave of so-and-so," "the wife of so-and-so," and "the friend of so-and-so"?
b: They are: (1) attribution of ownership (iḍāfat al-milk), such as "the slave of so-and-so"; and (2) attribution of relationship (iḍāfat al-nisbah), such as "the wife of so-and-so" or "the friend of so-and-so."

f: 350. Why does the oath not remain regarding a slave after the slave is sold?
b: Because the oath was connected to the slave being attributed as belonging to that person. Once ownership ends, the described object no longer exists in that form.

f: 351. What is Muḥammad's view regarding an oath involving "the wife of so-and-so" or "the friend of so-and-so"?
b: Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ says that he does break his oath because these descriptions are merely for identifying the person, and the oath remains attached to the individual.

f: 352. How does Muḥammad explain the case of "the wife of so-and-so" or "the friend of so-and-so"?
b: He argues that the attribution is only a method of identification, similar to saying "this person." The relationship itself is not the basis of the oath.

f: 353. Why does the earlier Hanafi narration not make the person break his oath after the relationship ends?
b: Because it is possible that the person's intention was to avoid the person specifically due to their relationship with the named individual. Since he did not specify his intention, there is doubt, and doubt prevents the oath from being considered broken.

f: 354. If someone swears not to speak to a person described through ownership or relationship, what happens if the description later disappears?
b: If the oath was general and not directed at a specific individual, then according to the earlier narration he does not break his oath when the ownership or relationship disappears. This is because the thing mentioned no longer exists in the form upon which the oath was based.

f: 355. What is the difference between an attribution of ownership (iḍāfat al-milk) and an attribution of relationship (iḍāfat al-nisbah) in oaths?
b: Ownership attribution, such as "the slave of so-and-so," is connected to ownership itself. Relationship attribution, such as "the wife of so-and-so" or "the friend of so-and-so," may only serve to identify the person. Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considered the latter still binding even after the relationship ends because the person remains identifiable.

f: 356. If someone swears not to speak to the slave of so-and-so, and so-and-so sells the slave, does speaking to the former slave break the oath?
b: According to the narration of al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, he does not break the oath because the ownership attribution no longer exists.

f: 357. According to Muḥammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does speaking to a former wife or friend still break the oath after the relationship ends?
b: Because the relationship was only a means of identifying the person. The oath is actually connected to the individual himself, similar to pointing directly at someone.
