f: 358. If someone swears not to speak to a specific slave, such as saying "this slave of so-and-so," and then speaks after the slave is sold, does he break the oath?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, he does not break the oath. According to Muḥammad and Zufar رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, he does break the oath because the identification of the person remains.

f: 359. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ distinguish between a slave and a wife or friend in oaths?
b: They argue that a person avoids a slave because of the owner connected to him, not because of the slave himself. A wife or friend, however, is avoided because of the person himself, so the relationship only identifies the individual.

f: 360. If someone swears not to enter a particular house of so-and-so, then so-and-so sells the house and he enters it, what is the ruling?
b: This follows the same disagreement as the case of the specific slave. Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ consider the ownership connection relevant, while Muḥammad and Zufar رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ consider the house itself identified by the wording.

f: 361. Why do Muḥammad and Zufar رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that a house attribution is only for identification?
b: They argue that pointing to something is even stronger than attribution for identification. Since pointing to a specific object is considered binding, the attribution "of so-and-so" should not remove the ruling.

f: 362. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say ownership attribution affects the oath?
b: Because the reason for avoiding the object is connected to the owner. A person does not normally dislike a slave, house, or similar thing because of its own essence, but because of its connection to its owner.

f: 363. If someone swears not to speak to the owner of a certain cloak, then the cloak is sold and he speaks to him, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. The attribution to the cloak is only for identifying the person, so the oath remains attached to that individual.

f: 364. Why does the oath regarding the owner of a cloak remain after the cloak is sold?
b: Because a person is not avoiding someone because of the cloak itself. The cloak merely identifies the person, similar to pointing directly at him.

f: 365. If someone swears not to speak to this young man and later speaks to him after he becomes old, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. The oath applies to the specific person who was pointed out. The description "young" does not affect the ruling because the person himself was intended.

f: 366. Why is the description "young" ignored when someone points to a specific person?
b: Because descriptions attached to a present and identified person are normally not the basis of the ruling. The reference is to the individual, not the temporary description.

f: 367. Why does becoming old not remove the oath concerning "this young man"?
b: Because the description was only incidental. The person remains the same person who was identified when the oath was made.

f: 368. What is the ruling if someone swears: "I will not speak to him for a while" (ḥīnan)?
b: According to the Hanafi position, it means six months.

f: 369. What meanings can the word ḥīn have?
b: The word ḥīn can refer to a short period, forty years, or six months.

f: 370. Why is ḥīn interpreted as six months in an oath?
b: Six months is the middle meaning. A very short period is not intended because people naturally avoid speaking for short periods anyway, while an endless period would effectively mean forever. Therefore, the moderate meaning is selected.

f: 371. What evidence is used for the different meanings of ḥīn?
b: The Qur'an uses ḥīn for a long period in "Has there not come upon man a period of time..." (76:1), and for six months in "It produces its fruit every while..." (14:25), according to the interpretation mentioned by the jurists.

f: 372. If someone swears "I will not speak to him for a period" (zamānan), what duration does it mean?
b: It has the same ruling as ḥīn and means six months.

f: 373. Why does zamān have the same ruling as ḥīn?
b: Because people use it in similar expressions, such as "I have not seen you for a while," indicating a general period whose customary meaning is similar.

f: 374. If someone intends a different duration when saying ḥīn or zamān, is his intention accepted?
b: Yes. If he intended another meaning, the oath follows his intention because he intended the actual meaning of his words.

f: 375. What is the ruling of the word dahr in an oath according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: According to them, dahr has the same ruling as ḥīn and zamān, meaning it refers to six months when used indefinitely.

f: 376. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ give dahr the same ruling as ḥīn and zamān?
b: Because people use expressions like "I have not seen you for a while" and "I have not seen you for a dahr" with similar meanings.

f: 377. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position regarding the word dahr?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ said: "I do not know what dahr means." He did not assign it a fixed duration.

f: 378. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hesitate regarding dahr?
b: Because language cannot be established through analogy, and there is no consistent custom fixing its meaning, as its usage differs.

f: 379. Does the ruling of dahr change when it is used with the definite article al- (al-dahr)?
b: Yes. When used as al-dahr, it commonly means eternity.

f: 380. If someone swears: "I will not speak to him days," what does it mean?
b: It means three days.

f: 381. Why does "days" mean three days in an oath?
b: Because it is an indefinite plural, and the minimum number of a plural is three.

f: 382. If someone swears: "I will not speak to him the days," what duration does it mean according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, it means ten days.

f: 383. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret "the days" as ten days?
b: Because a definite plural refers to the greatest number normally expressed by that plural, and the greatest commonly expressed plural number is ten.

f: 384. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding "the days"?
b: According to them, it refers to the seven days of the week.

f: 385. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ interpret "the days" as the days of the week?
b: Because the definite article (al-) indicates something known and specific, and the known days are the seven days of the week.

f: 386. If someone swears: "I will not speak to him the months," what duration does it mean according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, it means ten months.

f: 387. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding "the months"?
b: According to them, it means twelve months, referring to the known months of the year.

f: 388. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret "the months" as ten months?
b: Because he applies the principle that a definite plural refers to the highest number normally expressed by that plural, which is ten.

f: 389. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ interpret "the months" as twelve months?
b: Because the definite article points to the known months, namely the twelve months of the year.

f: 390. If someone swears: "I will not speak to him the years," what does it mean according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, it means ten years.

f: 391. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding "the years"?
b: According to them, it refers to one's lifetime.

f: 392. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ interpret "the years" as one's lifetime?
b: Because there is no known lower limit for "the years" comparable to the days of the week or months of the year, so it refers to the longest known period connected to a person.

f: 393. If someone says to his slave: "If you serve me many days, then you are free," what does "many days" mean according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, it means ten days.

f: 394. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret "many days" as ten days?
b: Because ten is the greatest number normally included under the word "days."

f: 395. What is the position of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ regarding "many days"?
b: According to them, it means seven days.

f: 396. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ interpret "many days" as seven days?
b: Because anything beyond seven days is merely repetition of the same weekly cycle.

f: 397. How is the expression "many days" understood if the oath is made in Persian?
b: Some scholars say that in Persian it means seven days because the expression is treated as a singular form rather than a plural.

f: 398. If a man says to his wife: "When you give birth to a child, you are divorced," and she gives birth to a stillborn child, is she divorced?
b: Yes, she is divorced because the condition was fulfilled: a child was born.

f: 399. If a man says to his slave woman: "When you give birth to a child, you are free," and she gives birth to a stillborn child, does freedom occur?
b: Yes, freedom occurs because the condition of giving birth to a child was fulfilled.

f: 400. Why does the word "child" (walad) include a stillborn child in these rulings?
b: Because the word applies linguistically, according to common usage, and legally.

f: 401. What legal evidences show that a stillborn child is considered a child?
b: The waiting period (ʿiddah) ends through childbirth, postnatal bleeding (nifās) occurs after childbirth, and the mother becomes an umm walad through giving birth to the master's child.

f: 402. If someone says: "If she gives birth to a child, then he is free," and she gives birth first to a dead child and then to a living child, what is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, only the living child becomes free.

f: 403. If someone says: "If she gives birth to a child, then he is free," and she gives birth first to a dead child and then to a living child, what is the view of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ?
b: According to them, neither child becomes free.

f: 404. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that neither child becomes free?
b: Because the condition was already fulfilled by the birth of the dead child. The oath ended before a suitable recipient of freedom existed.

f: 405. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ restrict the word "child" to a living child in the case of emancipation?
b: Because the purpose of the statement was to establish freedom, and freedom only applies where another person's authority can be removed. A dead person has no such legal capacity.

f: 406. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not apply the same restriction to divorce or the freedom of the mother (umm walad)?
b: Because divorce and the freedom of the mother can be connected to childbirth itself without requiring the recipient of the consequence to possess legal capacity.

f: 407. If someone says: "The first slave whom I purchase is free," and he purchases one slave, what is the ruling?
b: That slave becomes free because he is the first individual purchased.

f: 408. Why does the first slave purchased become free when only one slave is purchased?
b: Because "first" refers to an individual who precedes others, and the single slave possesses this quality.

f: 409. If someone says: "The first slave whom I purchase is free," and he purchases two slaves together and then another slave later, does any slave become free?
b: No slave becomes free.

f: 410. Why do the two slaves purchased together not become free as the first slave?
b: Because neither one has individuality in being first; they share the first position.

f: 411. Why does the third slave purchased later not become free as the first slave?
b: Because he does not have precedence over anyone, so he is not first.

f: 412. If someone says: "The first slave whom I purchase alone is free," and he purchases several slaves, which slave becomes free?
b: The third slave becomes free if he is the first slave purchased individually.

f: 413. What does the word "alone" (waḥdahu) add to the meaning of "first slave"?
b: It means that the slave must be the first one purchased individually, not as part of a group purchase.

f: 414. If someone says: "The last slave whom I purchase is free," and he purchases only one slave then dies, does the slave become free?
b: No, the slave does not become free.

f: 415. Why does a single slave not become the "last" slave purchased?
b: Because "last" implies a later individual, and without another purchase there is no later position.

f: 416. If someone purchases one slave, then another slave, and then dies after saying: "The last slave whom I purchase is free," which slave becomes free?
b: The second slave becomes free because he is the later and therefore the last slave purchased.

f: 417. What is required for a slave to qualify as "the last slave purchased"?
b: There must be a later individual in comparison to another purchase, so the quality of being last exists.

f: 418. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, when does the slave become free in the case of "the last slave whom I purchase"?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the slave becomes free on the day he was purchased.

f: 419. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, when does the slave become free in the case of "the last slave whom I purchase"?
b: According to them, he becomes free on the day of the master's death.

f: 420. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ say that freedom occurs at death in the case of "the last slave"?
b: Because being "last" is only known after it becomes certain that no further purchase will occur, and this certainty only exists at death.

f: 421. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say that freedom occurs from the time of purchase?
b: Because death does not create the quality of being last; it only reveals that the slave was already last from the time of purchase.

f: 422. What practical difference results from the disagreement about when the "last slave" becomes free?
b: It affects whether the slave is considered part of the master's wealth from the time of purchase or only from death, especially regarding whether he is included in the entire estate or only one-third of it.

f: 423. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, is the slave who becomes free through being "last" considered from the entirety of the wealth or one-third?
b: He is considered from the entirety of the wealth because freedom occurred on the day of purchase.

f: 424. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ, is the slave who becomes free through being "last" considered from the entirety of the wealth or one-third?
b: He is considered from one-third of the wealth because freedom occurred at death.

f: 425. Does the same disagreement apply if three divorces are made conditional upon the last slave being purchased?
b: Yes, the same disagreement applies.

f: 426. What benefit appears in the disagreement regarding conditional divorce upon the last purchase?
b: The benefit appears regarding whether inheritance is prevented or not, depending on when the divorce is considered to occur.

f: 427. If someone says: "Every slave who gives me glad tidings of the birth of so-and-so is free," and three people separately give him the news, who becomes free?
b: The first person who gives the news becomes free.

f: 428. Why does only the first person become free when people give glad tidings separately?
b: Because glad tidings refers to news that causes happiness and changes the expression of the face, and this occurs from the first person who informs him.

f: 429. If three people give glad tidings of the birth together, who becomes free?
b: All of them become free because the glad tidings occurred from all of them together.

f: 430. If someone says: "If I purchase so-and-so, he is free," and he purchases him intending the purchase as expiation for an oath, does it count as kaffārah?
b: No, it does not suffice as expiation.

f: 431. Why does purchasing the specified slave not count as expiation when the oath was conditional upon purchasing him?
b: Because the condition is the purchase, while the intention of expiation must accompany the actual cause of emancipation.

f: 432. If someone purchases his father intending it as expiation for an oath, does it suffice according to the Hanafis?
b: Yes, according to the Hanafis it suffices.

f: 433. Who disagrees with the Hanafi position regarding purchasing one's father as expiation?
b: Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ disagree.

f: 434. What is the argument of Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ against counting the purchase of one's father as emancipation?
b: They argue that purchase is only the condition for freedom, while the actual cause of freedom is the relationship. They also argue that ownership and removing ownership are contradictory actions.

f: 435. What is the Hanafi evidence that purchasing one's father counts as emancipation?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "A child cannot repay his father except that he finds him enslaved, buys him, and frees him." The Prophet ﷺ treated the purchase itself as equivalent to emancipation.

f: 436. Why do the Hanafis say that purchasing one's father is equivalent to freeing him?
b: Because no additional act is required after the purchase; the purchase itself removes the father's enslavement.

f: 437. If someone purchases his Umm Walad intending expiation for an oath, does it count as kaffārah?
b: No, it does not count as kaffārah.

f: 438. Why does purchasing an Umm Walad not count as expiation?
b: Because her freedom already occurs due to her status as an Umm Walad, so the freedom cannot be fully attributed to the oath.

f: 439. Why does purchasing an ordinary female slave count as expiation but purchasing an Umm Walad does not?
b: An ordinary slave has no other cause requiring freedom, so the emancipation can be attributed to the oath. An Umm Walad already has another cause of freedom.

f: 440. If someone says: "If I take a slave woman as a concubine, then she is free," and he takes a slave woman he already owns as a concubine, does she become free?
b: Yes, she becomes free.

f: 441. Why does an already-owned slave woman become free when he takes her as a concubine under this oath?
b: Because the oath applies to any slave woman, and she falls under the indefinite wording.

f: 442. If someone purchases a slave woman and then takes her as a concubine, does she become free through the oath?
b: According to the Hanafi position, no, she does not become free through this oath.

f: 443. Who disagrees regarding a purchased slave woman later taken as a concubine?
b: Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disagrees and considers the oath applicable.

f: 444. What is Zufar's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument regarding the oath: "If I take a slave woman as a concubine, then she is free," when the slave woman was purchased first and then taken as a concubine?
b: Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argues that concubinage cannot exist except through ownership, so ownership is included within the meaning of the statement. Therefore, purchasing the slave woman should also be included.

f: 445. How does Zufar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ compare ownership in concubinage to marriage in divorce statements?
b: He compares it to someone saying to an unmarried woman: "If I divorce you, my slave is free." Marriage is implied because divorce cannot occur without marriage. Likewise, ownership is implied because concubinage cannot occur without ownership.

f: 446. What is the Hanafi response to Zufar's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argument regarding ownership and concubinage?
b: The Hanafis respond that ownership is only mentioned because it is necessary for concubinage to be valid. It is restricted to that necessity and does not extend to the consequence, which is emancipation.

f: 447. Why does ownership in the statement about concubinage not cause the purchased slave woman to become free?
b: Because ownership is only a condition for the act of concubinage, not part of the intended consequence of freedom.

f: 448. If someone says to a woman: "If I marry you, you are divorced three times," and then marries her, does divorcing her once cause three divorces?
b: No. If he marries her and divorces her once, she is only divorced once.

f: 449. Why does the example of marriage and divorce resemble the issue of ownership and concubinage?
b: Because in both cases the implied matter (marriage or ownership) is only required for the condition to occur, not for the consequence attached to it.

f: 450. If someone says: "Every slave owned by me is free," which slaves become free?
b: His umm walads, mudabbars, and ordinary slaves become free.

f: 451. Why do umm walads become free under the statement "Every slave owned by me is free"?
b: Because unrestricted ownership applies to them, as ownership of their persons and possession is established.

f: 452. Why do mudabbars become free under the statement "Every slave owned by me is free"?
b: Because they remain owned in terms of person and possession, even though their freedom is connected to the master's death.

f: 453. Do mukātab slaves become free under the statement "Every slave owned by me is free"?
b: No, unless the owner specifically intends them.

f: 454. Why do mukātab slaves not automatically become free under unrestricted ownership?
b: Because ownership over a mukātab is incomplete regarding possession. The master does not own the mukātab's earnings and cannot have intercourse with a mukātabah.

f: 455. Why is intention required for including mukātab slaves in the statement "Every slave owned by me is free"?
b: Because the ownership attribution is deficient, so the general wording does not automatically include them.

f: 456. If someone says to his wives: "This one is divorced, or this one and this one," which wife is definitely divorced?
b: The last wife mentioned is definitely divorced.

f: 457. What choice does the husband have regarding the first two wives mentioned in the statement: "This one is divorced, or this one and this one"?
b: He has the choice to decide which of the first two is divorced.

f: 458. Why is the last wife definitely divorced in the statement using "or"?
b: Because "or" establishes one of the first two persons, and the third person is joined to the chosen divorced person through conjunction, making her share in the ruling.

f: 459. Why does conjunction not apply equally to all three wives in the statement: "This one is divorced, or this one and this one"?
b: Because conjunction only applies where it is grammatically connected. The conjunction joins the third wife to the already established divorced person, not to both earlier options.

f: 460. If someone says regarding his slaves: "This one is free, or this one and this one," what is the ruling?
b: The last slave becomes free, and the owner has the choice regarding the first two.

f: 461. Why is the ruling the same for slaves as for wives in the statement: "This one is free, or this one and this one"?
b: Because the grammatical structure is the same: the conjunction joins the final person to the established ruling, while the earlier persons remain subject to choice.

f: 462. If a person says, "This slave is free if I sell him," then sells the slave while giving the buyer an option (khiyār), does the slave become free?
b: Yes. The sale occurred, and ownership still remains with the seller during the option period, so the condition is fulfilled and the emancipation takes effect.

f: 463. Why does a slave become free if his owner says, "This slave is free if I sell him," and then sells him with an option (khiyār)?
b: Because the condition—the sale—occurred, while ownership still exists in the seller during the option period.

f: 464. If a buyer says, "If I purchase this slave, he is free," then buys him with an option (khiyār), does the slave become free?
b: Yes. The purchase occurred, ownership is established, and the condition is fulfilled.

f: 465. Why does a slave become free if the buyer says, "If I purchase him, he is free," and purchases him with an option (khiyār)?
b: Because the purchase occurred and ownership is established despite the option.

f: 466. Why is conditional emancipation effective when a slave is purchased with an option (khiyār)?
b: Because a conditional emancipation is treated like an immediate declaration, and immediate emancipation requires ownership to exist first.

f: 467. If a person says, "If I do not sell this slave (or slave woman), then my wife is divorced," then emancipates or makes the slave a mudabbar, does his wife become divorced?
b: Yes. By making the slave free or a mudabbar, the possibility of selling is lost, so the condition of "not selling" is fulfilled.

f: 468. Why does emancipating or making a slave a mudabbar trigger the statement, "If I do not sell this slave, then my wife is divorced"?
b: Because those actions remove the possibility of selling the slave, so the condition of not selling has occurred.

f: 469. If a wife says to her husband, "You married another woman over me," and he replies, "Every woman I have is divorced three times," is the questioning wife divorced according to the judicial ruling?
b: Yes. According to the apparent narration, all of his wives, including the one who questioned him, are divorced.

f: 470. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, is the wife who questioned her husband divorced if he replies, "Every woman I have is divorced three times"?
b: No. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that the statement should be restricted to the woman who was the subject of the discussion.

f: 471. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hold that the questioning wife is not divorced when the husband says, "Every woman I have is divorced three times"?
b: Because the statement was given as an answer to her complaint, and his purpose was presumably to satisfy her by divorcing another wife.

f: 472. Why does the apparent narration hold that all wives are divorced when the husband says, "Every woman I have is divorced three times"?
b: Because the wording is general, he added words beyond the immediate answer, and the statement is treated as an independent declaration.

f: 473. If a husband who said, "Every woman I have is divorced three times," claims that he intended only one particular wife, is his claim accepted?
b: It is accepted between himself and Allah but not in court, because it specifies a general expression.

f: 474. If a person says, "Walking to the House of Allah is upon me," what becomes obligatory?
b: A Hajj or an ʿUmrah becomes obligatory, and it should be performed while walking.

f: 475. If a person says, "Walking to the Kaʿbah is upon me," what becomes obligatory?
b: A Hajj or an ʿUmrah performed while walking becomes obligatory.

f: 476. If someone vows, "Walking to the House of Allah is upon me," may he ride instead of walking?
b: Yes. He may ride, but he must offer a sacrificial animal (dam).

f: 477. Why does saying, "Walking to the House of Allah is upon me," make Hajj or ʿUmrah obligatory according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because of a report from ʿAlī (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) and because people customarily use this wording to make Hajj or ʿUmrah binding upon themselves.

f: 478. According to analogy (qiyās), what would be the ruling on someone saying, "Walking to the House of Allah is upon me"?
b: Nothing would become obligatory, because walking itself is not an independent act of worship.

f: 479. If a person says, "Going out to the House of Allah is upon me," does a Hajj or ʿUmrah become obligatory?
b: No. Nothing becomes obligatory.

f: 480. If a person says, "Travelling to the House of Allah is upon me," does a Hajj or ʿUmrah become obligatory?
b: No. Nothing becomes obligatory.

f: 481. Why does saying, "Going out to the House of Allah is upon me," not make Hajj or ʿUmrah obligatory?
b: Because this wording is not customarily used to make Hajj or ʿUmrah binding.

f: 482. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, if a person says, "Walking to the Ḥaram is upon me," does a Hajj or ʿUmrah become obligatory?
b: No. Nothing becomes obligatory.

f: 483. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, if a person says, "Walking to the Ḥaram is upon me," what becomes obligatory?
b: A Hajj or an ʿUmrah becomes obligatory.

f: 484. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, if a person says, "Walking to Ṣafā and Marwah is upon me," what becomes obligatory?
b: Nothing becomes obligatory.

f: 485. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, does the disagreement regarding "Walking to the Ḥaram is upon me" also apply to saying, "Walking to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām is upon me"?
b: Yes. The same disagreement applies.

f: 486. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad hold that saying "Walking to the Ḥaram is upon me" makes Hajj or ʿUmrah obligatory?
b: Because the Ḥaram includes the Kaʿbah by virtue of its connection to it, so mentioning the Ḥaram is like mentioning the House of Allah itself.

f: 487. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad hold that saying "Walking to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām is upon me" makes Hajj or ʿUmrah obligatory?
b: Because al-Masjid al-Ḥarām includes the Kaʿbah, making it equivalent to mentioning the House itself.

f: 488. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad distinguish Ṣafā and Marwah from the Ḥaram and al-Masjid al-Ḥarām?
b: Because Ṣafā and Marwah are separate from the Kaʿbah, whereas the Ḥaram and al-Masjid al-Ḥarām include it.

f: 489. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hold that saying "Walking to the Ḥaram is upon me" does not make Hajj or ʿUmrah obligatory?
b: Because making iḥrām obligatory through such expressions is not customary, and the obligation cannot be established merely from the literal wording.

f: 490. If a person says, "My slave is free if I do not perform Hajj this year," then claims to have performed Hajj while two witnesses testify that he sacrificed that year in Kūfah, does the slave become free according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. The slave does not become free.

f: 491. If a person says, "My slave is free if I do not perform Hajj this year," then claims to have performed Hajj while two witnesses testify that he sacrificed that year in Kūfah, does the slave become free according to Muḥammad?
b: Yes. The slave becomes free.

f: 492. Why does Muḥammad hold that the slave becomes free when witnesses testify that the person sacrificed in Kūfah during the Hajj season?
b: Because the testimony establishes that he sacrificed in Kūfah, which necessarily means he did not perform Hajj, fulfilling the condition.

f: 493. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reject testimony that someone sacrificed in Kūfah as proof that he failed to perform Hajj?
b: Because they view the testimony as really being testimony about a negation (that he did not perform Hajj), and testimony based on negation is insufficient in this context.

f: 494. If a person swears, "I will not fast," then forms the intention to fast, fasts for one hour, and breaks the fast before sunset, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes. He has broken his oath because the reality of fasting came into existence.

f: 495. Why does fasting for only one hour break an oath of "I will not fast"?
b: Because fasting consists of abstaining from things that invalidate the fast with the intention of worship, and that condition was fulfilled.

f: 496. If a person swears, "I will not fast a day" (or "I will not fast a fast"), then fasts for one hour and breaks the fast, has he broken his oath?
b: No.

f: 497. Why does fasting for only one hour not break an oath of "I will not fast a day"?
b: Because the oath refers to a complete Sharʿī fast, which requires continuing until the end of the day.

f: 498. What is the difference between swearing "I will not fast" and "I will not fast a day"?
b: "I will not fast" is broken by beginning a fast, whereas "I will not fast a day" requires completing an entire legally valid fast.

f: 499. If a person swears, "I will not pray," then stands, recites Qur'an, and bows (rukūʿ) but does not prostrate, has he broken his oath?
b: No.

f: 500. If a person swears, "I will not pray," then stands, recites, bows, prostrates, and then stops before completing the prayer, has he broken his oath?
b: Yes.

f: 501. Why does merely beginning the prayer not break an oath of "I will not pray"?
b: Because prayer consists of multiple pillars, and it is not called prayer until those essential pillars have been completed.

f: 502. Why is prayer treated differently from fasting regarding the beginning of the act?
b: Because fasting consists of one continuous act of abstention, whereas prayer consists of several distinct pillars.

f: 503. If a person swears, "I will not pray a prayer," when is the oath broken?
b: Only after he performs a legally valid prayer consisting of at least two rakʿahs.

f: 504. Why is an oath of "I will not pray a prayer" only broken after completing at least two rakʿahs?
b: Because the minimum legally valid prayer consists of two rakʿahs, and an incomplete prayer (ṣalāt al-batīrah) is prohibited.

f: 505. If a man says to his wife, "If you wear from what you spun, then it is a sacrificial offering (hadī)," and she buys cotton, spins it, weaves it, and he wears it, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It becomes a hadī (sacrificial offering), meaning it must be given in charity in Makkah.

f: 506. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, when does the statement "If you wear from what you spun, then it is a hadī" become binding?
b: Only if she spun cotton that her husband already owned at the time he made the oath.

f: 507. What is meant by hadī in the statement "it is a hadī"?
b: It means the item must be given as charity in Makkah, since a hadī is something offered there.

f: 508. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad require the cotton to have been owned at the time of the oath for the vow to be valid?
b: Because a vow is only valid regarding something already owned or connected to a cause of ownership, and the wife's spinning and weaving are not causes of ownership.

f: 509. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hold that the vow is binding even if the wife bought the cotton after the oath?
b: Because customarily a wife spins her husband's cotton, and customary meaning is what governs oaths.

f: 510. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why is the wife's spinning considered connected to the husband's ownership?
b: Because customarily a wife spins cotton belonging to her husband, making it a customary cause of ownership.

f: 511. If someone swears, "I will not wear jewelry," then wears a silver ring, does he break his oath?
b: No. A silver ring is not considered jewelry linguistically or according to customary usage.

f: 512. Why does wearing a silver ring not break an oath of "I will not wear jewelry"?
b: Because a silver ring is not regarded as jewelry in language or custom, and men are permitted to wear it as a signet ring.

f: 513. If someone swears, "I will not wear jewelry," then wears a gold ring, does he break his oath?
b: Yes. A gold ring is considered jewelry.

f: 514. Why does wearing a gold ring break an oath of "I will not wear jewelry"?
b: Because gold is regarded as jewelry, and its use is prohibited for men.

f: 515. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, if someone swears, "I will not wear jewelry," then wears a pearl necklace without gemstones, does he break his oath?
b: No.

f: 516. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, if someone swears, "I will not wear jewelry," then wears a pearl necklace without gemstones, does he break his oath?
b: Yes.

f: 517. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad consider a pearl necklace to be jewelry?
b: Because it is genuinely called jewelry, including in the Qur'an.

f: 518. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not consider a plain pearl necklace to be jewelry?
b: Because according to custom it is only regarded as jewelry when decorated with precious settings, and oaths are interpreted according to customary usage.

f: 519. According to later fatwā, whose opinion is followed regarding wearing a plain pearl necklace?
b: The opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, because wearing a plain pearl necklace as adornment became customary.

f: 520. If someone swears, "I will not sleep on a bed," then sleeps on the bed while there is a curtain (qirām) hanging above it, does he break his oath?
b: Yes.

f: 521. Why does sleeping under a curtain above the bed still break an oath of "I will not sleep on a bed"?
b: Because the curtain is considered an accessory of the bed and does not remove the attribution.

f: 522. If someone swears, "I will not sleep on a bed," then places another bed on top of it and sleeps on the upper bed, does he break his oath?
b: No.

f: 523. Why does placing another bed on top prevent breaking an oath of "I will not sleep on a bed"?
b: Because another bed is not merely an accessory; it is an independent object that removes the attribution to the lower bed.

f: 524. If someone swears, "I will not sit on the ground," then sits on a mat or reed mat, does he break his oath?
b: No.

f: 525. Why does sitting on a mat not break an oath of "I will not sit on the ground"?
b: Because a person sitting on a mat is not customarily described as sitting on the ground.

f: 526. Why does clothing not prevent breaking an oath of "I will not sit on the ground"?
b: Because clothing is considered part of the person and is therefore not treated as a barrier.

f: 527. If someone swears, "I will not sit on a bed," then sits on a mat placed on top of the bed, does he break his oath?
b: Yes.

f: 528. Why does sitting on a mat placed on a bed still break an oath of "I will not sit on a bed"?
b: Because the mat is considered an accessory of the bed, so he is still regarded as sitting on the bed.

f: 529. Why is sitting on a mat placed on a bed treated differently from sitting on another bed placed on top?
b: Because a mat is merely an accessory to the bed, whereas another bed is an independent object that removes the attribution to the first bed.

f: 530. If someone says, "If I strike you, then my slave is free," and the person dies before being struck, then he strikes the dead body, does the oath take effect?
b: No. The oath applies only while the person is alive because striking is an act that causes pain, and pain cannot be inflicted on the dead.

f: 531. Why does striking a dead person not fulfill an oath conditioned on striking him?
b: Because striking (ḍarb) is defined as an action that causes pain and affects a living body, which is impossible after death.

f: 532. Why is the punishment of the grave not evidence that a dead person can be "struck"?
b: Because, according to the scholars, Allah creates a special life for the deceased in the grave for that punishment; it does not mean ordinary worldly striking applies after death.

f: 533. If someone swears to clothe a person, does clothing a dead person fulfill the oath?
b: No, because unrestricted clothing (kiswah) means transferring ownership of clothing, which cannot occur after death.

f: 534. When could clothing a dead person fulfill such an oath?
b: If the person intended covering the body rather than transferring ownership.

f: 535. According to one reported view, how is the word clothing (kiswah) understood in Persian?
b: It refers to putting clothing on someone (wearing/dressing) rather than transferring ownership.

f: 536. If someone swears to speak to another person, does speaking to him after his death fulfill or break the oath?
b: No, because the purpose of speech is communication and understanding, which no longer exists after death.

f: 537. If someone swears to enter upon (visit) a person, does visiting his grave count?
b: No. After death one visits the grave, not the person himself.

f: 538. If someone says, "If I wash you, then my slave is free," and washes the person after death, does the oath take effect?
b: Yes. Washing applies to the dead because washing means pouring water and cleansing, which is still possible after death.

f: 539. Why does washing a dead person fulfill an oath when striking him does not?
b: Because washing remains possible after death, whereas striking (in its legal sense) requires causing pain to a living person.

f: 540. If someone swears not to strike his wife, then pulls her hair, has he broken the oath?
b: Yes. Pulling the hair is treated as striking because it causes pain.

f: 541. If someone swears not to strike his wife, then chokes her, has he broken the oath?
b: Yes. Choking causes pain and therefore falls under striking.

f: 542. If someone swears not to strike his wife, then bites her, has he broken the oath?
b: Yes. Biting causes pain and is included under striking.

f: 543. According to one opinion, when would pulling hair, choking, or biting not break the oath?
b: If they occur merely playfully, since they would then be described as joking rather than striking.

f: 544. If someone says, "If I do not kill so-and-so, then my wife is divorced," while that person is already dead and he knows it, does he break the oath?
b: Yes. The oath is considered established because Allah could theoretically restore life, but he breaks it through practical inability.

f: 545. Why does someone who knowingly swears to kill a person already dead still break the oath?
b: Because the act is theoretically possible through Allah's power, even though it is practically impossible under normal circumstances.

f: 546. If someone swears to kill a person who is already dead but does not know the person is dead, does he break the oath?
b: According to the text, no, because he based the oath on a life that no longer existed.

f: 547. To which earlier issue is the case of unknowingly swearing to kill a dead person compared?
b: It is compared to the issue of the empty water jug, where fulfillment was impossible from the outset.

f: 548. What is the preferred (correct) view regarding swearing to kill someone already dead?
b: The stronger view is that knowledge makes no difference; the ruling should not differ based on whether the person knew of the death.

f: 549. If someone swears, "I will repay my debt soon," what is meant by "soon"?
b: It means less than one month.

f: 550. If someone swears, "I will repay my debt after a long time," what is meant by "a long time"?
b: It means more than one month.

f: 551. Why is less than a month considered "soon" and a month or more considered "a long time"?
b: Because in customary usage, less than a month is regarded as near, while a month or more is regarded as distant.

f: 552. If someone swears to repay a debt today, pays it, and some of the coins are later discovered to be defective (zuyūf), has he broken his oath?
b: No. Defective coins are still considered money, so repayment has occurred.

f: 553. If someone repays a debt with counterfeit mixed coins (nabhuraj) that are later discovered, has he broken his oath?
b: No. They are still treated as money for this purpose if accepted in payment.

f: 554. If someone repays a debt with coins belonging to someone else, has he broken his oath?
b: No. Once the creditor validly received them, repayment occurred even if the coins are later returned to their true owner.

f: 555. Why do defective coins or another person's coins still fulfill repayment?
b: Because they remain within the category of money, and valid receipt establishes repayment.

f: 556. If someone repays a debt with lead coins or imitation counterfeit coins (stūqah), has he fulfilled his oath?
b: No. These are not legally considered dirhams, so repayment has not occurred.

f: 557. Why do lead or imitation coins not fulfill repayment?
b: Because they are not legally recognized as currency and cannot serve as valid exchange money.

f: 558. If a debtor sells a slave to his creditor in satisfaction of the debt and the creditor takes possession, has the debtor fulfilled an oath to repay the debt?
b: Yes. The debt is discharged through offsetting (muqāṣṣah).

f: 559. Why does selling property to the creditor fulfill repayment?
b: Because the debt is settled through legal offsetting, which counts as repayment.

f: 560. If the creditor forgives (gifts) the debt, has the debtor fulfilled an oath to repay it?
b: No. Waiving a debt is the creditor's act, not repayment by the debtor.

f: 561. Why does forgiving a debt not count as repayment?
b: Because repayment must be an action of the debtor, whereas remission is the creditor's action.

f: 562. If someone swears that he will not collect his debt except dirham by dirham, does taking only part of the debt break the oath?
b: No. The oath concerns collecting the entire debt in that manner.

f: 563. When does someone break an oath not to collect a debt except dirham by dirham?
b: When he collects the entire debt in a way contrary to the stated condition.

f: 564. Why does taking only part of the debt not break this oath?
b: Because the oath is attached to the entire known debt, not merely part of it.

f: 565. If the debt is collected in two weighings with only the normal interruption needed for weighing, is this considered separate collections?
b: No. Such a brief interruption is ignored by custom.

f: 566. Why are two consecutive weighings treated as one collection?
b: Because collecting everything in one weighing is often impractical, so the brief interruption is customarily disregarded.

f: 567. If someone says, "If I own anything except one hundred dirhams, then my wife is divorced," while owning only fifty dirhams, does he break the oath?
b: No. The statement is understood to deny ownership beyond one hundred dirhams.

f: 568. Why does owning only fifty dirhams not trigger the oath?
b: Because the expression customarily means "I own nothing beyond one hundred dirhams."

f: 569. If someone uses the expressions "other than one hundred" or "besides one hundred," do they have the same ruling as "except one hundred"?
b: Yes. All of these are treated as expressions of exception and have the same legal ruling.

f: 570. If someone swears that he will not do something, how long does the oath remain binding?
b: Forever, unless the oath itself specifies a time limit.

f: 571. Why does an oath to avoid an action continue indefinitely?
b: Because an unqualified negation includes every future instance of refraining from that action.

f: 572. If someone swears that he will do something, how many times must he perform it to fulfill the oath?
b: Once. A single performance fulfills the oath.

f: 573. Why is one performance sufficient when someone swears to do an act?
b: Because the oath commits him to one unspecified occurrence of the action.

f: 574. When does someone who swore to perform an act actually break the oath?
b: When all hope of performing it disappears, such as through death or permanent impossibility.

f: 575. If a ruler makes someone swear to report every immoral person entering the town, how long does the oath remain in effect?
b: Only during the ruler's period of authority.

f: 576. Why does such an oath end when the ruler's authority ends?
b: Because its purpose is to protect the ruler or the public, and that purpose ends with the ruler's authority.

f: 577. According to the apparent narration, what ends a ruler's authority for the purpose of this oath?
b: His death or his removal from office.

f: 578. If someone swears to gift his slave to another person, then offers the gift but the recipient refuses to accept it, has he fulfilled his oath?
b: Yes. The donor has fulfilled the oath by making the gift.

f: 579. Why does offering a gift fulfill the oath even if it is not accepted?
b: Because a gift (hibah) is a gratuitous act, and the donor's act itself demonstrates generosity.

f: 580. Why did Zufar disagree regarding gifting a slave?
b: He viewed it like a sale, which requires acceptance from both parties to be completed.

f: 581. Why is a gift treated differently from a sale?
b: A gift is a voluntary transfer completed by the donor's act, whereas a sale is an exchange requiring participation from both sides.

f: 582. If someone swears not to smell rayḥān (fragrant plants), then smells roses, has he broken his oath?
b: No. Roses are not included under rayḥān in this context.

f: 583. If someone swears not to smell rayḥān, then smells jasmine, has he broken his oath?
b: No. Jasmine is likewise excluded.

f: 584. Why are roses and jasmine excluded from the term rayḥān?
b: Because rayḥān refers to fragrant plants without stems, whereas roses and jasmine have stems.

f: 585. If someone swears not to buy violet (banafsaǧ) without specifying what he means, what does the oath ordinarily refer to?
b: It refers to violet oil, according to customary usage.

f: 586. Why is an oath regarding violets understood to refer to violet oil?
b: Because custom identifies buying violets with purchasing their oil, and sellers are known as sellers of violets on that basis.

f: 587. According to another opinion, what may the word violet (banafsaǧ) refer to?
b: It may refer to the leaves according to local custom.

f: 588. If someone swears regarding roses, what does the oath apply to?
b: It applies to the rose petals (or leaves).

f: 589. Why does an oath regarding roses apply to the petals?
b: Because this is both the literal meaning and the meaning supported by custom, unlike violets where custom changes the default understanding.

f: 1. What does the word ḥadd mean linguistically?
b: Prevention or restriction.

f: 2. Why is a ḥaddād (gatekeeper) called by that name?
b: Because he prevents people from entering.

f: 3. What is the Sharʿī definition of a ḥadd?
b: A prescribed punishment that is the right of Allah Most High.

f: 4. Why is qiṣāṣ (retaliation) not classified as a ḥadd?
b: Because it is the right of a human being, not the right of Allah.

f: 5. Why is taʿzīr (discretionary punishment) not classified as a ḥadd?
b: Because it is not a fixed, prescribed punishment.

f: 6. What is the primary wisdom behind legislating the ḥudūd?
b: To deter people from harmful actions that harm Allah's servants.

f: 7. Is purification of the offender the primary purpose of the ḥudūd?
b: No. Deterrence is the primary purpose.

f: 8. What shows that purification is not the primary purpose of the ḥudūd?
b: The fact that ḥudūd are also applied to non-Muslims, for whom ritual purification is not the objective.

f: 9. Through what two means is zina established before the judge?
b: Testimony and confession.

f: 10. What is meant by saying zina is "established"?
b: It means its establishment before the ruler or judge.

f: 11. Why is testimony accepted as proof of zina?
b: Because it is an outward legal proof recognized by the Sharīʿah.

f: 12. Why is confession accepted as proof of zina?
b: Because truthfulness is more likely in a confession, especially since it exposes the confessor to punishment and disgrace.

f: 13. Why is outward evidence accepted even though absolute certainty may not exist?
b: Because absolute certainty is generally unattainable, so the Sharīʿah accepts sufficient outward proof.

f: 14. How many witnesses are required to establish zina through testimony?
b: Four witnesses.

f: 15. Must the four witnesses testify against both men and women accused of zina?
b: Yes. Four witnesses are required whether the accused is a man or a woman.

f: 16. Which Qur'anic verses establish the requirement of four witnesses for zina?
b: Qur'an 4:15 and Qur'an 24:4.

f: 17. Which Prophetic instruction confirms the requirement of four witnesses in accusations of zina?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said to the accuser of his wife: "Bring four witnesses who testify to the truth of what you say."

f: 18. Why does the Sharīʿah require four witnesses rather than fewer?
b: To preserve concealment (satr) and discourage the spread of accusations.

f: 19. When witnesses testify to zina, what is the first thing the Imam asks them?
b: "What is zina?"

f: 20. Why does the Imam ask the witnesses to define zina?
b: To ensure they are describing actual legal zina, not some lesser act.

f: 21. What details does the Imam ask the witnesses about the alleged zina?
b: He asks what happened, how it happened, where it occurred, when it occurred, and with whom it occurred.

f: 22. Why does the Imam investigate how the alleged zina occurred?
b: To determine whether actual intercourse took place as required for the legal ruling.

f: 23. Why does the Imam investigate where the alleged zina occurred?
b: Because the location may affect the ruling, such as if it occurred in enemy territory (Dār al-Ḥarb).

f: 24. Why does the Imam investigate when the alleged zina occurred?
b: Because the passage of time or other circumstances may affect the legal case.

f: 25. Why does the Imam investigate with whom the alleged zina occurred?
b: To determine whether there was a possible legal doubt (shubhah) affecting liability.

f: 26. Give an example of a possible legal doubt that the Imam investigates before applying the ḥadd.
b: A case such as intercourse with one's son's slave-girl, where a legal doubt may exist.

f: 27. Which Companion did the Prophet ﷺ question in detail regarding the nature of the alleged zina?
b: Māʿiz (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ).

f: 28. Why is the judge required to investigate the case thoroughly before imposing the ḥadd?
b: Because the Sharīʿah seeks to prevent the application of the ḥadd whenever a legitimate doubt exists.

f: 29. What level of uprightness (ʿadālah) must the judge verify in witnesses before imposing the ḥadd punishment for zinā?
b: The judge must verify that all four witnesses are upright both privately and publicly before ruling on their testimony.

f: 30. Why must the judge investigate the private and public uprightness of witnesses in zinā cases instead of relying only on their apparent character?
b: Because ḥudūd are prevented whenever possible, extra precaution is required. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Avoid the prescribed punishments as much as you can."

f: 31. Does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ require private and public verification of witnesses in all legal cases?
b: No. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, this heightened level of verification is specific to ḥudūd cases, not ordinary rights.

f: 32. What does al-Hidāyah recommend the judge do while the witnesses in a zinā case are being investigated?
b: The judge should imprison the accused until the witnesses' reliability has been investigated.

f: 33. Why is imprisoning the accused during the investigation of witnesses in a zinā case recommended?
b: Because there is suspicion of a serious crime, and the Prophet ﷺ imprisoned a man on the basis of an accusation.

f: 34. Why is a person not imprisoned before witnesses are verified in ordinary debt cases?
b: Because debt cases are treated differently from ḥudūd cases, which require greater precaution due to the severity of the punishment.

f: 35. Who may validly confess to zinā so that the confession can establish the offence?
b: Only a mature and sane person. The confession of a child or an insane person is not legally valid.

f: 36. How many confessions are required to establish zinā according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: Four confessions.

f: 37. How many separate sittings are required for a valid confession of zinā according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Four separate sittings.

f: 38. Whose gatherings are considered when requiring four separate sittings for a confession of zinā?
b: The gatherings of the confessor, not those of the judge.

f: 39. What must the judge do after each confession of zinā according to the Sunnah described in al-Hidāyah?
b: The judge sends the confessor away after each confession so that he leaves and later returns to confess again.

f: 40. How far must the confessor leave between confessions according to the narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: He should leave until he is no longer visible, then return for the next confession.

f: 41. Why do the Ḥanafīs require four confessions to establish zinā?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ did not carry out the punishment of Māʿiz until he had confessed four times in four separate gatherings.

f: 42. Why is a single confession insufficient to establish zinā according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because the Sunnah establishes four confessions, and the seriousness of zinā requires greater caution and preserves concealment.

f: 43. What is Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding the number of confessions required to establish zinā?
b: One confession is sufficient.

f: 44. Why does Imām al-Shāfiʿī consider one confession sufficient to establish zinā?
b: Because confession merely reveals the truth, and repeating it does not make it clearer, unlike increasing the number of witnesses.

f: 45. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to Imām al-Shāfiʿī's view that one confession is sufficient?
b: They cite the case of Māʿiz, in which the Prophet ﷺ required four confessions before enforcing the punishment.

f: 46. Why do the Ḥanafīs draw a parallel between four witnesses and four confessions in zinā cases?
b: Because just as testimony requires an increased number of witnesses due to the gravity of zinā, confession likewise requires repeated admissions to preserve concealment and exercise caution.

f: 47. What does the judge ask a person after he has completed four valid confessions of zinā?
b: The judge asks what the zinā was, how it occurred, where it occurred, and with whom it occurred.

f: 48. When does the ḥadd punishment become obligatory after a confession of zinā?
b: It becomes obligatory once the confessor has completed four valid confessions and has explained the details of the offence.

f: 49. Why does al-Hidāyah not explicitly mention asking about the time of the zinā during a confession?
b: Because the passage of time prevents testimony from being accepted but does not prevent a confession from being accepted.

f: 50. Why might the judge still ask about the time of the zinā even in a confession case?
b: Because it is possible the act occurred while the confessor was still a child, in which case the ḥadd would not apply.

f: 51. What happens if a person retracts his confession before the ḥadd for zinā is carried out?
b: His retraction is accepted, and he is released.

f: 52. What happens if a person retracts his confession while the ḥadd for zinā is already being carried out?
b: His retraction is accepted, and the punishment is stopped.

f: 53. What is Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding a confession of zinā that is later retracted?
b: He holds that the punishment should still be carried out because it became obligatory through the original confession.

f: 54. Which other jurist agreed with Imām al-Shāfiʿī that retracting a confession does not cancel the ḥadd?
b: Ibn Abī Laylā.

f: 55. Why do the Ḥanafīs accept a retraction of a confession for zinā?
b: Because the retraction may be truthful, creating doubt, and ḥudūd are not enforced when doubt exists.

f: 56. Why is retracting a confession treated differently from cases involving qiṣāṣ or ḥadd al-qadhf?
b: Because those involve the rights of other people who may contradict the retraction, whereas zinā is a pure right of Allah in this context.

f: 57. Why is it recommended for the ruler to encourage a person confessing to zinā to retract his confession?
b: Because the Sharīʿah encourages avoiding the enforcement of ḥudūd whenever a valid doubt exists.

f: 58. What wording did the Prophet ﷺ use to encourage Māʿiz to reconsider his confession?
b: He asked: "Perhaps you only touched her or kissed her."

f: 59. According to al-Aṣl, what other questions should the ruler ask someone confessing to zinā?
b: He should ask whether the woman was his wife or whether intercourse occurred due to a legal doubt (shubha).

f: 60. What is the punishment for a muḥṣan (legally married) person who commits zinā after the offence is established?
b: He is stoned until he dies.

f: 61. What evidence establishes stoning as the punishment for a muḥṣan adulterer?
b: The Prophet ﷺ stoned Māʿiz after he had been muḥṣan, and the Companions unanimously agreed upon this ruling.

f: 62. Where is the punishment of stoning carried out?
b: In an open area.

f: 63. Who begins the stoning after the sentence has been issued?
b: The witnesses begin first, then the Imam, then the people.

f: 64. Why do the witnesses begin the stoning before everyone else?
b: Because if they hesitate or refuse, it may indicate they have retracted their testimony, preventing the punishment.

f: 65. What is Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding the witnesses beginning the stoning?
b: He does not consider it a condition, comparing it to flogging.

f: 66. How do the Ḥanafīs distinguish stoning from flogging regarding the role of the witnesses?
b: Flogging requires skill and is not intended to kill, whereas stoning is itself a method of execution, so the witnesses beginning it serves as a safeguard against enforcing the punishment after a retraction.

f: 67. What happens if the witnesses refuse to begin the stoning?
b: The punishment is dropped because their refusal is treated as evidence of retraction.

f: 68. What is the apparent narration regarding the punishment if the witnesses die or disappear before the stoning begins?
b: The punishment is dropped because one of its required conditions is no longer present.

f: 69. Who begins the stoning when the ḥadd for zinā is established by confession rather than testimony?
b: The Imam begins the stoning, followed by the people.

f: 70. What evidence supports the Imam beginning the stoning after a confession of zinā?
b: It is narrated from ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and the Prophet ﷺ threw the first small pebble at the Ghamidiyyah woman after her confession.

f: 71. What is done with the body of a person who is executed by stoning for zinā?
b: He is washed, shrouded, and the funeral prayer is performed over him.

f: 72. Why is a person executed for zinā washed and prayed over?
b: Because he was lawfully killed, like someone executed in qiṣāṣ, and the Prophet ﷺ instructed this for Māʿiz and prayed over the Ghamidiyyah woman.

f: 73. What is the ḥadd punishment for a free person who commits zinā without being muḥṣan?
b: One hundred lashes.

f: 74. What is the Qur'anic evidence for one hundred lashes for a non-muḥṣan adulterer?
b: Allah says: "The adulterer and the adulteress, flog each one of them with one hundred lashes." (Qur'an 24:2)

f: 75. Why does the verse prescribing one hundred lashes not apply to a muḥṣan adulterer according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because its ruling was abrogated with respect to the muḥṣan, who is punished by stoning.

f: 76. What type of whip should be used when carrying out the ḥadd of flogging?
b: A whip without knots.

f: 77. How forcefully should the lashes be delivered during the ḥadd?
b: With moderate force—neither excessively harsh nor so light that they fail to cause pain.

f: 78. Why must the lashes during the ḥadd be of moderate severity?
b: Because excessive force may cause death, while insufficient force fails to achieve the purpose of deterrence.

f: 79. What clothing is removed from a man before the ḥadd of flogging?
b: Everything except the waist covering (ʿawrah covering).

f: 80. Why is the waist covering left on during flogging?
b: To prevent exposing the person's private parts.

f: 81. Why are ordinary clothes removed before carrying out the ḥadd of flogging?
b: So that the punishment reaches the body effectively and fulfils its deterrent purpose.

f: 82. Why must the lashes be distributed across the body instead of concentrated in one place?
b: Because concentrating them in one place may cause death, whereas the purpose is deterrence, not destruction.

f: 83. Which parts of the body must not be struck during the ḥadd of flogging?
b: The head, face, and private parts.

f: 84. Why are the head, face, and private parts excluded from flogging?
b: Because they are vulnerable to fatal injury or permanent damage, and the Sharīʿah intends deterrence rather than destruction.

f: 85. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding striking the head during the ḥadd?
b: He held that the head should be struck and later returned to this opinion.

f: 86. What evidence did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ cite for allowing the head to be struck?
b: The statement of Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: "Strike the head, for there is a devil in it."

f: 87. How do the Ḥanafīs answer Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence about striking the head?
b: They interpret it as referring to someone whose killing was lawful, or to a disbelieving warrior calling people to disbelief, not to the ordinary ḥadd punishment.

f: 88. In what position is a man flogged during the ḥadd?
b: Standing.

f: 89. Why is a man flogged while standing?
b: Because it better fulfils the purpose of public deterrence.

f: 90. What did ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ say regarding the position of men and women during the ḥadd?
b: "Men are struck standing in the punishments, and women sitting."

f: 91. What are the three explanations of the statement that the punished person is 'not stretched out'?
b: (1) He is not laid on the ground and stretched out. (2) The striker does not raise the whip above his head. (3) The striker does not excessively extend the whip after striking.

f: 92. Why are these excessive methods of flogging prohibited?
b: Because they exceed the punishment prescribed by the Sharīʿah.

f: 93. How many lashes does a slave receive for zinā?
b: Fifty lashes.

f: 94. What Qur'anic evidence establishes fifty lashes for a slave?
b: Allah says: "Then upon them is half of the punishment of free married women." (Qur'an 4:25)

f: 95. Why is the punishment for a slave reduced compared to a free person?
b: Because slavery is considered a deficiency in worldly blessing, reducing the legal punishment.

f: 96. Are men and women equal in the number of lashes for the ḥadd of zinā?
b: Yes, both receive the same prescribed number according to their legal status.

f: 97. How is a woman's clothing treated during the ḥadd of flogging?
b: She is not stripped except for thick outer garments such as a fur coat or padded clothing.

f: 98. Why are thick outer garments removed from a woman during flogging?
b: Because they prevent the punishment from reaching her body effectively.

f: 99. Why is a woman not completely stripped before the ḥadd?
b: To preserve her modesty and avoid exposing her ʿawrah.

f: 100. In what position is a woman flogged during the ḥadd?
b: Sitting.

f: 101. Why is a woman flogged while sitting?
b: Because it provides greater concealment and modesty while carrying out the punishment.

f: 102. Is it permissible to dig a pit for a woman before carrying out the ḥadd of stoning?
b: Yes. It is permissible to dig a pit for her.

f: 103. What evidence supports digging a pit for a woman during stoning?
b: The Prophet ﷺ dug a pit for the Ghamidiyyah woman up to her chest, and ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ dug a pit for Sharāḥah al-Hamdāniyyah.

f: 104. Is digging a pit for a woman during stoning obligatory?
b: No. Leaving it does not affect the validity of the punishment because the Prophet ﷺ did not command it as an obligation.

f: 105. Why is digging a pit for a woman during stoning recommended?
b: Because it provides greater concealment and protection.

f: 106. How deep should the pit be when dug for a woman during stoning?
b: Up to her chest.

f: 107. Is a pit dug for a man during the ḥadd of stoning?
b: No.

f: 108. Why is no pit dug for a man during stoning?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ did not dig one for Māʿiz, and public exposure and deterrence are intended for men without restraining them.

f: 109. May a master carry out the ḥadd punishment upon his slave without the permission of the Imam?
b: No. He may only do so with the permission of the Imam.

f: 110. What is Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding a master carrying out the ḥadd on his slave?
b: He holds that the master may carry it out because of his authority over the slave.

f: 111. What evidence do the Ḥanafīs use to show that a master may not independently carry out the ḥadd?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Four matters belong to the rulers," and among them are the prescribed punishments.

f: 112. Why do the Ḥanafīs restrict the implementation of ḥudūd to the Imam or his deputy?
b: Because ḥudūd are rights of Allah intended to protect society, so they are enforced by the representative of the Sharīʿah.

f: 113. Why does the ruling on taʿzīr differ from the ruling on ḥudūd regarding a master's authority?
b: Because taʿzīr is primarily an individual's right, whereas ḥudūd are rights of Allah.

f: 114. Can a child receive taʿzīr even though ḥudūd do not apply to him?
b: Yes. A child may receive taʿzīr, but the rights of Allah represented by ḥudūd do not apply to him.

f: 115. What are the conditions required for a person to be considered muḥṣan and therefore eligible for the punishment of stoning?
b: The person must be free, sane, mature, Muslim, have contracted a valid marriage, and have had intercourse in that marriage while both spouses possessed the qualities of iḥṣān.

f: 116. Why are sanity and maturity conditions for iḥṣān?
b: Because legal responsibility does not exist without sanity and maturity.

f: 117. Why are freedom, Islam, valid marriage, and lawful intercourse conditions for iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because they represent complete blessings and lawful means that strongly deter zinā, making the crime more serious when committed despite them.

f: 118. Why does the Ḥanafī school connect the punishment of stoning to these conditions of iḥṣān?
b: Because the greater the blessings and lawful opportunities available, the more serious the denial of those blessings through committing zinā.

f: 119. Why are qualities such as honour or knowledge not conditions for iḥṣān?
b: Because the Sharīʿah did not designate them as conditions, and legal rulings cannot be established by personal opinion alone.

f: 120. How does freedom contribute to the status of iḥṣān?
b: It enables a person to contract a valid marriage.

f: 121. How does a valid marriage contribute to the status of iḥṣān?
b: It provides lawful access to sexual relations.

f: 122. How does lawful intercourse contribute to the status of iḥṣān?
b: It provides lawful satisfaction, making zinā less excusable and therefore more blameworthy.

f: 123. How does Islam contribute to the status of iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It allows marriage to a Muslim spouse and strengthens awareness of the prohibition of zinā.

f: 124. Does Imām al-Shāfiʿī consider Islam to be a condition of iḥṣān?
b: No. He does not regard Islam as a condition.

f: 125. Which Ḥanafī jurist also has a narration agreeing that Islam is not a condition for iḥṣān?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, in one narration.

f: 126. What evidence do Imām al-Shāfiʿī and the opposing narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to argue that Islam is not a condition of iḥṣān?
b: They cite the report that the Prophet ﷺ stoned two Jewish adulterers.

f: 127. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to the evidence of the Jewish adulterers who were stoned?
b: They say the ruling was according to the Torah and was later abrogated for this issue.

f: 128. What prophetic statement do the Ḥanafīs cite in support of Islam being a condition of iḥṣān?
b: "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not muḥṣan."

f: 129. What level of intercourse is required to establish the condition of iḥṣān?
b: Penetration into the private part in a manner that obligates ghusl.

f: 130. Must both spouses possess the qualities of iḥṣān at the time of intercourse for iḥṣān to be established?
b: Yes. Both parties must possess the qualities of iḥṣān at the time of intercourse.

f: 131. Does a man become muḥṣan by having intercourse with a non-Muslim wife according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: No. He does not become muḥṣan.

f: 132. Does a man become muḥṣan by having intercourse with a slave wife according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: No. He does not become muḥṣan.

f: 133. Does a man become muḥṣan by having intercourse with an insane wife according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: No. He does not become muḥṣan.

f: 134. Does a man become muḥṣan by having intercourse with a wife who is still a child according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: No. He does not become muḥṣan.

f: 135. Does a woman become muḥṣan if her husband is a disbeliever, slave, insane, or a child?
b: No. She does not become muḥṣan because both spouses must possess the qualities of iḥṣān.

f: 136. Why does intercourse with a non-Muslim, slave, insane person, or child not establish iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because the blessings that complete iḥṣān are not fully present in those situations.

f: 137. Why does marriage to an insane spouse not establish iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because human nature is repelled by companionship with an insane person, so the intended blessing is incomplete.

f: 138. Why does marriage to a child not establish iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because a child lacks normal sexual interest, so the intended lawful satisfaction is incomplete.

f: 139. Why does marriage to a slave woman not establish iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because there is fear that any child born will be enslaved, reducing the completeness of the blessing.

f: 140. Why does marriage to a non-Muslim spouse not establish iḥṣān according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because full harmony is lacking due to the difference in religion.

f: 141. Which Ḥanafī jurist differed regarding whether marriage to a non-Muslim woman establishes iḥṣān?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, who held a different opinion.

f: 142. What prophetic evidence do the Ḥanafīs cite to show that marriage to a Jewish or Christian woman does not establish iḥṣān?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "A Muslim man is not made muḥṣan by a Jewish or Christian woman, nor is a free man made muḥṣan by a slave woman, nor is a free woman made muḥṣan by a slave man."

f: 143. Is a muḥṣan adulterer punished with both flogging and stoning according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No. Only stoning is carried out.

f: 144. Why do the Ḥanafīs not combine flogging and stoning for a muḥṣan adulterer?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ did not combine them, and stoning alone fully achieves deterrence.

f: 145. Why does flogging serve no additional purpose when combined with stoning?
b: Because public deterrence is already achieved by stoning, and personal deterrence is meaningless after death.

f: 146. Is an unmarried adulterer punished with both flogging and exile according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No. Only flogging is imposed.

f: 147. What is Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding the punishment of an unmarried adulterer?
b: He holds that the punishment is one hundred lashes together with one year's exile.

f: 148. What ḥadīth does Imām al-Shāfiʿī use as evidence for combining flogging and exile?
b: "The unmarried person with the unmarried person: one hundred lashes and exile for a year."

f: 149. Why does Imām al-Shāfiʿī consider exile beneficial in the punishment of zinā?
b: Because it removes the social circumstances that facilitate adultery.

f: 150. What Qur'anic evidence do the Ḥanafīs use to argue that flogging alone is the punishment for an unmarried adulterer?
b: Allah says: "Flog each one of them with one hundred lashes." (Qur'an 24:2).

f: 151. Why do the Ḥanafīs say the Qur'anic verse indicates that flogging alone is the complete punishment?
b: Because the verse mentions only flogging and presents it as the full prescribed punishment.

f: 152. Why do the Ḥanafīs argue that exile may actually increase the risk of adultery?
b: Because separation from family and community removes shame and may even lead a person to use adultery as a means of livelihood.

f: 153. Which Companion's statement do the Ḥanafīs cite in support of not combining exile with flogging?
b: The statement of ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: "Exile alone is enough of a trial."

f: 154. How do the Ḥanafīs reconcile the ḥadīth mentioning both flogging and exile with their own ruling?
b: They hold that the ḥadīth has been abrogated, just as the narration combining flogging with stoning for the muḥṣan was abrogated.

f: 155. What is the ruling on exiling an unmarried adulterer according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: The unmarried adulterer is not subject to both flogging and exile as fixed ḥadd punishments. However, if the Imam considers exile beneficial, he may impose it as a discretionary (taʿzīr/siyāsah) measure.

f: 156. Why may the Imam exile an unmarried adulterer according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Exile is not a prescribed ḥadd punishment in the Ḥanafī school, but it may be imposed by the Imam as a discretionary measure if he sees a public benefit in doing so.

f: 157. How do the reports of exile from some Companions fit into the Ḥanafī position?
b: The Ḥanafīs interpret the reports of Companions exiling offenders as acts of discretionary political judgment (taʿzīr/siyāsah), not as fixed ḥadd punishments.

f: 158. Is a sick adulterer exempt from the punishment of stoning?
b: No. If the punishment is stoning, illness does not prevent its implementation because the punishment itself results in death.

f: 159. Is a sick adulterer flogged immediately if the punishment is one hundred lashes?
b: No. If the punishment is flogging, it is postponed until the person recovers to avoid causing death through illness.

f: 160. Why is flogging delayed for a sick person while stoning is not?
b: Flogging is delayed because illness may cause it to become fatal, whereas stoning is already intended to result in death.

f: 161. Why is amputation also delayed during extreme heat or cold?
b: Because such conditions increase the risk of death or excessive harm, so the punishment is postponed until safer circumstances exist.

f: 162. Is a pregnant woman punished for zina before giving birth?
b: No. Whether the punishment is stoning or flogging, it is postponed until she gives birth in order to protect the life of the unborn child.

f: 163. Why is the punishment of a pregnant adulteress delayed until after childbirth?
b: Because the unborn child is an innocent protected soul whose life must not be endangered by carrying out the punishment.

f: 164. When is a woman who must receive flogging punished after giving birth?
b: She is not flogged until her postnatal bleeding (nifās) has ended and she has recovered.

f: 165. Why is flogging delayed until nifās has ended?
b: Because postnatal bleeding is regarded as a form of illness, and punishments involving flogging are delayed until recovery.

f: 166. Why is stoning not delayed after childbirth due to nifās?
b: Because the reason for delaying stoning was to protect the unborn child. Once the child is born, that reason no longer exists.

f: 167. According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, when may the punishment of a woman with a newborn be delayed beyond childbirth?
b: If no one else can care for the infant, the punishment may be delayed until the child is no longer dependent upon its mother.
