f: 168. Which hadith supports delaying punishment until a child no longer depends on its mother?
b: The Prophet ﷺ told the Ghamidiyyah woman after childbirth: "Return until your child is no longer dependent upon you."

f: 169. Is a pregnant woman detained while awaiting punishment if zina was established by testimony?
b: Yes. If the offence was proven by witnesses, she is detained until childbirth to prevent her from fleeing.

f: 170. Why is a pregnant woman proven guilty by testimony detained until childbirth?
b: Because testimony cannot be withdrawn, so detention prevents escape before the punishment is carried out.

f: 171. Is a pregnant woman detained if zina was established only through her own confession?
b: No. Since a confession may be retracted, imprisonment is not considered necessary.

f: 172. Why is imprisonment unnecessary when zina is established by confession?
b: Because the confessor may retract the confession, and such retraction is legally effective in preventing the ḥadd punishment.

f: 173. What type of intercourse requires the ḥadd punishment according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: The intercourse that requires the ḥadd is zinā: a man having intercourse in the vagina with a woman outside ownership or a valid semblance of ownership (shubhat al-milk).

f: 174. How is zinā defined in the Sharīʿah and Arabic language according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Zinā is vaginal intercourse between a man and a woman without ownership or a legally recognized semblance of ownership.

f: 175. Why does ownership or a semblance of ownership prevent the ḥadd of zinā?
b: Because ownership or a legally recognized doubt removes the act from being absolutely prohibited, and the ḥadd is warded off by doubts (shubuhāt).

f: 176. What prophetic principle forms the basis for dropping the ḥadd due to doubt?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Ward off the prescribed punishments by means of doubts (shubuhāt)."

f: 177. How many categories of legal doubt (shubha) prevent the ḥadd of zinā?
b: There are two: shubhat al-fiʿl (doubt concerning the act) and shubhat al-maḥall (doubt concerning the legal status of the object).

f: 178. What is shubhat al-fiʿl (doubt concerning the act)?
b: It is when a person genuinely but mistakenly believes an unlawful act is lawful by treating something invalid as if it were valid.

f: 179. What is another name for shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: It is also called shubhat al-ishtibāh (mistaken belief).

f: 180. Does shubhat al-fiʿl require the offender to genuinely believe the act was lawful?
b: Yes. This type of doubt exists only if the person actually believed the act was lawful.

f: 181. What is shubhat al-maḥall (legal doubt concerning the object)?
b: It is a legal doubt arising from the status of the woman or property itself, where some legal evidence prevents the prohibition from being absolute.

f: 182. Does shubhat al-maḥall depend on the offender's personal belief?
b: No. It exists because of the legal status of the object itself, regardless of what the offender believed.

f: 183. Does either type of shubha prevent the ḥadd punishment?
b: Yes. Both shubhat al-fiʿl and shubhat al-maḥall prevent the ḥadd based on the general wording of the hadith.

f: 184. When is a child's lineage (nasab) established despite unlawful intercourse?
b: Lineage is established under shubhat al-maḥall if the man acknowledges the child.

f: 185. Is lineage established under shubhat al-fiʿl if the man claims the child?
b: No. Lineage is not established because the act remains pure zinā, and only the offender's mistaken belief prevented the ḥadd.

f: 186. Why is lineage not established under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Because the act itself remains true zinā, and the doubt relates only to the offender's mistaken belief, not to the legal nature of the relationship.

f: 187. Why is lineage established under shubhat al-maḥall?
b: Because the act is not regarded as pure zinā due to the legal doubt concerning the woman or property involved.

f: 188. How many situations constitute shubhat al-fiʿl according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Eight situations are listed.

f: 189. Does intercourse with one's father's slave-girl fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes. If the man genuinely believed she was lawful, the ḥadd is not carried out.

f: 190. Does intercourse with one's mother's slave-girl fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes, provided he genuinely believed she was lawful.

f: 191. Does intercourse with one's wife's slave-girl fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes, if he genuinely believed she was lawful.

f: 192. Does intercourse with a woman divorced by three divorces during her ʿiddah fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes, if he believed she was lawful for him.

f: 193. Does intercourse with a woman separated by khulʿ or divorce for compensation during her ʿiddah fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes, if he genuinely believed she was lawful.

f: 194. Does intercourse with an umm walad whom her master has freed while she is in her ʿiddah fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes, if the offender believed she was lawful.

f: 195. Does intercourse by a slave with his master's slave-girl fall under shubhat al-fiʿl?
b: Yes, if the slave genuinely believed she was lawful for him.

f: 196. Does intercourse by a pledgee with a pledged slave-girl fall under shubhat al-fiʿl according to Kitāb al-Ḥudūd?
b: Yes, according to that narration, if he believed she was lawful.

f: 197. In cases of shubhat al-fiʿl, what happens if the offender says, "I thought she was lawful for me"?
b: The ḥadd is not carried out because the genuine mistaken belief creates a valid doubt.

f: 198. In cases of shubhat al-fiʿl, what happens if the offender admits he knew the act was unlawful?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because the required mistaken belief no longer exists.

f: 199. How many situations constitute shubhat al-maḥall according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Six situations are listed.

f: 200. Does intercourse with one's son's slave-girl fall under shubhat al-maḥall?
b: Yes. The ḥadd is not carried out even if the offender knew she was unlawful.

f: 201. Does intercourse with a woman irrevocably divorced through kināyah fall under shubhat al-maḥall?
b: Yes. The legal doubt prevents the ḥadd even if the prohibition was known.

f: 202. Does intercourse with a slave-girl sold but not yet delivered remain under shubhat al-maḥall for the seller?
b: Yes. The seller is not subject to the ḥadd because of the legal doubt.

f: 203. Does intercourse with a slave-girl given as mahr before the husband has taken possession fall under shubhat al-maḥall?
b: Yes. The legal doubt prevents the ḥadd.

f: 204. Does intercourse with a jointly owned slave-girl fall under shubhat al-maḥall?
b: Yes. Joint ownership creates a legal doubt that prevents the ḥadd.

f: 205. Does intercourse by a pledgee with a pledged slave-girl fall under shubhat al-maḥall according to Kitāb al-Rahn?
b: Yes. According to that narration, the legal doubt prevents the ḥadd.

f: 206. In cases of shubhat al-maḥall, does admitting knowledge of the prohibition make the ḥadd obligatory?
b: No. The ḥadd is still not carried out because the legal doubt exists independently of the offender's belief.

f: 207. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can a marriage contract itself create a legal doubt preventing the ḥadd?
b: Yes. A marriage contract creates legal doubt even if the marriage is unanimously invalid and the parties know it is prohibited.

f: 208. How do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad differ from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding an invalid marriage contract?
b: They hold that if the parties know the marriage is prohibited, the contract does not create legal doubt preventing the ḥadd.

f: 209. Where does the discussion of marriage contracts creating legal doubt continue?
b: It is discussed later in the chapter dealing with marriage to unmarriageable relatives (maḥārim).

f: 210. What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with his wife during the ʿiddah after divorcing her three times and admits he knew she was unlawful?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because the marriage has completely ended, no legal doubt remains, and her prohibition is established by the Qur'an and consensus.

f: 211. Why is the ḥadd carried out if a man knowingly has intercourse with his thrice-divorced wife during her ʿiddah?
b: Because the ownership that previously made intercourse lawful has completely ceased, leaving no legal doubt.

f: 212. What is the ruling if a man says he believed his thrice-divorced wife was still lawful during her ʿiddah?
b: The ḥadd is not carried out because his mistaken belief creates shubhat al-fiʿl (a mistaken-belief doubt).

f: 213. Why can a mistaken belief prevent the ḥadd after a triple divorce during the ʿiddah?
b: Because some legal effects of the marriage still remain during the waiting period, such as lineage, maintenance, and the obligation of ʿiddah, making the mistaken belief conceivable.

f: 214. Which legal effects of marriage remain during the ʿiddah after a triple divorce?
b: Lineage (nasab), the obligation of the waiting period (ʿiddah), and maintenance (nafaqah) remain.

f: 215. Does the same ruling apply to an umm walad freed by her master who is still in her ʿiddah?
b: Yes. If the man genuinely believed she was lawful, the ḥadd is not carried out.

f: 216. Does the same ruling apply to a woman separated by khulʿ who is still in her ʿiddah?
b: Yes. A genuine mistaken belief prevents the ḥadd.

f: 217. Does the same ruling apply to a woman divorced in exchange for compensation (ṭalāq ʿalā māl) during her ʿiddah?
b: Yes. A genuine mistaken belief prevents the ḥadd.

f: 218. Why do these ʿiddah cases prevent the ḥadd despite the women being unlawful?
b: Because although their prohibition is established by consensus, some legal effects of marriage still remain during the waiting period, making the mistaken belief conceivable.

f: 219. What is the ruling if a man divorces his wife using indirect expressions (kināyāt), she chooses separation, and he later has intercourse with her during the ʿiddah?
b: The ḥadd is not carried out, even if he admits he knew she was unlawful.

f: 220. Why does intercourse after divorce by kināyah not require the ḥadd?
b: Because the Companions differed regarding the legal effect of such divorces, creating a legal doubt (shubhat al-maḥall).

f: 221. Which Companion held that certain indirect divorce expressions amounted to only one revocable divorce?
b: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: 222. Does intending three divorces with indirect expressions remove the legal doubt?
b: No. The disagreement among the Companions still exists, so the ḥadd is not carried out.

f: 223. Is there a ḥadd for a man who has intercourse with the slave-girl of his son?
b: No. The legal doubt prevents the ḥadd, even if he admits he knew she was unlawful.

f: 224. Does the same ruling apply to intercourse with the slave-girl of a grandson?
b: Yes. Grandfatherhood has the same legal effect as fatherhood in this ruling.

f: 225. What evidence creates the legal doubt regarding a son's slave-girl?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "You and your wealth belong to your father."

f: 226. Is the child's lineage established if a man has intercourse with his son's slave-girl?
b: Yes. The child's lineage is established from him.

f: 227. Must a man compensate for intercourse with his son's slave-girl?
b: Yes. He must pay the value of the slave-girl.

f: 228. What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with the slave-girl of his father, mother, or wife believing she was lawful?
b: The ḥadd is not carried out because his mistaken belief is considered conceivable.

f: 229. Why is a mistaken belief conceivable regarding the slave-girl of one's father, mother, or wife?
b: Because there is normally a degree of mutual freedom in benefiting from each other's property within these close relationships.

f: 230. What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with the slave-girl of his father, mother, or wife while admitting he knew she was unlawful?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because the mistaken-belief doubt no longer exists.

f: 231. Does the same ruling apply if a slave has intercourse with his master's slave-girl?
b: Yes. If he genuinely believed she was lawful, there is no ḥadd; if he knew she was unlawful, the ḥadd is carried out.

f: 232. Is intercourse with the slave-girl of one's father, mother, wife, or master considered actual zinā?
b: Yes. The act remains true zinā, but the ḥadd may be prevented by a genuine mistaken belief.

f: 233. Is someone who accuses such a person of zinā punished for slander (qadhf)?
b: No. Because the act is in reality zinā, the accuser is not liable for the ḥadd of qadhf.

f: 234. What if the slave-girl says she believed the man was lawful for her, but the man makes no such claim?
b: The same ruling applies, because the act is one and the same; the mistaken belief prevents the ḥadd.

f: 235. What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with the slave-girl of his brother believing she was lawful?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because such a mistaken belief is not legally recognized.

f: 236. What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with the slave-girl of his paternal uncle believing she was lawful?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because there is no customary freedom in benefiting from one another's property.

f: 237. Why does intercourse with the slave-girl of a brother or paternal uncle not create a valid mistaken-belief doubt?
b: Because there is no customary mutual freedom in using one another's property between such relatives.

f: 238. Does the same ruling apply to relatives other than ascendants and descendants?
b: Yes. The mistaken-belief excuse is not accepted for other relatives, and the ḥadd is carried out if the conditions are met.

f: 239. What is the ruling if a man is presented with a woman as his bride, is told she is his wife, and has intercourse with her?
b: There is no ḥadd upon him because he relied on evidence that reasonably caused confusion, but he must pay her dower (mahr).

f: 240. Why is there no ḥadd when a man has intercourse with a woman mistakenly presented as his wife?
b: Because he relied on the women's statement, which constitutes evidence in a situation where genuine confusion is possible.

f: 241. Must the woman observe an ʿiddah if she was mistakenly treated as the man's wife?
b: Yes. She must observe an ʿiddah because the intercourse occurred under a legally recognized doubt (shubhah).

f: 242. Why is the woman required to observe an ʿiddah after mistaken intercourse based on deception?
b: Because the man relied on legally recognized evidence and is treated as someone who was deceived rather than as a fornicator.

f: 243. Is someone who accuses such a man of zinā liable for the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: No, according to the relied-upon view, because the intercourse occurred under legal doubt. One narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ differs.

f: 244. What is the ruling if a man finds a woman on his bed and assumes she is his wife before having intercourse with her?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because this assumption is not based on legally recognized evidence.

f: 245. Why does finding a woman on one's bed not create a valid legal doubt?
b: Because after a long period of marriage there is ordinarily no legitimate confusion, and another woman may be sleeping there.

f: 246. Does blindness excuse a man who mistakes another woman for his wife in his own bed?
b: No. A blind man can verify her identity by asking or by other means, so the ḥadd is still carried out.

f: 247. What is the ruling if a man calls for his wife, another woman answers saying, "I am your wife," and he has intercourse with her?
b: There is no ḥadd because her statement provides legally recognized evidence that creates doubt.

f: 248. Why does a woman's false claim to be a man's wife prevent the ḥadd?
b: Because her statement serves as evidence upon which the man reasonably relied.

f: 249. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if a man marries a woman who is permanently unlawful for him (maḥram) and has intercourse with her?
b: The ḥadd is not carried out, but if he knew the marriage was unlawful he receives severe taʿzīr.

f: 250. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Muḥammad, and al-Shāfiʿī, what is the ruling if a man knowingly marries and has intercourse with a permanently prohibited woman?
b: The ḥadd is carried out because they regard the marriage contract as legally void and incapable of creating doubt.

f: 251. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider an invalid marriage contract sufficient to create legal doubt?
b: Because the contract still concerns a human female capable of fulfilling the intended purpose of marriage (procreation), creating a resemblance to a valid contract that prevents the ḥadd.

f: 252. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why does an invalid marriage contract create shubhah?
b: Because it resembles a valid marriage contract even though it does not actually make intercourse lawful.

f: 253. What punishment does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ impose for knowingly marrying a permanently prohibited woman?
b: Severe discretionary punishment (taʿzīr), since no fixed ḥadd applies according to his view.

f: 254. What is the ruling on sexual contact below the private parts with a non-maḥram woman?
b: It does not incur a ḥadd but is punished with taʿzīr because it is unlawful without a prescribed fixed punishment.

f: 255. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling for anal intercourse with a woman?
b: It does not incur the ḥadd of zinā but is punished with taʿzīr.

f: 256. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling for the act of the people of Lūṭ (male same-sex intercourse)?
b: It does not incur the ḥadd of zinā but is punished with taʿzīr, and according to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, imprisonment is also imposed.

f: 257. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, how is the act of the people of Lūṭ punished?
b: It is treated like zinā, and the ḥadd is carried out.

f: 258. What was one opinion of al-Shāfiʿī regarding liwat (the act of the people of Lūṭ)?
b: Both participants are executed in all cases based on the relevant hadith reports.

f: 259. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad analogize liwat to zinā?
b: Because it involves complete sexual gratification in a prohibited manner and place without any lawful basis.

f: 260. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reject treating liwat as zinā?
b: Because the Companions differed about its punishment, it does not involve confusion of lineage, and it differs significantly from zinā in nature and motive.

f: 261. What evidence does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ cite to show that liwat is not legally classified as zinā?
b: The Companions differed over its punishment, demonstrating that no single fixed ḥadd equivalent to zinā was established.

f: 262. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say liwat is unlike zinā with respect to lineage?
b: Because it cannot result in pregnancy or confusion of lineage (ikhtilāṭ al-ansāb), one of the major harms of zinā.

f: 263. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ interpret the hadiths commanding execution for liwat?
b: He interprets them as referring to political punishment (siyāsah) or to habitual repeat offenders rather than as establishing a fixed ḥadd.

f: 264. What is the ruling on intercourse with an animal according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It does not incur the ḥadd but is punished with taʿzīr.

f: 265. Why is intercourse with an animal not treated as zinā?
b: Because it is fundamentally different from zinā, lacks a normal human sexual motive, and is not analogous to it.

f: 266. According to the Ḥanafīs, what motivates intercourse with an animal?
b: Extreme foolishness or overwhelming lust rather than normal human desire.

f: 267. Is slaughtering and burning the animal obligatory after intercourse with it?
b: No. According to the Ḥanafīs, reports mentioning this are understood as preventing public gossip, not as establishing an obligatory legal ruling.

f: 268. What is the Hanafi ruling if someone commits zinā in Dār al-Ḥarb or Dār al-Baghy and later enters Muslim territory?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, no ḥadd is carried out because the offence occurred where the Imam's authority did not extend, so the punishment never became binding.

f: 269. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hold that zinā committed in Dār al-Ḥarb is not punished after returning to Muslim lands?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ said that prescribed punishments are not carried out in Dār al-Ḥarb, and the purpose of ḥudūd is deterrence, which cannot be achieved where the Imam has no authority.

f: 270. When can the ḥadd for zinā committed during a military expedition be carried out in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: If the commander has independent judicial authority, such as the Caliph or a provincial governor, he carries out the punishment within his military camp.

f: 271. Can an ordinary military commander enforce the ḥadd for zinā committed during a campaign?
b: No. An ordinary commander or detachment leader lacks delegated authority to implement ḥudūd.

f: 272. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, is a non-Muslim visitor (mustaʾmin) punished for committing zinā in Muslim lands?
b: No. A mustaʾmin is not subject to the ḥadd for zinā because he accepts only those rulings connected with the rights of people, not purely the rights of Allah.

f: 273. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, is a dhimmī punished for committing zinā in Muslim territory?
b: Yes. A dhimmī is subject to the ḥadd because he permanently lives under Islamic authority.

f: 274. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens if a mustaʾmin commits zinā with a dhimmī woman?
b: The dhimmī woman is punished, but the mustaʾmin is not.

f: 275. According to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, what is the ruling if a mustaʾmin commits zinā with a dhimmī woman?
b: Neither of them receives the ḥadd because the principal offender (the mustaʾmin) is not punishable, so the follower is not punished either.

f: 276. According to Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later opinion, are mustaʾmins subject to the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Yes. His later view is that all such offenders are punished because a mustaʾmin accepts the legal rulings of Islamic law while residing in Muslim territory.

f: 277. Why does Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later opinion subject a mustaʾmin to the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Because he accepts Islamic legal authority during his stay, just as he is subject to qiṣāṣ and the punishment for false accusation (qaḏf).

f: 278. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish between a mustaʾmin and a dhimmī regarding the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Because the mustaʾmin resides only temporarily for a specific purpose and accepts only rulings relating to the rights of people, whereas zinā is purely the right of Allah.

f: 279. According to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, why does the punishment sometimes depend on the male offender in cases of zinā?
b: Because he considers the man's act to be the principal act and the woman's participation secondary; if the principal cannot be punished, the follower cannot be punished either.

f: 280. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why can a willing woman still be punished even if her partner is not fully accountable?
b: Because the man's act is still legally zinā, and the woman knowingly participated in an act that legally constitutes zinā.

f: 281. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if a minor or insane person commits zinā with a consenting adult woman?
b: Neither party receives the ḥadd.

f: 282. According to Zafar and al-Shāfiʿī, what is the ruling if a consenting adult woman commits zinā with a minor or insane male?
b: The woman receives the ḥadd because she is personally accountable for her own act.

f: 283. According to one narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if a consenting adult woman commits zinā with a minor or insane male?
b: The woman is subject to the ḥadd.

f: 284. What is the Hanafi ruling if a sane adult man commits zinā with an insane woman?
b: Only the sane man receives the ḥadd.

f: 285. What is the Hanafi ruling if a sane adult man commits zinā with a minor capable of intercourse?
b: Only the sane man receives the ḥadd.

f: 286. Why is only the sane adult punished when he commits zinā with a minor or insane woman?
b: Because the minor or insane person is not legally accountable, while the sane adult fully bears legal responsibility.

f: 287. What principle underlies the Hanafi distinction between accountable and non-accountable participants in zinā?
b: Legal accountability (taklīf) is required for the prescribed punishment, so minors and the insane are exempt from ḥudūd.

f: 288. According to the Hanafis, why is the act of zinā primarily attributed to the man rather than the woman?
b: Because the man performs the act of intercourse (waṭʾ), while the woman is the object of the act. Therefore, he is literally called the fornicator (zānī), whereas her description as a fornicator (zāniyah) is only figurative.

f: 289. Why do the Hanafis consider the term zāniyah (female fornicator) to be figurative?
b: Because she is either described using the name of the agent for the object, or because she causes the act through her consent rather than performing the physical act itself.

f: 290. According to the Hanafis, upon what is the woman's liability for the ḥadd of zinā based?
b: It is based upon her willingly permitting a sinful act of zinā committed by someone who is legally accountable (mukallaf).

f: 291. Why is a consenting woman not punished if her sexual partner is a minor according to the Hanafis?
b: Because the minor's act is not legally considered a sinful act of zinā by a legally accountable person, so the woman's liability cannot attach to it.

f: 292. What is the Hanafi ruling if the ruler coerces a man into committing zinā?
b: The man is not subject to the ḥadd because coercion by the ruler creates legal doubt (shubhah).

f: 293. What was Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ original opinion regarding a man coerced by the ruler into committing zinā?
b: He originally held that the ḥadd still applied because erection appeared to indicate willingness, but he later retracted this opinion.

f: 294. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ later exempt a man coerced by the ruler from the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Because coercion is clearly established, while erection is only an equivocal sign that may occur involuntarily, creating legal doubt sufficient to prevent the ḥadd.

f: 295. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if someone other than the ruler coerces a man into committing zinā?
b: The ḥadd still applies because such coercion is ordinarily not considered irresistible.

f: 296. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what is the ruling if a private individual coerces a man into committing zinā?
b: The ḥadd does not apply because genuine coercion can exist regardless of whether the threat comes from the ruler or another person.

f: 297. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish between coercion by the ruler and coercion by a private individual?
b: Because a victim can ordinarily seek protection from the ruler or the Muslim community against a private individual, whereas protection from the ruler himself is generally impossible.

f: 298. What is the Hanafi ruling if a man confesses four times to zinā with a particular woman, but she claims he married her?
b: No ḥadd is carried out on either of them because the claim of marriage creates legal doubt, and the dowry (mahr) becomes due.

f: 299. What is the Hanafi ruling if a woman confesses to zinā while the man claims he married her?
b: Neither receives the ḥadd because the claim of marriage creates legal doubt, and the dowry is due.

f: 300. Why does a claim of marriage prevent the ḥadd after a confession of zinā?
b: Because the claim could be true and concerns both parties, creating sufficient legal doubt (shubhah) to prevent the prescribed punishment.

f: 301. Why is the dowry (mahr) due when the ḥadd is dropped because of a possible marriage?
b: Because the sanctity of the sexual relationship is recognized once the fixed punishment is removed through legal doubt.

f: 302. What is the Hanafi ruling if a man commits zinā with a slave woman and kills her during the act?
b: The ḥadd is carried out for zinā, and he must also pay her value because the killing and the zinā are separate offences.

f: 303. Why do the two companions hold that both the ḥadd and payment of the slave woman's value apply when she is killed during zinā?
b: Because paying her value is compensation for killing, not ownership of her, so it does not create legal doubt preventing the ḥadd.

f: 304. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why is there no ḥadd if a man kills the slave woman during zinā and becomes liable for her value?
b: Because liability for her value is treated like acquiring ownership, and ownership arising before execution of the ḥadd creates legal doubt that prevents the punishment.

f: 305. Why do the two companions distinguish between killing a slave woman and merely injuring her after zinā?
b: Because killing creates only blood-compensation, whereas injuring her while she remains alive causes ownership to attach to her living body, creating legal doubt that prevents the ḥadd.

f: 306. What is the Hanafi ruling if a man commits zinā with a slave woman and blinds her instead of killing her?
b: He must pay her value, and the ḥadd is dropped because ownership attaches to her living body, creating legal doubt.

f: 307. Why is the supreme Imām not subject to the prescribed ḥudūd according to the Hanafis?
b: Because enforcing ḥudūd belongs exclusively to the Imām, and there is no higher authority to enforce them upon him, nor can he meaningfully enforce them upon himself.

f: 308. Which legal claims can still be enforced against the supreme Imām according to the Hanafis?
b: Retaliation (qiṣāṣ) and financial liability for property, because these are rights belonging to people rather than purely rights of Allah.

f: 309. Why is the supreme Imām still liable for qiṣāṣ and property claims?
b: Because these are enforced by the injured party or the Muslim community, not exclusively by the Imām himself.

f: 310. Why is the ḥadd for false accusation (qadhf) generally treated like the other prescribed punishments regarding the supreme Imām?
b: Because the Hanafi jurists considered its dominant aspect to be the right of Allah, so it follows the same ruling as the other ḥudūd.

f: 311. According to the Hanafis, what is the ruling if witnesses testify to a ḥadd offence after a long delay?
b: Their testimony is not accepted for Allah's-right punishments such as zinā, theft, and drinking wine, but this does not apply to the ḥadd of qadhf.

f: 312. Which ḥudūd are invalidated by prolonged delay in testimony according to the Hanafis?
b: The ḥudūd for zinā, theft, and drinking wine.

f: 313. Does prolonged delay invalidate testimony for the ḥadd of qadhf according to the Hanafis?
b: No. Testimony for qadhf remains admissible despite delay.

f: 314. According to al-Shāfiʿī, does prolonged delay invalidate testimony for ḥudūd?
b: No. He treats them like the rights of individuals and like confession, so delay does not invalidate the testimony.

f: 315. Why do the Hanafis reject delayed testimony in Allah's-right punishments?
b: Because the witness either delayed to conceal the offence, suggesting later hostility, or delayed without excuse and became sinful by withholding testimony, making his testimony unreliable.

f: 316. Why is delayed confession treated differently from delayed testimony?
b: Because a person has no hostility toward himself, so the suspicion affecting delayed witnesses does not exist in confession.

f: 317. Why are zinā, theft, and drinking wine grouped together regarding delayed testimony?
b: Because their prescribed punishments are considered purely the rights of Allah.

f: 318. Why does prolonged delay not invalidate testimony in cases of qadhf?
b: Because qadhf includes the right of the individual, and witnesses may have delayed simply because the victim had not yet brought a claim.

f: 319. Why is a victim's claim relevant in cases of qadhf but not for the ḥadd of theft?
b: Because a claim is a condition for the punishment of qadhf, whereas for theft it is required only to recover the stolen property, not to establish the ḥadd.

f: 320. Why does concealing knowledge of a theft make a witness sinful according to the Hanafis?
b: Because theft is usually committed secretly, so the witness has a duty to inform the owner, and concealing it amounts to withholding testimony.

f: 321. What principle determines whether delayed testimony is accepted according to the Hanafis?
b: Whether the prescribed punishment is primarily the right of Allah or includes the right of an individual.

f: 322. According to the Hanafis, does prolonged delay only prevent testimony before judgment?
b: No. It also prevents execution of the remaining punishment after judgment if a long period passes.

f: 323. What happens if someone partially receives a ḥadd punishment, flees, and is captured after a long delay according to the Hanafis?
b: The remainder of the punishment is not carried out because execution is treated as part of the judicial ruling in ḥudūd.

f: 324. What was Zafar's opinion regarding completing a ḥadd after a long delay?
b: He disagreed with the Hanafis and held that the remaining punishment should still be carried out.

f: 325. Did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ specify a fixed period for when testimony becomes too stale to be accepted?
b: No. He left the determination to the judge according to the circumstances of the time.

f: 326. According to Muḥammad, what period generally constitutes excessive delay in testimony?
b: One month.

f: 327. Which opinion regarding the period of delay is reported as the preferred narration?
b: That one month constitutes excessive delay, as narrated from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 328. Which works indicate that six months may constitute excessive delay in testimony?
b: Al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr and al-Ṭaḥāwī's narration.

f: 329. Does the one-month rule apply if the witnesses live farther than one month's travel from the judge?
b: No. Their testimony is accepted because the delay is explained by the distance rather than suspicion.

f: 330. According to Muḥammad, how is delayed testimony treated in cases of drinking wine?
b: The same rule of prolonged delay applies as in the other Allah's-right punishments.

f: 331. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what determines whether testimony for drinking wine is still admissible?
b: The disappearance of the smell of wine rather than the mere passage of time.

f: 332. According to the Hanafis, what is the ruling if witnesses testify that a man committed zinā with a specific absent woman?
b: The man is still subjected to the ḥadd because the woman's presence or claim is not a condition for establishing zinā.

f: 333. According to the Hanafis, what is the ruling if witnesses testify that a man stole from an absent owner?
b: His hand is not cut off because the owner's claim is a condition for imposing the ḥadd of theft.

f: 334. Why is an absent woman's absence ignored in testimony for zinā but an absent owner's absence prevents the ḥadd for theft?
b: Because the owner's claim is a condition for the ḥadd of theft, whereas no such claim is required from the woman in zinā.

f: 335. Why does the possibility that an absent woman might claim a legal excuse not prevent the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Because it is merely a hypothetical possibility and is not legally considered.

f: 336. What is the ruling if witnesses testify that a man committed zinā with an unidentified woman?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed because she could have been his wife or slave-woman.

f: 337. Why does unidentified testimony regarding the woman prevent the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Because there remains the possibility of a lawful sexual relationship, creating legal doubt (shubhah).

f: 338. What is the ruling if a man himself confesses to committing zinā with an unidentified woman?
b: The ḥadd is imposed because he certainly knows whether she was lawfully permissible to him.

f: 339. If two witnesses testify that a woman was coerced into zinā while two testify that she consented, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ ruling?
b: The ḥadd is waived from both the man and the woman because the testimonies contradict each other regarding the act.

f: 340. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, who is punished when witnesses disagree over whether the woman consented to zinā?
b: Only the man is punished, while the woman is not.

f: 341. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad punish only the man when witnesses disagree about coercion and consent?
b: Because all witnesses agree that the man committed zinā, while the contradiction concerns only the woman's consent.

f: 342. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ waive the ḥadd from both parties when witnesses disagree over coercion and consent?
b: Because the contradiction concerns the very act testified to, and zinā is a single act involving both participants.

f: 343. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why are the witnesses who testified to the woman's consent not punished for slander?
b: Because the testimony of those who said she was coerced removes their liability by negating her responsibility for zinā.

f: 344. What is the ruling if two witnesses testify that zinā occurred in Kūfah while two testify it occurred in Baṣrah?
b: The ḥadd is waived because the testimonies concern two different acts, and neither act has the required four witnesses.

f: 345. Why does disagreement over different cities prevent the ḥadd for zinā?
b: Because the differing locations indicate different incidents, so no single act is proven by four witnesses.

f: 346. Are witnesses punished for slander when they disagree about whether zinā occurred in Kūfah or Baṣrah?
b: No, because it is still possible that each group is referring to the same occurrence.

f: 347. What is the ruling if witnesses differ only about which corner of the same house the zinā occurred in?
b: The ḥadd is imposed on both the man and the woman according to istiḥsān.

f: 348. Why does istiḥsān allow the ḥadd when witnesses differ only about different parts of the same house?
b: Because the testimonies can reasonably be reconciled by assuming the participants moved during the act or that the witnesses viewed the location differently.

f: 349. What would strict analogy (qiyās) require if witnesses disagreed about different corners of the same house?
b: It would require that the ḥadd not be imposed because the reported locations differ.

f: 350. What is the ruling if four witnesses testify that zinā occurred at Nakhlah at sunrise while another four testify that it occurred at Dayr Hind at the same time?
b: The ḥadd is waived because one of the two groups must necessarily be mistaken.

f: 351. Why are neither group of witnesses punished for slander when two complete groups testify to impossible simultaneous incidents?
b: Because each group could individually be truthful even though one must ultimately be mistaken.

f: 352. What is the ruling if four witnesses testify that a woman committed zinā but female examiners establish that she remains a virgin?
b: The ḥadd is waived from both the woman and the man, and the witnesses are not punished.

f: 353. Why does proven virginity prevent the establishment of zinā?
b: Because the act of zinā requiring the ḥadd cannot be established while virginity remains intact.

f: 354. Why is the testimony of female examiners accepted in this case?
b: Because their testimony is sufficient to remove the ḥadd, even though it cannot independently establish one.

f: 355. What is the ruling if four blind men testify to zinā?
b: The accused is not punished, and the witnesses are punished for slander (qadhf).

f: 356. What is the ruling if four people previously punished for false accusation testify to zinā?
b: The accused is not punished, and the witnesses are punished for slander.

f: 357. What is the ruling if one of the four witnesses is a slave or someone previously punished for qadhf?
b: The accused is not punished, and the witnesses are punished for slander.

f: 358. Why do legally unqualified witnesses become liable for slander when they testify to zinā?
b: Because their testimony is legally invalid and cannot establish even financial rights, let alone a ḥadd.

f: 359. Why does invalid testimony not create legal doubt sufficient to prevent liability for slander?
b: Because zinā can only be established through valid testimony, and invalid witnesses have no legal standing to establish it.

f: 360. Why is a slave completely disqualified from testimony according to the Hanafis?
b: Because a slave is not legally qualified either to bear testimony or to deliver it before the court.

f: 361. What is the Hanafi ruling if the witnesses to zinā are open sinners (fussāq)?
b: They are not punished for slander, and the accused is not subjected to the ḥadd because their testimony creates legal doubt.

f: 362. What is the ruling if witnesses are later discovered to have been open sinners after testifying to zinā?
b: They are not punished for slander because their testimony still creates sufficient doubt to prevent both the ḥadd of zinā and the ḥadd of qadhf.

f: 363. Why are sinful witnesses not punished for slander according to the Hanafis?
b: Because a sinner is still legally qualified to bear and deliver testimony, even though his testimony is deficient due to suspicion arising from his sinfulness.

f: 364. According to the Hanafis, is a judge's ruling based on the testimony of a sinner valid?
b: Yes. The ruling is considered legally valid.

f: 365. Why does the testimony of sinful witnesses prevent both the ḥadd of zinā and the ḥadd of slander?
b: Because their testimony creates doubt regarding the zinā, while their sinfulness creates doubt regarding the reliability of the testimony.

f: 366. How does al-Shāfiʿī differ from the Hanafis regarding testimony by open sinners?
b: He considers a sinner completely unqualified to testify, treating him like a slave.

f: 367. What is the ruling if fewer than four witnesses testify to zinā?
b: They are punished for slander because their accusation does not amount to valid testimony.

f: 368. Why are fewer than four witnesses punished for slander in a zinā case?
b: Because testimony requiring four witnesses becomes mere accusation when the required number is lacking.

f: 369. What happens if four witnesses secure a conviction for zinā, but one is later discovered to have been a slave or previously punished for qadhf?
b: The witnesses are punished for slander because there were effectively only three valid witnesses.

f: 370. Why are the witnesses punished if one is later found to have been legally disqualified?
b: Because the required four valid witnesses never actually existed.

f: 371. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, who pays compensation if a person is wrongly stoned because one witness was later found to be legally disqualified?
b: The public treasury (Bayt al-Māl) pays the blood-money.

f: 372. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, who pays compensation if wrongful flogging causes injury after one witness is found to be legally disqualified?
b: Neither the witnesses nor the public treasury pays compensation.

f: 373. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, who pays compensation for injuries caused by wrongful flogging?
b: The public treasury pays compensation.

f: 374. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, does the same ruling apply if the victim dies from wrongful flogging?
b: Yes. The same principle applies.

f: 375. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, are witnesses liable if they later retract testimony that led to wrongful flogging?
b: No. They are not liable.

f: 376. According to the two companions, are witnesses liable if they retract testimony that led to wrongful flogging?
b: Yes. They become liable for the resulting injury or death.

f: 377. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad attribute injuries from flogging to the witnesses' testimony?
b: Because the sentence authorized ordinary flogging, which inevitably includes the possibility of injury, so the injury is legally attributed to their testimony.

f: 378. Why does Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad place liability on the public treasury when witnesses do not retract?
b: Because the executioner's act is legally attributed to the judge, who acts on behalf of the Muslim community.

f: 379. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not attribute injuries from flogging to the witnesses' testimony?
b: Because the prescribed punishment consists only of painful blows that neither wound nor kill, so any injury is outwardly due to the executioner's lack of skill.

f: 380. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, why is the executioner generally not required to compensate for injuries caused during flogging?
b: To prevent people from refusing to carry out prescribed punishments out of fear of financial liability.

f: 381. What is the Hanafi ruling if four witnesses testify to the testimony of another four eyewitnesses in a zinā case?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed because testimony upon testimony creates additional legal doubt.

f: 382. Why is testimony upon testimony (shahādah ʿalā al-shahādah) not accepted in cases of zinā?
b: Because it introduces additional doubt, and there is no necessity for using substitute testimony in such cases.

f: 383. What happens if the original eyewitnesses later appear and testify personally after substitute witnesses had already testified?
b: The ḥadd is still not imposed because the earlier rejection affects the original testimony regarding the same incident.

f: 384. Why does the later testimony of the original witnesses still not establish the ḥadd?
b: Because the substitute testimony concerning the same incident had already been rejected, affecting the legal standing of the original testimony.

f: 385. Are the original witnesses punished for slander when their testimony is rejected after substitute testimony?
b: No. Their number is complete, and only legal doubt prevents the ḥadd.

f: 386. Why are the witnesses not punished for slander when testimony upon testimony is rejected?
b: Because the complete number of witnesses exists, and the rejection is based only on legal doubt, not on false accusation.

f: 387. What happens if four witnesses secure a stoning sentence and one later retracts his testimony?
b: The retracting witness alone is punished for slander and must pay one-quarter of the victim's blood-money.

f: 388. Why must a retracting witness pay only one-quarter of the blood-money?
b: Because three-quarters of the legal cause remains through the testimony of the other three witnesses, so only one-quarter of the death is attributed to him.

f: 389. How does al-Shāfiʿī differ regarding witnesses who retract after a stoning?
b: He holds that only retaliation (qiṣāṣ), not financial compensation, applies according to his legal principles regarding witness liability.

f: 390. According to the three Hanafi Imams, is a witness who retracts his testimony after a stoning punished for slander?
b: Yes. The retracting witness is punished for slander (qadhf).

f: 391. What was Zufar's opinion regarding a witness who retracts after a stoning has been carried out?
b: He held that the retracting witness is not punished for slander.

f: 392. Why did Zufar believe a retracting witness is not liable for slander after execution?
b: Because if the accusation concerns a living person, the person is now dead, and if it concerns a dead person, the judicial ruling of stoning creates legal doubt.

f: 393. Why do the three Hanafi Imams hold that a retracting witness is punished for slander after execution?
b: Because retraction invalidates the testimony, causing it to become slander against a dead person, and the previous judgment no longer creates doubt with respect to the retracting witness.

f: 394. Why does the standing judicial ruling not protect the retracting witness from liability for slander?
b: Because his own retraction invalidates the proof upon which the judgment was based with respect to him.

f: 395. Why is someone else who slanders the executed person after the judgment not punished in the same way?
b: Because the executed person is no longer legally regarded as chaste toward others due to the existing judicial ruling.

f: 396. What happens if one witness retracts before the accused has received the ḥadd?
b: The ḥadd is dropped from the accused, and all the witnesses are punished for slander.

f: 397. According to Muḥammad, who is punished if one witness retracts before execution of the sentence?
b: Only the retracting witness is punished for slander.

f: 398. Why does Muḥammad punish only the retracting witness before execution?
b: Because he considers the testimony strengthened by the judicial ruling and invalidated only with respect to the witness who retracts.

f: 399. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ punish all the witnesses if one retracts before execution?
b: Because execution is considered part of the judicial process, making retraction before execution equivalent to retraction before judgment.

f: 400. What happens if one witness retracts before the judge has even issued judgment?
b: The ḥadd is dropped from the accused, and all the witnesses are punished for slander.

f: 401. According to Zufar, who is punished if one witness retracts before judgment?
b: Only the retracting witness, because only he has admitted to lying.

f: 402. Why do the Hanafis punish all the witnesses when one retracts before judgment?
b: Because without a judicial ruling, their statements remain mere accusations rather than legally effective testimony.

f: 403. What is the ruling if there were five witnesses and only one retracts?
b: Nothing is due from the retracting witness because four valid witnesses still remain.

f: 404. Why does a single retraction among five witnesses have no legal effect?
b: Because the remaining four witnesses still constitute the complete legal proof required for zinā.

f: 405. What happens if a second witness retracts after there were originally five witnesses?
b: Both retracting witnesses are punished for slander and together bear one-quarter of the blood-money.

f: 406. Why do two retracting witnesses bear only one-quarter of the blood-money?
b: Because three-quarters of the legal proof remains through the three witnesses who continue to testify.

f: 407. What determines financial liability when some witnesses retract?
b: The amount of legal proof remaining through those who continue to testify, not the number who retract.

f: 408. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, who pays the blood-money if false certification of witnesses leads to an unlawful stoning?
b: The people who certified the witnesses' reliability (tazkiyah), if they later retract their certification.

f: 409. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, who pays the blood-money if false certification leads to an unlawful stoning?
b: The public treasury (Bayt al-Māl).

f: 410. According to one interpretation, when are the certifiers liable for compensation?
b: When they admit that they knowingly certified the witnesses despite knowing they were unqualified.

f: 411. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad not hold the certifiers personally liable?
b: Because they merely praised the witnesses, similar to someone testifying that the accused was muḥṣan.

f: 412. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hold the certifiers liable?
b: Because witness testimony only becomes legally effective through certification, making certification the cause of the cause of the judgment.

f: 413. Why is certification different from testimony establishing iḥṣān?
b: Because certification creates the legal effectiveness of testimony, whereas proving iḥṣān is merely one condition of the punishment.

f: 414. Does it matter whether the certifiers formally testified or simply informed the judge of the witnesses' reliability?
b: No. The ruling is the same in either case.

f: 415. When are certifiers liable for wrongly approving witnesses?
b: When they specifically certify that the witnesses are free and Muslim, and this later proves false.

f: 416. Are certifiers liable if they merely describe witnesses as "upright" and the witnesses later turn out to be slaves?
b: No. A slave may still be personally upright, so that statement is not necessarily false.

f: 417. Why do the original witnesses incur no liability when the certifiers of their testimony are held liable?
b: Because their statements never amounted to legally valid testimony.

f: 418. Why are the original witnesses not punished for slander after the accused has died?
b: Because they accused a living person, and the punishment for slander (qadhf) is not inherited after death.

f: 419. What is the ruling if a judge orders a man stoned for zinā, but someone instead beheads him, and it is later discovered that the witnesses were slaves?
b: The killer must pay the blood-money (diyah).

f: 420. According to strict analogy (qiyās), what would be the ruling for someone who beheads a man later found to have been wrongfully sentenced?
b: Retaliation (qiṣāṣ) would be required because he intentionally killed an innocent protected person.

f: 421. Why does juristic preference (istiḥsān) require only blood-money instead of retaliation in this case?
b: Because the judicial ruling appeared valid at the time of the killing, creating legal doubt that prevents retaliation.

f: 422. Why is beheading after the judge's order different from killing before judgment?
b: Because before judgment the witnesses' testimony had not yet become legally effective proof.

f: 423. Why is the killer excused from retaliation after acting on the judge's order?
b: Because he believed the victim's blood was lawful based on an apparent legal proof.

f: 424. Why is the blood-money for intentional beheading paid from the killer's own wealth?
b: Because intentional homicide is not covered by the ʿāqilah (male relatives).

f: 425. Over what period is the blood-money for intentional beheading paid?
b: Over three years.

f: 426. Why is the blood-money payable over three years in this case?
b: Because the liability arose directly from the act of killing.

f: 427. If the condemned person is actually stoned according to the judge's order and the witnesses are later found to have been slaves, who pays the blood-money?
b: The public treasury (Bayt al-Māl).

f: 428. Why does the public treasury pay when the execution is carried out by stoning?
b: Because the executioner merely carried out the judge's lawful order, so his act is legally attributed to the judge.

f: 429. Why is beheading treated differently from carrying out the ordered stoning?
b: Because the executioner exceeded the judge's command by using a different method of execution.

f: 430. Is the testimony of witnesses accepted if they admit they intentionally watched the act of zinā in order to testify?
b: Yes. Their testimony is accepted.

f: 431. Why is intentionally observing zinā permissible for witnesses?
b: Because looking is allowed out of necessity for bearing testimony, just as it is for physicians and midwives.

f: 432. What is the ruling if a man denies being muḥṣan, but his wife has borne him a child?
b: He is considered muḥṣan and is stoned if the other conditions are fulfilled.

f: 433. Why does a wife bearing a child establish iḥṣān despite the husband's denial?
b: Because established lineage is itself a judicial determination that consummation took place.

f: 434. What other situation establishes consummation for proving iḥṣān besides childbirth?
b: If a husband divorces his wife immediately after taking her back during a revocable divorce (rajʿah).

f: 435. What is the ruling if there is no child, but one man and two women testify that the accused is muḥṣan?
b: He is considered muḥṣan and is stoned.

f: 436. How does al-Shāfiʿī differ regarding testimony establishing iḥṣān?
b: He does not accept women's testimony for iḥṣān because he limits it largely to financial matters.

f: 437. Why does Zufar reject the testimony of one man and two women for establishing iḥṣān?
b: Because he considers iḥṣān a condition resembling an effective legal cause that aggravates the punishment, requiring stricter proof.

f: 438. Why do the Hanafis accept one man and two women as witnesses for iḥṣān?
b: Because iḥṣān consists of praiseworthy qualities that restrain a person from zinā rather than functioning as an effective legal cause.

f: 439. Why is testimony establishing emancipation different from testimony establishing iḥṣān?
b: Because emancipation itself is the legal cause being established, whereas iḥṣān is only a qualifying condition.

f: 440. According to the Hanafis, are witnesses who established iḥṣān liable if they later retract?
b: No. They incur no liability.

f: 441. How does Zufar differ regarding witnesses who later retract testimony establishing iḥṣān?
b: He holds them liable, unlike the Hanafis.

f: 442. When is the ḥadd for drinking wine imposed according to the Hanafis?
b: When a person is apprehended while the smell of wine is still present or while intoxicated, and witnesses testify to it.

f: 443. Is the ḥadd imposed if a person confesses to drinking wine while the smell is still present?
b: Yes. The ḥadd is imposed.

f: 444. Why is the ḥadd imposed when the smell of wine or intoxication is still present?
b: Because the offence is clearly established and insufficient time has passed to cast doubt upon it.

f: 445. What prophetic evidence supports imposing the ḥadd for drinking wine?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever drinks wine, flog him; and if he returns to it, flog him."

f: 446. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if a person confesses after the smell of wine has disappeared?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 447. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling if a person confesses after the smell of wine has disappeared?
b: The ḥadd is still imposed.

f: 448. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the ruling if witnesses testify after the smell of wine has disappeared or the intoxication has ended?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 449. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling if witnesses testify after the smell of wine has disappeared or the intoxication has ended?
b: The ḥadd is imposed.

f: 450. According to Muḥammad, how is delay (taqādum) measured in the ḥadd for drinking?
b: By the passage of time, by analogy with the ḥadd for zinā.

f: 451. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how is delay measured in the ḥadd for drinking?
b: By the disappearance of the smell of wine rather than by elapsed time.

f: 452. What evidence do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use for measuring delay by the smell of wine?
b: The statement of Ibn Masʿūd: "If you find the smell of wine, then flog him."

f: 453. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ rely on the smell rather than elapsed time?
b: Because the continued smell is the strongest indication that the drinking occurred recently.

f: 454. Why does Muḥammad treat delayed confession to drinking like delayed confession to zinā?
b: Because he considers delay not to invalidate confession, just as in zinā.

f: 455. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reject delayed confessions after the smell disappears?
b: Because the Companions' consensus regarding the ḥadd for drinking was based on Ibn Masʿūd's condition that the smell still be present.

f: 456. What is the ruling if witnesses apprehend a drunken person and transport him to another city, but the smell disappears before reaching the ruler?
b: According to all three Imams, the ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 457. Why is the ḥadd not imposed when the smell disappears during necessary travel to the judge?
b: Because the delay resulted from necessity rather than neglect, so no suspicion falls upon the witnesses.

f: 458. How is necessary travel in drinking cases compared to zinā cases?
b: It is treated like long-distance travel in zinā, which excuses delay in presenting testimony.

f: 459. Is a person who becomes intoxicated from nabīdh subject to the ḥadd?
b: Yes.

f: 460. What historical evidence supports imposing the ḥadd for intoxication caused by nabīdh?
b: ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ imposed the ḥadd upon a Bedouin who became intoxicated from nabīdh.

f: 461. Does merely smelling of wine establish the ḥadd?
b: No. Mere smell alone does not establish the ḥadd.

f: 462. Does vomiting wine by itself establish the ḥadd?
b: No. Vomiting wine alone does not establish the ḥadd.

f: 463. Why do smell or vomiting alone not establish the ḥadd for drinking?
b: Because they admit alternative explanations, and the drinking may have occurred under coercion or necessity.

f: 464. Is every intoxicated person automatically subject to the ḥadd?
b: No. The cause of the intoxication must first be established.

f: 465. What must be established before an intoxicated person can receive the ḥadd?
b: That the intoxication resulted from nabīdh (or an intoxicant requiring the ḥadd) and that it was consumed voluntarily.

f: 466. Is someone intoxicated from a lawful substance, such as henbane or mare's milk, subject to the ḥadd?
b: No.

f: 467. Is a person who was compelled to drink an intoxicant subject to the ḥadd?
b: No. Coercion prevents the ḥadd.

f: 468. Why is an intoxicated person not punished until his intoxication has passed?
b: So that the objective of deterrence is achieved, since a drunk person cannot fully comprehend the punishment.

f: 469. What is the ḥadd punishment for drinking wine or becoming intoxicated for a free person?
b: Eighty lashes.

f: 470. What is the evidence for prescribing eighty lashes for a free person who drinks wine?
b: The consensus (ijmāʿ) of the Companions.

f: 471. How are the lashes for the ḥadd of drinking distributed over the body?
b: They are distributed over the body in the same manner as the ḥadd for zinā.

f: 472. According to the well-known Hanafi narration, is a person stripped of his outer garments before the ḥadd for drinking?
b: Yes. He is stripped of his outer garments.

f: 473. What was Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's opinion regarding stripping clothing during the ḥadd for drinking?
b: He held that the offender is not stripped, as an act of leniency since no explicit text requires it.

f: 474. Why does the well-known Hanafi narration require removing the offender's outer garments during the ḥadd for drinking?
b: Because sufficient leniency has already been shown elsewhere, so no further leniency is given.

f: 475. What is the ḥadd punishment for a slave who drinks wine or becomes intoxicated?
b: Forty lashes.

f: 476. Why is a slave's punishment for drinking reduced to forty lashes?
b: Because slavery halves the prescribed punishment.

f: 477. What is the ruling if someone confesses to drinking wine or becoming intoxicated and then retracts the confession?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 478. Why does retracting a confession prevent the ḥadd for drinking?
b: Because it is purely the right of Allah, so doubts prevent enforcement.

f: 479. How is the offence of drinking wine established in the Hanafi school?
b: By the testimony of two witnesses or by a single confession.

f: 480. What alternative opinion did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ narrate regarding confession to drinking wine?
b: That two confessions are required, by analogy with theft.

f: 481. Is the testimony of women together with men accepted to establish the ḥadd for drinking?
b: No.

f: 482. Why is the testimony of women not accepted in establishing the ḥadd for drinking?
b: Because of the possibility of substitution and concerns about error or forgetfulness in ḥudūd cases.

f: 483. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how is the intoxication requiring the ḥadd defined?
b: It is when a person cannot understand any speech at all and cannot distinguish a man from a woman.

f: 484. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, how is intoxication requiring the ḥadd defined?
b: It is when a person's speech becomes irrational and confused in the ordinary sense of drunkenness.

f: 485. Which definition of legal intoxication was preferred by most later Hanafi scholars?
b: The definition of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad.

f: 486. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ adopt a stricter definition of intoxication for imposing the ḥadd?
b: To maximize certainty and avert the prescribed punishment whenever doubt exists.

f: 487. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the highest degree of intoxication that justifies the ḥadd?
b: When intoxication completely overcomes the intellect so that all ability to distinguish things is lost.

f: 488. What definition of intoxication is used when determining whether drinking itself was unlawful?
b: The definition of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, out of precaution.

f: 489. How does al-Shāfiʿī determine whether someone is intoxicated?
b: By the visible effects on the person's walking, movements, and limbs.

f: 490. Why do the Hanafis reject al-Shāfiʿī's definition of intoxication?
b: Because physical signs vary greatly between individuals and are therefore not a reliable legal standard.

f: 491. Is an intoxicated person's confession sufficient to establish the ḥadd for drinking?
b: No.

f: 492. Why is an intoxicated person's confession not accepted for imposing the ḥadd for drinking?
b: Because intoxication increases the possibility that the confession is false, and doubts prevent punishments that are purely Allah's rights.

f: 493. Why is the intoxicated person's confession treated differently in the ḥadd of qadhf (false accusation)?
b: Because qadhf includes the rights of another person, so the intoxicated person is treated like a sober person.

f: 494. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, does an intoxicated person's apostasy dissolve his marriage?
b: No. His wife does not become separated from him.

f: 495. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad not recognize an intoxicated person's apostasy?
b: Because disbelief requires genuine belief and conviction, which cannot truly exist while intoxicated.

f: 496. According to the apparent narration in the Hanafi school, is an intoxicated person's apostasy legally valid?
b: Yes. According to the apparent narration, it is considered valid.

f: 497. What conditions must be met for the ḥadd of false accusation (qadhf) to be imposed on an accuser?
b: The accuser must explicitly accuse a legally chaste (muḥṣan) man or woman of zinā, the accused must demand the punishment, and the accusation must be proven before the judge.

f: 498. What is the punishment for a free person who falsely accuses a muḥṣan person of zinā?
b: A free person is flogged with eighty lashes after the accused demands the punishment.

f: 499. What Qur'anic verse establishes the punishment for false accusation (qadhf)?
b: Allah says: "And those who accuse chaste women... then flog them with eighty lashes." (Qur'an 24:4).

f: 500. Why is the accusation in the verse understood specifically as an accusation of zinā?
b: Because the verse requires four witnesses, and the requirement of four witnesses applies specifically to accusations of zinā.

f: 501. Why must the accused person demand the punishment before the ḥadd of qadhf is carried out?
b: Because the punishment includes a personal right of the accused by removing the disgrace caused by the accusation.

f: 502. Is legal chastity (iḥṣān) required in the accused person for the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: Yes. The accused must possess iḥṣān for the punishment of qadhf to apply.

f: 503. How are the lashes distributed when carrying out the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: The lashes are distributed over the limbs, as explained previously for the punishment of zinā.

f: 504. Is a person punished for qadhf stripped of all clothing before being flogged?
b: No. He is not stripped of his normal clothing.

f: 505. Which garments are removed from a person receiving the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: His fur garment and heavily padded clothing are removed because they prevent the pain from reaching him.

f: 506. Why is a person punished for qadhf not stripped as completely as a person punished for zinā?
b: Because the cause for qadhf is not established with absolute certainty, so the punishment is not carried out with maximum severity.

f: 507. What is the punishment for a slave who commits qadhf?
b: A slave is flogged with forty lashes.

f: 508. What does iḥṣān (legal chastity) mean in the chapter on qadhf?
b: It means the accused is free, sane, adult, Muslim, and chaste from zinā.

f: 509. Why is freedom a condition of iḥṣān in qadhf?
b: Because the term muḥṣan in this context refers to a free person, as indicated by Qur'an 4:25.

f: 510. Why are sanity and adulthood conditions of iḥṣān in qadhf?
b: Because a child or insane person is not legally capable of committing zinā, so such an accusation does not bring legal disgrace.

f: 511. Why is Islam a condition of iḥṣān in qadhf according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because of the Prophet's ﷺ statement: "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not a muḥṣan."

f: 512. Why is chastity from zinā a condition of iḥṣān in qadhf?
b: Because only a chaste person suffers legal disgrace from a false accusation of zinā; if the accusation is true, the accuser is not guilty of qadhf.

f: 513. What is the ruling if someone says to another, "You are not your father's son," thereby denying his lineage?
b: The speaker is subject to the ḥadd of qadhf if the legal conditions are met.

f: 514. Under what condition does denying another person's lineage by saying, "You are not your father's son," incur the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: When the person's mother is a free, Muslim, and legally chaste woman.

f: 515. Why does denying someone's lineage constitute qadhf?
b: Because denying lineage is, in reality, an accusation that the person's mother committed zinā.

f: 516. What is the ruling if someone angrily says, "You are not the son of so-and-so," referring to the person's father?
b: The speaker is subject to the ḥadd of qadhf.

f: 517. Why does saying, "You are not the son of so-and-so," in anger incur the ḥadd?
b: Because in anger the statement is understood literally as an accusation against the person's lineage and mother.

f: 518. What is the ruling if someone calmly says, "You are not the son of so-and-so," outside a state of anger?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 519. Why does saying, "You are not the son of so-and-so," outside of anger not incur the ḥadd?
b: Because it is understood as reproaching the person's character rather than literally denying his lineage.

f: 520. What is the ruling if someone says, "You are not the son of so-and-so," intending the person's grandfather?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 521. Why is there no ḥadd when someone denies a person's relationship to his grandfather?
b: Because the statement is literally true, as a person is not the direct son of his grandfather.

f: 522. What is the ruling if someone attributes a person to his grandfather instead of his father?
b: The ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 523. Why does attributing someone to his grandfather not constitute qadhf?
b: Because people may figuratively be attributed to their grandfathers.

f: 524. What is the ruling if someone says, "O son of the adulteress," and the person's deceased mother was legally chaste?
b: The accuser is subject to the ḥadd if the son demands it.

f: 525. Why does saying, "O son of the adulteress," constitute qadhf when the mother is deceased?
b: Because it is an accusation of zinā against a legally chaste woman after her death.

f: 526. Who may demand the ḥadd for qadhf on behalf of a deceased person according to the Hanafi school?
b: Only a parent or child whose own lineage is impugned by the accusation.

f: 527. Why may a parent or child demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against a deceased relative?
b: Because the disgrace reaches them through their direct line of descent, so the accusation includes them in meaning.

f: 528. According to al-Shāfiʿī, who may demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against a deceased person?
b: Every heir, because he considers the right to the ḥadd of qadhf to be inherited.

f: 529. According to the Hanafi school, why may a parent or child demand the ḥadd for qadhf against a deceased relative?
b: Not because the right is inherited, but because the accusation directly impugns their own lineage.

f: 530. According to the Hanafi school, does a person who is barred from inheritance because he killed the deceased still have the right to demand the ḥadd for qadhf?
b: Yes.

f: 531. Why does a person disqualified from inheritance still have the right to demand the ḥadd for qadhf according to the Hanafi school?
b: Because the right is based on the disgrace to his lineage, not on inheritance.

f: 532. According to the Hanafi school, does a daughter's child have the right to demand the ḥadd for qadhf against a deceased grandparent?
b: Yes.

f: 533. Which Hanafi jurist differed by denying a daughter's child the right to demand the ḥadd for qadhf?
b: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan.

f: 534. According to the Hanafi school, may a grandchild demand the ḥadd for qadhf even if the deceased's own child is still alive?
b: Yes.

f: 535. Which Hanafi jurist held that a grandchild may not demand the ḥadd while the deceased's child is still alive?
b: Zufar.

f: 536. If a muḥṣan person is falsely accused of zinā and later dies, may his son demand the ḥadd of qadhf according to the Hanafi school?
b: Yes, even if the son is a non-Muslim or a slave.

f: 537. According to the Hanafi school, may a non-Muslim son demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against his muḥṣan parent?
b: Yes. Disbelief does not prevent him from possessing this right.

f: 538. According to the Hanafi school, may a slave son demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against his muḥṣan parent?
b: Yes. Slavery does not prevent him from possessing this right.

f: 539. Why may a son demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against his muḥṣan parent according to the Hanafi school?
b: Because the complete insult directed at the muḥṣan parent extends to the child.

f: 540. Why is the iḥṣān of the person accused of zinā important when determining whether the insult extends to the child?
b: Because only a complete insult against a muḥṣan person extends to his child and gives the child the right to demand the ḥadd.

f: 541. Why may a child not demand the ḥadd if the accusation was directed at the child himself while he lacked iḥṣān?
b: Because the insult is incomplete when the accused person is not muḥṣan.

f: 542. Which Hanafi jurist disagreed with allowing a non-Muslim or slave son to demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against his muḥṣan parent?
b: Zufar.

f: 543. According to Zufar, why should a non-Muslim or slave son not demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against his parent?
b: Because the insult reaches the child only indirectly, and the right is not inherited.

f: 544. May a slave demand the ḥadd from his master for falsely accusing the slave's free mother of zinā?
b: No.

f: 545. Why may a slave not demand the ḥadd from his master for accusing the slave's mother?
b: Because a master is not punished on account of his slave.

f: 546. May a son demand the ḥadd from his father for falsely accusing the son's free Muslim mother of zinā?
b: No.

f: 547. Why may a son not demand the ḥadd from his father for accusing his mother?
b: Because a father is not punished on account of his son.

f: 548. Which legal principle is illustrated by the rule that a son cannot demand the ḥadd from his father?
b: Just as a parent is not executed in qiṣāṣ for killing his child, a father is not punished on account of his son.

f: 549. Which legal principle is illustrated by the rule that a slave cannot demand the ḥadd from his master?
b: Just as a master is not executed in qiṣāṣ for killing his slave, he is not punished on account of his slave.

f: 550. If a woman has a son from another man, may that son demand the ḥadd against someone who falsely accused her of zinā?
b: Yes.

f: 551. Why may a son from another husband demand the ḥadd for qadhf committed against his mother?
b: Because the legal cause exists and no preventing factor is present.

f: 552. What is the ruling if a person falsely accused of zinā dies before the ḥadd of qadhf is carried out?
b: The ḥadd is cancelled according to the Hanafi school.

f: 553. According to al-Shāfiʿī, is the ḥadd of qadhf cancelled if the falsely accused person dies?
b: No. He holds that it is not cancelled.

f: 554. What happens if the falsely accused person dies after part of the ḥadd of qadhf has already been carried out?
b: The remainder of the punishment is cancelled according to the Hanafi school.

f: 555. Why does the Hanafi school cancel the ḥadd of qadhf upon the death of the falsely accused person?
b: Because the right to demand it is not inherited.

f: 556. What is the basis of the disagreement between the Hanafi school and al-Shāfiʿī regarding cancellation of the ḥadd of qadhf after the victim's death?
b: Whether the right to demand the punishment is inheritable.

f: 557. According to al-Shāfiʿī, why is the ḥadd of qadhf not cancelled when the victim dies?
b: Because he considers the right to demand it to be inherited by the heirs.

f: 558. According to the Hanafi school, does the ḥadd of qadhf contain both the right of Allah and the right of an individual?
b: Yes.

f: 559. Why is the ḥadd of qadhf considered to contain the right of the individual?
b: Because it removes the disgrace suffered by the falsely accused person.

f: 560. Why is the ḥadd of qadhf considered to contain the right of Allah?
b: Because it serves as a deterrent and protects society from corruption.

f: 561. Why is qadhf classified as a ḥadd despite containing an individual's right?
b: Because one of its purposes is general deterrence, which is characteristic of the rights of Allah.

f: 562. What is the Hanafi ruling when the rights of Allah and the rights of individuals conflict in the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: The Hanafis give precedence to the right of Allah, while al-Shāfiʿī gives precedence to the individual's right.

f: 563. Why do the Hanafis give precedence to Allah's right over the individual's right in the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: Because Allah safeguards the individual's interests, whereas individuals cannot independently enforce Allah's rights except as His representatives.

f: 564. Why does al-Shāfiʿī give precedence to the individual's right in the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: Because the individual has a personal need for the right, whereas Allah is free of need.

f: 565. How does the Hanafi principle regarding Allah's right affect inheritance of the right to demand the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: The right is not inherited because it is predominantly the right of Allah.

f: 566. How does al-Shāfiʿī's principle affect inheritance of the right to demand the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: The right is inherited because he treats it primarily as the individual's right.

f: 567. According to the Hanafis, can the victim pardon the offender in a case of qadhf?
