b: No. The victim's pardon does not prevent the ḥadd from being carried out.

f: 568. According to al-Shāfiʿī, can the victim pardon the offender in a case of qadhf?
b: Yes. The victim's pardon is valid because he considers the punishment primarily the individual's right.

f: 569. According to the Hanafis, may compensation be accepted in exchange for waiving the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: No. Accepting compensation in place of the prescribed punishment is not permissible.

f: 570. According to the Hanafis, does the principle of tadākhul (merging multiple punishments into one) apply to repeated acts of qadhf?
b: Yes. Multiple punishments may merge into a single ḥadd.

f: 571. According to al-Shāfiʿī, does tadākhul apply to repeated acts of qadhf?
b: No. Multiple offenses do not merge into one punishment.

f: 572. Which Hanafi scholar agreed with al-Shāfiʿī that the victim may pardon the offender in qadhf?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that the victim's pardon is valid.

f: 573. Did all Hanafi scholars agree that Allah's right predominates in the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: No. Some Hanafi scholars regarded the individual's right as predominant, though the first opinion is considered stronger.

f: 574. What is the preferred Hanafi opinion regarding whether Allah's right or the individual's right predominates in qadhf?
b: The preferred opinion is that Allah's right predominates.

f: 575. What is the Hanafi ruling if a person confesses to qadhf and then retracts the confession?
b: The retraction is not accepted, and the confession remains effective.

f: 576. Why is retraction of a confession to qadhf not accepted in the Hanafi school?
b: Because the accused person has a personal right and contradicts the retraction, unlike purely Allah-right cases.

f: 577. Why is retraction accepted in ḥudūd that are purely the rights of Allah but not in qadhf?
b: Because in purely Allah-right offenses no individual contradicts the retraction, allowing doubt to avert the punishment.

f: 578. Does calling an Arab "O Nabataean" constitute qadhf in the Hanafi school?
b: No. It is understood as criticism of character or eloquence rather than an accusation of zinā.

f: 579. Is saying to someone, "You are not an Arab," considered qadhf?
b: No. It is interpreted as an insult unrelated to zinā.

f: 580. Does saying, "O son of the water of the sky," constitute qadhf?
b: No. It is a figurative expression praising nobility, generosity, and purity.

f: 581. Why is the expression "Water of the Sky" not considered slander?
b: Because it is a well-known title associated with purity and generosity rather than an accusation of fornication.

f: 582. Does attributing someone to his paternal uncle constitute qadhf?
b: No. A paternal uncle may figuratively be called a father in Islamic usage.

f: 583. What Qur'anic evidence supports figuratively calling a paternal uncle a father?
b: Allah's statement mentioning Abraham عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, Ishmael, and Isaac as "your fathers" (Qur'an 2:133), even though Ishmael was a paternal uncle.

f: 584. Does attributing someone to his maternal uncle constitute qadhf?
b: No. A maternal uncle may also be called a father.

f: 585. What hadith supports referring to a maternal uncle as a father?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said, "The maternal uncle is a father."

f: 586. Does attributing someone to his mother's husband constitute qadhf?
b: No. A mother's husband may figuratively be called a father because he raises the child.

f: 587. What if someone says to another, "You zanāʾta (زَنَأْتَ) on the mountain," claiming he meant climbing the mountain?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, he is still liable for ḥadd al-qadhf. Muḥammad held that he is not liable. They argued that although zanāʾa can literally mean "to climb," it is also used by some Arabs for zinā, and the context of anger indicates the accusation of fornication. Mentioning "the mountain" only clearly indicates climbing when accompanied by ʿalā ("upon").

f: 588. What if he says, "You climbed upon the mountain (zanāʾta ʿalā al-jabal)"?
b: Two opinions are reported. One says no ḥadd, because the wording clearly indicates climbing. Another says ḥadd still applies, based on the possibility that the expression was intended as an accusation of fornication.

f: 589. What if someone says, "O adulterer," and the other replies, "No, rather you"?
b: Both receive the ḥadd for slander. The reply means: "No, rather you are the adulterer." The particle bal ("rather") transfers the accusation to the speaker.

f: 590. What if a husband says to his wife, "O adulteress," and she replies, "No, rather you"?
b: The wife receives the ḥadd for slander, and liʿān is not carried out. Since both have exchanged accusations, beginning with the ḥadd upon the wife removes her qualification to perform liʿān, thereby preventing it. This order is preferred because it avoids combining punishments.

f: 591. What if the wife replies, "I committed fornication with you" after he accuses her?
b: Neither the ḥadd nor liʿān is carried out. Her statement creates legal doubt. It may refer to fornication before marriage (which would support his accusation but not require liʿān), or she may mean, "My only illicit intercourse after marriage was with you," implying no accusation against him. This uncertainty prevents both rulings.

f: 592. What is the ruling if a man acknowledges a child as his and then later denies him?
b: He must perform liʿān, because the child's lineage became established through his acknowledgment. By denying the child afterwards, he has effectively accused his wife, making liʿān obligatory.

f: 593. What if he first denies the child and then later acknowledges him?
b: He receives the ḥadd for qadhf (false accusation). By admitting he was mistaken, he invalidates the basis for liʿān. Since liʿān is only an exceptional substitute due to mutual contradiction, once that contradiction disappears, the law returns to the original ruling, namely the ḥadd for slander.

f: 594. Is the child considered his in both situations?
b: Yes. The child remains legally his because of his acknowledgment, whether it came before or after the denial. Liʿān remains valid even without severing lineage, just as it can occur even when no child exists.

f: 595. What if he says, "He is neither my son nor your son"?
b: Neither the ḥadd for qadhf nor liʿān applies, because he is denying the birth itself rather than accusing his wife of fornication.

f: 596. What is the ruling for accusing a woman who has children whose father is unknown?
b: No ḥadd for qadhf is imposed upon the accuser because the existence of such a child is treated as an indication suggesting fornication, meaning the condition of chastity (ʿiffah) required for iḥṣān is considered absent.

f: 597. What if someone accuses a woman who underwent liʿān regarding a child, whether the child is alive or has died?
b: No ḥadd for qadhf applies because the child whose lineage was denied through liʿān remains an indication suggesting fornication, preventing the establishment of the woman's legal chastity (iḥṣān).

f: 598. What if someone accuses a woman who underwent liʿān but there was no child involved?
b: The ḥadd for qadhf applies because there is no indication suggesting fornication, so the woman's iḥṣān remains intact.

f: 599. What is the general rule regarding accusing someone who has committed unlawful intercourse outside ownership?
b: The accuser is not liable for ḥadd al-qadhf, because the accused has lost the chastity required for iḥṣān. Since the accusation is true, the accuser is not punished.

f: 600. What principle governs when an accusation of zinā incurs the ḥadd for qadhf?
b: Whoever commits intercourse that is intrinsically unlawful (ḥarām li-ʿaynihi) loses the protection of iḥṣān, so accusing him does not incur the ḥadd. If the prohibition is only external (ḥarām li-ghayrihi), the accusation still incurs the ḥadd because such intercourse is not legally considered zinā.

f: 601. What kinds of intercourse are considered intrinsically unlawful (ḥarām li-ʿaynihi)?
b: Intercourse entirely or partially outside ownership, and intercourse within ownership where the prohibition is permanent, are intrinsically unlawful.

f: 602. What kinds of intercourse are prohibited only due to an external factor (ḥarām li-ghayrihi)?
b: Intercourse within ownership where the prohibition is temporary is prohibited due to an external reason rather than intrinsically, so accusing such a person still incurs ḥadd al-qadhf.

f: 603. What additional condition does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ place on permanent prohibitions?
b: The permanent prohibition must be established by consensus (ijmāʿ) or a well-known (mashhūr) ḥadīth, so that the prohibition is certain and free from legal doubt.

f: 604. What is the punishment for falsely accusing a muḥṣan (chaste) Muslim of explicit zinā in the Hanafi school?
b: If a free person falsely accuses a muḥṣan (free, sane, adult, Muslim, and chaste) man or woman of explicit zinā, and the accused demands the punishment, the accuser receives 80 lashes. If the accuser is a slave, he receives 40 lashes.

f: 605. What are the conditions of iḥṣān (legal chastity) required for the victim of qadhf?
b: The accused must be free, sane, adult, Muslim, and chaste from zinā.

f: 606. Why are freedom, adulthood, sanity, Islam, and chastity conditions for iḥṣān in qadhf?
b: Freedom is required because the Qur'an uses muḥṣan for free persons; children and the insane cannot legally commit zinā; Islam is required based on the hadith, "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not a muḥṣan"; chastity is required because the accusation only disgraces one who is chaste.

f: 607. Is the victim's demand required before the ḥadd of qadhf is carried out? Why?
b: Yes. The accused must demand it because qadhf contains a personal right whose purpose is to remove the disgrace suffered by the victim.

f: 608. How is the ḥadd of qadhf carried out?
b: The lashes are distributed across the body. The offender is not stripped, although heavy clothing such as fur garments and padded clothing is removed so the punishment is effective.

f: 609. Why is the offender not stripped for qadhf as he is in zinā?
b: Because the cause for qadhf is not established with the same level of certainty as zinā, so the punishment is carried out with less severity.

f: 610. When does denying someone's lineage become qadhf?
b: Saying, "You are not your father's son," is qadhf if it amounts to accusing the person's mother of zinā, provided she was a free Muslim woman.

f: 611. Why is denying someone's lineage treated as accusing the mother of zinā?
b: Because legitimate lineage is only denied on the basis of fornication, making the statement effectively an accusation against the mother.

f: 612. When does saying, "You are not the son of so-and-so," incur the ḥadd of qadhf?
b: If said in anger about the person's father, it is treated as an accusation of illegitimacy. If said calmly, it is understood as criticism rather than denial of lineage, so no ḥadd applies.

f: 613. Does saying, "You are not the son of your grandfather," incur the ḥadd?
b: No. It is literally true, and likewise attributing someone to his grandfather is permissible figuratively.

f: 614. Who may demand the punishment if someone says, "O son of an adulteress," after the mother has died?
b: The parent or child of the deceased may demand it, because the insult directly affects their lineage. This right is not inherited but exists because the disgrace reaches them.

f: 615. Who may demand qadhf on behalf of a deceased person according to the Hanafi school?
b: Only the parent or child whose own lineage is implicated by the accusation. Other heirs do not acquire this right merely through inheritance.

f: 616. Can a son who is a slave or non-Muslim demand qadhf for his muḥṣan father?
b: Yes. If the father was muḥṣan, even a slave or non-Muslim son may demand the punishment because the completed insult extends to the child.

f: 617. Can a son demand qadhf against his own father for accusing the son's mother? Can a slave demand it against his master?
b: No. A son cannot demand qadhf against his father, and a slave cannot demand it against his master, because a father is not punished on account of his child nor a master on account of his slave. However, another son from a different husband may demand it.

f: 618. What happens if the victim of qadhf dies before or during execution of the punishment?
b: The punishment is cancelled. If part of it has already been carried out, the remainder is not completed because, according to the Hanafis, the right is not inherited.

f: 619. Why does the Hanafi school regard the ḥadd of qadhf as non-inheritable?
b: Although qadhf contains both the right of Allah and the right of the individual, the Hanafi school considers the right of Allah predominant, so it is not inherited after the victim's death.

f: 620. What practical rulings follow from considering Allah's right predominant in qadhf?
b: The right is not inherited, pardon is generally ineffective, compensation cannot replace the punishment, multiple accusations may merge (tadākhul), and retracting a confession is not accepted.

f: 621. Is retraction accepted after confessing to qadhf?
b: No. Because another person's right is involved, retracting the confession does not remove the punishment.

f: 622. Do insults such as "O Nabataean," "You are not an Arab," or "O son of the water of the sky" constitute qadhf?
b: No. These expressions are understood as insults, comparisons, or figurative speech rather than accusations of zinā.

f: 623. Does attributing someone to his paternal uncle, maternal uncle, or mother's husband constitute qadhf?
b: No. Each of these may figuratively be called a father in Arabic and Islamic usage.

f: 624. If someone says, "You zanāʾta on the mountain," claiming he meant "You climbed the mountain," what is the ruling?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the ḥadd applies because the wording can also mean zinā and insulting context indicates that meaning. Muḥammad held that no ḥadd applies because the phrase literally refers to climbing.

f: 625. If two people exchange the accusation, "You are an adulterer," by saying, "No, rather you," what is the ruling?
b: Both receive the punishment for qadhf because each has accused the other of zinā.

f: 626. What happens if a husband accuses his wife of zinā and she replies, "No, rather you"?
b: The wife receives the ḥadd for qadhf first, and liʿān is no longer performed, because someone punished for qadhf is not eligible for liʿān.

f: 627. If the wife replies to her husband's accusation by saying, "I committed zinā with you," what is the ruling?
b: Neither qadhf nor liʿān is carried out because the statement is open to multiple interpretations, creating legal doubt.

f: 628. What happens if a man first acknowledges a child as his, then later denies him?
b: The child's lineage remains established, but the father must perform liʿān, since denying the child amounts to accusing the mother.

f: 629. What happens if a man first denies a child, then later acknowledges him?
b: The child is still considered his, but the father receives the ḥadd of qadhf, because his later acknowledgment invalidates the basis for liʿān.

f: 630. If a husband says of a child, "He is neither my son nor your son," does qadhf or liʿān apply?
b: No. He is denying the birth itself rather than accusing the mother of zinā.

f: 631. When does accusing a woman not incur the ḥadd of qadhf because iḥṣān is absent?
b: No ḥadd applies if she has children with no known father, or if she underwent liʿān regarding a child (whether the child is alive or deceased), because these circumstances indicate possible zinā and thus negate iḥṣān.

f: 632. If a woman underwent liʿān without any child being involved, does accusing her incur qadhf?
b: Yes. Without a child there is no indication of zinā, so her iḥṣān remains intact.

f: 633. What principle determines whether accusing someone of unlawful intercourse constitutes qadhf?
b: If the intercourse was intrinsically unlawful (ḥarām li-ʿaynihi), then accusing the person is truthful and no qadhf applies. If it was only prohibited due to an external or temporary reason (li-ghayrihi), qadhf still applies because the act is not legally zinā.

f: 634. Give examples where accusing someone does not incur qadhf because the intercourse counts as zinā.
b: Examples include intercourse with a jointly-owned slave woman, intercourse committed by a woman while still a Christian, and intercourse with a slave woman who is also one's foster sister (according to the preferred Hanafi view).

f: 635. Give examples where accusing someone does incur qadhf because the intercourse is not legally zinā.
b: Examples include intercourse with one's Magian slave woman, one's menstruating wife, or one's mukātabah, since ownership remains and the prohibition is only temporary.

f: 636. What is the ruling on accusing a mukātab who dies leaving enough wealth to complete his emancipation?
b: The accuser is not punished because there is legal doubt regarding whether the mukātab had become free.

f: 637. What is the Hanafi ruling on accusing a Magian who married his mother before embracing Islam?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the accuser is punished because the marriage is treated as legally valid among Magians. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, no punishment applies.

f: 638. Is a ḥarbī under amān (safe-conduct) punished for falsely accusing a Muslim of zinā? Why?
b: Yes. Because qadhf primarily protects the rights of individuals, and by accepting amān he undertakes to respect the rights of those living under Muslim protection.

f: 639. What is the Hanafi ruling on the testimony of a Muslim who has received the ḥadd for qadhf (false accusation)?
b: His testimony is permanently rejected, even if he later repents. (Al-Shāfiʿī accepts his testimony after sincere repentance.)

f: 640. What is the ruling on the testimony of a non-Muslim who receives the ḥadd for qadhf?
b: His testimony is no longer accepted against members of his own religious community (Ahl al-Dhimmah), since rejection of testimony forms part of completing his punishment.

f: 641. What happens if a non-Muslim who was punished for qadhf later embraces Islam?
b: His testimony is accepted against both Muslims and non-Muslims, because his legal capacity to testify as a Muslim is a new qualification acquired after Islam and is not affected by the earlier punishment.

f: 642. Why does a former non-Muslim regain the ability to testify after embracing Islam, while a slave punished for qadhf does not after emancipation?
b: The former acquires a new legal capacity to testify after embracing Islam. By contrast, a slave had no legal capacity to testify while enslaved, so rejection of his testimony continues after emancipation as part of completing the punishment.

f: 643. If a non-Muslim receives part of the lashes for qadhf, then embraces Islam and completes the remaining lashes as a Muslim, is his testimony accepted?
b: Yes. According to the preferred Hanafi opinion, rejection of testimony is an attribute completing the punishment, and since the punishment was completed after Islam, his testimony is accepted. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that it remains rejected.

f: 644. Do multiple acts of the same ḥadd offence require multiple punishments?
b: No. If someone repeatedly commits the same offence (such as repeated qadhf, repeated zinā, or repeated drinking) before being punished, one ḥadd suffices for all.

f: 645. Why do repeated acts of the same offence merge into one ḥadd in the Hanafi school?
b: Because the purpose of the ḥadd is deterrence, and one punishment may achieve that objective. This creates sufficient doubt to prevent imposing multiple identical ḥudūd.

f: 646. Do different categories of ḥadd offences merge into one punishment?
b: No. If someone commits different offences (e.g., zinā, qadhf, theft, and drinking), each offence has its own distinct legal purpose, so each receives its own prescribed punishment.

f: 647. Why does the Hanafi school allow multiple qadhf offences to merge into one punishment?
b: Because the Hanafi school regards the right of Allah as predominant in qadhf, making it analogous to zinā and drinking, where repeated offences merge into one ḥadd before execution.

f: 648. How does al-Shāfiʿī differ regarding repeated acts of qadhf?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī treats the individual's right as predominant. Therefore, if either the person slandered or the specific accusation differs, the punishments do not merge and separate ḥudūd are required.

f: 649. When is taʿzīr imposed instead of the ḥadd for slander (qadhf)?
b: Taʿzīr is imposed when someone falsely accuses of zinā a person who is not legally muḥṣan, such as a male slave, female slave, umm walad, or a non-Muslim, because the condition of iḥṣān required for the ḥadd is absent.

f: 650. What types of non-zinā insults require taʿzīr?
b: Insulting a Muslim with expressions such as "O sinner," "O unbeliever," "O vile one," or "O thief" incurs taʿzīr because they cause harm and disgrace, even though they do not amount to qadhf.

f: 651. Why is taʿzīr imposed for insults other than qadhf?
b: Because the insult causes harm and dishonor, while no prescribed ḥadd exists for such speech. Since ḥudūd are not established by analogy, the offence is punished with taʿzīr.

f: 652. How does the amount of taʿzīr differ between false accusations against non-muḥṣans and ordinary insults?
b: False accusations of zinā against someone lacking iḥṣān receive the maximum taʿzīr, since they resemble an offence that normally carries a ḥadd. Ordinary insults are left to the Imām's discretion.

f: 653. Is taʿzīr imposed for calling someone "O donkey" or "O pig"?
b: The basic Hanafi ruling is no, because everyone knows the statement is literally false and therefore not inherently disgraceful. However, later jurists held that custom (ʿurf) may justify taʿzīr if such insults are considered degrading.

f: 654. How does social custom affect taʿzīr for insults like "O donkey" or "O pig"?
b: Some later jurists held that if such expressions are regarded as insulting in a particular society, taʿzīr should be imposed. A preferred view further distinguishes that taʿzīr is especially appropriate when the insult is directed at people of high standing, such as scholars or descendants of the Prophet ﷺ.

f: 655. What are the Hanafi limits for the number of lashes in taʿzīr?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, the minimum is 3 lashes and the maximum is 39 lashes.

f: 656. Why is the Hanafi maximum for taʿzīr set at 39 lashes?
b: Because of the hadith: "Whoever reaches a prescribed punishment in a case that is not subject to a prescribed punishment is among the transgressors." Since the lowest ḥadd is 40 lashes (for a slave in qadhf), taʿzīr must remain below it, making the maximum 39 lashes.

f: 657. How did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ differ regarding the maximum taʿzīr?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ based the limit on the lowest ḥadd for free persons, allowing taʿzīr up to 75 lashes. One narration deducts one lash by analogy, while another deducts five lashes, following a report from ʿAlī (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu).

f: 658. What is the minimum number of lashes in taʿzīr according to the author of al-Hidāyah, and what did later Hanafi scholars say?
b: The author states the minimum is 3 lashes, because fewer would not achieve deterrence. However, later Hanafi scholars held that there is no fixed minimum; rather, the Imām determines the number that best achieves deterrence, since people differ.

f: 659. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, how should the amount of taʿzīr be determined?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ narrated that it should correspond to the seriousness of the offence. Another narration from him says each offence should be brought close to the ḥadd of the most similar prescribed offence (e.g., unlawful touching close to zinā, lesser slander close to qadhf).

f: 660. May the Imām combine imprisonment with flogging in taʿzīr?
b: Yes. Since imprisonment is itself a valid form of taʿzīr, it may be imposed alone or combined with flogging whenever the Imām considers it beneficial.

f: 661. Why is imprisonment permitted in taʿzīr even before an offence is fully proven?
b: Because imprisonment is a discretionary punishment, not a prescribed ḥadd. Therefore, it may be used even on the basis of strong suspicion, unlike the ḥudūd, which require strict proof.

f: 662. Which type of flogging is carried out most severely in the Hanafi school?
b: Taʿzīr flogging is the most severe in its manner of execution. Since leniency has already been shown by reducing the number of lashes below the ḥudūd, no further leniency is shown in how the blows are delivered.

f: 663. How does the manner of taʿzīr flogging differ from the flogging of the ḥudūd?
b: In taʿzīr, the blows are not given additional leniency, such as distributing them over different limbs, because doing so would weaken the deterrent purpose after the number of lashes has already been reduced.

f: 664. What is the Hanafi order of severity among the three major flogging punishments (ḥudūd), and why?
b: The order is: (1) Zinā, because it is established directly by the Qur'an and is the gravest offence (even allowing stoning for the muḥṣan); (2) Drinking intoxicants, because its cause is established with certainty; (3) Qadhf (false accusation), because its cause is only probable (the accuser may actually be truthful), and its severity is already increased through the rejection of the offender's testimony.

f: 665. If a person dies while the Imām lawfully carries out a prescribed punishment (ḥadd) or discretionary punishment (taʿzīr), is anyone financially liable according to the Hanafi school?
b: No. If the punishment was lawfully carried out by the Imām and the offender dies, no blood-money (diyah) is due, because the Imām was carrying out the command of the Sharīʿah.

f: 666. Why is no liability incurred when someone dies during a lawfully administered ḥadd or taʿzīr?
b: Because the Imām acts by the command of Allah. One carrying out a divinely prescribed punishment is not required to guarantee the person's survival, just as a cupper or one performing bloodletting is not liable if death unexpectedly results.

f: 667. Why is the Imām not compared to a husband disciplining his wife in cases of liability?
b: A husband's authority is general and unrestricted, so it is conditioned upon causing no harm. The Imām, however, acts under a specific command of the Sharīʿah, so his lawful execution of a punishment is not subject to that condition.

f: 668. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion if someone dies during the lawful execution of a punishment, and how did the Hanafis respond?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī held that the diyah is paid from the public treasury, treating the death as accidental during a lawful public duty. The Hanafis replied that since the Imām is executing Allah's right by His command, the death is legally attributed to that divine command, so no compensation is due.

f: 1. What is the linguistic meaning of theft (sariqah), and how does the Sharīʿah define it?
b: Linguistically, theft (sariqah) means secretly and stealthily taking another person's property. The Sharīʿah retains this basic meaning but adds further legal conditions, such as a minimum value, removal from a secure place, absence of ownership doubt, and other requirements before the prescribed punishment applies.

f: 2. How is the linguistic meaning of theft reflected in both ordinary theft and highway robbery?
b: In ordinary theft, the property is secretly taken from the owner's (or his representative's) notice. In highway robbery, the theft is considered, in a sense, hidden from the sight of the Imām, who is responsible for protecting the roads through his officials.

f: 3. What are the conditions for the amputation penalty for theft according to the Hanafi school?
b: Amputation becomes obligatory when a sane, adult person steals ten coined dirhams or property worth ten coined dirhams from a secure place (ḥirz), while no legal doubt (shubhah) regarding ownership exists.

f: 4. Why are sanity and adulthood conditions for the punishment of theft?
b: Because criminal liability (taklīf) only exists for a sane adult, and amputation is the legal consequence of that criminal responsibility.

f: 5. Why does the Hanafi school require a minimum value before amputation is imposed?
b: Because insignificant items are generally not strongly desired, are less likely to be secretly stolen, and do not fully realize the wisdom of deterrence. The prescribed punishment is therefore limited to thefts of significant value.

f: 6. What is the minimum value for theft requiring amputation according to the Hanafi, Shāfiʿī, and Mālikī schools?
b: Hanafis: ten coined dirhams (or equivalent value). Al-Shāfiʿī: one-quarter of a dīnār. Mālik: three dirhams.

f: 7. Why do the Hanafis adopt ten dirhams rather than the lower thresholds mentioned by other schools?
b: Because greater caution is required in applying prescribed punishments (ḥudūd). A higher threshold avoids imposing amputation where doubt exists regarding whether the theft is sufficiently serious. The Hanafis also rely on the hadith: "There is no amputation except for a dīnār or ten dirhams."

f: 8. Why do the Hanafis specify "ten coined dirhams" rather than simply "ten dirhams"?
b: Because, by customary usage, the term dirhams refers to coined currency, making coined dirhams the standard mentioned in the apparent narration (ẓāhir al-riwāyah), which is regarded as the sounder opinion.

f: 9. What is theft (sariqah) linguistically and legally according to al-Hidāyah?
b: Linguistically, theft means secretly taking another person's property. The Sharīʿah adds further conditions beyond the linguistic meaning, including minimum value, secure custody, and absence of legal doubt.

f: 10. How does al-Hidāyah explain the difference between ordinary theft and highway robbery?
b: Ordinary theft is committed secretly from the owner or his representative, whereas highway robbery is regarded as theft from the authority of the Imām, who is responsible for protecting public roads.

f: 11. What conditions must exist before the hadd of amputation becomes obligatory for theft?
b: The thief must be a sane adult, steal at least ten coined dirhams (or property worth that amount), take it from secure custody (ḥirz), and there must be no legal doubt (shubhah) regarding ownership.

f: 12. Why are sanity and adulthood conditions for the hadd of theft?
b: Because criminal liability only exists for legally accountable persons, and amputation is the legal consequence of that liability.

f: 13. Why does the Ḥanafī school require a minimum of ten dirhams for amputation?
b: Because a higher threshold provides greater caution in avoiding wrongful implementation of the hadd, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no amputation except for a dīnār or ten dirhams."

f: 14. What are the opinions of the four schools regarding the minimum value for theft?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ: ten dirhams; Mālik: three dirhams; al-Shāfiʿī: one-quarter of a dīnār.

f: 15. Why does the Ḥanafī school prefer the higher minimum value despite reports mentioning a shield worth three dirhams?
b: Because hudūd are averted by doubt, so adopting the higher threshold is considered safer and more cautious in applying the prescribed punishment.

f: 16. Must the stolen dirhams be coined for the hadd to apply?
b: Yes. The apparent and preferred Ḥanafī narration requires coined currency, since the Prophet's ﷺ wording refers to coined dirhams.

f: 17. What if someone steals ten uncoined pieces of silver worth less than ten coined dirhams?
b: Amputation is not obligatory because the required monetary value has not been reached.

f: 18. How is the value of stolen property other than silver determined?
b: All other property—including gold—is valued according to the equivalent value of ten dirhams.

f: 19. Why must the stolen property come from secure custody (ḥirz) and without legal doubt?
b: Because legal doubt prevents implementation of the prescribed punishment, and secure custody is one of the conditions that completes the legal definition of theft.

f: 20. Are slaves and free persons treated differently regarding amputation for theft?
b: No. Both receive amputation if all conditions are fulfilled, since the Qur'an makes no distinction and the punishment cannot be halved.

f: 21. How is theft established through confession according to the three Ḥanafī Imāms?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad require only one confession. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ requires two confessions, and according to one narration they must occur in separate sittings.

f: 22. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad accept a single confession for theft?
b: Because a single confession fully establishes the offense, just as in qiṣāṣ and qadhf, and repeating it adds no further certainty.

f: 23. Why does Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ require repeated confessions for theft?
b: He analogizes confession to testimony, arguing that just as multiple witnesses are required in some hudūd, repeated confession should likewise strengthen the proof.

f: 24. Why is repeated confession for zinā not used as evidence for requiring repeated confession in theft?
b: Because the requirement for repeated confession in zinā is an exceptional ruling established by revelation and is therefore not extended to other offenses by analogy.

f: 25. Does retracting a confession affect the property rights arising from theft?
b: No. Retraction is ineffective regarding the owner's financial rights because the owner denies the retraction; only the hadd aspect may be affected.

f: 26. How is theft established through witness testimony?
b: By the testimony of two qualified witnesses.

f: 27. What precautions should the judge take before ordering amputation based on testimony?
b: He should question the witnesses about the exact manner, nature, time, and place of the theft, investigate their reliability, and detain the accused during that investigation.

f: 28. How is the hadd applied when several people jointly commit theft?
b: If each person's individual share reaches ten dirhams, each has his hand amputated. If each share is less than ten dirhams, no amputation is carried out.

f: 29. Why must each participant individually steal the full niṣāb for amputation?
b: Because each person's liability is based upon his own offense, so the complete minimum value must exist with respect to each individual separately.

f: 30. Which items do not incur the ḥadd of amputation because they are considered insignificant or commonly available in Dār al-Islām according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Things originally available for common use, such as wood, grass, reeds, fish, birds (including chickens, ducks, and pigeons), game animals, arsenic, red ochre, and lime. These are considered of lesser legal significance because they are naturally abundant, imperfectly protected, retain traces of common ownership, or are not normally the subject of secure storage.

f: 31. Why is there no amputation for stealing naturally abundant items like wood, birds, or fish?
b: Several reasons combine: (1) they are generally regarded as insignificant; (2) people are less likely to steal them secretly; (3) their protection (ḥirz) is often incomplete (e.g., wood left outside, birds can fly away); and (4) they retain a trace of original common ownership, creating legal doubt (shubhah), which prevents the ḥadd.

f: 32. What evidence do the Ḥanafīs cite for exempting such items from amputation?
b: They rely on the report of ʿĀʾishah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhā): "During the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the hand was not amputated for something insignificant." They also cite the general ḥadīth: "There is no amputation for stealing birds."

f: 33. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and al-Shāfiʿī regarding these commonly available items?
b: They held that amputation applies to all property of value, with Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ excepting only clay, earth, and manure, unlike the main Ḥanafī position.

f: 34. Which perishable items do not incur amputation when stolen?
b: Milk, meat, fresh fruit, prepared food, and other foods that spoil quickly do not incur the ḥadd because of their perishable nature.

f: 35. What textual evidence supports exempting perishable foods from amputation?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no amputation for dates or for kathar," and "There is no amputation for food." The Ḥanafīs interpret "food" here as food that spoils quickly.

f: 36. Why don't the Ḥanafīs interpret the ḥadīth "There is no amputation for food" as including all food?
b: Because there is consensus (ijmāʿ) that stealing durable foods such as wheat and sugar does incur amputation when the other conditions are met. Therefore, the ḥadīth is understood to refer only to perishable foods.

f: 37. How do the Ḥanafīs answer al-Shāfiʿī's proof that the Prophet ﷺ allowed amputation for fruit once it reached the drying area (jarīn)?
b: They explain that the ḥadīth refers to fruit after it has been dried and stored, since that is the customary use of a drying area. Thus, the ruling concerns preserved fruit, not fresh, perishable fruit.

f: 38. Which types of property do not incur the ḥadd of amputation because they are considered insignificant or commonly available?
b: There is no amputation for stealing items regarded as insignificant and freely available in Dār al-Islām, such as wood, grass, reeds, fish, birds, game, arsenic, red ochre, and lime. These are originally common resources, attract little desire, often lack complete secure storage (ḥirz), and retain traces of common ownership, creating legal doubt (shubhah), which prevents the ḥadd.

f: 39. Why is there no amputation for stealing birds or game animals?
b: Birds and game are excluded because they can easily escape, their protection is incomplete, and there is a specific ḥadīth stating: "There is no amputation for stealing birds."

f: 40. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding stealing commonly available property?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ (and al-Shāfiʿī) held that amputation applies to every kind of valuable property except things like clay, earth, and manure, whereas the Ḥanafī school exempts naturally common and insignificant items.

f: 41. Which perishable goods do not incur amputation if stolen, and why?
b: There is no amputation for quickly perishable items such as milk, meat, and fresh fruit. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no amputation for dates or for kathar," and "There is no amputation for food." The Ḥanafīs interpret this as referring to foods that spoil quickly. However, durable foods like wheat and sugar are not included in this exemption.

f: 42. Does amputation apply to stealing fruit still on the tree or unharvested crops?
b: No. Fruit on trees and crops before harvest are not yet in secure storage (ḥirz), so the ḥadd does not apply.

f: 43. Why is there no amputation for stealing intoxicating beverages?
b: Because the thief may claim he intended to destroy them, and some intoxicants are not legally recognized as property while others are disputed in that regard. This legal doubt prevents the ḥadd.

f: 44. Why is there no amputation for stealing a musical instrument such as a ṭunbūr?
b: Because the thief may claim he intended to destroy it as an act of forbidding evil, creating legal doubt that prevents the prescribed punishment.

f: 45. Why does the Ḥanafī school not impose amputation for stealing a muṣḥaf, even if it is ornamented?
b: The thief may claim he intended to read or benefit from it rather than steal it. The Qur'ānic text itself is not treated as property in this context, and the ornamentation and binding are merely accessories to what is primarily protected—the Qur'ān. Therefore the ḥadd is not imposed.

f: 46. What were the opinions of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding stealing an ornamented muṣḥaf?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī held that amputation applies because it is valuable property whose sale is lawful. One narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ agrees, while another says amputation applies if the ornamentation alone reaches the niṣāb. The apparent Ḥanafī position rejects amputation.

f: 47. Why is there no amputation for stealing mosque doors or property kept inside a mosque?
b: Mosque doors are not regarded as secure storage (ḥirz), since they do not primarily protect property. Consequently, property kept inside a mosque likewise does not receive the level of protection required for the ḥadd.

f: 48. Why is there no amputation for stealing a gold cross, chessboard, or backgammon set?
b: Because the thief may claim he intended to destroy objects associated with prohibited use or false worship, creating legal doubt that prevents the prescribed punishment.

f: 49. How did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguish between different locations of a cross?
b: If the cross is kept in a place of worship, there is no amputation because its secure storage is deficient. If it is stored elsewhere with complete protection, amputation applies because both its value and secure storage are complete.

f: 50. Why is stealing a coin bearing an image treated differently from stealing a cross?
b: A coin bearing an image is not made for worship, so there is no justification for claiming it was taken to destroy an object of false worship. Therefore, the legal doubt that exists with a cross does not arise.

f: 51. For which types of property is amputation not imposed because they are considered insignificant, commonly available, or insufficiently protected?
b: There is no amputation for stealing things commonly available in the Abode of Islam, such as wood, grass, reeds, fish (fresh or salted), birds (including chickens, ducks, and pigeons), game, arsenic, red ochre, and lime. These are originally common resources, are not highly desired, often lack proper secure storage (ḥirz), and retain traces of common ownership, creating legal doubt (shubhah).

f: 52. Why does the Ḥanafī school not require amputation for stealing these naturally available items, unlike Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and al-Shāfiʿī?
b: Because such items are generally of little importance, are imperfectly protected, and retain traces of common ownership, all of which create legal doubt preventing the ḥadd. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and al-Shāfiʿī generally require amputation for all valuable property except a few items like clay and manure.

f: 53. Which perishable items do not incur amputation if stolen, and what is the reasoning?
b: There is no amputation for milk, meat, fresh fruits, dates, palm hearts (kathar/jummār), and other food that spoils quickly. The Prophet ﷺ exempted such items, and the jurists understood this to refer to perishable food. However, durable foods such as wheat and sugar are excluded from this exemption because of scholarly consensus.

f: 54. Does amputation apply to stealing fruit from trees or standing crops?
b: No. Fruit still on the tree and crops not yet harvested are not considered to be in secure storage (ḥirz), so amputation does not apply.

f: 55. Why is there no amputation for stealing intoxicating beverages?
b: Because the thief may claim he intended to destroy them, and because some intoxicants are not legally recognized as property while others are disputed in that regard. This legal doubt prevents the ḥadd.

f: 56. Which religious or recreational objects are exempt from amputation if stolen, and why?
b: There is no amputation for stealing musical instruments (such as a ṭunbūr), a muṣḥaf, mosque doors, crosses of gold, chessboards, or backgammon sets. The thief may claim he intended to remove or destroy objects of wrongdoing, or the items are not regarded as protected property in the relevant legal sense.

f: 57. Why is there no amputation for stealing a muṣḥaf, even if it is decorated with valuable ornamentation?
b: The muṣḥaf is preserved primarily because of the Qur'anic writing, which is not treated as property. The ornamentation and binding are merely accessories, and the thief may also claim he intended to read from it. Therefore legal doubt prevents amputation. One narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ differs if the ornamentation alone reaches the niṣāb.

f: 58. Why is there no amputation for stealing mosque doors or property kept inside a mosque?
b: Because mosque doors are not regarded as secure storage (ḥirz). Since the mosque itself is not a protected place for storing property in this legal sense, theft from it does not incur amputation.

f: 59. Why is there no amputation for stealing a free child, even if the child wears valuable jewelry?
b: A free child is not property, and the jewelry is legally subordinate to the child. The thief may also claim he merely intended to care for or return the child. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ disagreed if the jewelry alone reached the niṣāb.

f: 60. What is the ruling on stealing slaves of different ages?
b: Stealing an adult slave does not incur amputation because it resembles usurpation or deception rather than theft. Stealing a young slave who can express himself does incur amputation because true theft is realized. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held by istiḥsān that even a very young slave does not incur amputation due to his human status.

f: 61. Which written materials incur amputation if stolen, and which do not?
b: Ordinary books, registers, and notebooks do not incur amputation because the intended object is the writing, which is not property. Account books are an exception because the paper itself is ordinarily the valuable object sought.

f: 62. What is the ruling on stealing animals such as dogs or hunting leopards?
b: There is no amputation for stealing dogs or hunting leopards because such animals were originally common, their legal financial value is disputed, and this disagreement creates legal doubt.

f: 63. Which musical instruments are specifically exempt from amputation?
b: There is no amputation for stealing a tambourine (duff), drum (ṭabl), lute (barbaṭ), or flute (mizmar). According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad they lack legal financial value, while Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasons that the thief may claim he intended to destroy them.

f: 64. Which valuable materials definitely incur amputation if stolen?
b: Amputation applies for stealing valuable woods such as teak, bamboo cane, ebony, and sandalwood because they are prized property kept in secure storage and are not naturally available in the Abode of Islam.

f: 65. What precious stones incur amputation if stolen?
b: Stealing emeralds, rubies, and chrysolite (zabarjad) incurs amputation because they are among the most valuable forms of wealth and are treated like gold and silver with respect to theft.

f: 66. Which items made from wood require amputation if stolen, and which do not?
b: Amputation applies for stealing manufactured wooden items (such as utensils and doors) because craftsmanship gives them significant value and they are kept in secure storage. It does not apply to ordinary mats because the raw material predominates and they are often left unsecured. However, finely crafted Baghdad mats are an exception, since their workmanship predominates, making them valuable enough for amputation.

f: 67. What conditions apply before amputation is imposed for stealing large manufactured items?
b: The ruling applies only to non-composite items and only if the object is light enough for one person to carry. If it is so heavy that one person normally cannot carry it, amputation is not imposed because such items are generally not the target of thieves.

f: 68. Is amputation imposed for breach of trust, open snatching, or quick seizure? Why?
b: No. There is no amputation for a trustee who betrays a trust (khāʾin), one who openly snatches property (muntahib), or one who steals by quick seizure (mukhtalis). These acts lack the element of secret theft from secure custody required for the ḥadd. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no amputation for the one who snatches openly, the one who seizes stealthily by quick snatching, or the one who betrays a trust."

f: 69. What is the ruling on the grave robber (nabbāsh), and why do the jurists differ?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad: No amputation. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and al-Shāfiʿī: Amputation applies. The latter argue that the burial shroud is valuable property kept in secure storage and cite the report: "Whoever robs graves, we amputate his hand." Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad reply that the Prophet ﷺ also said: "There is no amputation for the hidden thief," understood in the Madinan dialect to refer to the grave robber. They further argue that ownership of the shroud is legally doubtful (the deceased no longer owns it fully, while the heirs' ownership is not yet complete) and that the rarity of the crime weakens the rationale for deterrence. They interpret the contrary report either as weak or as referring to discretionary state punishment (siyāsah), not the prescribed ḥadd.

f: 70. Does the ruling on grave robbery change if the grave is inside a locked house or if the deceased is in a coffin during travel?
b: No. According to the preferred opinion, the same juristic disagreement remains whether the grave is inside a locked house or the deceased is in a coffin in a caravan, because the underlying legal reasoning regarding ownership and the nature of the offense remains unchanged.

f: 71. Who is exempt from amputation because of a share in the property or a personal entitlement to it?
b: Amputation is not carried out for someone who steals from the public treasury (Bayt al-Māl), steals property in which he himself has a share, or takes an equal amount of dirhams from someone who owes him that amount. This is because he has an ownership interest or is taking his own right. The same applies whether the debt is due immediately or deferred (istiḥsān).

f: 72. If a creditor steals more dirhams than he is owed, is amputation carried out?
b: No. Since he is considered a partner in the property to the extent of his own debt, the resulting legal doubt prevents the prescribed punishment.

f: 73. If a creditor steals merchandise instead of money from his debtor, is amputation carried out?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, yes, because he has no right to satisfy his debt by taking merchandise without mutual agreement. Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that no amputation applies, citing opinions allowing such taking as payment or security. However, the Ḥanafīs only accept this as a legal doubt if the thief actually bases his defense on that scholarly opinion. One opinion also states that if the debt is in dirhams but he steals dīnārs, amputation applies, while another treats all coined currency as one category and does not impose amputation.

f: 74. If someone steals an item, returns it, then later steals the very same item again, is amputation carried out?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, no. The first theft and its consequences create a legal doubt concerning that specific item, since it is the same object and owner. Although analogy—and one narration from Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and al-Shāfiʿī—would require amputation because the second theft is complete in itself, the Ḥanafīs hold that the earlier amputation removed the item's legal inviolability with respect to that thief, and the resulting doubt prevents a second amputation. This differs from a case where ownership changed in between (e.g., through sale and repurchase), because then the legal relationship to the item has changed. The jurists also note that repeating theft after already enduring amputation is rare, reducing the need for deterrence.

f: 75. When is amputation not imposed for theft because of family relationships?
b: There is no amputation if a person steals from his parents, children, or any unmarriageable blood relative (dhū raḥim maḥram), because close relatives have customary access to one another's homes and property, creating legal doubt (shubhah).

f: 76. Why are parents/children and other maḥram relatives exempt from amputation for theft?
b: Parents and children: because of unrestricted access to each other's property and homes. Other blood maḥram relatives: because of unrestricted access to the place of secure custody (ḥirz), even if not to the property itself.

f: 77. Does al-Shāfiʿī agree that stealing from other maḥram relatives prevents amputation?
b: No. Al-Shāfiʿī treated them like more distant relatives and did not exempt them on this basis.

f: 78. Does friendship prevent the hadd of theft?
b: No. Friendship creates no legal doubt, since stealing from a friend is itself evidence that the friendship has effectively been abandoned.

f: 79. What is the ruling if someone steals another person's property from the house of his own maḥram relative?
b: No amputation, because the legal doubt relates to entering that place of custody (ḥirz), to which he has customary access.

f: 80. What if someone steals his maḥram relative's property from someone else's house?
b: Amputation applies, because the legal doubt regarding entry into the place of custody no longer exists.

f: 81. Does stealing from a foster mother (through breastfeeding) prevent amputation?
b: According to the apparent (ẓāhir al-riwāyah) Hanafi position, no—amputation applies, because foster relationships do not receive the same legal treatment as blood relationships.

f: 82. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding theft from a foster mother?
b: He held that amputation does not apply, since a person commonly enters his foster mother's house without formal permission, creating a similar customary access.

f: 83. Why does the relied-upon Hanafi view distinguish foster relatives from blood relatives?
b: Because there is no blood relationship, and foster relationships are often not widely known. Therefore, unrestricted access (basūṭah) is not legally recognized in the same way, so no legal doubt prevents the hadd.

f: 84. Are foster sisters treated like blood sisters regarding theft?
b: No. The apparent Hanafi view does not equate foster relationships with blood relationships for this ruling, even though both create unmarriageability.

f: 85. Does stealing from one's spouse invalidate the hadd of theft? What about a slave stealing from his master or from his master's wife?
b: No amputation is carried out if one spouse steals from the other, or if a slave steals from his master, his master's wife, or the husband of his mistress. This is because there is normally permission to enter and access property in these relationships, creating legal doubt (shubhah).

f: 86. If spouses do not share the same house or storage area, does amputation apply if one spouse steals from the other?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, no amputation applies, even if the stolen property was kept in a separate place of custody. This is because spouses are assumed to have unrestricted access to one another's property. Al-Shāfiʿī disagreed and treated such property as protected.

f: 87. Why is there no amputation if a master steals from his mukātab slave?
b: Because the master still has a legal right connected to the mukātab's earnings, creating doubt regarding complete ownership of the stolen property.

f: 88. Why is there no amputation for stealing from war booty (ghanīmah)?
b: Because the person stealing from the war booty has a share in it. This ruling is reported from ʿAlī (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ) both as a precaution against applying the hadd and as the legal reasoning behind the ruling.

f: 89. What are the two types of secure custody (ḥirz) required for the hadd of theft?
b: Secure custody is of two types: (1) custody by place, such as houses, shops, storage areas, and chests; and (2) custody by guardian, such as a person protecting his property while carrying it or sitting beside it.

f: 90. Why is secure custody (ḥirz) required before the hadd of theft can be applied?
b: Because theft requires secretly taking protected property. Without secure custody, the essential element of theft and the reason for deterrence are incomplete.

f: 91. What is an example of property protected by a guardian rather than by a place?
b: A person sitting in a mosque or on the road with his belongings beside him has protected them through his guardianship. The Prophet ﷺ amputated the hand of the person who stole Ṣafwān's cloak from beneath his head while he was sleeping in the mosque.

f: 92. If property is stored in a building, is a guardian required for the hadd of theft to apply?
b: No. According to the correct Hanafi position, custody by the place itself is sufficient. A guardian is not required, even if the house has no door or the door is left open, because the building itself exists for protecting property.

f: 93. When does amputation become obligatory for stealing property from a house or building?
b: Amputation only becomes obligatory after the thief removes the property from the building. While the property remains inside, the owner's possession is still considered present, so the theft is not yet complete.

f: 94. Why is theft from a house different from theft from property guarded by a person?
b: In a house, the owner's possession continues until the thief removes the item outside. In the case of a guardian, the owner's possession ends immediately when the thief takes the property, completing the theft.

f: 95. Does the hadd of theft require the guardian to be awake?
b: No. A sleeping person still counts as a guardian if the property is beneath him or beside him, because people normally consider him to be guarding it.

f: 96. Is a depositary (mūdaʿ) or borrower (mustaʿīr) responsible if entrusted property is stolen while beside them?
b: No, provided they were not negligent. Since a person sleeping beside property is still considered a guardian, the loss is not attributed to negligence.

f: 97. What is the difference between custody by place and custody by guardian regarding completion of theft?
b: With custody by place, the theft is only complete when the item is removed from that protected place. With custody by guardian, the theft is complete as soon as the thief takes possession of the item away from the guardian.

f: 98. If someone steals property whose owner is present guarding it, is amputation applied even if the property itself is not in a secure place?
b: Yes. Amputation applies because the property is protected through one of the two forms of secure custody (ḥirz): either the place itself or the personal guardianship of the owner.

f: 99. Why is there no amputation for stealing from a bathhouse, public building, merchants' shops, or inns?
b: Because these places have general permission of entry, either by custom or explicit permission, which weakens the secure custody (ḥirz).

f: 100. Does stealing from a bathhouse or public building at night require amputation?
b: Yes. At night, these places are considered secure custody because they are constructed for protecting property, while the permission to enter is normally limited to daytime.

f: 101. If someone steals property from a mosque while the owner is present with it, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. The mosque itself is not a place of secure custody for property because it was not built for safeguarding possessions. However, the owner's presence creates personal guardianship (ḥirz by guardian), so amputation applies.

f: 102. Why does theft from a mosque differ from theft from a bathhouse or similar public building?
b: A mosque is not considered a place built for protecting property, so only personal guardianship can provide ḥirz. A bathhouse or similar building is designed for safeguarding property, so the place itself provides ḥirz.

f: 103. Is amputation applied if a guest steals from his host?
b: No. A guest has permission to enter the house and is treated like part of the household, so the house is not considered secure custody against him. His act is treated as betrayal of trust (khiyānah), not technical theft.

f: 104. Why is amputation not applied if a thief takes property inside a house but does not remove it from the house?
b: Because the entire house is considered one place of secure custody. The owner's possession legally continues over everything inside the house, creating doubt as to whether the theft has been completed.

f: 105. If a house has separate rooms and a thief moves property from one room into the courtyard, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. Each separate room is considered its own secure custody with respect to its occupant. Removing the property from that room completes the theft.

f: 106. If a resident steals from another resident's separate room in the same house, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. Since each room functions as a separate place of custody for its occupant, the thief has removed property from another person's secure custody.

f: 107. If one thief enters a house, takes property, and gives it to an accomplice outside the house, are either of them subject to amputation?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, neither is subject to amputation. The person inside did not personally remove the property from the secure place, because another legally recognized hand took possession of it. The person outside did not violate the secure custody, so the theft is incomplete with respect to both individually.

f: 108. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding a thief inside a house handing stolen property to someone outside?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ distinguished between two cases: if the person inside extends his hand outside and gives the property to the outside person, the person inside is subject to amputation. If the outside person reaches inside and takes the property from the inside person's hand, then both are subject to amputation.

f: 109. If a thief throws stolen property outside a house, then leaves and later picks it up, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, amputation applies because throwing the property outside is considered part of the theft when done as a common strategy to escape with the property. Since no legally recognized hand took possession in between, the actions are treated as one continuous act.

f: 110. Why did Zufar disagree regarding a thief who throws stolen property outside and later retrieves it?
b: Zufar held that no amputation applies because throwing the property outside alone does not require amputation, and picking it up from the street alone would also not require amputation. Therefore, he viewed the two acts separately.

f: 111. Why does abandoning stolen property after throwing it outside differ from retrieving it?
b: If the thief throws out the property and leaves without retrieving it, he is considered someone who abandoned the property rather than someone who completed a theft. Amputation therefore does not apply.

f: 112. If a thief loads stolen property onto a donkey and drives it out of the secure place, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. Amputation applies because the movement of the donkey is attributed to the thief since he is controlling and driving it.

f: 113. If several thieves enter a secure place but only one of them physically carries away the stolen property, are all of them subject to amputation?
b: Yes, according to the Hanafi position based on istiḥsān (juristic preference). Although analogy would restrict the punishment to the person who carried the property, all participants are punished because their assistance makes the removal of the property attributable to all of them.

f: 114. Why does analogy require only the person carrying the stolen property to be amputated when several thieves act together?
b: Because the actual removal of the property from secure custody was physically performed only by that person, so the essential act of theft occurred through his action alone. This was the view of Zufar.

f: 115. Why does istiḥsān require amputation for all thieves who participate in a group theft?
b: Because thieves commonly divide roles: some carry the property while others guard, threaten resistance, or assist the escape. Treating only the carrier as liable would make the hadd difficult to apply and would allow others to avoid punishment through cooperation. This resembles the ruling in highway robbery.

f: 116. If someone breaks through a wall, inserts only his hand into a house, and steals property without entering the house, is amputation applied?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, no amputation applies because the violation of secure custody (hatk al-ḥirz) is incomplete. Complete violation requires entering the protected place itself.

f: 117. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding a thief who inserts his hand through a wall and steals property?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that amputation applies because the essential factor is removing the property from secure custody, and entering the place itself is not required.

f: 118. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ require the thief to enter the protected place before amputation is applied?
b: Because the violation of secure custody must be certain and complete to avoid doubt. Entering the place is the normal and customary method of theft and therefore is required when possible.

f: 119. Why is inserting a hand into a money chest different from inserting a hand through a wall of a house?
b: A money chest cannot normally be entered, so taking property by inserting the hand is the only possible method and completes the violation of custody. A house, however, can be entered, so entry is required.

f: 120. Why is the requirement of entering a place not applied to group theft where only one person carries the property?
b: Because dividing roles among thieves is the customary method of committing such crimes. The assistance of the others makes the act legally attributable to all of them.

f: 121. If someone cuts off a money pouch hanging outside a person's sleeve, is amputation applied?
b: No. Amputation does not apply because the pouch is outside the sleeve and therefore not protected by secure custody (ḥirz). The thief took the property from an exposed place.

f: 122. If someone inserts his hand into a person's sleeve and cuts off or takes a money pouch, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. Amputation applies because the sleeve itself functions as secure custody, and the thief removed the property from within that protected area.

f: 123. Why does the ruling differ between a pouch outside the sleeve and a pouch inside the sleeve?
b: Because the sleeve is considered the secure custody protecting the property. A pouch outside the sleeve is exposed, while a pouch inside the sleeve is protected by the garment.

f: 124. If a thief unties the fastening of a money pouch rather than cutting it, does the ruling change?
b: Yes. The ruling is reversed in both cases because the legal reason changes. What matters is whether the thief took the property from a protected place or from an exposed place.

f: 125. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding stealing a pouch from a sleeve?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that amputation applies in all cases because the property is protected either by the sleeve or by the owner himself.

f: 126. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad reject Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ view regarding a pouch?
b: They argued that the true secure custody is the sleeve, because that is what the owner relies upon for protection. The owner wears the sleeve for travel and rest, not specifically to guard the property, making it similar to a saddlebag.

f: 127. If someone steals a camel or a load from a caravan, is amputation applied?
b: No. Amputation does not apply because the goods in a caravan are not intentionally kept in secure custody. The people accompanying the caravan are usually concerned with travel and transport, not guarding the goods.

f: 128. When does stealing from a caravan become subject to amputation?
b: If someone accompanies the caravan specifically for the purpose of guarding the goods, then amputation applies because secure custody exists through the guardian.

f: 129. If someone cuts open a camel's pack (jawlāq) and steals property from inside, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. The pack itself serves as secure custody because goods are placed inside it for protection, similar to property kept inside a sleeve.

f: 130. If someone steals a saddlebag while its owner is guarding it and sleeping on it, is amputation applied?
b: Yes. This applies when the saddlebag is in a place without physical secure custody, such as a road. The owner's personal guardianship protects the property.

f: 131. Does sleeping beside property count as guarding it for the hadd of theft?
b: Yes. According to the preferred Hanafi view, sleeping beside or upon one's property counts as guarding because this is considered protection according to normal custom.

f: 132. What determines whether a person is considered to be guarding property?
b: The consideration is ordinary custom. Actions such as sitting beside property, sleeping upon it, or sleeping nearby are regarded as methods of guarding when people normally rely upon them for protection.

f: 133. How is the hadd punishment of theft carried out according to the Hanafi school?
b: The thief's right hand is amputated at the wrist, and the wound is cauterized to prevent death. The purpose of the punishment is deterrence, not killing.

f: 134. What is the evidence for amputating the thief's hand?
b: The basis is the Qur'anic verse: "As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands..." (Qur'an 5:38).

f: 135. Why is the thief's right hand amputated specifically?
b: The specification of the right hand is based on the recitation attributed to ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ) and transmitted legal understanding.

f: 136. Why is the hand amputated at the wrist rather than higher up the arm?
b: Because the word "hand" linguistically can refer to the entire arm up to the armpit. The wrist is the certain point intended, and reports from the Prophet ﷺ indicate amputation at the wrist.

f: 137. Why is the wound cauterized after the thief's hand is amputated?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ ordered that the hand be amputated and cauterized. Cauterization prevents the wound from causing death, since the hadd is intended as a deterrent rather than a means of execution.

f: 138. What happens if a person commits theft a second time after having his right hand amputated?
b: His left foot is amputated. This ruling is based on istiḥsān (juristic preference).

f: 139. What happens if a person commits theft a third time after already losing his right hand and left foot?
b: No further limb is amputated. Instead, he is imprisoned permanently until he repents, and scholars also mention that he receives discretionary punishment (taʿzīr).

f: 140. What was al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding repeated theft offenses?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī held that the left hand is amputated for the third theft and the right foot for the fourth theft.

f: 141. What evidence did al-Shāfiʿī use for amputating additional limbs after repeated theft?
b: He relied on the narration: "Whoever steals, amputate him. If he steals again, amputate him. If he steals again, amputate him." He argued that a third theft is still a criminal act and therefore still deserves the hadd punishment.

f: 142. What is the Hanafi evidence for not amputating further limbs after the second theft?
b: The statement of ʿAlī (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ): "I would be ashamed before Allah to leave him without a hand by which he eats and cleanses himself, and without a foot upon which he walks." The Companions accepted this reasoning, establishing consensus according to the Hanafi argument.

f: 143. Why does the Hanafi school reject amputating further limbs after the second theft?
b: Because removing more limbs would effectively destroy the person by eliminating essential bodily functions. The hadd is meant to deter crime, not destroy the offender.

f: 144. Why is repeated theft treated differently from retaliation (qiṣāṣ)?
b: Retaliation concerns an individual's right, so as much of the wrong as possible is restored. The hadd of theft is a right of Allah intended for deterrence, so it is limited to what achieves that purpose.

f: 145. How do Hanafis respond to the hadith used to justify repeated amputations?
b: Al-Ṭaḥāwī criticized its authenticity. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as referring to governmental discretionary punishment (siyāsah), not the fixed hadd punishment.

f: 146. Why is permanent imprisonment imposed on a repeat thief after two amputations?
b: Because further amputation would exceed the purpose of the hadd by destroying bodily function, while imprisonment continues to achieve deterrence and protection of society.

f: 147. If a thief's left hand is already paralyzed or amputated, is his right hand amputated for a theft?
b: No. Amputation is not carried out because this would remove an entire category of bodily function: the ability to grasp.

f: 148. If a thief's right foot has already been amputated, is his right hand amputated for theft?
b: No. Since walking has already been lost, removing another limb would eliminate another essential bodily function and go beyond the purpose of the hadd.

f: 149. If a thief's right foot is paralyzed, is his hand amputated for theft?
b: No. The same reasoning applies because removing another limb would cause excessive loss of bodily function.

f: 150. If the thumb of the thief's left hand is missing or paralyzed, is the right hand amputated for theft?
b: No. The thumb is the main instrument of grasping, so its loss significantly affects the hand's function.

f: 151. If two fingers other than the thumb on the thief's left hand are missing or paralyzed, is the right hand amputated?
b: No. Two fingers together reduce the effectiveness of grasping in a way comparable to the loss of the thumb.

f: 152. If only one finger other than the thumb on the thief's left hand is missing or paralyzed, is amputation still carried out?
b: Yes. The loss of one finger does not significantly impair the ability to grasp, so the hadd punishment remains applicable.

f: 153. Why does the loss of two fingers prevent amputation while the loss of one finger does not?
b: Because two fingers together significantly weaken grasping ability, while one missing finger does not create a major functional impairment.

f: 154. If a judge orders the executioner to amputate the thief's right hand, but the executioner mistakenly amputates the left hand, is the executioner liable according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, nothing is due from the executioner, because this is considered an excusable error in legal judgment (ijtihād).

f: 155. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding an executioner who amputates the wrong hand?
b: They held that there is no liability if it was a mistake, but if it was done intentionally, the executioner is liable because he deliberately destroyed a protected limb without legal justification.

f: 156. What was Zufar's opinion regarding an executioner who amputates the wrong hand?
b: Zufar held that the executioner is liable even if it was done by mistake, because he destroyed a protected limb and mistakes regarding people's rights are not excused.

f: 157. Why did Zufar consider the executioner liable for amputating the wrong hand?
b: Because the left hand was protected and there was no right to destroy it. In matters involving the rights of people, mistakes do not excuse liability.

f: 158. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to Zufar's argument regarding the wrong hand being amputated?
b: He argued that the executioner made a legal mistake because the revealed text does not explicitly specify the right hand. Errors in legal interpretation are excused.

f: 159. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad disagree with Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding the wrong hand being amputated?
b: They argued that the executioner did not merely make an interpretive error; he intentionally destroyed a protected limb without any valid legal basis.

f: 160. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning for not holding the executioner liable when the wrong hand is amputated?
b: Although one limb was destroyed, it was replaced by another limb of the same type that was more suitable for the intended punishment. Therefore, it is not treated as complete destruction.

f: 161. If someone other than the official executioner amputates the wrong hand of the thief, is he liable?
b: According to the preferred view, he is also not liable, following the same reasoning applied to the official executioner.

f: 162. If the thief himself extends his left hand and claims, "This is my right hand," is the executioner liable for amputating it?
b: No. All scholars agree that the executioner is not liable because he acted based on the thief's own instruction.

f: 163. If the thief falsely presents his left hand as his right hand and it is amputated, does he still owe the stolen property?
b: According to the view that this was intentional deception, he remains liable for the stolen property because the amputation was not the valid hadd punishment. According to the mistaken-opinion view, he is also liable. According to the view that treats it as a legitimate legal error, he is not liable.

f: 164. Is the thief's hand amputated without the owner of the stolen property being present and demanding prosecution?
b: No. The owner's legal claim (khuṣūmah) is required because establishing the offense against another person's property depends upon a dispute being brought forward by the person whose right was harmed.

f: 165. According to the Hanafi school, does the requirement of the owner's claim apply both when theft is proven by testimony and when it is proven by confession?
b: Yes. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his companions, there is no difference between proof through witnesses and proof through confession; both require the owner's legal claim.

f: 166. What was al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding theft established by confession?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī differed regarding confession and held that the owner's claim is not required in the same way when the thief confesses.

f: 167. Why is the owner's claim required before amputation for theft?
b: Because theft is an offense involving another person's property, and the legal offense is not fully established until the owner brings a claim.

f: 168. If the owner is absent when the amputation is about to be carried out, is the hadd punishment performed?
b: According to the Hanafi school, no. The owner's presence is required because carrying out the judgment is part of the judicial process for prescribed punishments.

f: 169. Can a depositary (mūdaʿ) demand the amputation of someone who steals the deposited property?
b: Yes, according to the Hanafi school. A depositary may bring the claim because he has a custodial relationship with the property and requires protection of that possession.

f: 170. Can a usurper (ghāṣib) demand the amputation of someone who steals the property he is holding?
