b: Because they treat the combined case according to the ruling of each item individually.

f: 622. What principle do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad apply to the case of a runaway slave carrying property?
b: The ruling of the whole case follows the ruling of each separate component.

f: 623. If an enemy non-Muslim enters Muslim territory under safe-conduct, purchases a Muslim slave, and takes him back to enemy territory, does the slave become free according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Yes, the slave becomes free according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 624. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what is the ruling if an enemy non-Muslim purchases a Muslim slave and takes him back to enemy territory?
b: The slave does not become free and remains a slave in the buyer's possession.

f: 625. What is the argument of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding an enemy purchasing a Muslim slave?
b: They argue that ownership was transferred through a legally valid sale.

f: 626. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad say the slave remains enslaved after being taken to enemy territory?
b: Because once the valid sale was completed, judicial authority over the matter ended, leaving the slave under the buyer's ownership.

f: 627. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ response regarding a Muslim slave under the authority of an enemy non-Muslim?
b: He argues that freeing the Muslim from humiliation under enemy authority is obligatory.

f: 628. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what replaces the normal legal cause of emancipation in this case?
b: The separation between Dār al-Islām and Dār al-Ḥarb is treated as standing in place of the legal cause of emancipation.

f: 629. What example does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to support the idea that territorial separation can substitute for a legal cause?
b: The example of three menstrual cycles substituting for judicial separation when one spouse embraces Islam while remaining in Dār al-Ḥarb.

f: 630. If an enemy slave accepts Islam and comes to Muslim lands, what happens to him?
b: He becomes free.

f: 631. If Muslims conquer enemy territory while an enemy slave is still there, what happens to the slave?
b: He becomes free.

f: 632. If enemy slaves leave their masters and come out to the Muslim army, what happens to them?
b: They become free.

f: 633. What report is used as evidence that enemy slaves who come to Muslims become free?
b: The report that slaves from Ṭāʾif accepted Islam and came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "They are the freed ones of Allah."

f: 634. Why does a slave become free when he comes over to the Muslims against his master's wishes?
b: Because he secures himself under Muslim protection by separating himself from his master's authority.

f: 635. Why does an enemy slave become free when Muslims conquer his territory?
b: Because he comes under the protection and authority of the Muslim forces.

f: 636. In the case of an enemy slave accepting Islam and coming to Muslims, whose possession is given priority: the slave's own possession or the Muslims' newly established possession?
b: The slave's own possession over himself is given priority.

f: 637. Why is the slave's own possession over himself preferred over the Muslims' possession?
b: Because his own control existed earlier and only requires reinforcement, while the Muslims' possession would be a new establishment of control.

f: 638. What principle explains why the slave's own legal control over himself is recognized?
b: Earlier existing possession has stronger legal recognition than a newly established possession.

f: 639. What does the phrase "his own legal possession over himself" mean in this context?
b: It means the slave's ability to control his own person after separating from his master's authority.

f: 640. What is the purpose behind freeing slaves who come under Muslim protection?
b: To remove them from subjugation under enemy non-Muslim authority.

f: 641. What does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider the legal status of a Muslim slave taken under enemy authority?
b: He considers the slave's continued enslavement under enemy authority impermissible due to the humiliation involved.

f: 642. What is a mustaʾmin in Islamic law?
b: A person from one territory who enters another territory under a guarantee of safety (amān).

f: 643. If a Muslim enters enemy territory as a merchant under safe-conduct, may he take their property or shed their blood?
b: No, it is not lawful for him to take their property or shed their blood.

f: 644. Why may a Muslim merchant under safe-conduct not violate the property or lives of the enemy?
b: Because accepting safe-conduct is a pledge not to betray their persons or property.

f: 645. What is the violation of safe-conduct by taking property or shedding blood considered?
b: It is considered treachery (ghadr).

f: 646. Is treachery after accepting safe-conduct permissible?
b: No, treachery is unlawful.

f: 647. When may a Muslim under safe-conduct retaliate against enemy property or persons?
b: When the enemy ruler himself betrays the treaty by confiscating wealth, imprisoning people, or similar actions with official approval.

f: 648. Why does betrayal by the enemy ruler cancel the safe-conduct agreement?
b: Because the enemy has broken the treaty themselves.

f: 649. Why is a Muslim prisoner of war different from a Muslim merchant under safe-conduct?
b: Because a prisoner is not in enemy territory under a covenant of protection.

f: 650. May a Muslim prisoner of war take opportunities against the enemy if released voluntarily?
b: Yes, because he was not bound by a safe-conduct agreement.

f: 651. If a Muslim merchant under safe-conduct betrays the enemy, takes property, and returns to Muslim lands, does he acquire ownership of the property?
b: Yes, he acquires ownership, but it is an unlawful ownership.

f: 652. Why does a Muslim who betrays safe-conduct acquire ownership of captured property?
b: Because conquest has occurred over property that was legally available for acquisition.

f: 653. Why is the ownership acquired through betrayal considered unlawful?
b: Because it was obtained through treachery and violation of the guarantee of safety.

f: 654. What must a Muslim do with property acquired through betrayal of safe-conduct?
b: He must give it away in charity.

f: 655. What legal principle does ownership through unlawful acquisition demonstrate?
b: A prohibition arising from an external factor does not prevent the legal cause of ownership from taking effect.

f: 656. If a Muslim under safe-conduct lends money to an enemy or borrows from him, will an Islamic judge later enforce the debt after both enter Muslim jurisdiction?
b: No, the judge will not adjudicate the claim.

f: 657. Why is a debt created between a Muslim mustaʾmin and an enemy not enforced by an Islamic judge?
b: Because Islamic judicial authority did not exist over them when the debt was created.

f: 658. Does an enemy entering Muslim lands under safe-conduct make Islamic courts responsible for actions completed before his arrival?
b: No, safe-conduct only subjects him to Islamic law for future conduct, not previous actions.

f: 659. If a Muslim and enemy non-Muslim usurp each other's property while under safe-conduct, will the judge rule on the usurpation claim?
b: No, the judge will not adjudicate the claim.

f: 660. Why is usurped property not returned through Islamic judgment in this case?
b: Because the usurper became the owner through conquest over property lacking legal protection.

f: 661. Does the same ruling apply if two enemy non-Muslims commit debts or usurpation among themselves and later enter Muslim lands under safe-conduct?
b: Yes, the same ruling applies.

f: 662. If two people who entered Muslim lands as Muslims had a debt between them from before, is the debt enforceable?
b: Yes, the debt is enforceable between them.

f: 663. Why is a debt between two Muslims enforceable after they enter Islamic jurisdiction?
b: Because it arose through a valid consensual contract and both parties become subject to Islamic judicial authority.

f: 664. Why is usurpation different from a debt when both parties later become Muslims?
b: Because the usurper had already acquired ownership of the property under the earlier legal rules.

f: 665. After a non-Muslim usurper becomes Muslim, is he required to return property he acquired through conquest?
b: No, he is not ordered to restore it.

f: 666. Why is a person not ordered to return property acquired through conquest after accepting Islam?
b: Because acquiring such ownership was not considered legally blameworthy for a non-Muslim enemy.

f: 667. What is a mustaʾmin?
b: A person who enters another territory under a guarantee of safety (amān).

f: 668. If a Muslim enters Dār al-Ḥarb as a merchant under amān, may he violate the property or blood of its people?
b: No, it is not lawful for him to violate their property or shed their blood.

f: 669. Why may a Muslim mustaʾmin not harm the people of Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Because by accepting their amān, he has implicitly guaranteed that he will not harm them.

f: 670. What does violating the terms of amān constitute?
b: It constitutes treachery (ghadr).

f: 671. Is treachery after receiving amān permissible?
b: No, treachery is unlawful.

f: 672. When is a Muslim no longer bound by an enemy's amān?
b: When the enemy ruler himself breaks the covenant by betraying Muslims.

f: 673. What examples are given of an enemy ruler breaking the covenant?
b: Confiscating Muslim wealth, imprisoning Muslims, or committing similar acts with the ruler's approval or without preventing them.

f: 674. Why does the Muslim no longer remain bound by the original amān if the enemy ruler betrays it?
b: Because the covenant has already been broken by the other side.

f: 675. How does a Muslim prisoner of war differ from a Muslim mustaʾmin?
b: A prisoner of war is not in Dār al-Ḥarb through a voluntary covenant of safe-conduct.

f: 676. May a Muslim prisoner of war take advantage of opportunities against the enemy?
b: Yes, because he is not bound by an amān agreement.

f: 677. Does the voluntary release of a Muslim prisoner by the enemy change his ruling?
b: No, voluntary release does not change the ruling.

f: 678. If a Muslim mustaʾmin betrays the enemy, takes property, and returns with it, does he acquire ownership?
b: Yes, he acquires ownership of it.

f: 679. What type of ownership does a Muslim acquire through betraying amān?
b: He acquires ownership that is legally effective but sinful and unlawful (malakan maḥẓūran).

f: 680. Why does ownership occur despite the betrayal?
b: Because valid seizure (istīlāʾ) occurred over property that was legally subject to acquisition.

f: 681. Why is the ownership acquired through betrayal considered unlawful?
b: Because it was obtained through the prohibited act of treachery.

f: 682. What should a Muslim do with property acquired through betrayal of amān?
b: He should give it away in charity.

f: 683. What legal principle does this case demonstrate?
b: A prohibition caused by an external factor does not prevent the legal cause of ownership from taking effect.

f: 684. If a Muslim mustaʾmin lends money to a ḥarbī, is the debt later enforced in Islamic courts?
b: No, no judgment is passed regarding the claim.

f: 685. If a ḥarbī lends money to a Muslim mustaʾmin, is the debt later enforced in Islamic courts?
b: No, no judgment is passed regarding the claim.

f: 686. Why are loans made between a Muslim mustaʾmin and a ḥarbī not judged by Islamic courts?
b: Because Islamic judicial authority (wilāyah) did not exist over them when the loan was made.

f: 687. Does a ḥarbī entering Dār al-Islām under amān create retroactive Islamic jurisdiction over previous transactions?
b: No, it only applies to future dealings.

f: 688. What does a ḥarbī accept when entering Dār al-Islām under amān?
b: He accepts Islamic rulings concerning his future conduct, not transactions completed before entering.

f: 689. What happens if one mustaʾmin usurps the property of another?
b: No judgment is passed regarding the usurped property.

f: 690. Why is a usurped item not returned through Islamic judgment in this case?
b: Because the usurper became the owner through seizing property that lacked legal protection in that jurisdiction.

f: 691. Does the same ruling apply if two ḥarbīs commit transactions or usurpation among themselves and later enter Dār al-Islām under amān?
b: Yes, the same ruling applies.

f: 692. If two people enter Islam, are debts between them enforceable?
b: Yes, judgments regarding debts are enforced between them.

f: 693. Why are debts between two Muslims enforceable after they embrace Islam?
b: Because the loan was originally concluded through valid consent and both parties become subject to Islamic judicial authority.

f: 694. Why is a debt treated differently from usurped property after both parties embrace Islam?
b: Because a debt arises from a valid contract, while usurped property had already transferred ownership to the usurper.

f: 695. If a non-Muslim combatant acquired property through conquest and later becomes Muslim, must he return that property?
b: No, he is not ordered to return it.

f: 696. Why is a convert not ordered to return property acquired by conquest before Islam?
b: Because such ownership was not considered legally blameworthy for a non-Muslim combatant under those rules.

f: 697. What is the difference between the legal treatment of a loan and usurpation after conversion to Islam?
b: The loan remains enforceable because it was a valid agreement, while usurped property is not returned because ownership had already transferred.

f: 698. If a Muslim mustaʾmin wrongfully seizes the property of a ḥarbī and both later embrace Islam, does the judge compel him to return the property?
b: No, the judge does not compel him to return it.

f: 699. If a Muslim mustaʾmin wrongfully seizes a ḥarbī's property and both later become Muslims, what is he instructed to do?
b: He is instructed to return the property.

f: 700. Why does the judge not issue a ruling requiring the return of the property?
b: Because ownership had already transferred through seizure according to the legal rules previously explained.

f: 701. Why is the Muslim instructed through fatwā to return the property despite owning it legally?
b: Because his ownership was morally corrupted by violating the covenant of safe-conduct.

f: 702. What is the difference between a legal judgment (qaḍāʾ) and fatwā in this case?
b: A judge does not compel the return, but a religious ruling instructs him to return it.

f: 703. If two Muslims enter Dār al-Ḥarb under safe-conduct and one kills the other, is any financial liability due?
b: Yes, blood-money (diyah) is due, and in accidental killing expiation (kaffārah) is also due.

f: 704. Does it matter whether the killing between two Muslim mustaʾmins is intentional or accidental?
b: Yes. Intentional killing requires diyah, while accidental killing requires diyah and kaffārah.

f: 705. Why is kaffārah required for accidental killing between Muslim mustaʾmins?
b: Because of the unrestricted wording of the Qur'ānic command regarding accidental killing.

f: 706. Why is diyah required when a Muslim kills another Muslim mustaʾmin in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Because the protection (ʿiṣmah) gained through residence in Dār al-Islām is not removed by temporarily entering Dār al-Ḥarb under safe-conduct.

f: 707. Is qiṣāṣ carried out when one Muslim mustaʾmin kills another in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: No, qiṣāṣ is not carried out.

f: 708. Why is qiṣāṣ not carried out between Muslims in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Because it requires the authority and protection of the Muslim ruler and community, which are absent there.

f: 709. Who pays the diyah when one Muslim mustaʾmin kills another Muslim mustaʾmin?
b: The killer himself pays the diyah from his own wealth.

f: 710. Why does the ʿāqilah not pay diyah for intentional killing in this case?
b: Because the ʿāqilah never bears liability for intentional homicide.

f: 711. Why does the ʿāqilah not pay diyah for accidental killing between Muslim mustaʾmins?
b: Because the ʿāqilah cannot realistically supervise or prevent incidents occurring across separate territories.

f: 712. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is due if one Muslim prisoner of war kills another Muslim prisoner?
b: Nothing is due from the killer, not even kaffārah for accidental killing.

f: 713. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, what is due if one Muslim prisoner kills another Muslim prisoner?
b: Diyah is due in both intentional and accidental killing.

f: 714. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding Muslim prisoners killing each other?
b: They hold that captivity does not remove a Muslim's legal inviolability.

f: 715. How do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad compare captivity with safe-conduct?
b: They argue that captivity, like safe-conduct, does not remove a Muslim's protection.

f: 716. Why do Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad still deny qiṣāṣ between Muslim prisoners?
b: Because Muslim judicial authority is absent in enemy territory.

f: 717. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad, who pays diyah between Muslim prisoners?
b: The killer pays it from his own wealth.

f: 718. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reasoning for not imposing liability when one Muslim prisoner kills another?
b: He argues that the captive becomes legally attached to the enemy due to their physical control over him.

f: 719. What evidence does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to show that a captive follows the enemy's legal status?
b: His legal residence and travel status follow theirs.

f: 720. What happens to a Muslim captive's previous territorial protection (iḥrāz) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It no longer exists because he has become under enemy control.

f: 721. To what case does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ compare a Muslim prisoner?
b: A Muslim who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb but never migrated to Dār al-Islām.

f: 722. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ deny kaffārah in accidental killing by a prisoner?
b: Because according to his view there is no liability even for accidental killing, and kaffārah is not prescribed for intentional killing in the Ḥanafī school.

f: 723. What is the main disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and his two companions regarding Muslim prisoners?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considers their protection removed due to enemy control, while Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad maintain that captivity does not remove Muslim inviolability.

f: 724. What is the overall principle behind Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ ruling on prisoners?
b: Legal protection follows territorial and political control, and captivity places the Muslim under enemy authority.

f: 725. What is the overall principle behind Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad's ruling on prisoners?
b: Muslim identity preserves legal inviolability even while under captivity.

f: 726. What is the ruling if a ḥarbī enters Muslim territory under amān, leaving behind his wife, children, and property in Dār al-Ḥarb, then embraces Islam and Muslims later conquer that land?
b: His remaining wife, children, and property become war booty (fayʾ).

f: 727. Why does the wife of a ḥarbī who embraces Islam in Dār al-Islām become fayʾ if she remains in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Because she remains a non-Muslim enemy subject and is not legally dependent upon her husband.

f: 728. Why do the adult children of a ḥarbī who embraces Islam become fayʾ?
b: Because they are independent adult non-Muslim enemy subjects.

f: 729. What happens to an unborn child if the wife of the convert is pregnant?
b: The unborn child follows the ruling of the mother and becomes fayʾ.

f: 730. Why do the minor children of a ḥarbī who embraces Islam in Dār al-Islām not become Muslim through their father?
b: Because a child follows the father's religion only while under his custody and legal authority.

f: 731. Why is the legal dependency between the father and his minor children absent in this case?
b: Because they are separated between Dār al-Islām and Dār al-Ḥarb.

f: 732. Does a person's Islam in Dār al-Islām automatically protect property he left behind in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: No, property remaining in Dār al-Ḥarb does not become protected merely because its owner entered Dār al-Islām.

f: 733. What happens to property left behind in Dār al-Ḥarb when the Muslims later conquer it?
b: It becomes fayʾ.

f: 734. If a ḥarbī embraces Islam while still in Dār al-Ḥarb, migrates to Muslim lands, and Muslims later conquer that territory, what happens to his minor children?
b: His minor children become free Muslims.

f: 735. Why do the minor children become free Muslims in the second case?
b: Because when he embraced Islam, they were still under his authority and in the same territory.

f: 736. What happens to property deposited with a Muslim or a dhimmī by a person who later embraces Islam?
b: It remains his property.

f: 737. Why does property deposited with a Muslim or dhimmī remain protected?
b: Because it is held by a legally recognized custodian whose possession is treated as the owner's possession.

f: 738. What happens to property left in the possession of a ḥarbī?
b: It becomes fayʾ.

f: 739. Why does property held by a ḥarbī not receive legal protection?
b: Because the possession of a hostile non-Muslim is not regarded as legally protected possession.

f: 740. What chapter topic follows these rulings on the mustaʾman?
b: The killing of a Muslim who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb.

f: 741. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is due if a ḥarbī accepts Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb and another Muslim kills him accidentally?
b: Only kaffārah is due.

f: 742. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is due if a Muslim intentionally kills someone who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Nothing is due.

f: 743. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, does accidental killing of a Muslim who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb require diyah?
b: No, only kaffārah is required.

f: 744. According to al-Shāfiʿī, what is due for accidental killing of a Muslim who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Diyah is due.

f: 745. According to al-Shāfiʿī, what is due for intentional killing of a Muslim who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Qiṣāṣ (retaliatory punishment) is due.

f: 746. What is al-Shāfiʿī's evidence for imposing diyah and qiṣāṣ in this case?
b: Islam itself establishes legal inviolability, because it is the basis of human dignity.

f: 747. What is the main disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and al-Shāfiʿī regarding a new Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considers territorial protection relevant, while al-Shāfiʿī considers Islam itself sufficient to establish full inviolability.

f: 748. What additional condition is mentioned for Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ ruling on the new Muslim killed in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: The victim must have Muslim heirs in that territory.

f: 749. What legal concept is central to the disagreement regarding the killed convert in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: The concept of ʿiṣmah (legal protection and inviolability).

f: 750. What Qur'anic verse does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ cite regarding the killing of a Muslim who accepted Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Allah's statement: "If he was from a people who are enemies to you while being a believer, then only the freeing of a believing slave..." (Qur'an 4:92).

f: 751. What does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ infer from the fact that Qur'an 4:92 mentions kaffārah but not diyah?
b: He infers that no blood-money (diyah) is due in this case.

f: 752. What are the two categories of legal inviolability (ʿiṣmah) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Moral inviolability (al-ʿiṣmah al-muʾaththimah) and financial inviolability (al-ʿiṣmah al-muqawwamah).

f: 753. What is moral inviolability (الْعِصْمَةُ الْمُؤْثِّمَةُ)?
b: It is the protection that makes unlawful killing a sin.

f: 754. Why does moral inviolability make killing sinful?
b: Because every human being with religious responsibility (taklīf) has inherent respect and protection.

f: 755. What is the basis of moral inviolability?
b: Being a human being who is subject to religious accountability.

f: 756. Does moral inviolability itself create financial liability?
b: No, it only makes the act sinful; it does not necessarily require compensation.

f: 757. How does property gain protection according to moral inviolability?
b: Property is protected as a consequence of the protection given to human life.

f: 758. What is financial inviolability (الْعِصْمَةُ الْمُقَوَّمَةُ)?
b: It is the type of protection that creates financial obligations such as diyah and compensation.

f: 759. What legal consequences result from financial inviolability?
b: Payment of blood-money (diyah) and other forms of financial compensation.

f: 760. Why is financial inviolability connected to property?
b: Because compensation replaces something lost, and replacement applies to things that have equivalents, such as wealth.

f: 761. Why is human life not considered the basis of financial compensation itself?
b: Because human life has no true equivalent that can replace it.

f: 762. What does financial inviolability depend upon according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It depends upon territorial protection (iḥrāz bi-l-dār).

f: 763. What is meant by iḥrāz bi-l-dār?
b: Protection gained through belonging to a territory under recognized Islamic authority and security.

f: 764. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not consider Dār al-Ḥarb to provide financial protection?
b: Because Islamic law does not recognize hostile political authority as creating this type of legal protection.

f: 765. Why does the Sharīʿah not recognize hostile political authority as creating financial protection?
b: Because one of the aims of the Sharīʿah is the removal of hostile political power.

f: 766. How are an apostate and a mustaʾman in Dār al-Islām treated regarding territorial affiliation?
b: They are legally considered connected to their original territory because their intended affiliation remains there.

f: 767. What is the ruling if someone accidentally kills a Muslim who has no heirs?
b: The killer's ʿāqilah pays the diyah to the Imām, and the killer must perform kaffārah.

f: 768. Why is diyah due when a Muslim without heirs is accidentally killed?
b: Because the victim was a legally protected person.

f: 769. Who receives the diyah when a Muslim with no heirs is killed?
b: The Imām receives it on behalf of the Muslim community.

f: 770. Why does the Muslim community receive the diyah when there are no heirs?
b: Because the Imām acts as the representative and guardian of the public interest.

f: 771. What is the ruling if a ḥarbī enters under amān, accepts Islam, and is accidentally killed while having no heirs?
b: The killer's ʿāqilah pays the diyah to the Imām, and the killer performs kaffārah.

f: 772. Who pays diyah in accidental killing of a protected person with no heirs?
b: The killer's ʿāqilah pays the diyah.

f: 773. Who performs kaffārah in accidental killing?
b: The killer himself performs kaffārah.

f: 774. If a person with no heirs is intentionally killed, what options does the Imām have?
b: The Imām may execute the killer or accept diyah.

f: 775. Why may the Imām accept diyah instead of qiṣāṣ in intentional killing?
b: Because the Imām acts as guardian of the person who has no guardian and may choose what benefits the Muslim community.

f: 776. What prophetic statement supports the Imām's guardianship over one without an heir?
b: "The ruler is the guardian of the one who has no guardian."

f: 777. What is the legal nature of accepting diyah instead of qiṣāṣ in intentional killing?
b: It is a settlement (ṣulḥ) between the parties.

f: 778. Why is accepting diyah considered beneficial in this situation?
b: Because the diyah benefits the Muslim community while the original punishment is qiṣāṣ.

f: 779. Can the Imām simply pardon the killer of a person with no heirs?
b: No, he cannot simply pardon the killer.

f: 780. Why can the Imām not pardon the killer without receiving compensation?
b: Because the right belongs to the Muslim public, not to the Imām personally.

f: 781. How is the Imām's authority over public rights described?
b: It is a trust exercised for the benefit of the Muslim community.

f: 782. Why may public rights not be abandoned without compensation?
b: Because a public authority cannot discard a public benefit without obtaining an equivalent benefit.

f: 783. What is the main legal distinction between moral and financial inviolability?
b: Moral inviolability makes wrongdoing sinful, while financial inviolability creates monetary liability.

f: 784. What is the main principle behind Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ position on diyah?
b: Financial liability depends on recognized territorial protection, not merely personal faith.

f: 785. What type of land is every land whose inhabitants embraced Islam considered?
b: It is considered ʿushr land.

f: 786. What type of land is land that was conquered by force and then divided among the conquering Muslims?
b: It is considered ʿushr land.

f: 787. Why is ʿushr imposed when the taxpayers are Muslims?
b: Because ʿushr resembles an act of worship and is lighter upon Muslims, as it is taken from actual agricultural produce.

f: 788. Why is ʿushr considered more suitable for Muslim-owned land?
b: Because Muslim lands are subject to a form of taxation connected to worship, and ʿushr fulfills that role.

f: 789. How is ʿushr calculated compared to kharāj?
b: ʿUshr is calculated from the actual agricultural produce.

f: 790. What type of land is land conquered by force whose inhabitants are left upon it?
b: It is considered kharāj land.

f: 791. What type of land is land whose inhabitants retain possession through a peace treaty?
b: It is considered kharāj land.

f: 792. Why is kharāj imposed when the taxpayers are non-Muslims?
b: Because kharāj is more appropriate for non-Muslim inhabitants whose land remains under their possession after conquest.

f: 793. What is the exception to the rule that conquered land left with its inhabitants becomes kharāj land?
b: Makkah is the exception.

f: 794. Why is Makkah not considered kharāj land despite being conquered by force?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ conquered it but left it in the possession of its inhabitants without imposing kharāj.

f: 795. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, what type of land is conquered land irrigated by river water?
b: It is kharāj land.

f: 796. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, what type of land is not reached by river water but irrigated by a dug spring?
b: It is ʿushr land.

f: 797. What determines whether agricultural land is subject to ʿushr or kharāj according to the irrigation discussion?
b: The source of irrigation connected to the land.

f: 798. Why does irrigation affect whether land is classified as ʿushr or kharāj land?
b: Because agricultural productivity depends upon irrigation, so the legal ruling follows the source that sustains the land.

f: 799. What is iḥyāʾ al-mawāt?
b: The revival and cultivation of dead (unused) land.

f: 800. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what determines the ruling of newly revived dead land?
b: The region in which the land is located.

f: 801. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens if revived land lies within an area of kharāj lands?
b: It becomes kharāj land.

f: 802. According to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what happens if revived land lies within an area of ʿushr lands?
b: It becomes ʿushr land.

f: 803. What did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider the land of Basra to be?
b: He considered Basra to be ʿushr land.

f: 804. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider Basra to be ʿushr land?
b: Because of the consensus of the Companions who imposed ʿushr upon it.

f: 805. What principle did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to determine the ruling of revived land?
b: The surrounding region (ḥīz) gives its legal ruling to adjacent land.

f: 806. What analogy did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use for the effect of surrounding land upon adjacent land?
b: The courtyard surrounding a house takes the legal status of the house itself.

f: 807. How does the legal status of surrounding land affect revived land according to Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The revived land follows the ruling of the surrounding area.

f: 808. Why would analogy suggest that Basra should have been kharāj land?
b: Because of its geographical surroundings.

f: 809. Why was analogy abandoned regarding Basra?
b: Because the consensus of the Companions established that it was ʿushr land.

f: 810. What principle does the case of Basra demonstrate?
b: Consensus (ijmāʿ) can take precedence over analogy (qiyās).

f: 811. What is the main difference between ʿushr land and kharāj land?
b: ʿUshr land is subject to a produce-based tithe, while kharāj land is subject to land taxation.

f: 812. What is the legal reason given for preferring ʿushr for Muslims?
b: It resembles worship and is lighter because it depends on actual produce.

f: 813. What is the legal reason given for preferring kharāj for non-Muslims?
b: It is the appropriate land tax for non-Muslim inhabitants whose land remains under their control.

f: 814. What was Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's opinion regarding land revived by a privately dug well?
b: He held that such land is ʿushr land.

f: 815. According to Muḥammad, what type of land results from revival through uncovering a spring?
b: It becomes ʿushr land.

f: 816. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling of land revived using water from the Tigris or Euphrates?
b: It is ʿushr land.

f: 817. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling of land irrigated by water from a great river belonging to no individual?
b: It is ʿushr land.

f: 818. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling of land irrigated by rainwater?
b: It is ʿushr land.

f: 819. What determines the ruling of revived land according to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan?
b: The source of irrigation used for the land.

f: 820. Why does the source of irrigation determine whether land is ʿushr or kharāj according to Muḥammad?
b: Because irrigation is the immediate cause of agricultural growth and productivity.

f: 821. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling of land revived through Persian-dug canals?
b: It is kharāj land.

f: 822. Which examples of Persian canals are mentioned as making land kharāj land?
b: The King's Canal (Nahr al-Malik) and the Canal of Yazdajird.

f: 823. Why does irrigation from a kharāj canal indicate that land carries kharāj according to Muḥammad?
b: Because kharāj cannot initially be imposed upon a Muslim against his will, so the irrigation source indicates an existing kharāj obligation.

f: 824. Who originally established the kharāj rates for the lands of the Sawād?
b: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: 825. What lands are referred to by the Sawād in this discussion?
b: The agricultural lands of Iraq.

f: 826. What was the kharāj imposed by ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ on ordinary cultivated land per jarīb?
b: One Hāshimī qafīz (equal to one ṣāʿ) plus one dirham.

f: 827. What was the kharāj imposed by ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ on vegetable gardens per jarīb?
b: Five dirhams.

f: 828. What was the kharāj imposed by ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ on continuous vineyards or dense date-palm groves per jarīb?
b: Ten dirhams.

f: 829. Who surveyed the Sawād lands of Iraq for ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: ʿUthmān ibn Ḥunayf.

f: 830. Who supervised the survey of the Sawād lands according to this account?
b: Ḥudhayfah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: 831. What was the total area surveyed in the Sawād according to this report?
b: Thirty-six million jarībs.

f: 832. Why did the kharāj rates established by ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ become considered authoritative?
b: Because they were established in the presence of the Companions without objection, constituting consensus.

f: 833. What principle explains why different crops have different kharāj rates?
b: Tax liability corresponds to productive capacity and agricultural expenses.

f: 834. Which type of crop requires the least agricultural expense according to this explanation?
b: Vineyards.

f: 835. Which type of crop requires the greatest agricultural expense according to this explanation?
b: Ordinary grain fields.

f: 836. Where do vegetable gardens fall in terms of agricultural expense?
b: They fall between vineyards and grain fields.

f: 837. Why were vineyards assigned the highest kharāj rate despite having the lowest expenses?
b: Because they have greater productive value and yield.

f: 838. Why were ordinary grain fields assigned the lowest kharāj rate?
b: Because they have the highest cultivation expenses.

f: 839. Why were vegetable gardens assigned an intermediate kharāj rate?
b: Because their expenses and productivity fall between grain fields and vineyards.

f: 840. What is the main legal principle behind Muḥammad's classification of revived land?
b: The legal ruling follows the source of irrigation.

f: 841. What is the main legal principle behind ʿUmar's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ different kharāj rates?
b: Taxation should correspond to the productive capacity of the land.

f: 842. What is the relationship between irrigation and agricultural productivity in this discussion?
b: Irrigation is considered the direct cause enabling cultivation and growth.

f: 843. Why is kharāj not initially imposed upon Muslims according to this discussion?
b: Because taxation of Muslims begins with ʿushr rather than kharāj.

f: 844. How is kharāj assessed for crops such as saffron and orchards?
b: It is assessed according to their productive capacity.

f: 845. Why are crops such as saffron and orchards assessed according to productive capacity?
b: Because no specific assessment from ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ exists for these crops.

f: 846. What principle is used when no fixed kharāj amount has been transmitted?
b: The tax is determined according to the land's ability to produce revenue.

f: 847. What is the maximum amount of produce that may be taken as kharāj according to the jurists?
b: No more than one-half of the produce.

f: 848. Why is one-half considered the maximum kharāj assessment?
b: Because taking half represents the limit of fairness.

f: 849. What is a bustān (orchard) according to the jurists?
b: Enclosed land surrounded by a wall containing scattered date palms along with other fruit trees.

f: 850. How were agricultural taxes often collected in later Muslim lands?
b: They were often assessed in monetary amounts rather than directly from produce.

f: 851. Why was assessing agricultural taxes in money accepted in later Muslim lands?
b: Because the essential consideration is the productive capacity of the land, not the specific form of payment.

f: 852. What does the Imam do if land can no longer bear its assessed kharāj?
b: He reduces the kharāj assessment.

f: 853. Is reducing kharāj when land productivity decreases accepted among the jurists?
b: Yes, it is accepted by consensus.

f: 854. What question did ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ ask his tax officials regarding land assessment?
b: "Perhaps you imposed upon the land more than it could bear?"

f: 855. How did ʿUmar's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ officials respond when asked if they had overburdened the land?
b: They replied that they had imposed only what it could bear.

f: 856. What did ʿUmar's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ officials say would happen if the assessment were increased?
b: They said the land could still bear more.

f: 857. What does the statement of ʿUmar's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ officials demonstrate regarding kharāj?
b: It demonstrates that assessments are based on the land's ability to bear taxation.

f: 858. What is Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's opinion if agricultural production substantially increases?
b: He permits increasing the kharāj.

f: 859. Why does Muḥammad permit increasing kharāj when production increases?
b: He reasons by analogy with the permissibility of reducing kharāj when production decreases.

f: 860. What is Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding increasing kharāj when production increases?
b: He does not permit increasing it.

f: 861. Why does Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not permit increasing kharāj after increased productivity?
b: Because ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ was informed that land could bear more but did not increase the assessment.

f: 862. What happens to kharāj if kharāj land is flooded?
b: No kharāj is due.

f: 863. What happens to kharāj if the water supply of kharāj land is cut off?
b: No kharāj is due.

f: 864. What happens to kharāj if crops are destroyed by a natural disaster?
b: No kharāj is due.

f: 865. Why is kharāj waived when land cannot be cultivated due to disaster?
b: Because the owner has lost the practical ability to produce from the land.

f: 866. Why does crop destruction remove kharāj liability for that year?
b: Because the presumed productivity upon which kharāj is based no longer exists.

f: 867. What does kharāj depend upon according to this discussion?
b: The presumed productive capacity of the land.

f: 868. How do jurists compare the waiver of kharāj after crop destruction with zakāh?
b: They compare it to zakāh, where productive ownership must continue throughout the year.

f: 869. What alternative reasoning do jurists give for waiving kharāj after crop destruction?
b: They consider the actual harvest that eventually appears.

f: 870. What is the main principle behind reducing or waiving kharāj?
b: Kharāj follows the actual ability of land to produce.

f: 871. Why is taking half of the produce considered the upper limit of kharāj?
b: Because beyond half would exceed fairness and become excessive taxation.

f: 872. What determines the amount of kharāj on unspecified crops?
b: The revenue-producing capacity of the land.

f: 873. Why can the form of agricultural tax payment differ while remaining valid?
b: Because the objective is assessing productive capacity, not a specific payment method.

f: 874. What is the difference between Muḥammad and Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding increased land productivity?
b: Muḥammad allows increasing kharāj, while Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ does not.

f: 875. What is the shared principle between reducing kharāj and assessing new crops?
b: Both are based on the productive ability of the land.

f: 876. If the owner leaves kharāj land uncultivated by his own choice, does kharāj remain due?
b: Yes, kharāj remains due.

f: 877. Why does kharāj remain due when the owner neglects cultivation?
b: Because the ability to cultivate still existed, and the failure to cultivate resulted from his own neglect.

f: 878. What is the difference between owner neglect and natural disaster regarding kharāj?
b: Owner neglect does not remove kharāj, while circumstances beyond his control may remove it.

f: 879. What are the two types of jizyah mentioned by the jurists?
b: Jizyah established by treaty and jizyah imposed by the Imam after conquest.

f: 880. What is the first type of jizyah?
b: A jizyah established through treaty and mutual agreement.

f: 881. How is the amount of treaty-based jizyah determined?
b: By whatever amount both parties agree upon.

f: 882. Why can more than the agreed treaty jizyah not be demanded?
b: Because its basis is mutual consent and agreement.

f: 883. Which people did the Prophet ﷺ conclude a treaty with requiring 1,200 ḥullahs?
b: The people of Najrān.

f: 884. What is the second type of jizyah?
b: Jizyah imposed by the Imam after conquering a non-Muslim people and allowing them to remain on their lands.

f: 885. According to the Hanafi position, how much jizyah is imposed annually upon the wealthy?
b: Forty-eight dirhams annually.

f: 886. According to the Hanafi position, how much does a wealthy person pay monthly for jizyah?
b: Four dirhams per month.

f: 887. According to the Hanafi position, how much jizyah is imposed annually upon those of moderate means?
b: Twenty-four dirhams annually.

f: 888. According to the Hanafi position, how much does a person of moderate means pay monthly for jizyah?
b: Two dirhams per month.

f: 889. According to the Hanafi position, how much jizyah is imposed annually upon the poor who can earn?
b: Twelve dirhams annually.

f: 890. According to the Hanafi position, how much does a poor but earning person pay monthly for jizyah?
b: One dirham per month.

f: 891. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding the amount of jizyah?
b: The Imam imposes one dīnār or its equivalent annually upon every adult.

f: 892. What evidence did al-Shāfiʿī use for a uniform jizyah amount?
b: The Prophet's ﷺ instruction to Muʿādh: "Take from every adult male and female one dīnār or its equivalent in Maʿāfir garments."

f: 893. Why did al-Shāfiʿī not distinguish between rich and poor in jizyah?
b: Because the hadith he relied upon mentions one fixed amount without distinction.

f: 894. What is the Hanafi evidence for graduated jizyah amounts?
b: It is transmitted from ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ.

f: 895. Why is the practice of the Rightly Guided Caliphs considered evidence for the Hanafi position?
b: Because none of the Muhājirūn or Anṣār objected to it.

f: 896. Why does jizyah differ according to financial ability according to the Hanafis?
b: Because it compensates for protection provided by the Muslim army, and people's financial capacities differ.

f: 897. What analogy is used to explain different jizyah amounts?
b: The variation of kharāj according to circumstances.

f: 898. How is jizyah described in relation to military service?
b: It is a substitute for military participation and financial contribution.

f: 899. Why does the substitute (jizyah) differ according to wealth?
b: Because the obligations it replaces differ according to people's financial ability.

f: 900. How do Hanafis respond to al-Shāfiʿī's hadith regarding one dīnār?
b: They interpret it as referring to a treaty settlement.

f: 901. Why do Hanafis interpret that hadith as referring to a treaty settlement?
b: Because it mentions collecting from adult women, whereas women are not normally subject to jizyah.

f: 902. Upon whom is jizyah imposed according to the author's statement?
b: Upon the People of the Book and the Magians.

f: 903. What Qur'anic verse is used as evidence for imposing jizyah upon the People of the Book?
b: "From those who were given the Scripture until they pay the jizyah..." (Qur'an 9:29).

f: 904. What is the evidence that jizyah is imposed upon the Magians?
b: The Prophet ﷺ imposed jizyah upon them.

f: 905. Does al-Shāfiʿī allow jizyah for non-Arab idol worshippers?
b: No, he disagrees with allowing jizyah for them.

f: 906. What is al-Shāfiʿī's argument against imposing jizyah upon non-Arab idol worshippers?
b: He argues that fighting unbelievers is the original ruling and jizyah is only an exception established for specific groups.

f: 907. According to al-Shāfiʿī, for whom is the exception of jizyah established?
b: The People of the Book by the Qur'an and the Magians by the Sunnah.

f: 908. What is the Hanafi response to al-Shāfiʿī's argument?
b: Since non-Arab idol worshippers may be enslaved, jizyah may also be imposed upon them.

f: 909. What similarity exists between slavery and jizyah according to the Hanafi response?
b: Both spare their lives while placing them under Muslim authority.

f: 910. How does slavery benefit Muslims according to this explanation?
b: The enslaved person works, their earnings benefit Muslims, and their maintenance is provided from that work.

f: 911. What principle allows jizyah to be imposed upon groups besides the People of the Book and Magians according to the Hanafis?
b: Anything that permits sparing life through slavery can also permit sparing life through jizyah.

f: 912. What is the main reason the Hanafis allow jizyah for non-Arab idol worshippers?
b: Because jizyah and slavery share the same purpose of preserving life while establishing Muslim authority.

f: 913. How does the Hanafi view of jizyah differ from al-Shāfiʿī's view?
b: Hanafis allow it for People of the Book, Magians, and non-Arab idol worshippers, while al-Shāfiʿī restricts it to those with specific textual evidence.

f: 914. What happens if Muslims conquer Arab idol-worshippers or apostates before they accept Islam?
b: They, their women, and their children become war booty (fayʾ).

f: 915. Why do the women and children of conquered Arab idol-worshippers or apostates become fayʾ?
b: Because they may lawfully be enslaved.

f: 916. Why are Arab idol-worshippers considered to have especially grave disbelief according to the Hanafis?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ arose among them, the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and the miracle was most evident to them.

f: 917. Why are apostates considered to have especially grave disbelief?
b: Because they rejected Allah after accepting Islam and witnessing its truth and excellence.

f: 918. What options are given to Arab idol-worshippers and apostates according to this ruling?
b: They are offered only Islam or fighting, not the option of paying jizyah.

f: 919. Why are Arab idol-worshippers and apostates not offered the option of paying jizyah?
b: Because their circumstances make their disbelief especially severe.

f: 920. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding Arab idol-worshippers?
b: He held that Arab idol-worshippers may be enslaved.

f: 921. How do the Hanafis respond to al-Shāfiʿī regarding Arab idol-worshippers?
b: They respond with the reasoning that their disbelief is especially severe due to the Prophet ﷺ and revelation being among them.

f: 922. Which Companion enslaved the women and children of Banū Ḥanīfah after their apostasy?
b: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: 923. What did Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ do with the women and children of Banū Ḥanīfah?
b: He enslaved them and distributed them among the Muslim fighters.

f: 924. What happens to the men of apostates who do not embrace Islam after being conquered?
b: They are executed.

f: 925. Why are the men of apostates executed according to this ruling?
b: Because of the previously mentioned ruling regarding apostates.

f: 926. Is jizyah imposed upon women according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, jizyah is not imposed upon women.

f: 927. Is jizyah imposed upon children according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, jizyah is not imposed upon children.

f: 928. Why is jizyah not imposed upon women and children?
b: Because jizyah substitutes either for liability to fighting/killing or for military service, and women and children are not subject to these due to lack of legal capacity.

f: 929. What is the legal reasoning behind jizyah according to the Hanafis?
b: It is a substitute for military obligation or the liability to be fought.

f: 930. Is jizyah imposed upon a chronically disabled person (zamin)?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 931. Is jizyah imposed upon a blind person?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 932. Who else is exempt from jizyah due to inability according to this discussion?
b: The paralysed and the extremely elderly.

f: 933. Why are the chronically disabled, blind, paralysed, and extremely elderly exempt from jizyah?
b: Because they lack the ability that forms the basis of the obligation.

f: 934. What was Abū Yūsuf's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion regarding wealthy disabled or blind people?
b: He held that jizyah is due from them if they are wealthy.

f: 935. Why did Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider wealthy disabled people liable for jizyah?
b: Because they may still be liable to be killed in some circumstances, such as if they provide military counsel.

f: 936. Is jizyah imposed upon a poor person who cannot earn?
b: No, according to the Hanafi position.

f: 937. Who disagreed with exempting poor people unable to earn from jizyah?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 938. What evidence did al-Shāfiʿī use for imposing jizyah upon all adults?
b: The general wording of the hadith of Muʿādh رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: 939. What is the Hanafi evidence that poor people unable to earn are exempt from jizyah?
b: ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ did not impose jizyah upon such people, and the Companions did not object.

f: 940. What analogy do the Hanafis use to explain why incapable poor people are exempt from jizyah?
b: Just as land incapable of producing crops is not taxed, a person incapable of earning is not subject to this head tax.

f: 941. How do Hanafis interpret the hadith of Muʿādh regarding jizyah?
b: They interpret it as referring to people who are capable of working and earning.

f: 942. What general principle connects kharāj and jizyah in this discussion?
b: Both are connected to ability and productive capacity.

f: 943. Why is jizyah called a "head tax" in this discussion?
b: Because it is imposed upon individuals rather than land.

f: 944. What distinguishes those who are liable for jizyah from those exempt?
b: Ability to participate, earn, or otherwise contribute to the obligations that jizyah represents.

f: 945. Upon whom is jizyah not imposed regarding slaves and those with partial freedom?
b: It is not imposed upon a slave, mukātab, mudabbar, or umm walad.

f: 946. What are the two possible explanations given for the basis of jizyah?
b: It is either a substitute for execution or a substitute for military service.

f: 947. Why is jizyah not imposed upon slaves according to the Hanafi reasoning?
b: Because the basis of military service does not apply to them, and obligations are not established when there is doubt.

f: 948. Do masters pay jizyah on behalf of their slaves?
b: No, because the obligation does not transfer to the owner merely because of ownership.

f: 949. Is jizyah imposed upon monks who live in seclusion and do not mix with people according to the stated ruling?
b: No, according to the ruling mentioned by the author.

f: 950. What is Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding secluded monks?
b: Jizyah is imposed upon them if they are physically capable of working.

f: 951. Who else held that physically capable secluded monks must pay jizyah?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.

f: 952. Why do those who impose jizyah upon capable secluded monks argue that it is due?
b: Because they possess the ability to earn but voluntarily abandon earning.

f: 953. What analogy is used for monks who abandon earning voluntarily?
b: The owner of taxable land who leaves it uncultivated but remains liable for kharāj.

f: 954. Why do those who exempt secluded monks from jizyah argue for exemption?
b: Because they are not fought while remaining secluded, and jizyah serves as a substitute for fighting.

f: 955. What condition is required for imposing jizyah upon a monk according to the view that requires it?
b: He must be capable of working for most of the year.

f: 956. What happens to jizyah if a non-Muslim embraces Islam while jizyah is due from him?
b: The jizyah is cancelled.

f: 957. What happens to jizyah if a non-Muslim dies while still a non-Muslim?
b: The jizyah is cancelled.

f: 958. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding jizyah after someone embraces Islam?
b: He held that it remains payable.

f: 959. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding jizyah after someone dies while owing it?
b: He held that it remains payable.

f: 960. Why did al-Shāfiʿī argue that jizyah remains due after Islam or death?
b: Because it became due in exchange for protection or residence, and receiving the benefit does not remove the obligation.

f: 961. What analogy did al-Shāfiʿī use to support keeping jizyah due?
b: He compared it to rent or blood-money agreed upon in a settlement of intentional homicide.

f: 962. What hadith did the Hanafis use as evidence that jizyah is cancelled after Islam?
b: The Prophet's ﷺ statement: "There is no jizyah upon a Muslim."

f: 963. How do Hanafis explain the word jizyah itself?
b: They relate it to jazāʾ (requital or recompense), indicating a penalty or compensation.

f: 964. Why do Hanafis describe jizyah as a legal penalty for disbelief?
b: Because it is attached to the condition of disbelief and falls away when disbelief ends.

f: 965. Why do worldly punishments cease after Islam or death according to the Hanafi reasoning?
b: Because their purpose is to repel continuing harm, and that harm ends through Islam or death.

f: 966. How does Islam remove the basis for jizyah if it is considered a substitute for military service?
b: After embracing Islam, the person becomes capable of fulfilling military obligations himself.

f: 967. Why do Hanafis reject the idea that jizyah is simply a payment for protection?
b: Because protection (ʿiṣmah) belongs to every human being by virtue of humanity.

f: 968. Why is charging jizyah merely for residence rejected by the Hanafis?
b: Because a dhimmī lives upon his own property, so residence itself is not a benefit requiring payment.

f: 969. What is the overall Hanafi principle regarding jizyah after Islam?
b: When the cause of jizyah (disbelief) disappears, the obligation disappears.

f: 970. What is the difference between the Hanafi and Shāfiʿī positions regarding conversion and jizyah?
b: The Hanafis cancel jizyah upon Islam, while al-Shāfiʿī maintains that it remains due because the benefit was already received.

f: 971. What is the connection between jizyah and military service according to the Hanafis?
b: Jizyah functions as a substitute for the military contribution expected from Muslims.

f: 972. Why does a Muslim no longer owe jizyah after conversion according to the Hanafis?
b: Because he is no longer receiving an exemption from military duty; he becomes part of those responsible for it.

f: 973. What happens if two years of unpaid jizyah become due according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The two years merge into one obligation.

f: 974. What is the ruling in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr if a person's jizyah is not collected for a year and another year arrives?
b: It is not collected.

f: 975. Whose opinion is that multiple years of jizyah merge into one?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ opinion.

f: 976. Who disagreed with Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding multiple years of unpaid jizyah?
b: Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Muḥammad, and al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 977. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Muḥammad, and al-Shāfiʿī regarding multiple years of unpaid jizyah?
b: Both years remain collectible.

f: 978. What happens if a person dies at the completion of the jizyah year according to all scholars mentioned?
b: Nothing is collected from him.

f: 979. What happens if a person dies during the jizyah year according to all scholars mentioned?
b: Nothing is collected from him.

f: 980. Why is no jizyah collected after death?
b: Because the ruling concerning death removes the obligation, as previously explained.

f: 981. Was the same disagreement about merging obligations extended by some scholars to kharāj?
b: Yes, some scholars extended it to kharāj.

f: 982. What did other scholars say regarding kharāj and merging?
b: They held that kharāj never merges, by consensus.

f: 983. What is the argument of Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad for collecting multiple years of jizyah?
b: Jizyah is a financial obligation, and multiple financial obligations are collected whenever collection is possible.

f: 984. What is the only exception recognized by Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Muḥammad regarding collecting accumulated jizyah?
b: When the person embraces Islam, because collection becomes legally impossible.

f: 985. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to the argument that jizyah is merely a financial obligation?
b: He argues that jizyah is fundamentally a punishment for persisting in disbelief.

f: 986. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ consider jizyah a punishment?
b: Because it is connected to continued disbelief rather than merely being a financial debt.

f: 987. According to the strongest narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, can jizyah be accepted if sent through an agent?
b: No, the dhimmī himself must come personally.

f: 988. How does the dhimmī pay jizyah according to the strongest narration?
b: He pays while standing, while the collector remains seated.

f: 989. What additional description is mentioned in another narration regarding collection of jizyah?
b: The collector takes hold of the dhimmī's collar, shakes him, and tells him to pay the jizyah.

f: 990. What does this method of collecting jizyah demonstrate according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: It demonstrates that jizyah has the nature of a punitive measure.

f: 991. What legal analogy does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ use to explain why multiple years of jizyah merge?
b: Multiple punishments merge, just as multiple legal punishments (ḥudūd) merge.

f: 992. Why do multiple years of jizyah merge according to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: Because jizyah is treated as a punishment rather than a normal financial debt.

f: 993. If jizyah is viewed as a substitute for execution, why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say it does not accumulate for past years?
b: Because execution relates to the current state of hostility, not a past state that has ended.

f: 994. If jizyah is viewed as a substitute for military service, why does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say it does not accumulate for past years?
b: Because protection and military benefit concern future circumstances, while past protection has already been received.

f: 995. How did some scholars interpret the phrase "another year comes" in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr?
b: They interpreted it figuratively as meaning "another year passes."

f: 996. Why did some scholars interpret "comes" as "passes"?
b: Because they held that jizyah becomes due only at the end of the year.

f: 997. How did others understand the phrase "another year comes" literally?
b: They understood it literally because Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ holds that jizyah becomes obligatory at the beginning of the year.

f: 998. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, when does jizyah become obligatory?
b: At the beginning of the year.

f: 999. According to al-Shāfiʿī, when does jizyah become obligatory?
b: At the end of the year.

f: 1000. What analogy does al-Shāfiʿī use for the timing of jizyah obligation?
b: He compares it to zakāh.

f: 1001. What is the Hanafi proof that jizyah begins at the start of the year?
b: The thing it substitutes for—protection and restraint from fighting—exists prospectively from the beginning of the year.

f: 1002. Why do Hanafis reject making jizyah obligatory only at the end of the year?
b: Because the obligation corresponds to future protection, not merely protection already received.

f: 1003. What is the key difference between the Hanafi and Shāfiʿī positions on when jizyah becomes due?
b: Hanafis consider it due at the beginning of the year, while al-Shāfiʿī considers it due at the year's completion.

f: 1004. What is the overall Hanafi reasoning behind merging unpaid jizyah years?
b: Since jizyah functions as a punishment for disbelief, accumulated punishments merge rather than accumulate like ordinary debts.

f: 1005. Is it permissible for dhimmīs to construct new synagogues or churches in Dār al-Islām according to the Hanafi ruling mentioned?
b: No, it is not permissible.

f: 1006. What prophetic statement is used as evidence for prohibiting the construction of new churches in Dār al-Islām?
b: The Prophet's ﷺ statement: "There is no castration in Islam and no church."

f: 1007. What does the phrase "there is no church" mean in the context of this ruling?
b: It means there is no establishment of a new church.

f: 1008. May dhimmīs rebuild an old church or synagogue if it collapses in Dār al-Islām?
b: Yes, they may rebuild it.

f: 1009. Why may dhimmīs rebuild an old church or synagogue after it collapses?
b: Because buildings naturally deteriorate, and permission to retain the original building includes permission to restore it when necessary.

f: 1010. May dhimmīs move an existing church or synagogue to another location?
b: No, they may not relocate it.

f: 1011. Why is relocating an existing church or synagogue considered equivalent to constructing a new one?
b: Because moving it creates a new religious structure in a new place.

f: 1012. What is the ruling of a monastic cell (ṣawmaʿah) used for religious seclusion?
b: It has the same ruling as a church.

f: 1013. Why is a prayer area inside a private home not treated like a church?
b: Because it is merely part of a private residence and not an independent religious building.

f: 1014. According to the author, where does the prohibition of constructing new churches primarily apply?
b: It primarily applies to cities (amṣār).

f: 1015. Why does the author distinguish between cities and villages regarding the construction of churches?
b: Because Islamic public symbols are established in cities and should not be opposed by publicly displaying other religious symbols.

f: 1016. What is another view mentioned regarding constructing churches in villages?
b: That dhimmīs should also be prevented from building them in villages within Muslim lands.

f: 1017. Why did some scholars prevent the construction of churches even in villages?
b: Because Islamic public rites are also established in villages.

f: 1018. What was the reported opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding churches in the villages of Kūfah?
b: Churches were permitted because most inhabitants were dhimmīs.

f: 1019. Are dhimmīs allowed to build churches in the Arabian Peninsula according to this ruling?
b: No, they are prevented from building them in both cities and villages.

f: 1020. What prophetic statement is used regarding religious coexistence in the Arabian Peninsula?
b: The Prophet's ﷺ statement: "Two religions shall not coexist in the Arabian Peninsula."

f: 1021. In which aspects must dhimmīs distinguish themselves from Muslims according to this ruling?
b: They must distinguish themselves in clothing, mounts, saddles, and headgear.

f: 1022. Are dhimmīs allowed to ride horses according to this ruling?
b: No, they are not allowed to ride horses.

f: 1023. Are dhimmīs allowed to carry weapons according to this ruling?
b: No, they are not allowed to bear weapons.

f: 1024. What distinctive garment or marker are dhimmīs required to wear according to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr?
b: The kustījāt, a distinctive waist-belt.

f: 1025. What type of saddles are dhimmīs required to use according to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr?
b: Saddles resembling pack-saddles.

f: 1026. Why are dhimmīs required to have distinctive clothing and appearance?
b: To display their subordinate legal status and prevent confusion between them and Muslims.

f: 1027. Why must dhimmīs be distinguishable from Muslims according to this legal framework?
b: Because Muslims receive public honor while dhimmīs do not receive the same public status.

f: 1028. Are Muslims required to initiate greetings of salām to dhimmīs according to this ruling?
b: No, they are not to greet them first with salām.

f: 1029. What road etiquette is required of dhimmīs according to this ruling?
b: They must give way on the road.

f: 1030. Why would failing to distinguish dhimmīs from Muslims cause a problem according to the jurists?
b: People might mistakenly treat them as Muslims in matters where the law distinguishes between them.

f: 1031. What material should the distinguishing waist-belt (kustījāt) be made from?
b: A thick woolen cord.

f: 1032. Why should the distinguishing belt not be made from silk?
b: Because silk is inappropriate for Muslims.

f: 1033. Must dhimmī women also be distinguished from Muslim women?
b: Yes, especially in public places.

f: 1034. In which places should dhimmī women be distinguishable from Muslim women?
b: Places such as roads and bathhouses.

f: 1035. Why should dhimmī houses have distinctive marks?
b: So that someone seeking charity does not unknowingly pray for forgiveness for their occupants.

f: 1036. What was the ideal ruling regarding dhimmīs riding animals according to the jurists?
b: They should not ride except when there is a necessity.

f: 1037. What should a dhimmī do if necessity requires him to ride through gatherings of Muslims?
b: He should dismount when passing through those gatherings.

f: 1038. What type of saddle should a dhimmī use if riding remains necessary?
b: The distinctive saddle prescribed for dhimmīs.

f: 1039. What types of clothing are dhimmīs prohibited from wearing?
b: Clothing distinctive of Muslim scholars, ascetics, or people of honor.

f: 1040. What is the general purpose of requiring dhimmīs to have distinguishing signs?
b: To preserve visible distinction between Muslims and dhimmīs within the Islamic state.

f: 1041. Does a dhimmī lose his covenant merely by refusing to pay the jizyah according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, his covenant is not annulled merely by refusing to pay the jizyah.

f: 1042. Does a dhimmī lose his covenant by killing a Muslim according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, his covenant is not annulled merely because he kills a Muslim.

f: 1043. Does a dhimmī lose his covenant by insulting the Prophet ﷺ according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, his covenant is not automatically annulled.

f: 1044. Does a dhimmī lose his covenant by committing adultery with a Muslim woman according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, his covenant is not annulled.

f: 1045. What is the reason the covenant of a dhimmī remains valid despite these actions according to the Hanafis?
b: Because the point at which fighting is stopped is his acceptance of the obligation of jizyah, not necessarily his actual payment of it.

f: 1046. What condition maintains the covenant of a dhimmī according to the Hanafi reasoning?
b: The continued legal commitment to the obligation of jizyah.

f: 1047. What was al-Shāfiʿī's position regarding a dhimmī who insults the Prophet ﷺ?
b: He held that insulting the Prophet ﷺ nullifies the covenant.

f: 1048. What argument did al-Shāfiʿī use for making insult of the Prophet ﷺ nullify the covenant?
b: Since insulting the Prophet ﷺ would invalidate a Muslim's faith, it should also invalidate the covenant that replaces it for a non-Muslim.

f: 1049. How do the Hanafis respond to al-Shāfiʿī's argument regarding insulting the Prophet ﷺ?
b: They argue that insulting the Prophet ﷺ is an act of disbelief, but the original disbelief did not prevent the covenant from being valid, so newly committed disbelief does not automatically end it.

f: 1050. According to the author, what two things definitely annul the covenant of a dhimmī?
b: Joining the Abode of War or their people seizing territory and waging war against Muslims.

f: 1051. Why does joining the Abode of War annul the covenant of a dhimmī?
b: Because he becomes an active enemy and the purpose of the covenant—to prevent hostility—no longer exists.

f: 1052. Why does a dhimmī's people waging war against Muslims annul the covenant?
b: Because the covenant's purpose of maintaining peace has been destroyed.

f: 1053. What does it mean that a dhimmī who breaks the covenant is treated like an apostate?
b: He is treated similarly regarding the legal consequences of joining enemy territory and his property.

f: 1054. In what respect is a covenant-breaking dhimmī treated like an apostate?
b: Regarding his joining enemy territory and the property he takes with him.

f: 1055. What is the difference between a covenant-breaking dhimmī and an apostate if they are captured?
b: A dhimmī may be enslaved, whereas an apostate may not.

f: 1056. What amount do the Christians of Banū Taghlib pay according to their treaty?
b: They pay double the amount that Muslims pay in zakāh.

f: 1057. What is the evidence for the special obligation upon Banū Taghlib?
b: The treaty concluded by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ with them in the presence of the Companions without objection.

f: 1058. Does the double payment of Banū Taghlib apply to their women?
b: Yes, it is collected from their women.

f: 1059. Does the double payment of Banū Taghlib apply to their children?
b: No, it is not collected from their children.

f: 1060. Why is the payment collected from Banū Taghlib women but not children?
b: Because the treaty established a doubled charitable levy, and ordinary zakāh applies to women but not children.

f: 1061. Who held that nothing should be collected from Banū Taghlib women?
b: Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 1062. What was Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī's reasoning for exempting Banū Taghlib women?
b: They argued that the payment is actually jizyah, and women are not normally subject to jizyah.

f: 1063. What statement from ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ did Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī use as evidence?
b: "This is jizyah—call it whatever you wish."

f: 1064. Why did Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī consider the Banū Taghlib payment to be jizyah?
b: Because its revenue is spent like jizyah and resembles a tax imposed upon non-Muslims.

f: 1065. How do the Hanafis respond to the argument that Banū Taghlib payment is jizyah?
b: They argue that it arises through treaty, not directly as jizyah.

f: 1066. Why can Banū Taghlib women be required to pay this treaty obligation according to the Hanafis?
b: Because women are legally capable of accepting financial obligations through agreement.

f: 1067. Where does the revenue from the Banū Taghlib payment go?
b: It goes to the public treasury (Bayt al-Māl).

f: 1068. Why do the Hanafis reject applying all jizyah rules to the Banū Taghlib payment?
b: Because not every type of revenue entering the public treasury follows the specific rulings of jizyah.

f: 1069. What is the main Hanafi distinction between Banū Taghlib's payment and ordinary jizyah?
b: Banū Taghlib's payment is based on a treaty obligation, whereas jizyah is a specific legal levy imposed upon non-Muslims.

f: 1070. What is the general Hanafi principle regarding the covenant of dhimmīs?
b: The covenant remains until there is a clear act of joining hostile forces or ending the peaceful relationship.

f: 1071. What type of jizyah does a client (mawlā) of Banū Taghlib pay according to the Hanafi position?
b: A client of Banū Taghlib pays ordinary jizyah, not the doubled payment of Banū Taghlib.

f: 1072. What type of land tax does a client of Banū Taghlib pay according to the Hanafi position?
b: He pays ordinary land tax (kharāj).

f: 1073. Who does the author compare the client of Banū Taghlib to regarding jizyah and kharāj?
b: The client of a Qurashī.

f: 1074. What was Zufar's opinion regarding the jizyah obligation of a client of Banū Taghlib?
b: Zufar held that the client should also pay the doubled amount paid by Banū Taghlib.

f: 1075. What prophetic statement did Zufar use to support extending Banū Taghlib's ruling to their clients?
b: "The client of a people is one of them."

f: 1076. What example did Zufar use to support his analogy about clients sharing the rulings of their patrons?
b: The client of Banū Hāshim shares their prohibition from accepting zakāh.

f: 1077. How do the Hanafis respond to Zufar's argument about the client of Banū Taghlib?
b: They argue that Banū Taghlib's doubled payment was an exceptional concession that does not extend to their clients.

f: 1078. Does a Christian client of a Muslim receive the same financial concession as Banū Taghlib according to the Hanafi position?
b: No, he pays ordinary jizyah.

f: 1079. Why do the clients of Banū Hāshim share the prohibition on accepting zakāh?
b: Because sacred legal prohibitions may be established through partial resemblance.

f: 1080. Why is the Banū Hāshim analogy not applied to Banū Taghlib's financial concession?
b: Because financial concessions are not extended merely due to resemblance.

f: 1081. Which sources of revenue are mentioned as being spent on the public interests of Muslims?
b: Kharāj, Banū Taghlib's payments, gifts from enemy states to the Imam, and jizyah.

f: 1082. Where are kharāj, Banū Taghlib payments, enemy gifts, and jizyah placed?
b: They are placed in Bayt al-Māl (the public treasury).

f: 1083. Why are kharāj, jizyah, and similar revenues used for general Muslim interests?
b: Because they belong to the public treasury and serve the welfare of the Muslim community.

f: 1084. Do the revenues of kharāj and jizyah come through direct military conquest?
b: No, they come to the Muslims without direct military conquest.

f: 1085. What military purpose may Bayt al-Māl revenue be used for?
b: Maintaining frontier defenses and paying soldiers.

f: 1086. What public construction projects may be funded from Bayt al-Māl revenue?
b: Canals and bridges.

f: 1087. What judicial expenses may be funded from Bayt al-Māl revenue?
b: Supporting Muslim judges.

f: 1088. What government expenses may be funded from Bayt al-Māl revenue?
b: Paying government officials.

f: 1089. What scholarly positions may receive support from Bayt al-Māl?
b: Scholars, teachers, and muftis.

f: 1090. Why are soldiers' families supported from Bayt al-Māl?
b: Because soldiers' normal maintenance obligations could distract them from military service if not provided for.

f: 1091. Why must provision be made for soldiers' families according to this explanation?
b: So soldiers can remain available for military duties rather than seeking other livelihoods.

f: 1092. What happens to the stipend (ʿaṭāʾ) of someone who dies halfway through the year?
b: He has no entitlement to it.

f: 1093. Why does a person's death during the year cancel his entitlement to the stipend (ʿaṭāʾ)?
b: Because the stipend is a discretionary grant, not a debt.

f: 1094. Why is the payment called ʿaṭāʾ (stipend/grant)?
b: Because it is given as a discretionary grant rather than being an established financial obligation.

f: 1095. When does ownership of the stipend (ʿaṭāʾ) become established?
b: Ownership is established only after the recipient takes possession of it.

f: 1096. Can an unpaid stipend be inherited after the recipient dies?
b: No, it is extinguished upon death before possession.

f: 1097. Which professions are mentioned as receiving stipends in later times?
b: Judges, teachers, and muftis.

f: 1098. What is the main purpose of Bayt al-Māl according to this section?
b: To provide for the general welfare and interests of the Muslim community.

f: 1099. What is the difference between a stipend (ʿaṭāʾ) and a debt?
b: A stipend is a discretionary grant, while a debt is an established obligation that must be paid.

f: 1100. Why does the author say a stipend is not like a debt?
b: Because no ownership exists until the stipend is actually received.

f: 1101. What principle explains why public treasury funds may be used for many different purposes?
b: They are designated for the general interests of Muslims rather than for a single specific category.

f: 1102. What should be done if a Muslim apostatizes from Islam according to this chapter?
b: Islam should be presented to him, and any doubts or misconceptions he has should be clarified.

f: 1103. Why are the doubts of an apostate clarified before dealing with him?
b: Because he may have fallen into apostasy due to a misunderstanding, and removing that misunderstanding may restore him to Islam.

f: 1104. Is presenting Islam to an apostate legally obligatory according to the Hanafi jurists?
b: No, it is not obligatory because the message of Islam has already reached him.

f: 1105. What happens if an apostate requests time before being dealt with?
